The Darpadalana ('Crushing of Pride') is a seven-chapter satirical and didactic poem (upadeśakāvya) composed by Kṣemendra. Each chapter (vicāra) targets one of seven traditional causes of conceit (madahetavaḥ)—noble birth (kula), wealth (vitta), erudition (śruta), physical beauty (rūpa), valor (śaurya), munificence (dāna), and asceticism (tapas)—demonstrating through general moral reflections and illustrative narratives (dṛṣṭānta) how excessive vanity leads to downfall and ridicule.

The Nyāyasiddhāñjana ('Collyrium of Nyāya Logic / Conclusions') is a foundational ontological prakaraṇa of the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta tradition composed by Vedānta Deśika. Functioning as the ontological counterpart to his epistemological treatise Nyāyapariśuddhi, the work classifies and analyzes knowable reality (prameya) across six chapters (paricchedas): material substance (triguṇadravya/jaḍadravya), individual souls (jīva), God (īśvara), transcendental eternal realm (nityavibhūti), consciousness/cognition (buddhi/dharmabhūtajñāna), and non-substance/attributes (adravya). It adapts and reforms Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika dialectic within Rāmānuja's metaphysics and is historically indispensable for citing and preserving substantial fragments of lost early Viśiṣṭādvaita texts, particularly Nāthamuni's Nyāyatattva.

## Contents

**Coverage:** unclear — Empty record (0 segment files, 0 segments, 0 characters); placeholder for the work.

The Bhagavadgītā ('Song of the Lord') is an eighteen-chapter philosophical dialogue embedded within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata (adhyāyas 23–40 in the critical edition). Set on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra on the brink of fratricidal war, the warrior Arjuna is overcome by moral despondency and is instructed by his charioteer Kṛṣṇa, revealed as the supreme deity. The text articulates a seminal synthesis of disciplined action without attachment to fruits (karma-yoga), metaphysical discernment (jñāna-yoga), and devotion (bhakti-yoga), culminating in the cosmic revelation of Kṛṣṇa's Viśvarūpa. As one of the three foundational authorities (prasthānatrayī) of Vedānta, it has generated continuous commentary across Indian philosophical schools and remains central to Hindu religious thought.

Appendix I of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition of the Harivaṃśa, the supplementary epic (khila) to the Mahābhārata detailing the genealogy, incarnations, and deeds of Kṛṣṇa. During critical editing by P. L. The Harivaṃśa ('Genealogy of Hari') is the canonical supplement (khila) to the Mahābhārata, bridging late epic narrative with the early Purāṇas. The Sabhāparvan ('Book of the Assembly Hall') constitutes the second book of the Mahābhārata, comprising 72 adhyāyas in the Pune Critical Edition. It recounts the construction of the magnificent assembly hall at Indraprastha by the dānava Maya, King Yudhiṣṭhira's imperial Rājasūya sacrifice, and Kṛṣṇa's slaying of Śiśupāla. The narrative culminates in the fateful dice match rigged by Śakuni and Duryodhana, the public humiliation of Draupadī, and the subsequent banishment of the Pāṇḍavas to twelve years of exile and a thirteenth year incognito.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa.

The Āraṇyakaparvan ('Book of the Forest', traditionally also known as the Vanaparvan) is the third and one of the longest books of the Mahābhārata. It chronicles the twelve years of forest exile endured by the five Pāṇḍava brothers and Draupadī following Yudhiṣṭhira's defeat in the game of dice. During this period, the narrative incorporates numerous celebrated inset episodes (upākhyānas) told to comfort and instruct the exiles, including the tales of Nala and Damayantī (Nalopākhyāna), Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Sāvitrī and Satyavān, as well as an abridged version of the Rāma story (Rāmopākhyāna). The book also details extensive pilgrimage circuits across sacred geography (Tīrthayātrā), divine encounters yielding celestial weapons for Arjuna, and the philosophical interrogation of Yudhiṣṭhira by the Yakṣa (Yakṣapraśna).

**Also known as:** Virāṭaparvan, Vairāṭaparvan

The Virāṭaparvan is the fourth book of the Mahābhārata, consisting of 67 chapters. It chronicles the thirteenth and final year of exile, which the five Pāṇḍava brothers and Draupadī are required to spend living in disguise (ajñātavāsa) without being recognized, seeking refuge at the court of King Virāṭa of Matsya. Assuming humble service personas—Yudhiṣṭhira as the courtier Kaṅka, Bhīma as the cook Ballava, Arjuna as the eunuch dance-instructor Bṛhannaḍā, Nakula and Sahadeva as stable masters, and Draupadī as the chambermaid Sairandhrī—they confront peril when the general Kīcaka attempts to violate Draupadī and is slain by Bhīma. The book reaches its climax during the dual cattle raids led by the Trigartas and the Kauravas, wherein Arjuna single-handedly routs the Kaurava forces, fulfilling their period of concealment and paving the way for diplomatic negotiations and the marriage of Abhimanyu to Princess Uttarā.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Droṇaparvan (Book 7 of the Mahābhārata) according to the Poona Critical Edition, comprising all 173 adhyāyas (adhyāyas 1–173; verses 07,001.001 to 07,173.107) along with the critical apparatus passages, including starred variant verses (*0001_01 through *1479_02) and Appendix I lines (marked with @).

**Also known as:** Droṇaparvan, Mahābhārata Book 7

The Droṇaparvan is the seventh major book of the Mahābhārata, narrating days eleven through fifteen of the eighteen-day Kurukṣetra war when the Kaurava martial preceptor Droṇa commands the army after Bhīṣma's fall. Critical episodes include the deadly circular military formation (cakravyūha) in which Arjuna's teenage son Abhimanyu is trapped and killed, Arjuna's retaliatory vow culminating in the slaying of Jayadratha before sundown, an intense night engagement marked by Ghaṭotkaca's death at the hands of Karṇa, and the moral turning point wherein Yudhiṣṭhira utters the ambiguous half-truth concerning the death of Aśvatthāman, causing Droṇa to lay down his arms before being decapitated by Dhṛṣṭadyumna. The book captures the breakdown of traditional kṣatriya battlefield codes (dharmayuddha) under extreme existential stakes.

The Mahābhārata is one of the two foundational Sanskrit epics (itihāsa) of ancient India, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyāsa. Comprising eighteen major books (parvans) and exceeding 75,000 stanzas in its Critical Edition, it centers on the bitter dynastic struggle and cataclysmic war between the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas at Kurukṣetra. Beyond its narrative framework, the epic serves as an encyclopedic exposition of dharma, statecraft, cosmology, and soteriology, incorporating major philosophical texts such as the Bhagavadgītā, Sanatsujātīya, and the Mokṣadharmaparvan of the Śāntiparvan.

The Āgamaḍambara ('Much Ado About Religion') is a satirical and philosophical Sanskrit drama composed by the Kashmiri philosopher Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. Set during the reign of King Śaṅkaravarman of Kashmir, the drama depicts ideological debates and socio-religious friction among Vedic Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists, Jains, Cārvākas, Kāpālikas, and antinomian Nīlāmbaras. The plot follows the zealous Vedic graduate Saṅkarṣaṇa as he campaigns to suppress heterodox movements, concluding with a state-mediated resolution that legitimizes multiple religious traditions conforming to common social morality.

The Saundarananda is an early Buddhist Sanskrit mahākāvya in 18 cantos by Aśvaghoṣa relating the conversion of Nanda, the Buddha's handsome half-brother. Deeply attached to his beautiful wife Sundarī, Nanda is drawn into the monastic saṅgha against his inclination; the Buddha then uses a pedagogical device (upāya), first showing him celestial nymphs in Indra's heaven before having him guided toward the realization that even heavenly realms are ephemeral and fraught with suffering. The second half of the epic serves as an exposition of Buddhist mental training, psychological analysis, and meditative praxis (śamatha and vipaśyanā), culminating in Nanda's attainment of arhatship. In the final verses (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa explicitly declares his poetic purpose: he employed the sweet ornamentation of kāvya to make the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa) palatable to worldly audiences.

The Daśakumāracarita ('Adventures of the Ten Princes') is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (gadyakāvya) by Daṇḍin, recounting the interwoven picaresque adventures of Prince Rājavāhana and his companions across India as they seek romantic conquests, wealth, and political power. Distinctive for its vivid portrayal of secular, sub-courtly, and underworld life—featuring thieves, gamblers, courtesans, corrupt ministers, ascetics, and charlatans—the work is also famous for rhetorical tours de force, notably the seventh chapter composed entirely without labial phonemes (aniroṣṭhya). The surviving text is framed by the introductory Pūrvapīṭhikā and concludes with the kathopasaṃhāra.

The Kaliviḍambana ('Mockery of the Kali Age') is an influential satirical poem of 102 anuṣṭubh verses composed by the 17th-century South Indian poet, polymath, and minister Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita. The Haṃsadūta ('The Swan Messenger') is a Sanskrit messenger poem (dūtakāvya) in 142 verses composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Modeled after Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, the poem describes Lalitā, a confidante of Rādhā, dispatching a swan from the banks of the Yamunā to Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā following his departure from Vraja. The bulk of the composition conveys Lalitā's message depicting Rādhā's distress in separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) and reproaching Kṛṣṇa for abandoning the gopīs, synthesizing courtly lyric conventions with Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology.

The Hitopadeśa is a celebrated Sanskrit collection of animal fables and gnomic maxims composed in prosimetric campū form by Nārāyaṇa under the patronage of Prince Dhavalacandra [3882, 3887]. Drawing largely on the Pañcatantra as well as the Kāmandakīyanītisāra and the epics [19], the work is framed as practical instruction in statecraft and ethics given by the sage Viṣṇuśarman to the errant sons of King Sudarśana of Pāṭaliputra [21, 28]. Renowned for its direct syntax and pragmatic political wisdom (nīti), it has served for centuries as an essential introductory reader for students of Sanskrit.

The Śukasaptati ('Seventy Tales of the Parrot') is a popular Sanskrit frame-tale narrative (kathā). When the young merchant Madanavinoda embarks on a lengthy commercial journey abroad, his wife Prabhāvatī is tempted by dissolute companions to pursue illicit liaisons; her wise parrot keeps her at home each night by narrating an ingenious story of wit, trickery, or adulterous escape, cunningly breaking off the tale until dawn. Over the course of seventy consecutive nights, the parrot deters her from infidelity until the merchant returns. Renowned for its realistic depiction of rogue life and practical cleverness, the collection enjoyed immense popularity throughout Asia and formed the direct basis for the Persian Ṭūṭī-nāma.

The Padmapurāṇa is one of the eighteen classical Mahāpurāṇas, traditionally ranking second in size with approximately 55,000 ślokas. Extant in distinct northern (five khaṇḍas) and western/southern (six or seven khaṇḍas) recensions, it comprises encyclopedic accounts of cosmogony, dynastic genealogies, pilgrimage guides (tīrthamāhātmya, notably for Puṣkara and the Gaṅgā), and substantial Vaiṣṇava narrative material including independent versions of the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa legends. While its oldest core dates to the Gupta period (c. 4th–8th centuries CE), extensive interpolations and sectarian expansions accrued well through the late medieval period.

The Agnipurāṇa is one of the eighteen canonical Mahāpurāṇas, framed as a discourse imparted by the fire god Agni to the sage Vasiṣṭha. Renowned for its encyclopedic scope, it combines traditional Puranic cosmogony, genealogies, and avatāra narratives with extensive epitomes of classical and medieval technical disciplines. These include comprehensive manuals of temple architecture and iconography (vāstu- and śilpaśāstra), Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva tantric ritual and initiation (dīkṣā), statecraft and military science (rājanīti, dhanurveda), medicine (āyurveda), poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra), metrics (chandaḥ), and grammar. While preserving earlier epic-Puranic material, the compilation reached its extant encyclopedic form largely between the 9th and 11th centuries CE.

The Garuḍapurāṇa is one of the eighteen major canonical Mahāpurāṇas of the Vaiṣṇava tradition, framed as a dialogue between Viṣṇu and his vahana Garuḍa, recounted by Sūta to the sages of the Naimiṣāraṇya. The composite work ranges in date from c. the 8th–10th century CE for the early encyclopedic core to the 14th–16th century CE for the late medieval Brahmakāṇḍa.

The Viṣṇupurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and is widely regarded by Indologists as the most unified exemplar of the classical pañcalakṣaṇa ('five characteristics') genre. Structured as a six-book dialogue between the sage Parāśara and his disciple Maitreya, the text articulates a Vaiṣṇava cosmology and theology identifying Viṣṇu as the supreme, all-encompassing Brahman. Book 5 contains one of the earliest continuous accounts of the life and legends of Kṛṣṇa Gopāla, serving as a vital foundation for the later Bhāgavatapurāṇa, and the text's theological consistency made it an authoritative pramāṇa for Vedānta commentators, particularly Rāmānuja.

The Arthaśāstra is ancient India's foundational treatise on statecraft, political economy, judicial administration, and diplomatic strategy. Divided into fifteen books (adhikaraṇas), it systematically covers the education and discipline of the king, ministerial appointments, internal civil and revenue administration, civil and criminal law (dharmasthīya and kaṇṭakaśodhana), espionage, interstate relations (the mandala theory and the sixfold foreign policy, ṣāḍguṇya), military logistics and warfare, and the methodological hermeneutics of treatises (tantrayukti). The Suśrutasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Āyurveda (the Bṛhat-trayī) and ancient India's premier authority on surgery (śalyatantra). Framed as instructions delivered by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his student Suśruta, it describes surgical instruments, practical anatomy through human cadaveric dissection, and operative procedures such as rhinoplasty, couching of cataracts, lithotomy, and abdominal suture. **Attribution:** The root treatise Manusmṛti (Mānavadharmaśāstra) is traditionally attributed to the sage Manu (revealed through Bhṛgu). The commentary Manubhāṣya was authored by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Vīrasvāmin (c. 9th–10th century CE). The Manusmṛti (or Mānava-Dharmaśāstra) is ancient India's foundational and most influential metrical code of socio-religious duty (dharma), statecraft, jurisprudence, and penance. Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya (c. 9th–10th century CE) represents the earliest surviving and most comprehensive commentary on the text, celebrated for its rigorous application of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to reconcile textual tensions and develop sophisticated legal reasoning. Surviving incompletely in manuscript witnesses, the commentary was partially restored under King Madanapāla and remained a primary benchmark for subsequent Dharmaśāstra commentarial traditions and digests.

The Baudhāyanadharmasūtra is one of the four surviving Vedic Dharmasūtras, forming part of the larger Baudhāyana Kalpasūtra within the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda. The text is celebrated for its explicit recognition of regional customary law (ācāra), highlighting contrasting customs between northern and southern Brahmins.

The Gautamadharmasūtra is one of the earliest extant aphoristic legal treatises of ancient India, traditionally affiliated with the Rāṇāyanīya and Kauthuma schools of the Sāmaveda. The Tantravārttika is the primary prose sub-commentary composed by the 7th-century philosopher Kumārila Bhaṭṭa on Śabarasvāmin's Śābarabhāṣya on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, covering Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 through Adhyāya 3, Pāda 8. Serving as the central work in Kumārila's tripartite commentary on the Bhāṣya (flanked by the verse Ślokavārttika on 1.1 and the concise notes of the Ṭupṭīkā on Adhyāyas 4–12), it develops a comprehensive defense of Vedic ritualism, textual exegesis, and Brahmanical orthopraxy. The work is renowned for its seminal analyses of the semantic force of Vedic injunctions (vidhi), the epistemological and evidentiary authority of explanatory passages (arthavāda) and mantras, the validity of Smṛti and regional customs (ācāra), and the formal criteria governing ritual subordination (śeṣatva).

The Tantrāloka ('Light on the Tantras') is the magnum opus of Abhinavagupta and the foundational encyclopedic exposition of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, synthesizing the Trika, Krama, and Pratyabhijñā traditions. Spanning 37 daily lectures (āhnikas) and nearly 5,800 metrical verses, the work organizes Śaiva ontology, theology, and ritual practice into four progressive means to realization (anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava) based primarily on the Mālinīvijayottaratantra. It integrates internal contemplative yogas with complex external ritual, mantra mechanics, and initiation procedures (dīkṣā) under an uncompromising philosophy of non-dual consciousness.

The Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (or Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya) is Śaṅkara's magnum opus and the foundational commentary of Advaita Vedānta on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa. Across four chapters (samanvaya, avirodha, sādhana, and phala), Śaṅkara harmonizes Upaniṣadic statements, refutes competing traditions (including Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, and Buddhism), and expounds knowledge of non-duality as the sole direct means to liberation.

The Jīvanmuktiviveka ('Discrimination of Liberation while Living') is an influential 14th-century Advaita Vedānta treatise by Vidyāraṇya. Across five prakaraṇas, the text examines the nature of and scriptural authority for living liberation, the eradication of latent mental impressions (vāsanākṣaya), the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), the five purposes served by liberation-in-life, and the renunciation of the enlightened knower (vidvatsaṃnyāsa). The work is celebrated for its synthesis of classical Advaita epistemology with the practical yogic disciplines of Patañjali's Yogasūtra and the Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha, maintaining that enduring experiential tranquility in life requires the coordinated practice of tattvajñāna, vāsanākṣaya, and manonāśa.

The Atharvavedasaṃhitā (Śaunaka recension) is the canonical fourth Veda of ancient India, comprising 730 hymns arranged across 20 kāṇḍas. The Atharvavedasaṃhitā is the fourth collection of the Vedic scriptural canon, preserved principally in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions. Unlike the sacrificial focus of the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda, it encompasses a wide range of domestic, magical, and medical hymns, including incantations for healing, apotropaic charms against hostile powers, blessings for prosperity and harmony, and royal coronation rites. It also preserves notable speculative, cosmogonic, and philosophical hymns—such as the Bhūmisūkta (hymn to the Earth) and hymns to Skambha and Prāṇa—that mark an important conceptual transitional phase toward early Upaniṣadic thought.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete Kauthuma ārcika text, verses numbered continuously 1–1875: Pūrvārcika (Āgneya, Aindra and Pāvamāna kāṇḍas, vv. 1–585), Āraṇyaka kāṇḍa and Mahānāmnyārcika (vv. 586–650, ending with the five purīṣapadas), and Uttarārcika (vv. 651–1875). Ends with the colophon 'iti sāmavedasaṃhitā samāptā'. Unaccented; no gāna (song-book) texts.

**Also known as:** Sāmaveda, Sāmaveda-Saṃhitā, Sāmavedasaṃhitā (Kauthumaśākhā)

The Sāmavedasaṃhitā is the liturgical verse collection (ārcika) providing the textual base (yoni) for the melodies (sāman) intoned by the Udgātṛ priest during Śrauta sacrificial rituals, particularly the Soma sacrifices. Preserved here in the standard Kauthuma recension, the collection comprises 1,875 mantras divided into the Pūrvārcika (single stanzas arranged by deity—principally Agni, Indra, and Soma Pavamāna—followed by the Āraṇyaka/Mahānāmnī section) and the Uttarārcika (strophes and triplets arranged according to ritual execution). With the exception of approximately 75 stanzas, all verses are drawn from the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā (predominantly Mandalas VIII and IX), frequently showing distinct dialectal and phonetic variations adapted to musical chant.

The Ṛgveda (or Ṛgvedasaṃhitā) is the oldest surviving work of Indo-Aryan literature and the foundational canonical text of the Vedic sacrificial tradition, composed in archaic Vedic Sanskrit in northwestern South Asia during the second millennium BCE. Arranged into ten books (maṇḍalas), its 1,028 hymns (sūktas) were primarily recited by the Hotṛ priest during Śrauta rituals to invoke deities such as Agni, Indra, Soma, and Varuṇa. In addition to liturgical praise, the collection contains dialogue hymns, riddles, and foundational cosmogonic and philosophical poetry, notably the Nāsadīyasūkta and Puruṣasūkta.

The Chāndogyopaniṣad is one of the oldest, largest, and most authoritative of the principal (mukhya) Upaniṣads, belonging to the Sāmaveda tradition where it constitutes chapters 3–10 of the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa. **Also known as:** Kaṭha-Upaniṣad

The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical mukhya Upaniṣad of the Kaṭha school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda, framed as an initiatory dialogue between the boy Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. When granted three boons, Naciketas bypasses earthly riches and longevity to demand knowledge of what transpires beyond death, prompting Yama to distinguish the path of spiritual good (śreyas) from the path of worldly pleasure (preyas) and reveal the immortal nature of the inner self (ātman). The text is renowned for its chariot allegory in Vallī 3—correlating the body with a chariot, the intellect with the charioteer, the mind with reins, and the senses with horses—and for providing one of the earliest textual formulations of proto-Sāṃkhya ontological gradations and the definition of yoga as steady sensorial restraint.

The Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Śāṅkhāyana branch of the Ṛgveda. The Kṛṣṇayajurveda ('Black Yajurveda') is one of the two primary branches of the Yajurveda, the Vedic liturgical corpus of mantras and formulas (yajus) used by the adhvaryu priest during solemn sacrificial rituals (śrauta). Unlike the Śuklayajurveda ('White Yajurveda'), which segregates mantras from their ritual explanations, the Kṛṣṇayajurveda characteristically interweaves liturgical mantras (saṃhitā) and brāhmaṇa-style prose ritual exegesis. Surviving recensions include the Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka, and Kapiṣṭhala schools, of which the Taittirīya is the most complete and widely recited.

The Taittirīyaprātiśākhya is the foundational phonological and phonetic treatise of the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda. Arranged in 24 chapters (adhyāyas), the text specifies the sound inventory, articulation points, euphonic combination (sandhi), and accentuation patterns necessary to derive the continuous recitation (saṃhitāpāṭha) from the word-by-word text (padapāṭha). It is a central monument of ancient Indian phonetic science (śikṣā).

The Vājasaneyisaṃhitā (Mādhyandina recension) is the foundational mantra collection of the White (Śukla) Yajurveda, preserving the formulas and verses recited by the adhvaryu priest during śrauta sacrificial rites. Unlike the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurvedic saṃhitās, which intermingle liturgical formulas with brāhmaṇa prose exposition, the White Yajurveda separates the liturgical mantras into this collection, relegating exegesis to the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa. The Bhaiṣajyavastu ('Chapter on Medicines') is the sixth section of the Vinayavastu in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. While opening with monastic regulations concerning permissible medicines, dietary schedules, and the care of ill monks, the vast majority of the chapter is narrative, incorporating numerous avadānas, jātakas, legendary travels of the Buddha to northwest India, apotropaic formulas (including an early version of the Mahāmāyūrī spell), and prophecy accounts. The Lalitavistara ('The Extensive Account of the [Buddha's] Play') is an elaborate Mahāyāna sūtra in 27 chapters composed in mixed Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit prose and verse. It narrates the sacred biography of Śākyamuni Buddha from his decision to descend from Tuṣita heaven, his miraculous conception and birth in Lumbinī, his luxurious princely youth, four encounters, and great renunciation, to his austerities, defeat of Māra, awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, and first turning of the wheel of Dharma in Ṛṣipatana. Blending early biographical accounts (primarily Sarvāstivādin) with a docetic Mahāyāna perspective, the sūtra depicts the Buddha's earthly career as the deliberate, compassionate sport (lalita) of an already fully enlightened being, and served as a major inspiration for classical Buddhist art and literature across Asia.

The Nairātmyaparipṛcchā ('Questions on Selflessness') is a short Mahāyāna scripture consisting of a prose opening dialogue and 26 verses. Departing from standard sūtra narrative conventions, it depicts non-Buddhist wanderers (tīrthikas) approaching Mahāyāna practitioners to question how bodily actions and affective states (laughter, crying, anger, jealousy) can arise if the body is devoid of a supreme self (paramātman). The Buddhist respondents elucidate the non-duality of existence and non-existence, the distinction between conventional reality (saṃvṛti) and ultimate reality (paramārtha), and the nature of all phenomena as illusory, dream-like appearances empty of intrinsic self-nature.

**Evidence:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the sūtra in 80 sections (pp. 21–105 of Lévi's 1932 edition). The commentary edited in the second part of the volume (Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa) is not included.

**Also known as:** Karmavibhaṅga, Karmavibhaṅgasūtra

**Attribution:** Canonical Buddhist discourse presented as the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) delivered to the brahmin youth Śuka Taudeyaputra in Śrāvastī.

The Mahākarmavibhaṅga (also referred to in manuscripts as Karmavibhaṅga or Karmavibhaṅgasūtra) is an early Buddhist discourse detailing the retributions of specific actions across cycles of rebirth. Expanding substantially upon the framework of the canonical Cūḷakammavibhaṅga-sutta (Majjhima-nikāya 135) and its Āgama parallels, the text presents 80 categories of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, frequently illustrating doctrinal points with narrative exempla and avadānas. The work was historically influential across Buddhist Asia and served as the direct textual source for the 160 relief panels carved on the hidden basement of Borobudur in Java.

The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra set in Vaiśālī, centered on the lay bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to receive visitors and instruct them. **Attribution:** Canonical Vajrayāna tantra (buddhavacana) revealed by the primordial Buddha / Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajra (Vajradhara) residing in the source/womb of the cosmic Vajrayoṣit.

The Śrīguhyasamājatantra (also known as the Tathāgataguhyaka) is the foundational scripture of esoteric Mahāyāna Buddhism belonging to the Anuttarayoga / Mahāyoga class of tantras. In eighteen chapters (paṭalas 1–17 forming the root tantra and paṭala 18 serving as the Uttaratantra or explanatory continuation), it expounds the maṇḍala of the five Tathāgata families, deity yoga, consecration rituals, and subtle-body inner yogic practices. The scripture became the central root source for two major Indian commentarial lineages—the Ārya school associated with Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, and the Jñānapāda school—profoundly shaping the development of Indo-Tibetan Vajrayāna scholasticism and meditative praxis.

**Attribution:** Canonical Vinaya scripture preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit belonging to the Lokottaravāda branch of the Mahāsāṃghika school.

The Mahāvastu ('The Great Story') is an extensive Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit canonical text preserved by the Lokottaravāda sub-sect of the Mahāsāṃghika school, nominally forming the opening section of their Vinayapiṭaka. It presents an expansive biography of the Buddha Gautama, tracing his past lives, his bodhisattva path across the ten spiritual stages (daśabhūmi), his vow under previous Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara, and his final awakening and initial teaching career. Rich in jātakas, avadānas, and early doctrinal discourses, the work was compiled and expanded over several centuries (c. 2nd century BCE to 4th century CE) and stands as a key witness for early Lokottaravāda supramundane buddhology and proto-Mahāyāna concepts.

The Sekoddeśa consists of 174 verses traditionally considered an excerpt from the fifth chapter of the lost Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddha). The Tattvasaṃgraha ('Compendium of Reality') by the 8th-century Madhyamaka-Yogācāra master Śāntarakṣita is a monumental verse treatise providing an exhaustive critique of classical Indian philosophical systems. Grounded in the Buddhist epistemological framework (pramāṇa) of Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, it systematically refutes rival theories regarding primordial nature (prakṛti), God (īśvara), the eternal Self (ātman), the categories of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, the eternity of sound and Vedic authority, and various non-Buddhist epistemologies, while establishing Buddhist tenets such as universal momentariness, nominal exclusion (apoha), dependent origination, and the omniscience of the Buddha. It serves as one of the most important doxographical sources for 8th-century Indian philosophy, preserving extensive fragments and doctrines of otherwise lost Brahmanical, Jaina, and materialist thinkers.

The Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā (Thirty Verses on Representation-Only) by Vasubandhu is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra Buddhism. In thirty concise kārikās, it expounds the threefold transformation of consciousness (vijñānapariṇāma)—the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the afflicted mentation (manas), and the six object-cognizing consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)—alongside the doctrine of the three natures (trisvabhāva). The Bodhisattvabhūmi constitutes the fifteenth and most influential section of the encyclopedic Yogācārabhūmi, composed in approximately the 4th century CE. The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi ('Proof of Mere Representation in Twenty Verses') is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda philosophy composed by Vasubandhu. - nyi shu pa'i 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 4057): translated by Jinamitra, Śīlendrabodhi, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains the complete work: introductory prose, all 22 stanzas, full autocommentary (vṛtti), and closing colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi (Vasubandhu, root text)
- Viṃśatikāvṛtti (Vasubandhu, commentary)

**Also known as:** Viṃśatikā, Viṃśikā, Viṃśatikāvṛtti, Viṃśikāvṛtti, Viṃśatikākārikā, Viṃśatikā vijñaptimātratāsiddhi, Vijñaptimātratāsiddhiḥ viṃśatikā savṛttikā

**Attribution:** Both the twenty-two stanzas (twenty doctrinal kārikās plus two concluding verses) and the prose autocommentary (vṛtti) are composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE), attested by the concluding Sanskrit colophon ('kṛtir iyam ācāryavasubandhoḥ') and ancient Tibetan (D 4056, D 4057) and Chinese translations (T 1588, T 1589, T 1590).

The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi with its autocommentary (Viṃśatikāvṛtti) is Vasubandhu's foundational defense of the Yogācāra doctrine that reality is cognition-only (vijñaptimātra) and devoid of external, mind-independent physical objects. The text systematically counters realist objections regarding spatiotemporal coordination, collective experience, and causal efficacy through analogies to dreams, collective torment in hell, and shared karmic fruition. It is especially famous for stanzas 11–15, which formulate a decisive refutation of atomism by demonstrating that physical atoms can neither possess parts nor be partless without rendering composite macroscopic extension conceptually impossible.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC) Project, input and proofread by Udip Shakya (2008); converted and integrated into GRETIL by Reinhold Grünendahl and Maximilian Mehner.

**Also known as:** Tattvasiddhiśāstra, Chengshi lun, Jōjitsuron

**Attribution:** Authored in Sanskrit by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE). The original Sanskrit text was lost in India, surviving in Kumārajīva's Chinese translation (T 1646, 成實論 Chengshi lun, 406–412 CE). This Sanskrit e-text represents the modern retroversion/reconstruction from Chinese into Sanskrit by N. Aiyaswami Sastri.

The Satyasiddhiśāstra (also reconstructed as Tattvasiddhiśāstra; Chinese: Chengshi lun) is an extensive Buddhist scholastic treatise by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE), reflecting Bahuśrutīya and Dārṣṭāntika/Sautrāntika doctrines. Organized around an introductory section and doctrinal topics, it expounds Buddhist tenets including the Four Truths, emptiness, and prajñaptisat. While lost in India, Kumārajīva's Chinese translation formed the foundational text of the Chinese Chengshi (Japanese Jōjitsu) school.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text containing all five chapters (paricchedas): 1. Lakṣaṇapariccheda, 2. Āvaraṇapariccheda, 3. Tattvapariccheda, 4. Phalanirdeśapariccheda / Pratipakṣabhāvanāpariccheda, and 5. Yānānuttaryapariccheda.

**Also known as:** Āgamānusāriṇī, Madhyāntavibhāgasūtrabhāṣyaṭīkā, Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣyaṭīkā

The Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā (subtitled Āgamānusāriṇī) is Sthiramati's Sanskrit sub-commentary on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya and the root verses attributed to Maitreya. Across five chapters, it expounds classical Yogācāra ontology and soteriology, giving extensive philosophical explanations of the constructive imagination of the unreal (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), emptiness (śūnyatā), obscurations to enlightenment and their antidotes, and the unexcelled Mahāyāna path. It constitutes one of the most comprehensive surviving Sanskrit expositions of early Vijñaptimātra thought.

This text contains the opening portion of chapter 4 of Sthiramati's Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā, an exegesis on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya. The chapter analyzes the cultivation of meditative antidotes (pratipakṣabhāvanā) formulated as the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyadharma). The present e-text covers the exegesis through the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), and four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) to the five spiritual faculties (pañcendriya), explaining their functions in entering the four noble truths and progressing through the stages of preparation and penetration.

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Mahayana, Yogacara)

**Genre:** tika (sub-commentary)

**Estimated date:** c. 6th c. CE

The fourth chapter (Pratipakṣabhāvanāpariccheda, 'Cultivation of the Antidotes') of Sthiramati's Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā, in the new critical edition prepared by Sebastian Nehrdich. The chapter treats the cultivation (bhāvanā) of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣya-dharma) as antidotes (pratipakṣa) to the obstacles set out earlier in the text: the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya) and powers (bala), the seven factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), glossing Vasubandhu's bhāṣya word by word.

**History:** Composed by Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE), the most prolific commentator of the early Yogācāra tradition. The ninth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled Ātmavādapratiṣedha ('Refutation of the Assertion of a Self') or Pudgalaviniścaya ('Investigation of the Person'), is an unversified prose treatise appended to Vasubandhu's masterwork. In this text, Vasubandhu defends the canonical Buddhist teaching of selflessness (anātman) against the personalist doctrines of the Buddhist Vātsīputrīya / Pudgalavādin tradition as well as non-Buddhist substantialist soul theories of the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika schools. The treatise is a foundational locus classicus in Indian Buddhist philosophy for arguments addressing personal identity, reductionism, and causal continuity.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: all kārikās of chapters 1–8 (VAkK_1.1–8.43; chapter 9 has no kārikās), with chapter colophons. Numbering slip: kārikā 2.32 is labelled 'VAkK_2.33' (so 2.33 occurs twice and 2.32 seems missing), but the text is present.

**Also known as:** Abhidharmakośa, Abhidharmakośamūlakārikā, Chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi tshig le'ur byas pa, Apidamo jushe lun ben song (阿毘達磨俱舍論本頌)

**Attribution:** Universally accepted as the work of the Buddhist master Vasubandhu, who also authored the auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya).

The Abhidharmakośakārikā consists of verses in eight chapters composed by Vasubandhu, synthesizing the doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika school of Abhidharma. The text classifies conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across eight subjects: ultimate constituents (dhātu), sensory and psychological faculties (indriya), cosmological realms (loka), intentional action (karma), underlying afflictions (anuśaya), noble spiritual paths and attainers (mārgapudgala), transcendent cognitions (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Designed for memorization, it served as the baseline verse manual upon which Vasubandhu constructed his famous auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) offering critical Sautrāntika critiques of Vaibhāṣika tenets, and it remains the fundamental Abhidharma textbook throughout East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the closing colophon ('iti nāgārjunapādaviracito 'yaṃ dharmasaṃgrahaḥ samāptaḥ').

The Dharmasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit Buddhist glossary consisting of 140 numbered entries categorizing doctrinal concepts and numerical dharmas (mātṛkā). It enumerates foundational Buddhist frameworks common to early Buddhism and Mahāyāna, including the three jewels, three vehicles, five Buddhas, four immeasurables (brahmavihāra), perfections (pāramitā), aggregates (skandha), sense fields (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditioned mental factors (caitasika). **Attribution:** The Bhagavadgītā is traditionally attributed to Vyāsa.

Chapter 3 (Karma-yoga) of the Bhagavadgītā contains 43 verses wherein Kṛṣṇa resolves Arjuna's perplexity regarding the relative merits of renunciation/knowledge (jñāna) versus engagement in action (karma). Kṛṣṇa establishes that physical inaction is impossible and prescribes selfless performance of duty without desire for fruit (niṣkāma karma) as a sacred sacrifice (yajña), warning against desire (kāma) and anger (krodha) as the primary obstacles. It introduces the celebrated simile of the disciplined mind resting steady like a lamp in a windless place, reassures Arjuna that an unsuccessful aspirant is preserved from destruction and reborn into propitious surroundings to resume spiritual pursuit, and concludes by designating the devotee absorbed in loving devotion to God as the foremost yogi. Chapter 7 of the Bhagavadgītā (traditionally titled Jñānavijñānayoga, comprising 30 verses) opens the middle six chapters of the poem by distinguishing between the divine lower nature (aparā prakṛti: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and ego) and higher nature (parā prakṛti: the living entities that sustain the world). Chapter 10 of the Bhagavadgītā, known as the Vibhūtiyoga ('Yoga of Divine Glories'), details Kṛṣṇa's cosmic manifestations and transcendent immanence at Arjuna's request. Declaring himself the origin of gods, great sages, and all cosmic faculties, Kṛṣṇa enumerates the foremost exemplars across diverse categories of existence as aspects of his supreme splendor, concluding that the entire universe is pervaded and sustained by a mere fraction of his power. In this digital text, each verse of chapter 10 is followed by four complete commentaries: the Advaitic yet bhakti-oriented expositions of Śrīdhara Svāmin (Subodhinī) and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (Gūḍhārthadīpikā), followed by the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics of Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī) and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (Gītābhūṣaṇa).

Chapter 11 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Viśvarūpadarśanayoga ('The Yoga of the Vision of the Universal Form'), forms the dramatic and theophanic climax of the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna. Arjuna asks to see the divine cosmic form of the Lord, whereupon Krishna grants him divine vision (divya-cakṣus) and reveals his all-encompassing body blazing with innumerable mouths, eyes, and weapons, into which all creatures and warring heroes are drawn to their demise as Kāla ('Time/Death'). Awestruck and terrified, Arjuna offers extensive stotras and begs Krishna to return to his gentle four-armed and two-armed human form. In this e-text, all 55 verses are accompanied verse-by-verse by four influential Sanskrit commentaries: Śrīdharasvāmin's Subodhinī, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā, Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa.

**Attribution:** The root text of the Bhagavadgītā is embedded within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa. The chapter includes commentaries by Śrīdharasvāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī), and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (titled in the colophon as Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītopaniṣad-bhāṣya).

Bhagavadgītā chapter 12 (Bhaktiyoga, 20 verses) evaluates the comparative spiritual efficacy of meditating upon the unmanifest, imperishable Absolute (nirguṇa / avyakta akṣara) versus worship of the personal Divine (saguṇa / vyakta). Kṛṣṇa explains that while both orientations lead to liberation, the contemplative path of the unmanifest is arduous for embodied beings, whereas single-minded devotion directed to the personal Lord brings swift liberation through divine grace. The chapter concludes with a delineation of the tranquil virtues—such as non-malice, friendliness, forbearance, detachment, and equanimity in pleasure and pain—that characterize the devotee dear to the Lord. The accompanying commentaries synthesize and contrast the Advaita-bhakti readings of Śrīdharasvāmin and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī with the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theological interpretations of Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

Bhagavadgītā chapter 15 (Puruṣottamayoga, 20 verses) expounds the metaphysical hierarchy of reality through the metaphor of an inverted cosmic fig tree (aśvattha), whose branches must be severed by detachment. Kṛṣṇa explicates the nature of the transmigrating self, the divine power sustaining the cosmos, and the distinction between the perishable (kṣara), the imperishable (akṣara), and the transcendent Supreme Person (puruṣottama). The accompanying commentaries in this e-text offer both classical Advaitic exegesis (Śrīdhara Svāmin and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī) and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theological exposition (Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa).

The Bhagavadgītā ('Song of the Lord') is an 18-chapter philosophical dialogue of 700 verses, set on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. Addressing the existential and moral crisis of the warrior Arjuna before the fratricidal battle, Kṛṣṇa expounds the nature of the imperishable self (ātman) and synthesizes the disciplines of detached action (karmayoga), knowledge (jñānayoga), and devotional surrender (bhaktiyoga). Culminating in the theophany of Kṛṣṇa's cosmic form (viśvarūpa), the work became a foundational text of classical Vedānta as the smṛtiprasthāna of the prasthānatrayī and one of the most widely commented-upon works in Indian religious literature.

The Udyogaparvan ('Book of Preparation/Effort') is the fifth major book of the Mahābhārata. Following the conclusion of the Pāṇḍavas' thirteen-year period of exile, it narrates the failed diplomatic efforts to avert conflict, the recruitment of allies across the subcontinent, and Kṛṣṇa's embassy to Hastināpura, where Duryodhana refuses any compromise. The Sauptikaparvan ('Book of the Nocturnal Attack') is the tenth of the eighteen books of the Mahābhārata, comprising 18 adhyāyas. Following Duryodhana's mortal defeat at the close of the Kurukṣetra war, the surviving Kaurava warrior Aśvatthāman, driven by grief and vengeance and accompanied by Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, conducts an unauthorized midnight raid on the sleeping Pāṇḍava encampment. Infused with the destructive power of Śiva, Aśvatthāman massacres Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the five sons of Draupadī (the Upapāṇḍavas), and the remaining allied army. When subsequently pursued by Arjuna and Krishna, Aśvatthāman discharges the apocalyptic brahmaśiras weapon; Krishna compels him to surrender his protective gem and curses him to wander the earth diseased and solitary for three thousand years, while ensuring the revival of Uttarā's unborn child Parīkṣit.

The Anuśāsanaparvan ('Book of Instructions') is the thirteenth book of the Mahābhārata, continuing and concluding Bhīṣma's post-war instructions to King Yudhiṣṭhira as the patriarch lies on his bed of arrows at Kurukṣetra. Diverging from the political and philosophical focus of the Śāntiparvan, it concentrates heavily on social, ritual, and religious duties, including exhaustive treatments of gift-giving (dānadharma), religious vows (vrata), funerary and ancestral rites (śrāddha), strict non-injury and vegetarianism (ahiṃsā), the conduct and status of women, and the veneration of brahmins. The parvan is particularly noted for preserving seminal Hindu devotional litanies, most famously the Viṣṇusahasranāmastotra (adhyāya 135) and the Śivasahasranāma, before culminating in the arrival of the auspicious winter solstice (uttarāyaṇa), Bhīṣma's ultimate yogic release, and his funerary rites.

The Aśvamedhikaparvan (Book 14 of the Mahābhārata) recounts the aftermath of the Kurukṣetra war and the death of Bhīṣma. Distressed by the catastrophic slaughter of his kin, King Yudhiṣṭhira is urged by Vyāsa and Kṛṣṇa to perform the royal horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) to expiate the sin of warfare and consolidate sovereign rule. The narrative then details Arjuna's military expeditions guarding the wandering sacrificial horse across the subcontinent, Kṛṣṇa's revival of Abhimanyu's stillborn son Parikṣit, the formal completion of the Vedic horse sacrifice, and the concluding fable of the golden-spotted mongoose (Nakulopākhyāna), which illustrates the spiritual superiority of humble, selfless charity over extravagant ritual pageantry.

The Nārāyaṇīya (Mahābhārata 12.321–339) is a major theological tract of 19 chapters located near the end of the Mokṣadharmaparvan in the Śāntiparvan. It provides the earliest comprehensive textual witness to early Pāñcarātra and Bhāgavata doctrine within the epic literature, extolling Nārāyaṇa as the supreme transcendent deity and cosmic source of all manifestations. Key theological contributions include the systematic exposition of the fourfold emanation theory (caturvyūha: Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha), the practice of unswerving devotion (ekāntikabhakti), and the allegorical voyage of the celestial seer Nārada to Śvetadvīpa ('the White Island').

The Uttarakāṇḍa is the seventh and concluding book of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, serving as an extensive narrative and mythological epilogue to the core epic. It begins with the sage Agastya narrating the origins, genealogy, and early exploits of Rāvaṇa and other rākṣasas, as well as the childhood deeds of Hanumān. **Attribution:** The work is ascribed to the 7th-century rhetorician Bhāmaha.

The Kāvyālaṃkāra of Bhāmaha (c. 7th century CE) is one of the earliest extant systematic treatises on classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), establishing poetics as an autonomous discipline distinct from dramaturgy. In six chapters (paricchedas) comprising approximately 400 verses, the work treats poetic genres, thirty-nine figures of speech (alaṃkāra), poetic defects (doṣa), logical and epistemological argumentation (nyāya, including a famous refutation of the Buddhist apoha doctrine), and grammatical correctness (śabdaśuddhi). Bhāmaha famously defines kāvya as the unified harmony of word and meaning (śabdārthau sahitau kāvyam) and identifies vakrokti ('oblique/striking expression') as the indispensable hallmark of genuine poetic language.

**Attribution:** Authored by Jayadeva, son of Mahādeva and Sumitrā, who bore the epithet Pīyūṣavarṣa ('rain of nectar'), dated to the 13th century CE. He is identical with the dramatist who composed the Prasannarāghava, but must not be confused with Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva, the 12th-century author of the Gītagovinda.

The Candrāloka is an elementary verse treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by Jayadeva Pīyūṣavarṣa in ten chapters (mayūkhas) in straightforward anuṣṭubh meter. It methodically surveys poetic causes and definitions, word-powers (śaktivṛtti), poetic faults (doṣas), virtues (guṇas), figures of speech (alaṃkāras), and sentiment (rasa). The fifth mayūkha, treating figures of speech, is celebrated for its didactic technique wherein each definition serves simultaneously as an illustration of the figure defined; this chapter served as the direct basis for Appayya Dīkṣita's influential Kuvalayānanda.

The Vakroktijīvita by Rājānaka Kuntaka is a landmark treatise in Sanskrit poetics that presents vakrokti ('oblique' or 'striking expression') as the essential life-principle (jīvita) of all literature. Composed in kārikā verses alongside Kuntaka's own prose commentary (svavṛtti) and hundreds of illustrative literary citations, the work systematizes creative poetic deviation (vakratā) across six hierarchical levels of linguistic organization: phoneme/letter arrangements (varṇavinyāsa), lexical stems (pada-pūrvārdha), inflectional morphology (pratyayāśraya), sentential composition (vākya), thematic episodes (prakaraṇa), and overall plot structure (prabandha). Responding to the dominant dhvani theory of Ānandavardhana, Kuntaka seeks to integrate alaṅkāra, guṇa, mārga, and rasa into an all-encompassing aesthetic framework centered on the imaginative faculty and creative activity of the poet (kavi-vyāpāra).

The Kāvyaprakāśa is an 11th-century masterpiece of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) authored by the Kashmiri scholar Mammaṭa and completed in its tenth chapter by Allaṭa. Divided into ten chapters (ullāsas), it systematically synthesizes the dhvani (poetic suggestion) theory developed by Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta with the older traditions of poetic faults (doṣa), qualities (guṇa), and figurative ornaments (alaṃkāra). Combining terse theoretical kārikās with an auto-commentarial vṛtti and hundreds of illustrative verses drawn from classical literature, it served as the foremost textbook of literary theory across the subcontinent and inspired dozens of subcommentaries.

Although Rājaśekhara projected an ambitious eighteen-adhikaraṇa treatise in chapter 1, only this first adhikaraṇa has survived in manuscript tradition (or was ever completed), making the e-text complete for the extant work.

**Also known as:** Kavirahasya

The Kāvyamīmāṃsā ('Inquiry into Poetry') by Rājaśekhara is a classic of Sanskrit literary theory focused on the practical training and culture of a poet (kaviśikṣā). Although planned on an encyclopedic scale of eighteen books, only the first book, the Kavirahasya ('The Poet's Secret') in eighteen chapters, is extant. The work offers valuable documentation of early medieval Indian literary life, describing the allegorical personification of poetry (Kāvyapuruṣa), the nature of innate poetic talent (pratibhā), royal assemblies and salons (kavisabhā), the classification of borrowing and plagiarism (haraṇa), poetic conventions (kavisamaya), and Pan-Indian cultural geography (deśavibhāga).

The Nāṭakacandrikā ('Moonlight of Drama') is a 16th-century dramaturgical treatise by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Synthesizing Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and especially the Rasapūrvasudhākara (Rasārṇavasudhākara)—while consciously rejecting the formulation of the Sāhitya-darpaṇa—the work systematizes plot structure (sandhi, sandhyaṅga), hero types, and emotional states for dramatic poetry. The Vyaktivivekavyākhyā is a commentary by Ruyyaka on Mahimabhaṭṭa's Vyaktiviveka. This text contains the second chapter (dvitīya vimarśa), which analyzes poetic defects (doṣas) and syntactic improprieties (śabdānaucitya), examining five major faults: vidheyāvimarśa (faulty predication/emphasis), prakramabheda (lack of syntactic parallelism), kramabheda (misplaced word order), paunaruktya (redundancy), and vācyāvacana / avācyavacana (omission or unwarranted inclusion of expressions). Although Mahimabhaṭṭa composed the root work as a polemic against Ānandavardhana's dhvani doctrine by seeking to subsume suggestion into logical inference (anumāna), Ruyyaka's commentary provides indispensable grammatical and rhetorical elucidations while critically scrutinizing Mahimabhaṭṭa's positions.

The Alaṅkārasarvasva is an influential 12th-century Kashmiri treatise on Sanskrit poetics by Ruyyaka (c. 1135–1150 CE). Composed in concise sūtras accompanied by a prose vṛtti, the work provides an analytical and exhaustive classification of over eighty figures of sense and sound (alaṅkāra), integrating traditional rhetorical taxonomies with the dhvani framework established by earlier theorists. Its introductory Bhūmikā offers a critical historical review of earlier poetic theories (including Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, Vāmana, Rudraṭa, and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka), demonstrating that ornamental figures are functionally related to suggested sense.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete work comprising all three vilāsas (1: Rañjakollāsa, 2: Rasollāsa, 3: Nāṭakollāsa), complete with kārikās, authorial vṛtti, and illustrative citations (udāharaṇas).

**Also known as:** Rasārṇava-sudhākara

**Attribution:** Attributed to Siṅgabhūpāla (1381), the Recarla King (also referenced as Siṃhabhūpāla / Śiṅgarāja).

The Rasārṇavasudhākara ('Nectar-Moon to the Ocean of Rasa') is an encyclopedic 14th-century Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy and aesthetics composed by King Siṃhabhūpāla II of the Recherla dynasty. Arranged into three comprehensive 'rays' (vilāsas)—Rañjakollāsa (dealing with dramatic personae, the typology of hero and heroine, and their aesthetic embellishments), Rasollāsa (treating the primary sentiments, transient emotions, excitant/ensuant factors, and the nature of aesthetic delight), and Nāṭakollāsa (treating plot structure, junctures/sandhis, and dramatic genres)—it synthesizes the traditions of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, Dhanañjaya's Daśarūpaka, and Bhoja's Śṛṅgāraprakāśa. The work is especially prized by later commentators (notably Mallinātha and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theorists such as Rūpa Gosvāmin) for its rigorous definitions and rich repertoire of illustrative quotations drawn from classical poetry and drama.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all five adhikaraṇas (comprising twelve adhyāyas): 1. Śārīra (3 adhyāyas), 2. Doṣadarśana (2 adhyāyas), 3. Guṇavivecana (2 adhyāyas), 4. Ālaṅkārika (3 adhyāyas), and 5. Prāyogika (2 adhyāyas, concluding at 5.2.91 with the author's final verses and colophon).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra (Vāmana, root text)
- Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti (Vāmana, commentary)

**Also known as:** Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti, Kavipriyā, Kāvyālaṅkārasūtrāṇi savṛttīni

**Attribution:** Vāmana composed both the root sūtras and the prose auto-commentary (vṛtti), which he designates as 'Kavipriyā' in the opening maṅgala stanza (1.1.3–4: 'praṇamya paramaṃ jyotir vāmanena kavipriyā / kāvyālaṅkārasūtrāṇāṃ teṣāṃ vṛttir vidhīyate'). Later tradition and manuscript colophons typically refer to the unitary work as the Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti.

The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra along with its auto-commentary (Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti or Kavipriyā) by Vāmana (fl. late 8th to early 9th century CE, Kashmir) constitutes the defining work of the Rīti school of classical Sanskrit poetics. Vāmana formulated the famous thesis that style (rīti) is the soul of poetry ('rītir ātmā kāvyasya', 1.2.6), distinguishing three primary styles (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, and Pāñcālī) based on the presence of specific poetic qualities (guṇas). Organised into five adhikaraṇas (Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika), the work presents a comprehensive taxonomy of poetic purpose, flaws (doṣas), aesthetic qualities (ten verbal and ten semantic guṇas), figures of speech (alaṅkāras), and rules for grammatical purity in poetry (śabdaśuddhi).

The second chapter (pariccheda) of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa investigates the grammatical and semantic foundations of poetic discourse, focusing on the definitions of the sentence (vākya) and the word (pada). It elaborates the three classical conditions for syntactic and semantic coherence: semantic compatibility (yogyatā), mutual expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), and contiguity (āsatti). It systematically analyzes the primary linguistic powers (śabdavṛtti)—denotation (abhidhā), metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā), and poetic suggestion (vyañjanā)—as well as the sentence-purport function (tātparyavṛtti) of the Abhihitānvayavādins. This digital file presents Viśvanātha's kārikās and autocommentary interwoven with two important traditional commentaries: the Locanā of the author's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā of Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra.

Pariccheda 3 (Rasādinirūpaṇa) of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa provides an in-depth exposition of rasa (aesthetic relish), analyzing how the sthāyibhāva is brought to relish via vibhāvas (determinants), anubhāvas (consequents), and vyabhicāribhāvas (transitory emotions). It also details the classification of the rasas (śṛṅgāra, hāsya, karuṇa, raudra, vīra, bhayānaka, bībhatsa, adbhuta, and śānta), dramatic character types, and the comprehensive taxonomy of heroes (nāyakas) and heroines (nāyikās). The fourth pariccheda of Viśvanātha's Sāhityadarpaṇa treats the classification of poetry based on the theory of aesthetic suggestion (dhvani), building upon the frameworks of Ānandavardhana and Mammaṭa. It defines first-rate poetry (dhvanikāvya or uttama kāvya) where implied meaning surpasses expressed meaning, detailing its major divisions (avivakṣitavācya and vivakṣitānyaparavācya) and their numerous varieties, and contrasts this with second-rate poetry of subordinate suggestion (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya or madhyama kāvya). This electronic text presents the root kārikās and Viśvanātha's autocommentary alongside two extensive Sanskrit commentaries: the Locana by the author's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā by Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra.

The commentary Vijñapriyā is by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya (also cited as Maheśvarabhaṭṭa or Maheśvaranyāyālaṅkāra). Chapter 5 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's 14th-century treatise on poetics, the Sāhityadarpaṇa, presented alongside the Vijñapriyā commentary of Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra and the Locana commentary of the author's son Anantadāsa. This chapter is devoted to vindicating the dhvani school's doctrine of suggestion (vyañjanāvyāpāra) as an autonomous semantic function (vṛtti) indispensable for conveying aesthetic relish (rasa), vastudhvani, and alaṅkāradhvani. Viśvanātha and his commentators systematically refute competing theories advanced by Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and other schools that attempt to reduce suggestion to literal denotation (abhidhā), sentence purport (tātparya), or syllogistic inference (anumāna).

Pariccheda 8 (Guṇavivecana) of Viśvanātha's fourteenth-century alaṅkāraśāstra treatise Sāhityadarpaṇa treats the poetic qualities (guṇa). Adopting the Kashmiri dhvani position elaborated by Mammaṭa, Viśvanātha argues that guṇas inhere essentially in the principal aesthetic emotion (rasa) rather than in mere sound or word configurations, reducing the traditional tenfold guṇa system of Daṇḍin and Vāmana to three primary qualities: mādhurya (sweetness/melting), ojas (vigor/expansion), and prasāda (perspicuity/clarity). - Coomaraswamy, Ananda K. 1917. New Delhi: Munishiram Manoharlal. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** unclear — The catalog entry contains no e-text data.

**Also known as:** Abhinaya darpaņa

The Abhinayadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Gesture'), attributed to the legendary sage Nandikeśvara, is an indispensable Sanskrit manual on classical Indian performing arts, particularly central to the tradition of Bharatanatyam. It is primarily devoted to āṅgikābhinaya (bodily and gestural expression), systematically enumerating and defining gestures of the single and combined hands (asaṃyuta- and saṃyuta-hastas), movements of the head (śirobheda), eyes (dṛṣṭibheda), neck (grīvābheda), and eyebrows, as well as postures (sthāna), movements (cārī), and gaits (gati). The work functions as a practical handbook connecting theoretical dramaturgy with dance choreography.

He is distinct from his contemporary Gauḍa Abhinanda (son of Śatānanda), the author of the epic Rāmacarita.

The Kādambarīkathāsāra is an eight-canto metrical epitome of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's celebrated prose romance Kādambarī, composed in Kashmir by Abhinanda, son of the Nyāya logician Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. It compresses Bāṇa's intricate, multilayered narrative of reborn lovers (Candrāpīḍa, Puṇḍarīka, Kādambarī, and Mahāśvetā) into accessible verse, omitting the extensive descriptive prose digressions of the original. The autobiographical prologue in canto 1 preserves valuable historical evidence for the author's family genealogy, recording their migration from Gauḍa to Dārvābhisāra and Kashmir, and noting that his ancestor Śaktisvāmin served as a minister under the Kārkoṭa ruler Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa.

**Also known as:** Saundaranandakāvya, Saundaranandaṃ Mahākāvyam

**Attribution:** Ascribed to the Buddhist poet and philosopher Aśvaghoṣa.

The Saundarananda ('Handsome Nanda') by Aśvaghoṣa is one of the earliest extant Sanskrit mahākāvya court epics, preserved complete in eighteen cantos. It dramatizes the conversion of the Buddha's handsome half-brother Nanda, who is deeply attached to his sensual love for his consort Sundarī. Through skilful pedagogy, meditation instruction, and visions of heavenly nymphs juxtaposed with the perils of cyclic existence, the Buddha leads Nanda step by step to spiritual maturity and arhatship. In the closing stanzas (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa articulates a seminal defense of Buddhist kāvya, explaining that ornate poetry serves merely as a sweet coating to administer the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa).

After Rājyavardhana defeats Mālava, he is treacherously assassinated by the Gauḍa ruler (Śaśāṅka). Urged by his commander-in-chief Siṃhanāda, Harṣa takes a solemn vow (rājapratijñā) to destroy the treacherous enemies of his house and announces his campaign for the conquest of the earth.

The Kādambarī is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance composed in the 7th century CE by Bāṇabhaṭṭa and finished by his son Bhūṣaṇabhaṭṭa. Renowned for its intricate sentence structure, ornate imagery, and complex nested frame stories spanning successive rebirths, it tells the intertwined tales of Prince Candrāpīḍa and Princess Kādambarī alongside Puṇḍarīka and Mahāśvetā. The Kirātārjunīya is an 18-canto mahākāvya composed by the poet Bhāravi, elaborating an episode from the Vanaparvan of the Mahābhārata. The epic narrates Arjuna's journey to Mount Indrakīla in the Himalayas to perform penance and procure divine weapons for the Pāṇḍavas, his duel and wrestling combat with Śiva disguised as a mountain hunter (kirāta) over a slain boar, and Śiva's revelation and bestowal of the Pāśupata weapon. Celebrated in classical Sanskrit literary theory for gravity of meaning (arthagaurava), political discourse (nīti), and virtuoso poetic ornamentation (especially the citrakāvya constraints of canto 15), it constitutes one of the traditional 'five great court epics' (pañcamahākāvya).

The Caurapañcāśikā is a famous classical Sanskrit lyrical sequence of fifty stanzas in the Vasantatilakā meter, each verse opening with the evocative anaphora 'adyāpi' ('even now'). Framed by tradition as the death-row lament of a clandestine lover awaiting execution after an illicit affair with a princess, each stanza presents a self-contained, vividly sensory recollection of the beloved's physical charms and their shared intimacy. Traditionally attributed to the 11th-century Kashmiri poet Bilhaṇa, the poem became one of the most celebrated works of classical Indian secular erotics (śṛṅgārakāvya), inspiring miniature painting cycles and vernacular adaptations throughout South Asia.

Chapters 12 through 22 of the Pūrvacampū of Jīva Gosvāmin's monumental campū work on the life and līlā of Kṛṣṇa in Vraja. Narrated within a frame story by two youth singers, Snigdhakaṇṭha and Madhukaṇṭha, this section chronicles Kṛṣṇa's transition into his youth (kaiśora), beginning with pasturing the calves and cows (gocāraṇa), the subduing of the serpent Kāliya, the slaying of Dhenukāsura and Pralambāsura, the lifting of Govardhana Hill, the extinguishing of the forest fire, and the granting of grace to the wives of the sacrificial brāhmaṇas (yajñapatnī-prasāda). The entire work is divided into the Pūrvacampū (33 pūraṇas) and the Uttaracampū (37 pūraṇas), portrayed as recitations by the bards Snigdhakaṇṭha and Madhukaṇṭha before Kṛṣṇa and his entourage in Goloka. This file comprises the first three pūraṇas of the Uttaracampū, covering the introductory narration, the prelude to Akrūra's visit to Vraja, and Kṛṣṇa's impending journey to Mathurā (Māthurapurasthānaprasthāna).

The Gītagovinda of Jayadeva (composed in late 12th-century Bengal) is a celebrated lyrical kāvya celebrating the passionate love, separation (viraha), and joyful reconciliation of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā. **Attribution:** Universally attributed to Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). This digital text presents the poem according to the recension commented on by Vallabhadeva.

The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') of Kālidāsa is the foundational lyric poem of the sandeśakāvya genre in classical Sanskrit literature, composed entirely in the mandākrāntā meter. Exiled to Mount Rāmagiri for neglecting his duties, an attendant yakṣa begs a passing monsoon cloud to deliver a message of love and reassurance to his pining wife in the celestial city of Alakā. The poem comprises two sections: the Pūrvamegha, charting the cloud's scenic journey across the rivers, mountains, and cities of northern and central India, and the Uttaramegha, depicting the mythological splendors of Alakā and conveying the yakṣa's tender message. This e-text preserves the 111-stanza Kashmiri recension commented on by Vallabhadeva.

**Also known as:** Raghuvamśa

**Attribution:** Work of Kālidāsa, referenced in the Aihole panegyric and commented on by early commentators including Vallabhadeva.

The Raghuvaṃśa is a nineteen-canto mahākāvya by Kālidāsa recounting the lineage of the solar kings (Sūryavaṃśa) of Ayodhyā. The narrative details the reign of Dilīpa, the world-conquest of Raghu, the tragic romance of Aja and Indumatī, Daśaratha, and the avatāra of Rāma (cantos 10–15), continuing through Kuśa down to the decline and death of the hedonistic Agnivarṇa and the accession of his pregnant queen. Renowned for its stylistic balance, evocative similes (upamā), and depiction of dharma, it is universally regarded as one of the twin pinnacles of classical Sanskrit epic poetry alongside the Kumārasambhava.

The Śiśupālavadha ('The Slaying of Śiśupāla') is a canonical 20-canto court epic (mahākāvya) composed by the poet Māgha. Expanding an episode from the Sabhāparvan of the Mahābhārata, the narrative recounts the slaying of the insolent king Śiśupāla of Chedi by Kṛṣṇa during Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya sacrifice. Celebrated in traditional Sanskrit literary criticism alongside Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, the work is renowned for its vigorous political debate (Canto 2), rich descriptive set pieces (Cantos 4–13), and intricate verbal pyrotechnics and visual poetry (citrakāvya, Canto 19).

The Mālatīmādhava is a ten-act drama of the prakaraṇa genre composed by the 8th-century poet Bhavabhūti. Set principally in the city of Padmāvatī, it depicts the fraught romance between Mādhava and Mālatī (alongside the subplot of Makaranda and Madayantikā), which faces obstacle from an imperial court betrothal and terror from Kāpālika sorcerers in cremation grounds before reaching resolution through the interventions of the Buddhist nun Kāmandakī and her disciple Saudāminī. - Siddharūpaṃ, Bālaprabodhaṃ, Samāsacakraṃ, vyākhyānavuṃ Śrīrāmodantavuṃ, ed. C. V. Ravisarma Raja, Thrissur: Kerala Sahitya Akademi, 1948 (repr. 2010). — Malayalam script edition preserving the shorter 156-verse recension.
- Śrīrāmodantaṃ (samīkṣā vyākhyānaṃ), ed. Pūvattūr Rāmakṛṣṇa Piḷḷa, Thiruvananthapuram – Kottayam: National Book Stall, 1990. — 153-verse recension with Malayalam commentary.

**Translations:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete; the e-text presents a comparative synoptic version incorporating the verses of both the shorter 156-verse Kerala recension and the expanded 199-verse 7-kāṇḍa recension with dual verse numbering.

**Also known as:** Śrīrāmodanta, Rāmodantam

**Attribution:** The work is anonymous in the pedagogical tradition of South India (especially Kerala); no historical author is named or reliably identified.

The Rāmodanta is an anonymous pedagogical Sanskrit poem summarizing the complete narrative of the Rāmāyaṇa in simple anuṣṭubh verse. Widely used across South India—particularly Kerala—as an introductory reader, it traditionally served as a student's first narrative text following the memorization of basic grammatical declensions and conjugations (such as the Siddharūpa). The original recension comprises 156 verses, encoded by the kaṭapayādi chronogram 'cinmayaḥ' (156) in the final verse, while popular later print editions expanded the text to 199 verses organized into seven kāṇḍas.

The Vāsavadattā of Subandhu (dated to the sixth century) is a classical Sanskrit prose romance (kathā). The narrative recounts how Prince Kandarpaketu and Princess Vāsavadattā experience dreams of each other, seek each other out, elope, undergo separation after Vāsavadattā is petrified into stone by an ascetic's curse, and are reunited once the touch of Kandarpaketu restores her to life. The work is famed for its extreme rhetorical display, notably pervasive paronomasia (śleṣa) across almost every syllable and sentence, which served as a major stylistic predecessor to Bāṇabhaṭṭa's prose romances.

**Evidence:**

- The e-text opening defines a tagging syntax: '[0] BhSv_(act).(verse)', '[1] :(prose / sentence)', '[2] {...} = stage directions', '[3] *{...}* = speakers', '[4] [...] = Sanskrit Chaya'.

- C.R. Devadhar (ed. & trans.), Svapnavāsavadatta of Bhāsa, Poona Oriental Series 27. — Mentioned in Mahāsubhāṣitasaṃgraha source list.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete drama in six acts (Acts 1–6), including opening stage directions, Prakrit dialogues accompanied inline by Sanskrit chāyā in square brackets, and concluding with the Bharatavākya (6.19) and colophon (iti svapnanāṭakam avasitam).

**Also known as:** Svapnavāsavadattam, Svapnanāṭaka

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the playwright Bhāsa. Bhāsa's authorship of a Svapnavāsavadatta is recorded by Rājaśekhara (Sūktimuktāvalī 4.48) and mentioned by Kālidāsa (Mālavikāgnimitra). T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī discovered and published 13 plays including the Svapnavāsavadatta, which he believed to be works of Bhāsa, though whether they represent the genuine works remains debated.

The Svapnavāsavadatta ('The Dream of Vāsavadattā') is a six-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) dramatizing episodes from the Udayana legend cycle of the Bṛhatkathā. To facilitate King Udayana's political alliance with King Darśaka of Magadha and recapture his kingdom from the usurper Āruṇī, Minister Yaugandharāyaṇa arranges the staged death of Queen Vāsavadattā in a fire at Lāvāṇaka and conceals her under the identity of Lady Āvantikā in the care of Princess Padmāvatī. The dramatic and psychological climax occurs in Act 5 (the dream act / svapnāṅka), where the sleeping Udayana addresses Vāsavadattā in what he believes to be a dream while she secretly comforts him, leading to their eventual reunion and royal restoration in Act 6.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Extremely fragmentary remains of three early plays preserved on palm-leaf fragments from the Berlin Turfan collection (SHT 16 and SHT 57). For the Śāriputraprakaraṇa, only scattered portions of acts 8 and 9 (including the final colophon) are preserved; the allegorical drama and courtesan drama survive only as isolated speech and verse fragments.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Śāriputraprakaraṇa (Aśvaghoṣa, root text)
- Allegorical Buddhist Drama (root text)
- Prakaraṇa with a Courtesan (root text)

**Also known as:** Bruchstücke buddhistischer Dramen, Śāriputraprakaraṇa, Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa, Buddhist Dramatic Fragments

**Attribution:** The Śāriputraprakaraṇa (or Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa) is explicitly attributed to Aśvaghoṣa (son of Suvarṇākṣī) in the surviving colophon of Act 9 (SHT 57). The two other plays preserved in the same manuscript find (SHT 16)—an allegorical play featuring personified qualities (Buddhi, Dhṛti, Kīrti) and a comedy featuring a courtesan (gaṇikā), a vidūṣaka (Komudagandha), and a rogue (duṣṭa)—are anonymous, though Lüders and subsequent scholarship suggest they stem from the same Kuṣāṇa-era Buddhist dramatic circle.

This e-text contains the oldest surviving specimens of Indian dramatic literature, discovered on palm-leaf fragments from Kizil near Turfan (Central Asia) and datable to the Kuṣāṇa period (c. 1st–2nd century CE). The principal identifiable play is Aśvaghoṣa's Śāriputraprakaraṇa (or Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa), a nine-act play dramatizing the conversion of the Buddha's foremost disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Preserved alongside it are fragments of two anonymous Buddhist plays: an allegorical drama featuring personifications (Buddhi, Dhṛti, Kīrti) and a prakaraṇa or social comedy involving a courtesan (gaṇikā), a rogue (duṣṭa), and a jester (vidūṣaka). These fragments are of foundational importance for the history of classical Sanskrit theatre and the early history of Middle Indo-Aryan dialects (archaic forms of Māgadhī, Ardhamāgadhī, and Śaurasenī).

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Sansarachandra (ed.), Motilal Banarsidas: Delhi 1997.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC) Project, Nagarjuna Institute of Buddhist Studies, Nepal and University of the West, Rosemead, California (proofread by Milan Shakya; version dated 2009-04-08); integrated into GRETIL by Reinhold Grünendahl and converted to TEI by Maximilian Mehner.

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL legacy file header (harnagau.htm): 'Based on the ed. by Sansarachandra, Motilal Banarsidas: Delhi 1997.'
- DSBC provenance notice in header: 'Input by members of the Sanskrit Buddhist Input Project. With kind permission of the Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon Project of Nagarjuna Institute, Nepal and University of the West... Version: 2009-04-08 15:07:19. Proof Reader: Milan Shakya.'

**Other editions:**

- Vidhusekhara Bhattacharya (ed.), Nāgānanda-nāṭaka of Śrīharṣadeva, Bibliotheca Indica, Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1957. — Edition of Sanskrit and Tibetan text.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains only the metrical verses across all five acts (Nā_1.1 to Nā_5.41), omitting all intervening Sanskrit and Prakrit prose dialogue and stage directions.

**Also known as:** Nāgānanda, Nāgānandanāṭaka

**Attribution:** Attributed to the 7th-century North Indian ruler Harṣadeva (Śrīharṣa).

The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Serpents') is a five-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) attributed to Harṣadeva (7th century CE), dramatizing the Buddhist legend of the Vidyādhara prince Jīmūtavāhana. The opening acts combine standard courtly kāvya romance with Jīmūtavāhana's courtship and marriage to Princess Malayavatī, while the fourth and fifth acts center on his Bodhisattva-like self-sacrifice: offering his own flesh on the slaughter stone to Garuḍa to rescue the young Nāga Śaṅkhacūḍa. Moved by Jīmūtavāhana's radical compassion and non-violence, Garuḍa renounces the slaughter of serpents and revives those previously consumed. Famous for invoking both the Buddha (munīndra / jina) and the Hindu goddess Gaurī, the work is an exceptional surviving exemplar of classical Buddhist dramatic literature.

The Priyadarśikā is a classical four-act court drama (nāṭikā) attributed to King Harṣadeva (Harṣavardhana of Kanauj, r. c. 606–647 CE). Drawing upon the popular romantic cycle of King Udayana of Vatsa, it depicts Udayana's romance with Princess Priyadarśikā of Aṅga, who lives incognito as the handmaiden Āraṇyakā in Queen Vāsavadattā's harem. The play is particularly noted for containing one of the earliest extant examples of a play-within-a-play (garbhanāṭaka) in Sanskrit dramatic literature (Act 3), which brings about the discovery of the lovers and the heroine's eventual royal marriage.

**Also known as:** Mattavilāsa

**Attribution:** The drama names its author as Śrī Mahendravikramavarman. He is identified with the Pallava king Mahendravarman I.

The Mattavilāsaprahasana ('The Farce of Drunken Sport') is a 7th-century one-act Sanskrit satire (prahasana) by the Pallava monarch Mahendravarman I, set in Kāñcīpuram. The plot follows a drunken Kāpālika ascetic, Satyasoma, and his consort Devasomā, who misplace their skull begging bowl (kapāla) and wrongly accuse a Buddhist monk, Nāgasena, of having stolen it. A Pāśupata ascetic is called in to arbitrate the dispute until a madman arrives with the bowl, which he had recovered from a stray dog, clearing the monk of blame. The play satirizes contemporary sectarian friction and religious hypocrisy among Kāpālikas, Pāśupatas, Buddhists, and Jains, and survives as a staple piece in Kerala's classical Kūṭiyāṭṭam theater.

The Mudrārākṣasa is a celebrated drama attributed to Viśākhadatta, dramatizing the statecraft of Cāṇakya following the overthrow of the Nanda dynasty. Uniquely devoid of romantic subplots or supernatural elements, the drama hinges on espionage, political psychology, and the minister Rākṣasa under emperor Candragupta.

The Pādatāḍitaka ('The Kick') by the late Gupta-era poet Śyāmilaka is the longest and most celebrated of the four satirical monologue plays preserved in the Caturbhāṇī. Spoken entirely by a viṭa (cosmopolitan man-about-town), the play recounts his journey through the streets of Sārvabhaumanagara (Ujjayinī) to convene a council of rogues to prescribe a comedic expiation (prāyaścitta) for a high-caste gentleman kicked on the head by a courtesan during a lovers' quarrel. Rich in social satire, vivid urban character sketches, and linguistic wit, it provides unparalleled insight into late classical Indian courtly and demi-monde life.

## Edition and provenance
