**Edition used (determined):** D. D. Kosambi and V. V. Gokhale (eds.), The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa Compiled by Vidyākara, Harvard Oriental Series 42, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1957.

**E-text:** Harunaga Isaacson (original input); adapted by Jan Brzezinski for Gaudiya Grantha Mandira; revised and compound-analyzed for GRETIL.

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL header: 'Based on the edition by D.D. Kosambi and V.V. Gokhale. Cambridge, Massachusetts 1957 (Harvard Oriental Series, 42). Input by Harunaga Isaacson.'
- Verse numbering 'VidSrk_0.1 *(1)' through 'VidSrk_50.41 *(1738)' precisely reflects the 1,738 numbered verses of the Kosambi–Gokhale critical edition.
- Final colophon matches HOS 42: 'samāpto 'yaṃ subhāṣita-ratna-koṣa iti // paṇḍita-śrī-bhīmārjuna-somasya //'.

**Other editions:**
- F. W. Thomas (ed.), Kavīndravacanasamuccaya, Bibliotheca Indica, Calcutta: Asiatic Society, 1912. — Editio princeps of the earlier recension based on a palm-leaf manuscript from Nepal.

**Translations:**
- Daniel H. H. Ingalls, An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry: Vidyākara's 'Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa', Harvard Oriental Series 44, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1965. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains all 50 vrajyās (thematic sections) and 1,738 verses comprising the complete expanded recension of the anthology as edited in HOS 42.

**Also known as:** Kavīndravacanasamuccaya

**Attribution:** Compiled by the Buddhist scholar-monk Vidyākara, associated with the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra in Bengal (fl. late 11th to early 12th century CE).

The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa ('Treasury of Well-Turned Verse') is an anthology of classical Sanskrit court poetry compiled by the Buddhist scholar Vidyākara around 1100 CE (with an expanded recension c. 1130 CE) in Bengal. Arranged into 50 thematic sections (vrajyās) encompassing 1,738 stanzas, it collects works from over two hundred poets, opening with Buddhist and Hindu devotional hymns and progressing through the seasons, love, social types, nature, gnomic sayings, and praise of poets. The work is a foundational witness to classical kāvya between 700 and 1050 CE, preserving extensive poetic material that would otherwise be entirely lost.

## GRETIL header

**Edition:** D.D. Kosambi and V.V. Gokhale. Cambridge, Massachusetts 1957 (Harvard Oriental Series, 42)

**Entered by:** Harunaga Isaacson

**Corrections by:** Corrected GRETIL version based on the adaptation by Jan Brzezinski (available from Gaudiya Grantha Mandira); in addition, parts left out in the course of that adaptation were restored, and the reference system was revised. Harunaga Isaacson's original e-text has been subjected to a large number of tacit changes in the Gaudiya Grantha Mandira version, apart from the missing verses. E.g., many b's have been changed to v's. In some cases the divergence may be on account of a different text. Quite a number these changes led to metrical corruptions, and have been revised in the present version. Nonetheless, it remains a hybrid between H. Issacson's text and other readings. The first skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa establishes the narrative, theological, and devotional frame for the scripture. At an assembly in Naimiṣa forest, the sages headed by Śaunaka ask the bard Sūta to recount the essence of all sacred teachings, leading to the framing narrative of Vyāsa, who after composing the Mahābhārata finds inner peace only when Nārada instructs him to celebrate Kṛṣṇa's divine manifestations directly. The skandha recounts the previous birth of Nārada, the birth and reign of King Parīkṣit, the departure of the Pāṇḍavas, and the curse placed upon Parīkṣit to die in seven days, prompting the king's renunciation on the banks of the Ganges and his reception of Śuka's teaching.

The sixth skandha (book) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa centers upon the themes of divine grace, the salvific efficacy of devotion (bhakti), and the repetition of the divine name (nāma-saṅkīrtana). Its central narratives begin with the deliverance of the wayward Brahmin Ajāmila through the utterance of 'Nārāyaṇa' at death, followed by the revelation of the protective Nārāyaṇa-kavaca, Dakṣa's genealogy, and his curse upon Nārada. The middle section narrates the war between the devas and the virtuous asura Vṛtra, who is slain by Indra using the vajra forged from the ascetic Dadhīci's bones, and recounts Vṛtra's previous life as King Citraketu. The book closes with Diti's performance of the Puṃsavana vrata and the miraculous emergence of the Maruts.

The twelfth and concluding skandha (book) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa opens with a prophetic account of post-Mahābhārata royal dynasties up through the Kali Yuga (including the Nandas, Mauryas, and Śuṅgas), followed by a description of the moral, spiritual, and physical degeneration of humanity in the Kali age and the advent of the Kalki avatāra. It includes the Bhūmigītā (Song of the Earth) on the transient folly of kings, expounds the four kinds of cosmic dissolution (pralaya), and concludes King Parīkṣit's narrative with his death by Takṣaka after receiving final teachings on the immortal Ātman from Śuka. The book then covers the lineage and preservation of the Vedic śākhās and the Purāṇas, the spiritual vision of sage Mārkaṇḍeya, an overall thematic summary of the entire purāṇa, and final benedictory verses extolling devotion through nāmasaṅkīrtana.

Chapters 29–33 of the tenth skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa, known as the Rāsa-pañcādhyāyī ('five chapters on the rāsa dance'), narrate Kṛṣṇa's autumn-night circle dance (rāsalīlā) with the cowherd maidens (gopīs) of Vraja, his temporary disappearance to dispel their pride, their anguished laments and song of longing (Gopīgīta), and his reunion with them in ecstatic devotional union. This section is universally regarded as the aesthetic and devotional climax of the Purāṇa. The included commentary, the Bhāvārthadīpikā by Śrīdharasvāmin (c. 14th century), interprets the erotic-devotional līlā within an Advaita-theistic framework as the triumph over desire (kāmavijaya) and served as the authoritative baseline for all subsequent Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics.

The Pretakhaṇḍa (variously styled Dharmakāṇḍa, Pretakalpa, or Uttarakhaṇḍa) forms the eschatological second division of the Garuḍapurāṇa, comprising 49 chapters in the Venkatesvara recension. ## Contents

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the mythical sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa (indicated in the opening mangala verse 'śrīmanmaharṣivedavyāsapraṇītaṃ'). The narrative frame is presented as an exposition given by four wise, dharma-abiding birds (Droṇa's sons) to Jaimini on the instruction of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya.

The Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa is considered one of the oldest and most narrative-driven of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, characterized by its general lack of sectarian bias. It opens with the sage Jaimini consulting four enlightened birds in the Vindhya mountains to resolve four perplexities left unresolved in the Mahābhārata, proceeding through discourses on cosmogony, dharma, eschatology, yoga, and the manvantara lineages. Adhyāyas 81–93 constitute the celebrated Devīmāhātmya (Durgāsaptaśatī), the seminal scripture of Hindu Śāktism celebrating the Supreme Goddess's subjugation of the demons Madhu, Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura, and Śumbha-Niśumbha.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GP12_skprevku`

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Oṅkārānanda Giri (ed.), Atha Bṛhat-Śrīnarmadāpurāṇam Revākhaṇḍam (parivardhita tṛtīya saṃskaraṇa). Hośaṅgābāda: Jñānasatra Prakāśana Nyāsa, 1994.

**E-text:** Jürgen Neuss (Freie Universität Berlin) for GRETIL

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL header explicitly cites: 'Based on the edition: Giri, Oṅkārānanda (ed.) - atha bṛhat śrīnarmadāpurāṇam revākhaṇḍam (parivardhita tṛtīya saṃskaraṇa). Jñānasatra Prakāśana Nyāsa, Hośaṅgābāda: 1994. Input and proof-reading by Juergen Neuss, Freie Universität Berlin.'
- The e-text contains all 116 chapters corresponding precisely to Giri's edition.

**Other editions:**
- Veṅkaṭeśvara Steam Press edition of the Skandapurāṇa (SkP 5.3), Bombay, 1910. — The first edition of the Skandapurāṇa (Veṅkaṭeśvara Steam Press, Bombay: 1910) wrongly assigned a different text of 232 adhyāyas originally belonging to the Vāyupurāṇa as SkP 5.3 instead of the genuine Skandapurāṇa Revākhaṇḍa.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete Revākhaṇḍa belonging to the Skandapurāṇa recension in 116 adhyāyas (1.1–116.22), which constitutes a single section of the vast Skandapurāṇa corpus.

**Also known as:** Revākhaṇḍa, Bṛhat-Śrīnarmadāpurāṇam Revākhaṇḍam

**Attribution:** Traditionally classified as a khaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa; framed primarily as a dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and King Yudhiṣṭhira.

The Revākhaṇḍa is a sacred geographical and pilgrimage text celebrating the holy sites along the course of the Narmadā (Revā) River in Central India. Structured largely around dialogues between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira, the work delineates pilgrimage and circumambulation along both the northern and southern banks, detailing origin legends, shrines, and devotional benefits. As noted by the contributor, Jürgen Neuss, this 116-chapter recension is the genuine Skandapurāṇa Revākhaṇḍa, distinct from the 232-chapter text of the Vāyupurāṇa tradition wrongly assigned to SkP 5.3 in the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition (Bombay: 1910).

## GRETIL header

**Edition:** Giri, Oṅkārānanda (ed.) - atha bṛhat śrīnarmadāpurāṇam revākhaṇḍam (parivardhita tṛtīya saṃskaraṇa). Jñānasatra Prakāśana Nyāsa, Hośaṅgābāda: 1994. Input and proof-reading by Juergen Neuss, Freie Universität Berlin. NOTE BY THE CONTRIBUTOR: This is the genuine Revākhaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa. Another text, originally belonging to the Vāyupurāṇa and comprising 232 adhyāyas, has been wrongly assigned to the Skandapurāṇa (i.e. SkP 5.3) in the latter's first edition (Veṅkateśvara Steam Press, Bombay: 1910) and ever since. (I have contributed an electronic version of that text to GRETIL, too.) Therefore the present text is not to be found in any of the editions of the SkP. (For further information on this group of texts, please contact the contributor of these e-texts at jneuss@arcor.de.)

# Vāmanapurāṇa

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GP12_vamp__u`

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** The Vāmana Purāṇa: Critically Edited, ed. Anand Swarup Gupta, Varanasi: All-India Kashiraj Trust, 1967.

**E-text:** Input by members of the SANSKNET project (sansknet.org); converted and contributed to GRETIL by Reinhold Grünendahl.

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL file header states: 'Based on the edition by A.S. Gupta, Varanasi : All India Kashiraj Trust 1967. Input by members of the SANSKNET-project (www.sansknet.org)'.
- TEI XML header (sa_vAmanapurANa1-69.xml) confirms identical source edition and SANSKNET data entry.
- Matches the 69-adhyāya chapter count and internal verse numbering of the All-India Kashiraj Trust critical edition, concluding with adhyāya 69.16 and 'iti śrīvāmanapurāṇaṃ samāptam'.

**Other editions:**
- Vāmana-Purāṇa, Bombay: Veṅkaṭeśvara Press, 1903. — Standard 95-adhyāya vulgate edition.

**Translations:**
- Vāmana-purāṇa, ed. Anand Swarup Gupta, trans. S. M. Mukhopadhyaya et al., Banaras: All-India Kashiraj Trust, 1968. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains all 69 adhyāyas of the critically constituted text of the Vāmanapurāṇa. The 28-adhyāya Saromāhātmya (dealing with Kurukṣetra tīrthas), which appears interpolated after adhyāya 23 in certain northern manuscripts and vulgate editions (yielding 95 chapters total), was edited as a separate section/appendix by Gupta and is provided separately in GRETIL as vamp_s_u.

**Also known as:** Vāmana Mahāpurāṇa, Vāmanamahāpurāṇa

**Attribution:** Within the internal narrative framework, the Purāṇa is narrated by the sage Pulastya in response to inquiries by Nārada.

The Vāmanapurāṇa is one of the eighteen traditional Mahāpurāṇas, nominally named after Viṣṇu's dwarf avatāra who subdues Bali. Despite its formal classification as a Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, the majority of its narrative content is eclectic, with substantial sections devoted to Śaiva and Śākta mythology, including the myths of Satī and Pārvatī, Śiva's penance, the birth of Kārttikeya, and the goddess's battles with Mahiṣāsura and Andhaka. It also contains detailed sacred geography and pilgrim itineraries (māhātmya), focusing heavily on Kurukṣetra, Sthāṇutīrtha, and Prayāga. Modern scholars assign the compilation of the surviving recension to between the 9th and 11th centuries CE.

**Attribution:** Framed as narrated by the Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa to the sages of Kurujāṅgala.

The Saromāhātmya is a 27-chapter pilgrimage manual (tīrthamāhātmya) preserved as an insertion or appendix to the Vāmanapurāṇa (placed between chapters 23 and 24 in the All-India Kashiraj Trust critical edition). Framed as a discourse delivered by the bard Lomaharṣaṇa to the ṛṣis assembled in Kurujāṅgala, it provides an elaborate eulogy of Kurukṣetra and its sacred lakes, notably Brahmasaras (identified with Rāmahrada and Samantapañcaka) and Sannihita-saras, alongside sacred sites along the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers. The text blends pilgrimage itineraries with local mythology, celebrating Sthāṇutīrtha and recounting both Vaiṣṇava legends (the Vāmana avatāra) and Śaiva myths.

The Viṣṇupurāṇa is one of the eighteen canonical Mahāpurāṇas and the classical exemplar of the traditional pañcalakṣaṇa structure (primary cosmogony, secondary creation, genealogies of gods and patriarchs, manvantara cycles, and dynastic histories). **Coverage:** complete — All 232 adhyāyas (RKV_1.1 – RKV_232.55), from the opening invocations ('śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ', 'oṃ namaḥ śrīnarmadāyai') to the final colophon of adhyāya 232 ('revākhaṇḍasamāpti-revākhaṇḍapustakadānādimāhātmyavarṇanaṃ nāma dvātriṃśadadhikadviśatatamo 'dhyāyaḥ').

**Also known as:** Skandapurāṇa, Āvantyakhaṇḍa: Revākhaṇḍa (SkP 5.3)

**Attribution:** Printed in the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition (1910) as part of the Skandapurāṇa (Āvantyakhaṇḍa 3) and retaining colophons naming the Skandapurāṇa ('iti śrīskānde mahāpurāṇa ekāśītisāhasryāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ pañcama āvantyakhaṇḍe revākhaṇḍe ...'); J. Neuss (GRETIL contributor note) states that all available manuscript evidence proves the text originally belonged to the Vāyupurāṇa. The final verse calls it 'pavanagaditam'. A separate, shorter Revākhaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa comprises 116 adhyāyas.

The Revākhaṇḍa is a purāṇic text in 232 chapters glorifying the Narmadā (Revā) river, its sacred places (such as Amarakaṇṭaka and Bhṛgukaccha), and associated rites and legends.

## GRETIL header

**Edition:** Śrīkṛṣṇadās, Kṣemrāj (ed.): Śrīskandamahāpurāṇam. Veṅkateśvara Steam Press, Bombay: 1910. and its reprint: Siṃha, Nāgaśaraṇa (ed.): Śrīskandamahāpurāṇam. pañcama bhāga: śrī āvantyakhaṇḍam. Nag Publishers, Delhi: 1986. Input and proof-reading by Juergen Neuss, Freie Universitaet Berlin.

**Corrections by:** Proof-reading and corrections by Oliver Hellwig, Freie Universitaet Berlin. NOTE BY THE CONTRIBUTOR: The text has been wrongly assigned in the Veṅkateśvara edition (and subsequently) to the Skandapurāṇa (i.e. SkP 5.3.); all available manuscriptual evidence, however, proves that the text was instead originally part of the Vāyupurāṇa. Nevertheless in the following text, the original colophones referring to the Skandapurāṇa have been retained. There is a Revākhaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa too, which, however, comprises 116 adhyāyas only. That text is almost forgotten; I have also contributed an electronic version of that text to GRETIL. (For further information on this group of texts, please contact the contributor at jneuss@arcor.de.)

**Evidence:**
- Explicit statement in the GRETIL header: 'Based on the ed. by K. K. Dixit, Ahmedabad : Lalbhai Dalpatbhai Bharatiya 1969 (L. D. Series, 22), Input by Yasunori Harada'

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete mūla text in 701 anuṣṭubh verses arranged across 11 stabakas (chapters). The electronic text also prefixes K. K. Dixit's Hindi table of contents (Viṣayasūcī) and preserves his section headers.

**Also known as:** Śāstravārttāsamuccaya

**Attribution:** A secure composition of the Śvetāmbara philosopher-monk Haribhadrasūri (c. 8th century CE). Haribhadra identifies himself by name in verse 699 (ācāryaharibhadreṇa śāstravārtāsamuccayam) and incorporates his customary sobriquet bhavaviraha in verse 700.

The Śāstravārtāsamuccaya ('Compendium of Philosophical Discourses') is a major 8th-century doxographical and polemical treatise in 701 anuṣṭubh verses across 11 chapters (stabakas) by the Śvetāmbara master Haribhadrasūri. The work presents a systematic survey and critique of non-Jain philosophical traditions, including Cārvāka materialism, theism (Īśvaravāda), Sāṃkhya dualism, Buddhist theories of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda) and idealism (vijñānavāda/śūnyavāda), Advaita monism, and Mīmāṃsā rejections of omniscience. Haribhadra examines each perspective critically while adhering to the Jain framework of non-one-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) and concludes with an exposition of the nature of omniscience and spiritual liberation.

The Bījanighaṇṭu (also termed Mantrakośa) is a tantric glossary in 87 verses containing cryptic names and esoteric designations for Sanskrit phonemes and mantric seed-syllables (bījas). Presented as a revelation spoken by Śiva and claiming derivation from the Bhūtaḍāmara and Yakṣaḍāmaratantra traditions, it supplies deity epithets and elemental associations for individual letters as well as composite syllables (such as śrīṃ, hrīṃ, krīṃ, and klīṃ). The work serves as a practical decoding key for reconstructing esoteric mantras (mantroddhāra) embedded in tantric ritual texts.

The Bhāvopahārastotra (or Bhāvopahāra, 'The Offering of Mental States') is a 47-verse non-dual devotional hymn to Śiva attributed to the Kashmirian master Cakrapāṇinātha (c. 11th–12th century), associated with the Krama and Trika traditions of Kashmir Śaivism. The stotra allegorically reinterprets the sequential ritual offerings of traditional pūjā—such as the bath, seat, arghya, incense, light, bell, and dakṣiṇā—into internal meditative processes, offering subjective cognitive states, perceptions, and vital breath as oblation to the supreme divine Consciousness. The Gorakṣaśataka is a foundational Sanskrit manual of Haṭhayoga attributed to Gorakṣanātha. This particular recension, recorded in Briggs (1938), consists of 101 verses describing postures (specifically siddhāsana and padmāsana), the subtle channels and energy centers (nāḍīs and cakras), kuṇḍalinī, and breath regulation (prāṇāyāma and nāḍīśodhana).

## Contents

**Attribution:** A regional Purāṇic sthalamāhātmya purporting to belong to a larger lost work, the Uttara-Pauṇḍra-khaṇḍa. The closing colophon attributes composition to Paraśurāma (paraśurāmaviracitam), framed within a dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka recounting an interlocution between Śiva and Pārvatī. The historical author is anonymous.

The Karatoyāmāhātmya is an early medieval regional sthalamāhātmya in 85 verses extolling the sacred Karatoyā river and the holy precinct of Pauṇḍravardhana (modern Mahasthangarh, Bogra District, Bangladesh). Set as a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī reported by Sūta to the sages, the text relates the mythic origin of the Karatoyā from the water poured onto Śiva's hands during his marriage to Pārvatī and surveys the holy bathing places, shrines, and lingas established by Paraśurāma in Pauṇḍrakṣetra. Verses from the text are cited in medieval dharmaśāstra and lexical commentaries as early as Sarvānanda's Ṭīkāsarvasva (1159 CE) and Devaṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā, confirming its currency in the twelfth century.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains the text of all three chapters (unmeṣas) following the recension of Kṣemarāja, each sūtra embedded within Varadarāja's versified vārttika commentary (concluding at SivSV 3.45:19).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Śivasūtra (Vasugupta, root text)
- Śivasūtravārttika (Varadarāja, commentary)

**Also known as:** Śivasūtravārtika, Śivasūtravārttika of Varadarāja, Śivasūtravārttika of Kṛṣṇadāsa, Shiva Sutra Vartika

**Attribution:** The Śivasūtra is the foundational text of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism (Trika), traditionally revealed to Vasugupta (c. 9th cent.). The Śivasūtravārttika is a metrical commentary in anuṣṭubh verses composed by Varadarāja (who also refers to himself as Kṛṣṇadāsa). In the concluding verses (3.45:17), the author explicitly notes that his commentary follows the interpretative path established in Kṣemarāja.

The Śivasūtra is the foundational revealed text of the non-dual Kashmiri Trika school, outlining the nature of supreme consciousness and the three successive means (upāyas)—śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava—by which the bound soul realizes its inherent identity with Śiva. This e-text pairs the root sūtras with the Śivasūtravārttika of Varadarāja (alias Kṛṣṇadāsa), a verse exposition that versifies and condenses the classic prose interpretation provided in Kṣemarāja's Śivasūtravimarśinī. Through accessible anuṣṭubh verses, Varadarāja systematically elucidates the metaphysical definitions of bondage, the dynamics of divine energy (spanda/mātṛkā), and yogic integration.

The Śivopaniṣad is an early medieval Śaiva treatise in seven chapters (adhyāyas) belonging to the eight-text Śivadharma corpus, preserved predominantly in Nepalese manuscripts. Framed as a dialogue between Mahākāla and the sage Ātreya, it outlines a path of liberation tailored for lay devotees, expounding the triadic ontology of paśu, pāśa, and pati/śiva, the recitation and power of the two-syllable name Śiva, external ritual and internal worship (mānasapūjā), yoga, and righteous conduct (śivācāra). ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the root verses (kārikās 1–322) of the Ratnatrayaparīkṣā. The prose commentary by Aghoraśiva (the Ullekhinī), printed alongside the kārikās in the source edition, was not keyed.

**Attribution:** The Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta scholar Śrīkaṇṭhasūri identifies himself in the concluding verse (v. 322: 'ratnatrayaparīkṣārthaḥ saṃkṣepeṇa prakāśitaḥ') and mentions his reliance on Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (vv. 321–322: 'rāmakaṇṭhakṛtālokanirmalīkṛtacetasā ... śrīrāmakaṇṭhasadvṛttiṃ mayaivamanukurvatā'). He is generally dated to the late 10th or 11th century CE.

The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is an influential 10th–11th-century Sanskrit doctrinal treatise in 322 verses by the Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta scholar Śrīkaṇṭhasūri. Instead of examining the school's general ontological triad (pati, paśu, and pāśa), the work focuses specifically on the 'three jewels' defined as bindu (the material cause of pure sound, language, and the pure universe), śakti (the conscious power of the Lord), and śiva (the supreme agent and consciousness). Drawing heavily on earlier Kashmirian exegesis (especially Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha), it provides a detailed metaphysical exposition of the pure path (śuddhādhvan), phonematic cosmogony, and soteriological initiation.

Framed as a dialogue between the sage Aṣṭāvakra and King Janaka of Videha, the text expounds an uncompromising, radical non-dualism (kevalādvaita) close to ajātavāda: the Self is pure, unattached witnessing consciousness (sākṣin), and liberation consists in the immediate recognition of one's innate freedom rather than the fruit of ritual action, meditation, or moral striving.

The Prakīrṇādhikāra is a foundational canonical manual belonging to the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava Āgama tradition, attributed to the sage Bhṛgu as part of the Bhṛgusaṃhitā. Arranged in 37 chapters (comprising roughly 6,000 verses), the work focuses on temple ritual praxis (kriyāpāda), expounding architectural and ground testing (bhūparīkṣā), iconography, image installation (pratiṣṭhā) of Viṣṇu and attendant deities, ceremonial processions and festivals (utsavas), and extensive expiatory procedures (prāyaścitta/niṣkṛti) for ritual deviations. ## Contents

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** Not determined.

**E-text:** Data entry by n.n.; initial normalization and conversion to legacy GRETIL formats by Reinhold Grünendahl; normalization and conversion to TEI by Maximilian Mehner.

**Evidence:**

- ilx_skt TEI header (gretil_sa/sa_bhaktivinoda-harinAmacintAmaNi.xml): data entry n.n., no source edition.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Paricchedas 1–15 complete to the final colophon (iti śrī-hari-nāma-cintāmaṇau bhajana-praṇālī-pradarśanaṃ nāma pañcadaśaḥ paricchedaḥ, HNC_15.115), except a lacuna of verses in pariccheda 11 (HNC 11.2–11.25), as flagged in the GRETIL header.

**Also known as:** Śrī Harināma-cintāmaṇi, Hari-nāma-cintāmaṇi

**Attribution:** Composed by Kedāranātha Datta, also known as Bhaktivinoda (1838–1914).

Structured as an extended theological dialogue at Jagannātha Purī between Caitanya Mahāprabhu and Haridāsa Ṭhākura. Across fifteen chapters, it provides a comprehensive manual on the theology and contemplative practice of chanting the holy name of Kṛṣṇa (harināma). The treatise details offenses against the holy name (nāmāparādha), semblance chanting (nāmābhāsa), pure devotional chanting, and a meditative progression (bhajana-praṇālī).

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** not determined

**E-text:** Input by ...; normalized and converted for GRETIL by Reinhold Grünendahl, converted to TEI by Maximilian Mehner.

**Evidence:**
- The header records: '[Jiva refers to this book as Kṛṣṇārcana-dīpikā in Brahma-saṃhitā commentary (verse 4).] Input by ...'

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Text in mixed prose and verse, concluding with the author's colophon followed by scribal/editorial cross-references.

**Also known as:** Kṛṣṇārcanadīpikā

**Attribution:** Firmly attributed to Jīva Gosvāmin in the colophon ('iti śrī-vṛndāvana-vāsinaḥ kasyacij jīvasya śrī-rādhā-kṛṣṇārcana-dīpikā...') and opening verse with invocation of Sanātana and Rūpa Gosvāmin. Jīva also refers to this work under the variant title Kṛṣṇārcanadīpikā in his commentary on Brahma-saṃhitā (verse 4).

The Rādhākṛṣṇārcanadīpikā ('Lamp Illuminating the Worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa') is a theological and ritual treatise in mixed prose and verse composed by Jīva Gosvāmin. It establishes the doctrinal justification for the paired worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa (specifically in the form of Rādhā-Dāmodara), drawing extensively on Purāṇic, Tantric, and Smṛti proof texts. Jīva argues that true worship of Bhagavān necessitates the worship of His devotees, establishes the gopīs as His foremost devotees, and demonstrates that Rādhā must be worshipped alongside Him.

# Kramadīpikā with Vivaraṇa

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GR14_krdipc_u`

**Author:** Keśava Kāśmīrī, Govindabhaṭṭācārya

**Collection / category:** Rellit / GR14 (GR14 Vaiṣṇava)

**Source:** GRETIL (Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages)

**Link:** [https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil/1_sanskr/4_rellit/vaisn/krdipc_u.htm](https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil/1_sanskr/4_rellit/vaisn/krdipc_u.htm)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Sudhākara Mālavīya (ed.), Kramadīpikā with the commentary by Govindabhaṭṭācārya, Benares: Krishnadas Academy, 1989 (Krishnadas Sanskrit Series, 119).

**E-text:** Jan Brzezinski for GRETIL

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL and TEI headers explicitly state: 'Based on the edition by Sudhakar Malaviya, Benares : Krishnadas Academy, 1989, (Krishnadas Sanskrit Series, 119). Input by Jan Brzezinski.'
- The introductory title line in segment 2 mirrors the title page of the 1989 edition: 'krama-dīpikā śrīmad-bhagavat-śrī-kṛṣṇārādhana-nirūpaṇa-pravaṇa āgama-nibandhaḥ vidyā-vinoda-śrī-govinda-bhaṭṭācārya-kṛta-vivaraṇa-sahitā'.

**Other editions:**
- Kramadīpikā, with the commentary by Govinda Bhatta, and with further commentaries called Gurubhaktimandākinī and a laudatory hymn Laghustavarājastotra, Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series. — Published together with Śrīnivāsācārya's Laghustavarājastotra and Puruṣottamaprasāda's Gurubhaktimandākinī.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all eight paṭalas of both the root Kramadīpikā and Govindabhaṭṭācārya's Vivaraṇa commentary.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kramadīpikā (Keśava Kāśmīrī, root text)
- Vivaraṇa (Govindabhaṭṭācārya, commentary)

**Also known as:** Kramadīpikāvivaraṇa

**Attribution:** The root manual is authored by Keśava Kāśmīrī, designated in the colophons as Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrī-Keśava-Kāśmīri-Bhaṭṭa-Gosvāmin. The commentary Vivaraṇa is by Vidyāvinoda Govindabhaṭṭācārya.

The Kramadīpikā is an eight-chapter Vaiṣṇava ritual and mantra manual (āgamanibandha) focused on the worship of Kṛṣṇa Gopāla, composed by Keśava Kāśmīrī. It expounds mantras (including the ten-syllable Gopāla mantra), daily worship, nyāsas, mudrās, and homa rites, accompanied in this e-text by Govindabhaṭṭācārya's commentary, the Vivaraṇa.

**Entered by:** Jan Brzezinski

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Prosimetric campū text, concluding with verses mentioning Rūpa, Jīva, and Kṛṣṇa-kavi-bhūpati.

**Also known as:** Muktācaritra, Muktā-caritram

**Attribution:** Attributed to Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī. The work concludes with verses dedicating the poem to Rūpa Gosvāmī, mentioning Jīva Gosvāmī, and expressing affection for Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja ('kṛṣṇa-kavi-bhūpati').

The Muktācarita ('The Tale of the Pearl') is a campū-kāvya combining Sanskrit prose and verse, composed by Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī. Framed as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and his queen Satyabhāmā in Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa recounts an incident from his youth in Vraja during the Dīpāvalī festival: when the gopīs refuse to give him pearls to ornament his beloved cows, Kṛṣṇa plants pearls in the earth and harvests bountiful pearl creepers, whereas the envious gopīs sow pearls with milk and butter but reap only thorny bushes. The work focuses on the witty banter, mock disputes, and commercial bargaining over the jewels between Kṛṣṇa, Subala, Madhumaṅgala, Rādhā, and Lalitā, illustrating the intimate erotic-devotional theology (mādhura-līlā) of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.

- Closing lines: 'Thank you for using a Gaudiya Grantha Mandir text. Remember, GGM is an open source network... Thank you, The Editors.'

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the root work (kārikās, prose introductions, and illustrative verses) across all four divisions (vibhāgas: pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara) and their component laharīs, concluding with the author's final stanzas and scribal/editorial colophon.

**Also known as:** Haribhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu

**Attribution:** Universally accepted as the work of Rūpa Gosvāmin.

The Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa'), composed by Rūpa Gosvāmin, is the foundational work of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology and aesthetics. Adapting the classical rasa theory of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and medieval alaṃkāraśāstra, Rūpa establishes devotion (bhakti) directed toward Kṛṣṇa not merely as a bhāva (transient emotional state), but as the supreme aesthetic and ontological sentiment (bhakti-rasa). Organised in four quadrants (pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara vibhāgas), the text comprehensively systematises the categories of devotional practice (sādhana, bhāva, prema), the constituent components of aesthetic emotion (vibhāva, anubhāva, sāttvikabhāva, vyabhicāribhāva), the primary rasas (śānta, dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya, madhura), and the secondary devotional sentiments along with discordant mixtures (rasābhāsa).

**Also known as:** Bhagavatsandarbha, Śrībhagavatsandarbha, Bhagavat-sandarbha, Ṣaṭsandarbha: 2. Bhagavatsamdarbha

**Attribution:** In the opening verses (vv. 2–3), Jīva Gosvāmī notes that he is re-organizing and completing an initial draft sketched by Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī ('dākṣiṇātyena bhaṭṭena pnuar etad vivicyate / tasyādyaṃ granthanālekhaṃ krāntam utkrānta-khaṇḍitam / paryālocyātha paryāyaṃ kṛtvā likhati jīvakaḥ').

The Bhagavatsandarbha is the second treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's foundational 16th-century theological work, the Ṣaṭsandarbha (or Bhāgavatasandarbha). Centering its inquiry around the tripartite definition of Absolute Reality in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.11 (brahmeti paramātmeti bhagavān iti śabdyate), the work establishes that Bhagavān—the supreme personal God possessed of all potencies—is the highest and most complete manifestation of Non-dual Consciousness (advaya-jñāna), whereas impersonal Brahman is an unmanifest, partial revelation. Across 118 anucchedas, Jīva details the intrinsic divine potency (svarūpa-śakti) with its threefold aspects of sandhinī (existence), saṃvit (knowledge), and hlādinī (bliss), expounds the trans-material nature of the divine realm (viśuddha-sattva), and defends the eternity of the Lord's transcendent anthropomorphic form (vigraha), abode (dhāman), and associates (parikara).

The Paramātmasandarbha is the third treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's sixfold Bhāgavatasandarbha, expounding the sambandha-jñāna (metaphysical ontology) of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism on the basis of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. Through detailed Purāṇic and Upaniṣadic exegesis, Jīva refutes Kevalādvaita monism and articulates the foundational tenets of the Gauḍīya acintyabhedābheda doctrine.

The Kṛṣṇasandarbha is the fourth treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's masterwork, the Ṣaṭsandarbha (or Bhāgavatasandarbha), composed in 16th-century Vrindavan. Serving as the primary theological defense of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ontology, the text systematically argues on the basis of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (particularly 1.3.28: 'kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam') that Kṛṣṇa is not merely an avatāra of Viṣṇu, but the ultimate and complete Godhead (Svayaṃ Bhagavān). ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text containing all 27 kārikās of the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi together with Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī's Vṛtti, concluding with Harabhaṭṭa's verse, the colophon, and Madhusūdan Kaul Śāstrī's editorial verse.

**Also known as:** Pramātṛsiddhi

**Attribution:** The root text consists of 27 kārikās by Utpaladeva, forming part of his Siddhitrayī. Utpaladeva's original auto-commentary being lost, the short Sanskrit Vṛtti accompanying the verses was composed in Śāka 1841 by the Kashmiri scholar Paṇḍit Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī, as recorded in the concluding verse (candrābdhyaṣṭenduśākābde śāstrī vṛttiṃ haro vyadhāt).

The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In 27 kārikās, Utpaladeva argues against Buddhist momentariness and static Vedāntic consciousness, maintaining that both cognition and practical causal efficacy (arthakriyā) require an active, self-reflective subject (vimarśa, ahaṃbhāva) rather than an insentient (jaḍa) continuum. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in Śāka 1841 by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

The Viṣṇudharma is an early Vaiṣṇava devotional and ritual handbook of approximately 4,200 verses in 105 chapters, generally dated to the 3rd–5th century CE. Framed as an exposition given by the sage Śaunaka to King Śatānīka, it instructs householders and lay devotees on the worship, liturgy, mental contemplation, vrata observances, and festivals dedicated to Viṣṇu. It represents one of the foundational texts of early non-sectarian Vaiṣṇavism, serving as a direct predecessor to the larger encyclopedic Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa and functioning alongside the roughly contemporary Śivadharmaśāstra as a crucial witness to early medieval devotional religion.

The Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā is a canonical Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava Āgama comprising 39 chapters and around 2,800 verses, named after Viṣvaksena, the celestial marshal and gatekeeper of Viṣṇu. The Vyākaraṇamahābhāṣya ('Great Commentary on Grammar') by Patañjali is the foundational exegetical and theoretical masterwork of the Pāṇinian school of Sanskrit grammar (vyākaraṇa). Composed in the form of a lively, dialectical dialogue across 85 daily lessons (āhnikas), it comments on 1,228 sūtras of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, critically assessing the critical glosses (Vārttikas) of Kātyāyana. The text addresses fundamental questions of syntax, morphology, phonetics, semantics, ontology, and the philosophy of language, establishing the definitive doctrinal standard of the Pāṇinian 'trimuni' (three sages) tradition.

The Laghusiddhāntakaumudī is an essential introductory primer of Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammar composed by Varadarāja in the seventeenth century. It condenses the comprehensive Siddhāntakaumudī of his teacher Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita into 1,279 select sūtras from Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, reorganized according to a topical, derivation-focused order (prakriyā) rather than the sequential order of the eight adhyāyas. Accompanied by Varadarāja's concise explanatory commentary (vṛtti) and standard grammatical derivations, the work has served for centuries as the primary pedagogical manual in traditional pāṭhaśālās and modern academic institutions.

Adyar Library Series 101. Madras: Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1971–1983. — South Indian commentaries.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete first kāṇḍa, spanning introductory verses 1.0.1–1.0.10 (maṅgalācaraṇa, prastāvanā, paribhāṣā), all ten vargas (svarga, vyoma, diś, kāla, dhī, śabda, nāṭya, pātālabhogi, naraka, vāri), and concluding summary verses 1.11.605–1.11.608.

**Also known as:** Amarakoṣa, Amarakośa

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Buddhist lexicographer Amarasiṃha (c. 6th century CE).

The Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (universally known as the Amarakoṣa) is classical India's most celebrated Sanskrit synonym dictionary and thesaurus, composed in śloka metre by the Buddhist lexicographer Amarasiṃha. This file contains the complete first division, which arranges nominal vocabulary conceptually into thematic sections (vargas): deities and heaven (svarga), sky and celestial bodies (vyoman), spatial directions (diś), time and seasons (kāla), intellect and mental states (dhī), speech and sound (śabda), theatre and musical performance (nāṭya), the subterranean realm and serpents (pātāla), hell (naraka), and water and aquatic flora (vāri). Alongside synonyms, the text systematically teaches grammatical gender (liṅgānuśāsana) through context, syntactic gender markers, and explicit exclusion rules.

The Tattvopaplavasiṃha ('The Lion that Devours all Principles/Categories') is a philosophical treatise of radical epistemological skepticism composed by Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa in the 8th or 9th century CE. Affiliated with the tradition of Bṛhaspati / Cārvāka, Jayarāśi turns dialectical reasoning against accepted instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇas)—including perception and inference—arguing against established principles/categories (tattvas).

**Translations:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete root text comprising 115 verses (numbered SAm_1–SAm_115).

**Also known as:** Devāgamastotra, Devāgama

**Attribution:** Attributed to Samantabhadra.

The Āptamīmāṃsā ('Critique of the Trustworthy Authority'), also known as the Devāgamastotra after its opening words, is a philosophical treatise by Samantabhadra. Beginning as a theological inquiry into what qualifies an individual as a truly omniscient, authoritative teacher (āpta), it establishes that miracles and external divine manifestations cannot establish authority; rather, true authority belongs only to one who has eradicated internal passions and whose teachings cannot be invalidated by reason or experience. Samantabhadra applies the sevenfold conditional predication (syādvāda / saptabhaṅgī) and many-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) to refute one-sided (ekānta) philosophical positions across rival Indian traditions, creating the dialectical framework that shaped subsequent Jain logic.

**Attribution:** Attributed to Vātsyāyana. Although the printed source edition includes Yaśodhara's Jayamaṅgalā commentary, only the root sūtras and concluding verses of Vātsyāyana were transcribed in this electronic text.

The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāma (erotic desire, pleasure, and aesthetic enjoyment), one of the traditional goals of human life (puruṣārtha). Divided into seven adhikaraṇas, the text surveys general principles of life, sexual union, courtship and marriage, the domestic conduct of wives, extramarital affairs, courtesans, and erotic/aphrodisiac recipes. Beyond physical intimacy, the work presents a detailed manual on urban sociology and the cultured lifestyle of the sophisticated citizen (nāgaraka), serving as the canonical source for all subsequent Indian erotic literature.

The Rasahṛdayatantra ('Heart of Mercury'), composed in 19 avabodhas (chapters) in āryā metre by Bhikṣu Govinda (Govindabhagavatpāda, c. 10th century CE), is the earliest surviving systematic treatise of the Sanskrit alchemical tradition (rasaśāstra). ## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Kalyāṇakārakam of Ugrādityācārya, ed./tr. Vardhaman Parshwanath Shastri, Sholapur: Seth Govindji Raoji Doshi, 1940 (Sakhārāma Nemacaṃda Digambara Jaina Graṃthamālā / SNGM 129).

**E-text:** Dharmamitra OCR

**Evidence:**
- Matches the 1940 Sholapur edition edited/translated by Vardhaman Parshwanath Shastri recorded in the source header and cited as SNGM 129 in EDSHP.
- Retains recurring 'bhāvārthaḥ' section headings and editorial variant notes ('... iti pāṭhāṃtaraṃ').
- Concludes at verse 38 of the Ariṣṭanirūpaṇa supplement ('iti jinabaktranirgatasuśāstramahāṃbunidheḥ...').

**Translations:**
- Vardhaman Parshwanath Shastri, Hindi translation accompanying the Sanskrit text in the 1940 Sholapur edition (Sakhārāma Nemacaṃda Digambara Jaina Graṃthamālā 129). (Hindi)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 25 chapters (paricchedas), comprising the Mūlatantra / Cikitsādhikāra (chapters 1–20) and the Uttaratantra (chapters 21–25), followed by the concluding supplementary section on death prognostication (Ariṣṭanirūpaṇa) and the author's final colophon verses.

**Also known as:** Kalyāṇakārakam

**Attribution:** Attributed to Ugrāditya. The work is placed around the 9th century CE (c. 825–875 CE in EDSHP; statistical model posterior median 811 CE).

The Kalyāṇakāraka is a comprehensive 9th-century Sanskrit Ayurvedic treatise composed by the Digambara Jain monk Ugrāditya. Divided into 25 chapters across two main divisions—the Mūlatantra (chapters 1–20) and Uttaratantra (chapters 21–25)—along with a concluding section on the prognostication of fatal signs (Ariṣṭanirūpaṇa), it is among the earliest surviving Indian medical compendia to detail the chemical purification (śodhana) and incineration (māraṇa) of mercury and other minerals for therapeutic formulations. Consistently framed within Jain ethics of non-harm (ahiṃsā), the work prohibits meat, alcohol, and honey in pharmacological treatments, replacing them with herbal and mineral substitutes while harmonising classical Ayurvedic eight-fold medicine with Jain doctrinal philosophy.

The Rasaprakāśasudhākara is a major 13-chapter Sanskrit treatise on alchemy and iatrochemistry (rasaśāstra), composed by Yaśodhara Bhaṭṭa in Saurashtra (Gujarat). It describes the origins, grades, and eighteen purification and transmutational processes (aṣṭādaśa-saṃskāra) of mercury, followed by treatments of primary and secondary minerals (mahārasas and uparasas), metals, gemstones, and apparatus (yantras, crucibles). The text holds an important position in the history of Indian chemistry for offering one of the earliest explicit accounts of zinc (yaśada/rasaka-sattva) distillation extraction and for key iatrochemical formulations such as Somanāthī tāmrabhasma and calomel (karpūrarasa).

Arranged into 106 chapters and comprising nearly 4,000 stanzas, it serves as an encyclopaedia of classical Indian material and ritual life, treating topics such as planetary movements, eclipses, meteorology, ground water and rainfall, temple and residential architecture (vāstuvidyā), iconometry (pratimālakṣaṇa), gemmology (ratnaparīkṣā), perfumery (gandhayukti), agriculture, and physiognomy. It is an indispensable primary source for the history of science, material culture, and religious society in Gupta-era India.

Verses 2 and 29 explicitly invoke Lagadha ('kālajñānaṃ pravakṣyāmi lagadhasya mahātmanaḥ' and 'vyākhyānaṃ lagadho 'bravīt'), indicating that the text is framed as an exposition of Lagadha's teachings, possibly redacted by a disciple (identified by some scholars as Śuci, named in verse 1).

The Ṛgvedavedāṅgajyotiṣa (also known as Ārcajyotiṣa) is the Ṛgvedic recension of the Vedāṅgajyotiṣa, the earliest surviving Indian text on mathematical astronomy and calendrical calculation, traditionally attributed to Lagadha. In 35 concise anuṣṭubh verses, it lays out a lunisolar calendar designed to determine the precise times for Vedic sacrifices, based on a five-year yuga consisting of 62 synodic months (including two intercalary months) and 1,830 civil days. The text details the coordinate system of 27 nakṣatras with their presiding deities, the positions of the solstices and equinoxes, rules for calculating tithis and nakṣatra portions, and seasonal variations in daytime length measurable by a water-clock (clepsydra).

The Nāradasmṛti is a classical Dharmaśāstra treatise uniquely devoted almost entirely to legal procedure and substantive law (vyavahāra), omitting the standard sections on customary conduct (ācāra) and expiation (prāyaścitta). It opens with an introductory section (mātṛkā) on the administration of justice, courts, plaint procedure, and evidence, followed by twenty chapters treating the eighteen traditional titles of law (vyavahārapadas) as well as theft and divine ordeals (divya). Dating to approximately the 5th–6th century CE, the work is notable for its sophisticated treatment of judicial evidence, contract law, and debt recovery, and for explicitly subordinating customary usage to royal edicts (rājaśāsana) in judicial disputes.

**Also known as:** Parāśarasmṛti, Pārāśaradharmasaṃhitā

The Parāśaradharmasaṃhitā (or Parāśarasmṛti) is an influential classical Dharmaśāstra text canonical for its claim to define the yugadharma specifically designated for the Kali age (Kalau Pārāśarāḥ smṛtāḥ, 1.24). Comprising 592 anuṣṭubh verses organized into 12 chapters, it expounds rules of customary conduct and purity (ācāra, chs. 1–11) and rites of expiation (prāyaścitta, ch. 12). The treatise is notable for introducing pragmatic modifications to classical law tailored to the diminished moral capacity of the Kali age, such as permitting agriculture to twice-born householders and outlining conditions for the remarriage of women. It does not contain an internal section on jurisprudence (vyavahāra), a lacuna that was famously supplemented in the 14th century by Mādhavācārya in his comprehensive commentary, the Parāśaramādhavīya.

The Mitākṣarā by the twelfth-century Sanskrit author Vijñāneśvara is a commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti (Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra). Its subject is dharma, legal and religious duty, encompassing ācāra, vyavahāra, and prāyaścitta. One regular change from the NSP is that Vijñāneśvara almost always has an introduction to each verse. Most often this consists of a substantive sentence. But frequently, the introduction consists of two brief introductions: kiṃ ca , api ca , and infrequently tathā ca . NSP and Pāṇḍeya place these in the commentary after the verse. This is an error. You will find that these are found only when there is no substantive introduction. Setlur is the only one who understood this; he places these connective phrases before the verse. So do I. The Mitākṣarā by Vijñāneśvara is an exhaustive running commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti and stands among the most influential works of Hindu legal literature. Spanning all three divisions of the smṛti—customary conduct (ācāra), judicial procedure and substantive law (vyavāhara), and penance (prāyaścitta)—the work harmonizes conflicting smṛti authorities using sophisticated Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles. The Mīmāṃsāsūtra (or Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra), traditionally attributed to Jaimini, is the foundational text of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā darśana. Arranged into twelve books (adhyāyas), hence known as the Dvādaśalakṣaṇī, the aphorisms formulate the rules of interpretation (nyāya) for the ritual injunctions (vidhi) of the Vedic corpus. The work provides systematic epistemological arguments for the intrinsicality of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya) and the eternality of language and the Veda, establishing hermeneutic canons that deeply influenced Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta, and Indian legal interpretation.

Adhyāya 3 of Mādhava's Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara, a metrical exposition and prose auto-commentary on the topical sections (adhikaraṇas) of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. In fifty verses, Śālikanātha argues for the intrinsic capacity of verbal communication—specifically Vedic revelation—to yield true knowledge of external facts (arthasaṃsparśitā). Nayavīthī ('The Path of Reasoning') is the third prakaraṇa of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, a foundational 9th-century treatise of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Composed entirely in 77 kārikās, this chapter articulates and defends the distinctive Prābhākara thesis that all cognitions are intrinsically veridical (sarvavijñānayathārthatva). Śālikanātha expounds the Prābhākara non-apprehension theory of error (akhyāti), arguing that experiential illusions (such as mistaking mother-of-pearl for silver) do not constitute a single mistaken cognition (anyathākhyāti), but rather two distinct mental episodes—an incomplete perceptual apprehension and a memory stripped of its temporal reference (smṛtipramoṣa)—whose difference goes unnoticed due to non-discrimination (vivekāgraha).

Prakaraṇa 4 of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, titled Jātinirṇaya ('Determination of Universals'), presents the Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā defense of realist ontology regarding universals (jāti / sāmānya). Śālikanātha systematically refutes Buddhist nominalism and the apoha doctrine, as well as the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and bhedābheda positions, establishing that a universal is real, ontologically distinct from its individual substrate (āśrayato bhinnā), and directly apprehended through recurrent perceptual cognition (anuvṛttākārāvabhāsinī buddhi).

Amṛtakalā ('The Digit of Nectar') is the fifth chapter of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, composed in 76 kārikās. It offers a concise metrical compendium of Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā epistemology, defining valid knowledge (pramāṇa) as apprehension distinct from memory (anubhūti) and defining the five pramāṇas admitted in the Prābhākara system: perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), scripture/verbal testimony (śāstra), comparison (upamāna), and presumption/postulation (arthāpatti). The chapter concludes with a systematic refutation of non-apprehension (anupalabdhi/abhāva) as an independent sixth pramāṇa, defending the Prābhākara doctrine that absence is identical with the bare locus.

Prakaraṇa 13 of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, titled Aṅgapārāyaṇa ('Investigation of Auxiliary Elements'), presents the Prābhākara school's comprehensive doctrine on the nature, function, and taxonomy of ritual accessories (aṅga). This text comprises the opening epistemological section (Tarkapāda, sūtras 1.1.1–5) of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra with the commentary of Śabarasvāmin (Śābarabhāṣya). **Attribution:** Pārthasārathi Miśra's authorship is confirmed by the opening maṅgala verse ('kumārilamatenāhaṃ kariṣye śāstradīpikām') and universal tradition in the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā school.

The Śāstradīpikā of Pārthasārathi Miśra (fl. c. late 11th century CE) is a major classical commentary on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra adhering strictly to the Bhāṭṭa school of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa. Its introductory section, the Tarkapāda (Adhyāya 1, Pāda 1), constitutes one of the foundational works of Mīmāṃsā epistemology and metaphysics, defending the intrinsic validity of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya), perception, realism concerning universals, and the eternal, uncreated nature of sound and the Vedas against Buddhist, Nyāya, and Advaita opponents. This file contains the Sanskrit text of the Tarkapāda from sūtras 1.1.1 to 1.1.23, ending at the conclusion of the section on the eternality of language (śabdanityatā).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the monograph spanning pages 1 to 76 in the printed edition, beginning with 'prayojanam uddiśyaiva' and terminating with the final colophon 'iti śrīmahāmahopādhyāyagadādharabhaṭṭācāryakṛtamuktivādaḥ samāptaḥ'.

The Muktivāda is an analytical Navya-Nyāya monograph composed by Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya investigating the soteriological concept of liberation (mukti / apavarga). Applying the school's precise formal definitions, Gadādhara demonstrates that liberation is fundamentally the absolute, permanent cessation of suffering (ātyantikaduḥkhanivṛtti) rather than experiential positive bliss. He critically refutes alternative doctrines from Advaita Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā, deliberates on whether the direct cause of release is self-knowledge (ātmatattvajñāna) or divine apprehension (paramātmasākṣātkāra), and assesses the causal role of ritual actions and auspicious death in holy places like Vārāṇasī.

The Nyāyabhūṣaṇa ('Ornament of Nyāya') is Bhāsarvajña's extensive auto-commentary (saṅgrahavārttika) on his concise epistemological treatise, the Nyāyasāra. Structured across three chapters according to the three pramāṇas accepted by the author (perception, inference, and verbal testimony), the work introduces several heterodox positions within Nyāya, including the rejection of comparison (upamāna) as a distinct means of knowledge and the assertion that final liberation involves the positive experience of eternal bliss (nityasukhasaṃvedana). The treatise is a primary source for philosophical controversies, featuring extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists as well as Cārvāka skeptics and rival Brahmanical systems.

**Attribution:** The root work Nyāyāvatāra was traditionally ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara. Modern scholarship distinguishes a logician Siddhasena Mahāmati who composed the Nyāyāvatāra. The commentary Nyāyāvatāravivṛti was authored by Siddharṣigaṇin. Note that while the opening mentions Devabhadrasūri's Ṭippana, this e-text contains only the Vivṛti.

The Nyāyāvatāra is a concise 32-verse Jain treatise on epistemology and logic (pramāṇaśāstra) treating perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), verbal testimony, internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), and the doctrine of perspectives (naya) in the context of anekāntavāda. Historically ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara, the text is also attributed to Siddhasena Mahāmati, who engaged systematically with Buddhist logic. Siddharṣigaṇin's commentary, the Nyāyāvatāravivṛti, provides an exposition of each verse, defending Jain epistemological positions against rival objections.

The third stabaka of Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali addresses the third major counter-position (vipratipatti), namely the contention of opponent schools (especially Mīmāṃsā and Buddhism) that there exist valid counter-proofs (bādhaka-pramāṇa) disproving God's existence. Udayana demonstrates that non-perception (anupalabdhi) only negates entities that are by nature perceptible (yogya), and cannot disprove an inherently supersensible (atīndriya) Lord. In the course of the chapter, Udayana defends the existence of an imperceptible self and mind, and systematically analyzes all recognized means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)—perception, inference, analogy, testimony, presumption, and absence—to prove that none constitutes an obstacle to the establishment of Īśvara.

**Also known as:** Kusumāñjali

**Attribution:** A work of Udayana.

The fourth chapter (Stavaka 4) of Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali refutes the Mīmāṃsaka challenge against divine omniscience. The opponent contends that God's cognition cannot be an instrument or instance of valid knowledge (pramā) because valid cognition requires apprehending what was not previously known (anadhigatārthagantṛ), an impossibility for an eternal, all-encompassing intellect. Udayana rejects both the anadhigatārthatva criterion and the Bhāṭṭa epistemological theory of cognizedness (jñātatā), defending the Nyāya definition of pramā as true experiential cognition (yathārthānubhava) independent of extraneous sources, and proving that continuous cognition (dhārāvāhikajñāna) and divine eternal awareness (nitya-sākṣātkāra) constitute genuine pramā.

The Tarkatāṇḍava by Vyāsatīrtha, accompanied by Rāghavendratīrtha's commentary Nyāyadīpa, is an advanced dialectical classic of Dvaita Vedānta that critically examines Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika logic and epistemology (especially Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi and Udayana) using Navya-Nyāya methods. This second section (Pariccheda 2) focuses on verbal testimony (śabdapramāṇa) and ontological categories, analyzing the prerequisites of sentential comprehension (ākāṅkṣā, āsatti, yogyatā), defending potency (śakti) as an autonomous category against Naiyāyika reductionism, examining universals (jāti), and dissecting the nature and motive force of Vedic injunctions (vidhivāda).

The Anuttarāṣṭikā ('Eight Verses on the Supreme/Absolute') is a concise philosophical stotra in Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre composed by the Kashmir Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). **Attribution:** The root work consists of 105 verses composed by Abhinavagupta. The commentary (vivṛti), explicitly titled Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti in the closing colophon, was composed by Rājānaka Yogarāja, who identifies himself in the concluding verses as a disciple of Kṣemarāja.

The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Reality') is an introductory compendium of 105 āryā stanzas by the Kashmiri master Abhinavagupta, articulating the metaphysical and soteriological core of nondual Trika Śaivism. Adapted from an earlier Vaiṣṇava work attributed to Ādiśeṣa, the treatise outlines the emanation of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) through the playful self-expression (krīḍā) and sovereign freedom (svātantrya) of Śiva-consciousness, the contracted state of worldly bondage (saṃsāra), and liberation through self-recognition (pratyabhijñā). Yogarāja's vivṛti commentary expands Abhinavagupta's compressed verses into a systematic philosophical treatise, refuting Advaita Vedānta and Buddhist positions while clarifying the nondual Śaiva doctrine of divine grace (śaktipāta / anugrahaśakti).

The Bodhapañcadaśikā ('Fifteen Verses on Awakening') is a succinct didactic treatise composed by the Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). As indicated in its concluding verse, it was written to introduce disciples of gentle intellect (sukumāramati) to the foundational non-dual metaphysics of Trika Śaivism. The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of the Supreme Truth') is a concise philosophical compendium consisting of 105 verses composed in the late 10th or early 11th century CE by the polymath Abhinavagupta. It serves as an introductory summary of nondual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika and Pratyabhijñā), setting forth the emanation of cosmic reality across thirty-six tattvas structured into four spheres (aṇḍas), the soul's contraction through the impurities (malas) and limiting veils (kañcukas), and liberation through spontaneous recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's identity with Paramaśiva. The Bhairavānukaraṇastotra ('Hymn on the Assimilation to Bhairava') is a 48-verse non-dual Śaiva hymn composed by Kṣemarāja in āryā metre. The Spandakārikā is the primary doctrinal and meditative manual of the Spanda branch of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed in the 9th century CE and attributed either to the sage Vasugupta or his disciple Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the foundational and most authoritative classical treatise of the Sāṃkhya darśana. In approximately 72–73 āryā stanzas, it systematically expounds the dualistic metaphysics of unmanifest and manifest primordial nature (avyakta- and vyakta-prakṛti) alongside the multiplicity of pure conscious subjects (puruṣa). The text establishes the satkāryavāda theory of causation, analyzes the triad of guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas), charts the 25 evolutionary principles (tattvas) and psychological schema (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, indriyas, tanmātras, mahābhūtas), and teaches that discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti) dissolves the misidentification of consciousness with nature to achieve final isolation and liberation (kaivalya).

The Sāṃkhyasūtra (or Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra) is an aphoristic treatise in six adhyāyas articulating Sāṃkhya metaphysics, traditionally attributed to Kapila. The Sarvopakāriṇī ('The All-Benefiting Gloss') is a concise, anonymous Sanskrit commentary on the Tattvasamāsa (also called Samāsasūtra or Kāpilasūtra), an ancient mnemonic outline of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It comments systematically on the 22 sūtras of this recension, expounding the 25 principles (tattvas), the forward and reverse evolutions of the guṇas (sañcāra and pratisañcara), the three kinds of suffering, the sources of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the nature of liberation (mokṣa). Its opening lines preserve a notable scholastic tradition asserting that this 22-sūtra work represents the original seed of the system taught by Kapila as an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa, in contrast to the six-chapter Sāṃkhyasūtra composed by Kapila as an avatāra of Vaiśvānara.

The Tattvasamāsa ('Compendium of Principles') is a very brief mnemonic outline consisting of between 23 and 27 aphorisms (sūtras) that summarize the central ontological, cosmological, and psychological categories of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It lists the fundamental categories including the eight material causes (prakṛti), the sixteen evolutes (vikāra), the conscious subject (puruṣa), the three constituents (guṇa), cosmic evolution and dissolution, and the faculties and conditions governing bondage and release. Traditionally attributed to the mythic sage Kapila, the surviving text represents a medieval scholastic syllabus that served as the basis for several commentaries, such as those by Kṣemānanda, Bhāvāgaṇeśa, and the author of the Kramadīpikā.

The Sāṅkhyasāra is an independent philosophical manual (prakaraṇa) of the Sāṅkhya system composed by the 16th-century synthesizer Vijñānabhikṣu. Structured into two parts—a Pūrvabhāga of four paricchedas and an Uttarabhāga of seven paricchedas—it sets out the nature of liberation (puruṣārtha), discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti), the material evolutes (prakṛti and tattvas), puruṣa, and the essential distinctions between self and non-self. The work encapsulates the core positions elaborated in his larger Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya, harmonizing classic Sāṅkhya dualism with theistic elements and Pātañjala Yoga.

Only Praśastapāda's bhāṣya is keyed; Śrīdhara's accompanying commentary Nyāyakandalī in the printed edition is omitted.

**Also known as:** Praśastapādabhāṣya, Dravyādiṣaṭpadārthabhāṣya

**Attribution:** Praśastapāda (c. 6th century CE) composed the Padārthadharmasaṃgraha. Although traditionally termed a bhāṣya on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, it is an independent, foundational treatise of classical Vaiśeṣika ontology and epistemology rather than a line-by-line commentary.

The Padārthadharmasaṃgraha (commonly known as the Praśastapādabhāṣya) is the definitive classical treatise of the Vaiśeṣika philosophical school, composed by Praśastapāda (c. 6th century CE). Rather than providing a sūtra-by-sūtra commentary on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, the work organizes Vaiśeṣika ontology topically into six categories (padārthas: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya), articulating their shared and distinctive attributes. It systematically incorporates advanced epistemology, natural philosophy, and atomistic theory, establishing the standard framework commented upon by Vyomaśiva, Śrīdhara, and Udayana.

The Vaiśeṣikasūtra is the foundational treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school of classical Indian philosophy, traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. Organised into ten adhyāyas of two āhnikas each, it elaborates an atomistic and pluralistic realist ontology structured around fundamental categories (padārtha): substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), motion/action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya). The work investigates physical causation, the elementary constituents of matter, and perception and inference, maintaining that spiritual liberation (niḥśreyasa) arises from discriminative knowledge of reality induced by dharma.

The Brahmasūtra (also known as the Vedāntasūtra or Śārīrakasūtra), traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, is the foundational systematizing text of the Vedānta school of Indian philosophy. Consisting of 555 terse aphorisms across four chapters (adhyāyas), it harmonizes Upaniṣadic statements regarding Brahman as the ultimate reality (samanvaya), defends Vedāntic doctrine against rival philosophical traditions such as Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhism, and Jainism (avirodha), outlines spiritual discipline and contemplative methods (sādhana), and delineates the nature and fruits of liberation (phala). This e-text preserves the full root text as isolated from Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya.

The Brahmasiddhi ('Establishment of Brahman') is a foundational treatise of early Advaita Vedānta composed by Maṇḍanamiśra in four chapters: Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa. Written in kārikā form accompanied by an autocommentary in prose, it defends the non-dual reality of Brahman against the realistic epistemology of Mīmāṃsā, Buddhist nominalism and momentariness, and rivals in linguistics. Maṇḍana formulates key tenets that distinguish his philosophy from Śaṅkara's, such as locating ignorance (avidyā) in individual selves (jīva) rather than in Brahman, and arguing for repeated meditation (prasaṅkhyāna) to transform propositional śabda-cognition into immediate realization. The work served as a primary point of departure for Vācaspati Miśra's commentary (Tattvasamīkṣā) and the subsequent Bhāmatī tradition.

The Śrībhāṣya is Rāmānuja's (ca. 11th–12th c. CE) fundamental commentary on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra and the foundational systematic treatise of Viśiṣṭādvaita ('qualified non-dualism') Vedānta. Rāmānuja argues that Brahman is the supreme personal deity (Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa), possessor of infinite auspicious attributes, related to individual souls (cit) and material reality (acit) as the embodied soul to its physical body (śarīra-śarīrī-bhāva). The work offers an extensive, systematic refutation of Advaita Vedānta's doctrine of an unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman and cosmic illusion (māyā/avidyā), particularly in the famous Mahāsiddhānta section of the opening adhyāya.

**Attribution:** Bādarāyaṇa is the credited author of the Brahmasūtras. The Ratnaprabhā (also styled Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā) is by Govindānanda. Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya is the commentary being explicated, but only its lemma words (pratīkas) are cited.

Adhyāya 2 (Avirodhādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra establishes the internal coherence and rational defensibility of Advaita Vedānta by systematically resolving objections. In the first pāda, attacks on Brahman as the sole material and efficient cause based on rival Smṛti doctrines (such as Sāṃkhya) and rational dialectic are rebutted. The second pāda offers a comprehensive philosophical critique of non-Vedāntic systems, including classical Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika atomism, Sarvāstivāda, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika Buddhism, as well as Jainism, Pāśupata theism, and Bhāgavata/Pāñcarātra doctrine. The third and fourth pādas reconcile conflicting Upaniṣadic statements regarding the genesis of the physical elements, the unoriginated and eternal nature of the individual soul (jīva), and the vital faculties (prāṇas). Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā provides a gloss on Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya.

Adhyāya 2 of the Brahmasūtra, known as the Avirodhādhyāya ('chapter on non-contradiction'), reconciles Advaita Vedānta against external criticisms and internal scriptural inconsistencies across four pādas. Pāda 1 answers objections based on smṛti and reasoning; Pāda 2 (Tarkapāda) critiques rival philosophical schools including Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Sarvāstivāda, Vijñānavāda, Jainism, and theistic traditions; while Pādas 3 and 4 resolve apparent scriptural contradictions concerning the creation of the elements, the nature of the jīva, and the sense faculties (prāṇas). Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī provides dialectical, logical, and grammatical analysis of Śaṅkara's bhāṣya, forming the foundational text of the Bhāmatī school of Advaita Vedānta.

**Also known as:** Gauḍapādakārikā, Gauḍapādīyakārikā, Māṇḍūkyakārikā

**Attribution:** Attributed to Gauḍapāda.

The Āgamaśāstra (commonly known as the Gauḍapādakārikā or Māṇḍūkyakārikā) is the earliest extant systematic treatise of Advaita Vedānta, consisting of 215 verses divided into four chapters (Āgamaprakaraṇa, Vaitathyaprakaraṇa, Advaitaprakaraṇa, and Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa). Elaborating on the states of consciousness outlined in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Gauḍapāda establishes the doctrine of absolute non-origination (ajātivāda), asserting that the unborn Self (ātman/brahman) alone is real while phenomenal multiplicity is an illusion akin to a dream or the circle traced by a whirling firebrand (alāta). The work is celebrated for its sophisticated dialectic, particularly in the fourth chapter, which draws heavily on Mahāyāna Buddhist concepts and terminology to articulate an orthodox Upaniṣadic non-dualism.

The Anuvyākhyāna is Madhva's versified dialectical supplement to his own prose Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, expounding Dvaita (Tattvavāda) Vedānta across four adhyāyas. The Vibhramaviveka ('Discrimination of Error') is a verse treatise in 164 kārikās by Maṇḍana Miśra examining the epistemology of perceptual error (khyātivāda). It critically evaluates rival classical theories—specifically Yogācāra ātmakhyāti, Mādhyamika asatkhyāti, and Prābhākara akhyāti—before analyzing anyathākhyāti / viparītakhyāti and demonstrating how the ultimate nature of error points toward indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva). The treatise is a fundamental document for the synthesis between late Mīmāṃsā epistemology and early Advaita Vedānta.

The Pañcadaśī is a verse prakaraṇa of Advaita Vedānta composed of fifteen chapters arranged into three pentads corresponding to the saccidānanda nature of Brahman: Viveka-pañcaka (discrimination of truth/reality, chs. 1–5), Dīpa-pañcaka (illumination of consciousness, chs. 6–10), and Ānanda-pañcaka (bliss of the Self, chs. 11–15). It serves as a comprehensive textbook explaining key Advaita concepts such as the mahāvākyas, cidābhāsa (reflected consciousness), māyā, and jīvanmukti.

The Bhagavadgītābhāṣya is Rāmānuja's commentary on the Bhagavadgītā and one of the central scriptural pillars of the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta tradition. Drawing on Yāmuna's Gītārthasaṅgraha, Rāmānuja expounds the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna as teaching that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme personal Brahman, possessing innumerable auspicious attributes, whose body (śarīra) consists of both sentient souls and insentient matter. The commentary demonstrates how disinterested performance of duty (karma-yoga) and self-knowledge (jñāna-yoga) culminate in continuous loving meditation (bhakti-yoga) and self-surrender (śaraṇāgati) as the direct means of release from saṃsāra.

**Translations:**
- J. A. B. van Buitenen, Rāmānuja's Vedārthasaṃgraha. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text across all 145 sections, from the opening maṅgalaślokas to the concluding verse (sārāsāravivekajñā ... kṛto vedārthasaṅgrahaḥ).

**Also known as:** Vedārthasaṅgraha

**Attribution:** Attributed to Rāmānuja.

The Vedārthasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Meaning of the Veda') is an independent prose treatise by Rāmānuja (11th–12th century CE) expounding the central philosophical doctrines of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. It harmonizes diverse Upaniṣadic passages by demonstrating that sentient beings (cit) and insentient matter (acit) form the body (śarīra) of the supreme Brahman (śarīrin), who is identified with Bhagavān Nārāyaṇa. The work offers extensive polemics against Advaita Vedānta (the unconditioned monism of Śaṅkara), Bhāskara's conditioned identity-in-difference (aupādhika-bhedābheda), and Yādavaprakāśa's essential identity-in-difference (svābhāvika-bhedābheda), concluding that devotional meditation (bhakti / parabhakti) is the ultimate means to liberation.

**Evidence:**

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Vidhiviveka (mūlakārikās and svavṛtti), spanning pp. 1–336 and ending with the final concluding colophon: <iti śrīmahāmahopādhyāyamaṇḍanamiśraviracito vidhivivekaḥ samāptaḥ>.

**Also known as:** Vidhivivekaḥ

**Attribution:** Authored by Maṇḍanamiśra (fl. c. 7th–8th century), who composed both the root verses (mūlakārikā) and the extensive prose autocommentary (svavṛtti).

The Vidhiviveka ('Discrimination of Injunction') is a seminal 8th-century treatise by Maṇḍanamiśra on Vedic hermeneutics and the philosophy of language. Composed in verse with an extensive prose autocommentary (svavṛtti), the work investigates the semantics of Vedic injunctions (vidhi) and the motive force that impels a person to act. Maṇḍanamiśra critically refutes rival theories—notably Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's concept of verbal efficient force (śabdabhāvanā) and the Prābhākara thesis of autonomous duty/obligation (niyoga/kārya)—establishing that prescriptive verbal forms convey that the enjoined act is an effective means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatā).

The Saṃvitsiddhi, the third treatise of Yāmuna's Siddhitraya, is a verse polemic against Advaita Vedānta. It takes the Upaniṣadic 'ekam evādvitīyam' to deny any equal or superior to Brahman, not the reality of the world. It then criticises the doctrines of avidyā, of contentless consciousness, and of the non-difference of cognition and object. The surviving text breaks off during the refutation of the sahopalambhaniyama argument. Rāmānuja drew on it in the Śrībhāṣya's Mahāsiddhānta.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — The extant text of the Saṃvitsiddhi, numbered YSvs_1–439 following Mesquita's lines (GRETIL: 'Line numbering follows ed.'). Each number is a half-verse line, not a kārikā. The text runs from 'ekam evādvitīyaṃ tad brahmety upaniṣadvacaḥ' to 'ghaṭād ṛte 'pi nirbhātaḥ paṭād iva ghaṭaḥ svayam'. The editor's short connective notes, lacuna markers and emendation notes (e.g. '(bādhanam)', '(...)') are kept. The Siddhitraya transmits the work incomplete, with lacunae, and Mesquita's attempted reconstruction of the lost portions is not part of the e-text.

**Also known as:** Siddhitraya (Saṃvitsiddhi section)

**Attribution:** Composed by Yāmunācārya (c. 10th–11th c. CE), predecessor of Rāmānuja in the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, as one of the three treatises comprising the Siddhitraya (alongside Ātmasiddhi and Īśvarasiddhi).

The Saṃvitsiddhi ('Proof of Consciousness') is the epistemological treatise of Yāmunācārya's Siddhitraya, presenting a systematic defense of Viśiṣṭādvaita realism against Advaita Vedānta and Buddhist Idealism. Yāmuna critiques Advaita interpretations of major Upaniṣadic statements (such as 'ekam evādvitīyam') and refutes the concept of anirvacanīyakhyāti, arguing that consciousness inherently reveals distinct, qualified objects. Surviving only as a fragment (439 half-verse lines in Mesquita's edition), it served as a direct conceptual and textual model for Rāmānuja's Mahāpūrvapakṣa and Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the surviving text of Saṃvitsiddhi accompanied by the Siddhāñjana commentary. The file contains only a section of the Siddhitraya. As noted by the commentator ('atra copakramamadhyāvasāneṣu bhūyān granthabhāgo luptaḥ'), the root text itself is preserved with major lacunae.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Attribution:** The root treatise Saṃvitsiddhi constitutes a section of the Siddhitraya by Yāmuna. The commentary Siddhāñjana was composed by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.

The Saṃvitsiddhi is the third treatise of Yāmunācārya's celebrated Siddhitraya ('Triad of Demonstrations'), a foundational work of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. Written primarily in verse with argumentative prose transitions, the work offers an extensive critique of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology, refuting the concept of contentless, undifferentiated consciousness (nirviśeṣa-cinmātra), the unreality of difference, and the doctrine of anirvacanīyatva. Instead, Yāmuna demonstrates that consciousness (saṃvit) is inherently qualified, intentional, and the attribute of an enduring knowing self (jñātṛ). This text directly influenced Rāmānuja's Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya. The digital file presents the surviving portions of the Saṃvitsiddhi accompanied by the Siddhāñjana commentary by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.

The Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā is a classical manual of Haṭha Yoga structured as a dialogue between the sage Gheraṇḍa and his disciple Caṇḍakāpāli. Departing from the fourfold or eightfold structures of other yoga treatises, it teaches a sevenfold discipline (saptāṅga) termed ghaṭastha yoga ('yoga centered on the body-vessel'), consisting of purification (ṣaṭkarma), posture (āsana), mudrā, sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra), breath regulation (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), and samādhi. Alongside the Haṭhapradīpikā and the Śivasaṃhitā, it stands as one of the three principal texts of premodern Haṭha Yoga.

The Yogasūtra with the Yogasūtrabhāṣya constitutes the foundational text of the classical Yoga darśana. Divided into four chapters—Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda—it establishes the philosophical definition of yoga as the cessation of mental fluctuations (cittavṛttinirodha) and elaborates the eightfold path (aṣṭāṅgayoga). **Attribution:** Traditional Vedic saṃhitā belonging to the Paippalāda school (śākhā) of the Atharvaveda, traditionally connected with the sage Pippalāda.

The Paippalādasaṃhitā is one of the two surviving recensions of the Atharvaveda (alongside the Śaunakasaṃhitā). Arranged into twenty kāṇḍas, it contains healing charms, protective spells, rituals for prosperity and defense, royal rites, and speculative cosmological hymns. Linguistically and historically belonging to the Mantra period of late Vedic Sanskrit, the corpus parallels the language of the Atharvaveda and the Yajurveda Saṃhitās. It preserves ritual and devotional hymns of major historical and liturgical significance, including the Śrīsūkta, the Medhāsūkta, the Śivasaṃkalpasūkta, and the Kuntāpa hymns recited during the Mahāvrata rite.

It expounds the nature of the non-dual Self (ātman/brahman) through an examination of the four states of consciousness—waking (viśva/vaiśvānara), dream (taijasa), deep dreamless sleep (prājña), and the transcendent fourth (turīya)—and correlates these states with the tripartite phonemes of the sacred syllable OM (A, U, M) and its partless silence (amātra).
