The second chapter (Vaitathyaprakaraṇa, 'Chapter on Unreality/Illusion', 38 kārikās) of Gauḍapāda's Āgamaśāstra along with the running commentary (bhāṣya) ascribed to Śaṅkara. **Attribution:** The kārikās are attributed to Gauḍapāda; the commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.

The third chapter (Advaitaprakaraṇa, 48 kārikās) of Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā, accompanied by the bhāṣya ascribed to Śaṅkara, establishes the absolute non-duality of Brahman through rational inquiry (tarka). Gauḍapāda expounds the doctrine of radical non-origination (ajātivāda), utilizing the classic analogy of ether enclosed in jars (ghaṭākāśa) to demonstrate that the apparent birth and manifold nature of individual souls (jīva) is illusory. The Aitareyopaniṣad is one of the earliest classical prose Upaniṣads belonging to the Ṛgvedic school, embedded as chapters 4 through 6 in the second book of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka. It opens with a cosmogonic account in which the solitary ātman creates the cosmic realms, their divine guardians, and the cosmic person (puruṣa), into whom the cosmic deities subsequently enter as perceptual and physiological faculties. After reflecting on the threefold birth of the individual soul and liberation through the legendary Ṛgvedic seer Vāmadeva, the Upaniṣad concludes with an inquiry into the fundamental nature of the Self, identifying all phenomena and faculties with consciousness in the famous mahāvākya 'consciousness is brahman' (prajñānaṃ brahma).

The Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya is Madhva's commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad of the Sāmaveda. In it, Madhva interprets the Upaniṣadic narrative and teachings from an uncompromising Dvaita (dualist) theistic perspective, equating the supreme Brahman exclusively with Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa). He famously offers an alternative reading and explanation of the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' as 'atat tvam asi' ('thou art not that'), emphasizing the eternal and essential ontological distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme Godhead.

The Garbhopaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad centered on embryology, human anatomy, and physiological contemplation integrated with Vedāntic and Sāṃkhya-Yoga soteriology. It details the month-by-month gestation of the embryo from conception to birth, the bodily components, humors, and tissues, and the fetus's awakening in the womb to memories of past lives and suffering, leading to a resolve to seek liberation through Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, or Yoga. The treatise concludes by homologizing the internal organs to the three Vedic fires and ritual instruments of the sacrificial arena and provides an enumeration of anatomical parts, identifying itself as a Paippalāda text on liberation.

The Atharvaśiropaniṣad ('Head of the Atharvaveda') is an early Śaiva and Pāśupata Upaniṣad traditionally attached to the Atharvaveda. It begins with the gods questioning Rudra about his identity, to which Rudra responds with a grandiose self-proclamation asserting that he is the sole eternal reality, transcendent and immanent in all deities, natural phenomena, and meters. The text expounds esoteric meditations on the sacred syllable Om (praṇava) and prescribes the observance of the Pāśupata vow (pāśupatavrata), including the application of sacred ashes (bhasmasnāna) for severance of worldly bondage (paśupāśa). Already cited in ancient Dharmasūtras (e.g. Gautama and Baudhāyana), it constitutes one of the foundational scriptural texts of early Śaivism.

The Abhisamācārikadharma is a Vinaya treatise preserved by the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravāda school outlining everyday rules of proper conduct, deportment, and etiquette (abhisamācāra) for Buddhist monks, functioning as a vital complement to the formal offenses of the Prātimokṣasūtra. **Coverage:** partial — Contains chapter 1 (Pravrajyāvastu) only, covering sūtras 1–647 along with their complete auto-commentary. The full Vinayasūtra contains over 4,000 sūtras covering seventeen vastus and the prātimokṣa rules.

The Saddharmapārājikā is a late medieval Newar Buddhist ritual and expiation tract belonging to the distinctive Nepalese cluster of 'Pārājikā' texts (alongside the Vajrasattva-, Mañjuśrī-, Tārā-, and Lokeśvarapārājikā). It specifies the penances and temporal periods required to purify grave sins (such as the slaughter of an arhat, a brahmin, or a cow), concluding with manual rites and mantras for purification with the five bovine products (pañcagavya) and kuśa water.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the work as edited by Gustav Roth (1970). It encompasses the foundational narrative of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the eight gurudharmas (§§ 1–28), the full Bhikṣuṇīprātimokṣavibhaṅga (§§ 29–255; colophon at line 7849), the Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka (§§ 256–289; colophon at line 8584), and the concluding Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka uddāna summary (§§ 290–294; colophon at line 8759).

**Attribution:** Canonical Vinaya scripture transmitted by the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school; regarded in tradition as Buddhavacana.

The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the sole Vinaya text governing Buddhist nuns preserved substantially in Sanskrit. It recounts the origin narrative of the nuns' order with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the formulation of the eight 'weighty rules' (gurudharma), followed by an extensive vibhaṅga (rule-by-rule casuistry and commentary) on the nuns' Prātimokṣa, miscellaneous disciplinary matters (Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka), and a concluding uddāna summary of the monks' miscellaneous section (Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka). Preserved in an 11th–12th century palm-leaf manuscript, its Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit idioms make it a cornerstone witness for early Buddhist sectarian law and linguistics.

The Pravrajyāvastu ('Chapter on Going Forth') is the opening section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, detailing the monastic protocols, criteria, and disqualifications for entering the Buddhist Order (pravrajyā) and receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā). Interspersed with the legal guidelines are extensive narrative episodes, including accounts of King Bimbisāra, early converts to the saṃgha, and the avadāna tales of Saṃgharakṣita and Nāgakumāra. The surviving Sanskrit text is preserved in fragmentary manuscript leaves from Gilgit.

**Attribution:** Traditional Mahāyāna scripture presented as the teaching of the Buddha, featuring interlocutors such as Subhūti, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and Śakra.

The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines') is the foundational and earliest extensive scripture in the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Centered on dialogues between the Buddha and disciples including Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Ānanda at Vulture Peak, it expounds the core Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā), the non-apprehension (anupalambha) of independent dharmas, and the altruistic path of the bodhisattva aiming at omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). Across 32 chapters, it promotes the veneration, recitation, and copying of Prajñāpāramitā manuscripts, culminating in the pilgrimage and self-sacrifice of Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita under the teacher Dharmodgata.

The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Diamond Sūtra or Triśatikā ('Three Hundred Lines'), is one of the most celebrated and influential scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and the venerable Subhūti in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī, it systematically dismantles attachment to conceptual signs and ontological categories, teaching that bodhisattvas must practice generosity and cultivate supreme enlightenment without abiding in notions of self, living being, or dharma. The text is renowned for its characteristic dialectical formula asserting that a dharma is designated as such precisely because it is empty of intrinsic existence. First translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 401/402 CE, the sūtra became a cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions—particularly Chan/Zen—and is celebrated for the 868 CE Dunhuang woodblock scroll, the world's earliest dated complete printed book.

**Other editions:**

**Translations:**

## Contents

**Also known as:** Vajracchedikāprajñāpāramitāsūtra, Diamond Sūtra

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna scripture, traditionally framed as the Buddha's discourse to the elder Subhūti in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī.

The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom') is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra presented as a discourse between the Buddha and Subhūti in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī. It expounds the core doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā) through radical deconstructive paradoxes, asserting that while bodhisattvas resolve to liberate all sentient beings, in ultimate reality no entities or self-subsisting dharmas exist. This e-text provides the critical transcription of an early Greater Gandhāran birchbark manuscript from Bamiyan (Schøyen Collection MS 2385/1/1, c. 5th–6th century CE), containing sections 1 through 16c before breaking off.

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra set at Gṛdhrakūṭaparvata in Rājagṛha, delivered by the Buddha Śākyamuni to Ānanda and Ajita (Maitreya).

The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra and the principal scriptural authority for Pure Land Buddhism. Set on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha, the Buddha Śākyamuni narrates to Ānanda how the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, generated the resolve for awakening and made forty-eight great vows to establish the western realm of Sukhāvatī and become the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus). The sūtra expounds the visual and spiritual splendors of this paradise, delineates the requirements for rebirth there through faith, recollection, and merits, and includes instructions addressed to the bodhisattva Ajita (Maitreya) on dispelling doubt.

The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is the primary canonical scripture of the Mahāyāna Pure Land tradition focusing on the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus) and his western realm, Sukhāvatī. The text depicts the wondrous topography, assemblies, and spiritual benefits of Sukhāvatī, while specifying the criteria for rebirth therein—chiefly generating the aspiration for awakening (bodhicittotpāda), sincere faith, ethical observance, and mindful recollection of Amitābha.

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra preserved as text 24 of the Ratnakūṭa collection (Toh 68; T 310[24]). Traditionally considered buddhavacana.

A Mahāyāna sūtra transmitted within the Ratnakūṭa collection that contrasts the monastic prātimokṣa rules of śrāvakas with the ethical conduct of bodhisattvas. The Buddha explains that while the śrāvaka discipline centers on strict detachment to avoid any rebirth in saṃsāra, bodhisattva discipline is guided by skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and intention, prioritizing the welfare and gathering of beings. Consequently, offenses rooted in aversion or hatred are considered severe for a bodhisattva because they cause abandonment of beings, whereas infractions rooted in desire can serve to gather beings and are deemed comparatively less obstructive. The sūtra concludes with an exposition by Mañjuśrī on the unconditioned, inherently pure nature of all dharmas.

The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra (also known as the Kāśyapaparivarta or Ratnakūṭasūtra) is an archaic and foundational Mahāyāna scripture presented as a dialogue between Śākyamuni Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak. A short Mahāyāna sūtra expounding the extraordinary karmic merit derived from erecting and venerating stūpas, images, and relics of a buddha. The Ahorātravratacaityasevānuśaṃsāvadāna is a Buddhist narrative poem (avadāna) preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts celebrating the spiritual merits and worldly rewards (anuśaṃsā) of the 'day-and-night vow' (ahorātravrata) performed during the worship and ritual service of caityas/stūpas. Framed as a dialogue between King Aśoka and the elder Upagupta, the text details the procedural rules of the vrata and illustrates its karmic efficacy through narratives of devotees whose stupa veneration purified negative karma and led to celestial rebirth and progress toward enlightenment. It constitutes a key textual witness for the devotional cult of the caitya and vow observances in Newar Buddhism.

The Āryānityatāsūtra is a short canonical discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī on the universal impermanence (anityatā) and inevitability of death for all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra). The Maitreyavyākaraṇa ('Prophecy Concerning Maitreya') is a metrical Buddhist scripture in anuṣṭubh verse setting forth the future advent of the bodhisattva Maitreya as the next buddha of the current cosmic era. The Caturdharmanirdeśasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Sudharmā council hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, in which the Buddha instructs the bodhisattva Maitreya on how to overcome and purify accumulated unwholesome actions. Frequently cited by Indian masters, notably Śāntideva in the Śikṣāsamuccaya, it serves as the primary canonical foundation for Buddhist confession and purification rituals.

A compilation of four canonical Āgama discourses reconstructed from Sanskrit manuscript fragments found in Central Asia (Turfan collection) expounding the ten powers (daśabala) of a Tathāgata. These powers—including perfect knowledge of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna), the ripening of karma (karmavipāka), the states of meditative attainment (dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti), the spiritual faculties of sentient beings (indriyaparāparatā), and the eradication of contaminants (āsravakṣaya)—form the foundation of the Buddha's authority to proclaim the wheel of Dharma and utter his lion's roar (siṃhanāda). Belonging to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda transmission, these discourses parallel texts in the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99, no. 684) and Pāli Dasabala suttas in the Saṃyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāyas.

The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna (Divyāvadāna Chapter 33) narrates how the low-caste Mātaṅga (Caṇḍāla) maiden Prakṛti falls in love with the Buddha's disciple Ānanda and attempts to entrap him with love sorcery, but is rescued by the Buddha, ordained as a bhikṣuṇī, and attains arhatship. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 38 avadānas as found in standard printed editions, opening with Avadāna 1 (Koṭikarṇāvadāna) and concluding with Avadāna 38 (Maitrakanyakāvadāna).

**Attribution:** An anonymous anthology of Buddhist narrative literature. Narrative material corresponds directly to sections of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, while other sections include well-known cycles such as the Aśokāvadāna and the Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna.

The Divyāvadāna ('Divine Narratives') is an anthology of 38 Buddhist avadāna stories composed in Sanskrit, illustrating the workings of karma, past births, and moral causation through the lives of the Buddha, his disciples, householders, and monarchs. A major portion of the text draws directly from the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition. Famous narrative components include the Aśokāvadāna cycle, Kuṇālāvadāna, Pūrṇāvadāna, and Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna.

The Dvāviṃśatyavadānakathā ('Narrative of Twenty-Two Avadānas') is a medieval Nepalese Buddhist narrative anthology organized around twenty-two core avadāna tales extolling the merits of donation (dāna), caitya and stūpa worship, and monastic veneration. Framed by an opening and closing dialogue between the Elder Upagupta and King Aśoka, it draws substantially on classical sources such as the Avadānaśataka and Divyāvadāna while also incorporating prose passages written in Newar Buddhist Sanskrit. The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, consisting of dialogues between the Buddha and the bodhisattvas Sarvaśūra and Bhaiṣajyasena. It emphasizes the spiritual perils of cyclic existence, the visionary experiences of dying and intermediate states, karmic retribution and purification, and the boundless merit accrued from hearing, reciting, or copying the text. The Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra ('Tantra of the Elimination of All Evil Destinies') is an influential Buddhist Yogatantra of the Vairocana cycle, dating roughly to the late 7th to 8th century CE. Set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the tantra opens with Śakra pleading with Śākyamuni to deliver the god Vimalamaṇiprabha, who has fallen into the lower realms upon his death. Centering on Sarvavid Vairocana and his maṇḍalas, the text provides elaborate ritual instructions—including initiations, sādhanas, apotropaic rites, and especially mortuary and post-mortem ceremonies—designed to purify negative karmic imprints and ensure liberation from adverse transmigrations.

## Contents

**Also known as:** Ekādaśamukham, Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya, Ekādaśamukhadhāraṇī

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara expounds the eleven-faced heart-spell (ekādaśamukhaṃ nāma hṛdayam) in the presence of the Buddha in Śrāvastī.

The Ekādaśamukha (also known as Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya) is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara reveals his eleven-faced heart-spell (hṛdaya) before the Buddha in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī. The text details ten mundane benefits (including freedom from illness, weapons, poison, fire, and untimely death) and four transcendental fruits (including beholding the Tathāgatas at death and rebirth in Sukhāvatī) promised to practitioners who recite the spell, followed by prescriptive ritual instructions for bali offerings, lustrations, and homa rites. Surviving in Sanskrit in a 5th- to 6th-century birch-bark manuscript unearthed at Gilgit, the scripture formed a foundational text for the cult of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara throughout Central and East Asia.

**Attribution:** Canonical Buddhist narrative (avadāna) belonging to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda textual lineage, preserved in a manuscript from Gilgit.

The Mahāsudarśanāvadāna is a Buddhist narrative preserved in the Gilgit manuscripts recounting a former existence of the Buddha as the righteous universal monarch (cakravartin) Mahāsudarśana. Endowed with the seven royal jewels and four supernatural faculties, the king establishes boundless charity, erecting magnificent palaces and ponds for all beings in his city of Kuśāvatī. Moving beyond temporal sovereignty, he renounces sensuality, cultivates the four immeasurable minds (brahmavihāras), enters the meditative absorptions (dhyānas), and attains rebirth in the Brahmā realm, with the Buddha identifying the tale as an exposition of the accumulation of merit (saṃbhāra) necessary for supreme awakening.

The Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (also known as the Vajrasattvasādhana) is a generation-stage (utpattikrama) meditation manual of the Guhyasamāja tantra, attributed to Candrakīrti. Structured across successive meditations including samādhirāja, maṇḍalarājāgrī, and karmarājāgrī, the practice systematically correlates ritual visualizations with canonical scriptural quotations cited across the chapters of the root Guhyasamājatantra.

The Pāṃśupradānāvadāna constitutes chapter 26 of the Divyāvadāna and serves as the opening section of the Aśokāvadāna cycle. The Sumāgadhāvadāna is an independent Buddhist narrative work (avadāna) in mixed prose and verse relating the story of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the prominent merchant and patron Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī. Married into the household of Vṛṣabhadatta in Puṇḍravardhana (Bengal), whose family reveres the Nirgranthas (Jains), she is repelled by the naked ascetics and miraculously summons the Buddha and his disciples from her roof. The aerial arrival and marvelous transformations of the Buddha and the arhats convert her husband's family and the entire city to Buddhism. The text concludes with karmic explanations by the Buddha, including Sumāgadhā's past lives and the ten prophetic dreams of King Kṛkin.

The Aṣṭamātṛkāstotra is an 11-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn venerating the Eight Mothers (Aṣṭamātṛkā), preserved in Nepalese Newar Buddhist manuscript and ritual collections. Following an opening salutation to Vighneśvara (Gaṇeśa), each stanza addresses one of the eight protective mother goddesses assigned to a compass direction (Brahmāṇī in the East, Vārāhī in the South, Indrāṇī in the West, Māheśvarī in the North, Kaumārī in the Southeast, Vaiṣṇavī in the Southwest, Cāmuṇḍā in the Northwest, and Caṇḍikā/Mahālakṣmī in the Northeast), identifying her vehicle, complexion, and emblems. The final verses invoke the goddesses collectively in connection with the eight pilgrimage seats (aṣṭapīṭha), sacred trees, and the eight Bhairavas, concluding with reverence to the planetary deities (navagraha) and Yama.

The Śākyasiṃhastotra (navagrahakṛtam) is a short Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of 10 stanzas composed in Toṭaka meter in praise of Śākyamuni Buddha (Śākyasiṃha). Verses 1–9 narrate key aspects of the Buddha's life and virtues: his golden appearance and destruction of Māra's army, his teaching of the ten pāramitās and four Noble Truths, his voluntary birth in the Śākya clan, his renunciation accompanied by Chandaka and Kaṇṭhaka, his forest austerities, his victory over Māra under the Bodhi tree, his reception of offerings from merchants, and his first turning of the wheel of the doctrine at the deer park in Vārāṇasī. The concluding phalaśruti stanza promises that whoever recites this hymn will be freed from disease and planetary afflictions (graharogabhaya) and will reach liberation.

**Attribution:** Traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna as part of his Catuḥstava hymn group. It is quoted under Nāgārjuna's name by Prajñākaramati (Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā) and other Indian commentators, and modern scholars (such as Lindtner and Seyfort Ruegg) generally accept its authenticity as an early Madhyamaka work.

The Acintyastava ('Hymn to the Inconceivable [Buddha]') is a philosophical stotra of 59 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to Nāgārjuna, belonging to the Catuḥstava collection. Styled as praise of the Buddha, it articulates quintessential Madhyamaka philosophy by equating dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) with the non-substantiality (naiḥsvābhāvya) of all factors of existence. It examines the relativity of existence and non-existence, the four extremes of the tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi), the illusion-like character of conventional experience, the distinction between provisional (neyārtha) and definitive (nītārtha) teachings, and ultimate reality as transcending all discursive proliferation.

**Attribution:** Traditionally regarded as the opening hymn of Nāgārjuna's Catuḥstava ('Four Hymns'). Its authenticity is widely accepted by modern scholarship (e.g. Christian Lindtner, who includes it among the core authentic works of Nāgārjuna), supported by frequent citations in Indian Madhyamaka works such as Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā and Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya.

The Lokātītastava ('Hymn to the World-Transcendent One') is a short hymn of 28 anuṣṭubh stanzas attributed to Nāgārjuna, traditionally ordered as the first text in the Catuḥstava collection. Framed as praise of the Buddha who has transcended worldly categories, it systematically presents foundational Madhyamaka philosophy: the five skandhas are revealed as dreamlike and illusory, subject and object lack intrinsic nature, and dependent arising (pratītyasamutpāda) is directly equated with emptiness (śūnyatā). Esteemed and cited by Candrakīrti and later commentators, it is considered one of the authentic works of Nāgārjuna.

The Niṣpannayogāvalī of Abhayākaragupta (abbot of Vikramaśīla, late 11th–early 12th c.) is a compendium of iconographic descriptions of 26 tantric maṇḍalas, complementing his ritual manual Vajrāvalī. This e-text contains only its first chapter, the 19-deity Mañjuvajramaṇḍala of the Guhyasamāja cycle: after the introductory verses on the 'perfected' (niṣpanna) yoga, it describes the protective circle with the ten wrathful deities, the palace, the central Mañjuvajra and the surrounding deities with their colours, faces and attributes, and closes with a discussion of whether the protective circle (rakṣācakra) is to be drawn in painted maṇḍalas.

**Attribution:** By Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, written in Nepal for an elder monk (sthavira) (v. 22 'nepālaviṣaye kṛtavān'). The work is transmitted in the Tibetan Tengyur (Spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma, D 3960).

The Caryāsaṅgrahapradīpa is a concise manual of daily Mahāyāna practice composed by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna during his stay in Nepal. Written for an elder monk who sought instruction focused on the Pāramitā path, the treatise lays out the daily routine of a bodhisattva: moral restraint, sensory control, division of the night for meditation and sleep, the sevenfold worship (saptāṅgapūjā), making stupas and images, and sharing food offerings with deities and beings. While acknowledging that Secret Mantra also attains awakening, it deliberately restricts its exposition to the exoteric Pāramitānaya.

The Mahāpratisarāvidyāvidhi is a short Vajrayāna ritual manual describing the preparation and design of a protective amulet-diagram (rakṣācakra) centered on Mahāpratisarā, the preeminent deity of the Pañcarakṣā pentad. The text sets forth specific geometric concentric circles (puṭa) to be drawn on birch bark (bhūrjatvac) or cloth, inscribed with seed-syllables, dhāraṇī formulas, names of guardian deities, and ritual emblems. Once inscribed and worn by the practitioner, the cakra is held to provide complete protection against calamities, evil spirits, and illness while fostering pacification (śānti) and prosperity (puṣṭi).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text consisting of opening salutation, introductory ritual prose, six metrical verses (Mvts 1–6), the ten-syllable mantra, and the closing colophon title; identified with Sādhanamālā no. 102.

**Also known as:** Sādhanamālā 102, Mṛtyuvañcanatārāsādhanam, 'Chi ba slu ba'i sgrol ma'i sgrub thabs

**Attribution:** Attributed to Vāgīśvarakīrti (BDRC P8946).

The Mṛtyuvañcanatārāsādhana is a concise Vajrayāna visualization manual devoted to White Tārā (Sitatārā) for averting untimely death and extending lifespan. Across six verses framed by prose ritual instructions, it outlines the preliminary contemplation of emptiness, the visualization of the sixteen-year-old goddess seated in vajraparyaṅka, the contemplation of an eight-spoked white wheel inscribed with syllables in her heart, and the six-month recitation of her ten-syllable mantra (oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā). Attributed to Vāgīśvarakīrti, the work constitutes a key liturgic summary of his 'cheating death' (mṛtyuvañcana) tradition, preserved independently in the Tengyur (Toh 3495) as well as within the Sādhanamālā anthology (no. 102).

The Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi of Śūnyasamādhipāda is an Anuttarayogatantra treatise and sādhana centered on the cult of Vajravārāhī and Caṇḍālī yoga, expounding the realization of non-dual gnosis (tattvajñāna) through internal yogic control of prāṇa, bindu, and innate bliss (sahajānanda). The Marmakalikāpañjikā by the Vikramaśīla scholar-monk Vīryaśrīmitra provides an extensive commentary on the root verses, elucidating the esoteric vital points (marman) of practice and quoting extensively from early Siddha songs, Caryāpadas, and the lineage of Śabarapāda.

The Tattvaratnāvalī ('Jeweled Garland of Reality') is a doxographical treatise composed by the scholar-siddha Advayavajra (Maitrīpa). It classifies the Buddhist path into three vehicles (Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Mahāyāna) and four philosophical tenets (Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka), dividing the Mahāyāna into Pāramitānaya and Mantranaya. The treatise sets out bipartite divisions within Yogācāra (Sākāra and Nirākāra) and Madhyamaka (Māyopamādvayavāda and Sarvadharmāpratiṣṭhānavāda), making it a key primary source for late Indian Buddhist doxographical literature (siddhānta).

The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a widely recited Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra centered on Vasudhārā, the goddess of wealth and grain. In the Kauśāmbī setting, the Buddha instructs the impoverished householder Sucandra on the protective incantation and ritual practices revealed by the ancient tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa to overcome poverty and dispel harm. This e-text preserves a unique recension copied in 1638 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1695) in Gujarat, documenting the cross-sectarian adoption and ritual use of the Buddhist prosperity spell by Jaina communities.

The Abhisamayālaṅkāranāmaprajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstra is a central Mahāyāna verse treatise of 273 kārikās in eight chapters outlining the hidden path-structure implicit in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras (specifically the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā). It classifies the spiritual path into eight clear realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy doctrinal topics (saptati padārthāḥ) leading from initial bodhicitta to complete omniscient buddhahood. Attributed to Maitreyanātha and transmitted to Asaṅga, it constitutes the foundational scholastic curriculum text for Prajñāpāramitā exegesis across Tibetan monastic institutions.

The Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha (also known as the Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārthasaṃgraha or Prajñāpāramitāsaṃgrahakārikā) is a 58-verse synopsis of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā composed by the Buddhist philosopher-epistemologist Dignāga. Dignāga organizes the scripture into thirty-two core thematic topics (dvātriṃśad arthāḥ), interpreting its insight through a Yogācāra doctrinal lens. The synthesis notably correlates the sūtra's teachings with sixteen aspects of emptiness, the counteracting of ten types of mental distraction (cittavikṣepa), and the three natures (trisvabhāva).

The Abhisamayālaṅkāra ('Ornament for Clear Realization') is a foundational Mahāyāna verse treatise composed of kārikās arranged across eight chapters (adhikāras). Attributed to Maitreya/Asaṅga, it serves as a systematic hidden-meaning commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, organizing the progressive path to enlightenment into eight clear realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy distinct topics (arthasaptati). Haribhadra's Sphuṭārthā (titled Abhisamayālaṅkārakārikāśāstravivṛti in the Sanskrit manuscript tradition) is a commentary (vṛtti) on the root kārikās of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra attributed to Maitreya. The Abhisamayālaṅkārāntaḥpātināṃ padārthānāṃ saṃkṣepato vivaraṇam is a modern Sanskrit scholastic manual written by Prof. Ram Shankar Tripathi as an appendix to his 1977 edition of Haribhadra's Abhisamayālaṅkāravṛtti Sphuṭārthā. ## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Carol Meadows (ed. and tr.), Ārya-Śūra's Compendium of the Perfections: Text, Translation and Analysis of the Pāramitāsamāsa. Indica et Tibetica 8. Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1986.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC book_280; input DSBC staff, proofread Miroj Shakya, Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West, 2008), passed to GRETIL as bsa050_u (Śāstra section, text no. 50) and converted with verse labels Ps_x.y.

- Editorial bracket "prajñāpāramitāsa[māsa]ś cāyaṃ" in the final colophon, from a printed edition.

**Other editions:**
- Alfonsa Ferrari (ed. and tr.), "Il «Compendio delle Perfezioni» di Āryaśūra", Annali Lateranensi 10 (1946). — Editio princeps with Italian translation.
- Naoki Saito, Das Kompendium der moralischen Vollkommenheiten: Vairocanarakṣitas tibetische Übertragung von Āryaśūras Pāramitāsamāsa samt Neuausgabe des Sanskrittextes. Indica et Tibetica 38. Marburg: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 2005. — New edition of the Sanskrit with the Tibetan translation.

**Translations:**
- Alfonsa Ferrari 1946 (see other_editions). (Italian)
- Carol Meadows 1986 (see edition_used). (English)
- Seiji Satoh, "Ārya Śūra's Compendium of the Perfections (Pāramitāsamāsa) The 1st chapter. A Japanese translation", Ronshū (1991). (Japanese)
- pha rol tu phyin pa bsdus pa zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 3944): translated by Vairocanavajra (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: six chapters (dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, prajñā) with 61/65/40/44/79/74 = 363 numbered stanzas (Ps_1.1–6.74), the final chapter colophon and the author's closing stanza.

**Also known as:** Pāramitāsamāsanāma, Prajñāpāramitāsamāsa

**Attribution:** The closing stanza names the author as Śūra ("śurabhramareṇa"); tradition identifies him with Āryaśūra, author of the Jātakamālā. Meadows (1986) discusses the authorship and date; whether he is the Jātakamālā poet is debated.

The Pāramitāsamāsa ("Compendium of the Perfections") is a kāvya-style verse treatise in six chapters on the six perfections of the bodhisattva: generosity, morality, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom. Each is presented as grounded in compassion and the bodhisattva's resolve, with the final chapter on prajñā. It is ascribed to (Ārya)Śūra and was translated into Tibetan by Vairocanarakṣita (D 3944).

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāsūtram with Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā of Ācārya Kamalaśīla, critically edited (Tibetan version) and restored into Sanskrit by Pema Tenzin, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1994 (Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica, 29).

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC) / Sanskrit Buddhist Input Project (proofread by Milan Shakya); converted to TEI/HTML for GRETIL by Reinhold Grünendahl and Maximilian Mehner.

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL legacy header: 'Based on the edition by Pema Tendzin: Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāsūtram, with Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā of Acārya Kamalaśīla. Sarnath 1994 (Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica, 29).'
- Colophon at line 3085 explicitly documents Pema Tenzin's Sanskrit reconstruction: 'viduṣāṃ vaśaṃvadena ācāryapemātenajinamahādayena bhoṭabhāṣātaḥ saṃskṛtabhāṣāyāṃ punaruddhṛtā sarvasattvahitasukhārtham iti.'
- Internal page/section references in the e-text correspond to the Sarnath edition (e.g., '(Vajraṭ_169)').

**Other editions:**
- Derge Tanjur (sde dge bstan 'gyur), dbu ma, vol. ma, fols. 204a1–267a7 (Tōhoku no. 3817). — Canonical Tibetan translation by Mañjuśrī, Jinamitra, and Ye shes sde.
- Peking Tanjur, fols. 209b4–285b5 (Ōtani no. 5216). — Canonical Tibetan translation by Indian upādhyāyas Mañjuśrī and Jinamitra, and translator-editor Ye shes sde.

**Translations:**
- phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa rdo rje gcod pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa (Derge Tengyur D 3817): translated by Mañjuśrī, Jinamitra, sna nam btsun pa ye shes sde (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary as reconstructed into Sanskrit by Pema Tenzin, from the introductory maṅgalācaraṇa through the final closing verses and modern restoration colophon.

**Also known as:** Vajracchedikāṭīkā, Āryavajracchedikāvistṛtaṭīkā, 'Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa rdo rje gcod pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa

**Attribution:** The work is an extensive commentary (vistṛtaṭīkā) by Ācārya Kamalaśīla on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā. The original Sanskrit text is lost; this Sanskrit version is a modern restoration/reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical translation by Ācārya Pema Tenzin (Pemā Tenjin). The Tibetan translation (D 3817) attributes the work to Jayasena (ka ma la shI la).

The Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā is an extensive commentary by the Indian master Kamalaśīla on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Following classical Indian scholastic structure—setting out the purpose (prayojana), concise overview (piṇḍārtha), word analysis (padārtha), internal connection (anusandhi), and answers to objections—Kamalaśīla expounds the sūtra from a Mādhyamika perspective. He details the path of the bodhisattva and refutes substantialist views while demonstrating two-fold selflessness. Because the ancient Sanskrit manuscript is lost, this e-text represents a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical version by Pema Tenzin.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains the complete verse treatise: 14 ślokas in total, consisting of 4 introductory stanzas, the 9 core stanzas (numbered 5[1] to 13[9]) illustrating the 9 similes of emptiness, and 1 concluding stanza (verse 14), with opening and closing colophons. The Garbhasaṅgraha is a concise 14-verse Mahāyāna work attributed in the colophon to Mahācārya Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa). It sets forth the essential path of the Bodhisattva: recognizing suffering caused by dualistic grasping and afflictions, cultivating emptiness and compassion, and generating bodhicitta to attain liberation.

The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā ('Verses on the Heart of Dependent Origination') is a concise seven-stanza Madhyamaka treatise that condenses the twelve links (nidāna) of dependent arising into three interrelated categories: defilements (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha). This discrepancy led Carmen Dragonetti to discuss authorship in favor of Śuddhamati, while Christian Lindtner has expressed doubt as to Nāgārjuna's authorship of the Vyākhyāna.

The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā with Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna is an epitome of the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna. It reduces the twelve links of existence into three fundamental categories: afflictions (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha), explaining how they perpetuate cyclic existence like an endlessly turning wheel without any permanent agent or substantial soul transmigrating between lives. Emphasizing that purely empty factors arise from empty conditions, the text concludes with well-known verses declaring that in ultimate reality nothing is to be removed and nothing added.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 123 verses of the Suhṛllekha in modern Sanskrit retroversion; does not include Mahāmati's commentary (Vyaktapadāṭīkā), which was edited alongside it in the 2002 CIHTS publication.

**Also known as:** Letter to a Friend, Bshes pa'i spring yig, bshes spring, Longshu pusa quan jie wang song (龍樹菩薩勸誡王頌)

**Attribution:** The original Sanskrit text of Nāgārjuna's Suhṛllekha is non-extant. The Sanskrit verses in this e-text are a modern retroversion (punaruddhāra / reconstruction) from the Tibetan translation (Bstan 'gyur, D 4182) by Padma Tendzin (Pema Tenzin) and published by CIHTS in 2002. Historically, the didactic epistle is attributed to Nāgārjuna and addressed to a king (variously identified as Śātavāhana / Gautamīputra / Udayana).

The Suhṛllekha ('Letter to a Friend') is a celebrated Buddhist didactic poem of 123 stanzas traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna and addressed to a king. Written in Āryāgīti metre, the text summarizes fundamental Mahāyāna and Buddhist lay ethics, including the six recollections, the ten virtuous actions, mindfulness, the hazards of sensory attachment, karma, the sufferings of cyclic existence (saṃsāra), and the bodhisattva path culminating in buddhahood. Because the original Sanskrit text has not survived in manuscript form and was preserved historically only in Tibetan and three Chinese translations, this electronic text reproduces a modern Sanskrit restoration (punaruddhāra) prepared by Padma Tendzin (CIHTS, 2002).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains all 73 kārikās in modern Sanskrit reconstruction. Although the source volume includes both the kārikās and the autocommentary (Śūnyatāsaptativṛtti, Toh 3831) — and the e-text retains the heading fragment 'svopajñavṛttyā samanvitā' and the commentary colophon 'śūnyatāsaptatervṛttiḥ ācāryanāgārjunapādakṛtā samāptā' — only the 73 verse kārikās were input, omitting the prose vṛtti.

**Attribution:** The original Sanskrit text of Nāgārjuna's Śūnyatāsaptati survives completely only in Tibetan translation (Toh 3827 / D 3827, P 5227). The Sanskrit text in this e-text is an artificial modern reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan by Ācārya Sempa Dorje (published 1985).

The Śūnyatāsaptati ('Seventy Verses on Emptiness') is one of the foundational works of the Yukti (reasoning) corpus attributed to Nāgārjuna. In 73 verses (predominantly in anuṣṭubh meter), the text argues that all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas—including the twelve links of dependent origination, time, the agent and object of action, and nirvāṇa itself—are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because they are dependently co-arisen (pratītyasamutpanna). Rather than promoting nihilism, Nāgārjuna explains that establishing ultimate emptiness (śūnyatā / paramārtha) enables the valid and unhindered operation of conventional transactional reality (laukikavyavahāra).

The Vigrahavyāvartanī is a philosophical work by Nāgārjuna defending the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā). The Bodhisattvādikarmikamārgāvatāradeśanā is a practical liturgical and behavioral handbook by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna outlining the progressive spiritual discipline required of a beginner bodhisattva (ādikarmika). It instructs the practitioner on cultivating calm abiding (śamatha) and special insight (vipaśyanā) according to the nine limbs set forth in Bodhibhadra's Samādhisambhāraparivarta, maintaining mindfulness of all phenomena as illusion-like (māyopama) in post-meditation, and promptly purifying ethical infractions.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete short treatise consisting of an introductory maṅgala verse, a summary verse setting out fifteen pedagogical topics (pañcadaśa vibhaktayaḥ) of refuge, interspersed prose explanations with illustrative verses (verses 3–9), and the author colophon.

The Śaraṇagamanadeśanā is a short instructional work on the practice and significance of going for refuge (śaraṇagamana) to the Three Jewels, composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna. The text structures the doctrine around fifteen headings: the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna), the twofold Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna states (sthiti), intentional disposition (āśaya), duration (avadhi), essence (svabhāva), standard measure (māna), method (naya), rules/precepts (śikṣā), etymological meaning (nirukti), functional role (kāritra), analogies (upamya), classification (bheda), faults of transgression (ādīnava), doctrinal meaning (artha), and twofold temporal benefits (anuśaṃsā).

The Gurukriyākrama (also called Saṃkṣiptagurukriyākrama) is a brief manual detailing the liturgical and instructional sequence (krama) to be followed by a spiritual master (ācārya / guru) when guiding a disciple in the generation of bodhicitta and the Mahāyāna path. It covers inspiring faith and enthusiasm in the disciple, making offerings and performing the preliminary sevenfold worship (saptāṅgapūjā), arousing relative and ultimate bodhicitta, and conferring instruction on the perfections (pāramitā), means of gathering disciples (saṃgrahavastu), immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the threefold training.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains the complete ten chapters of Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra (concluding at verse 10.58) and the complete extant nine chapters of Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā (chapters 1–9).

Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist treatise detailing the development and practice of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā is a Sanskrit commentary offering running glosses, citations, and Madhyamaka exegesis across chapters 1 through 9. **Coverage:** complete — Complete in all 27 chapters (prakaraṇas), running from Chapter 1 (Pratyayaparīkṣā) to Chapter 27 (Dṛṣṭiparīkṣā), ending with the full final colophons.

**Attribution:** The root verses of the Madhyamakaśāstra (commonly known as Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) are composed by Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE). The commentary Prasannapadā ('Clear Words', also known as Madhyamakavṛtti) is by Candrakīrti (c. 600–650 CE). The Tibetan translation (D 3860) attributes the work to Candrakīrti I (zla ba grags pa).

Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā ('Clear Words'), also titled Madhyamakaśāstravṛtti, is a 7th-century CE Sanskrit prose commentary on the 27 chapters of Nāgārjuna's fundamental Madhyamakaśāstra (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā). It is the only fully surviving Indian commentary on Nāgārjuna's root verses preserved in Sanskrit. Candrakīrti defines the Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka approach by defending Buddhapālita's method of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) against Bhāvaviveka's use of autonomous inference (svatantra), making the work an essential foundation for the study of Indian and Tibetan Madhyamaka philosophy.

The Niraupamyastava ('Hymn to the Incomparable One') is a devotional philosophical poem of 25 stanzas in anuṣṭubh metre composed by Nāgārjuna, forming part of his famous Catuḥstava ('Four Hymns'). Composed as an encomium praising the Buddha, the work formulates foundational Madhyamaka themes in a devotional idiom: praising the Tathāgata as having neither originated nor extinguished any dharma, having spoken not a single syllable while yet teaching all disciples, and being empty of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and conceptual proliferation (vikalpa). The hymn also contains prominent discussions of the two bodies of the Buddha (dharmakāya and janmakāya/rūpakāya) and affirms the ultimate unity of the vehicles (ekayāna) grounded in the non-differentiation of the dharmadhātu.

**Other editions:**

**Translations:**
- Giuseppe Tucci, 'Two hymns of the Catuḥstava of Nāgārjuna', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 1932, pp. 309–325. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 11 anuṣṭubh verses (verses 1–10 apophatic praise of the Buddha, verse 11 pariṇāmanā/dedication of merit), concluding with 'śrī paramārthastavaḥ samāptaḥ'.

**Also known as:** Catuḥstava (hymn 4), Don dam par bstod pa

**Attribution:** Attributed to Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE) in the Tibetan Tanjur (Toh 1122) and by Indian commentators such as Amṛtākara (Catuḥstavasamāsārtha). Modern scholarship (Tucci, Lindtner, Tola & Dragonetti) accepts it as a component of the Catuḥstava group.

The Paramārthastava ('Hymn to Ultimate Reality') is a short hymn of eleven verses attributed to Nāgārjuna and canonical as the fourth praise in the Catuḥstava quartet. It articulates Madhyamaka apophasis within devotional verse: because the Buddha is unarisen (anutpanna), unlocated (asthita), and beyond language (vākpathātīta), he cannot be praised in an ultimate sense (paramārtha). Consequently, praise can only take place conditionally via conventional designation (lokaprajñapti), culminating in the realization that in emptiness there is neither praised nor praiser.

The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way'), comprising 448 verses in 27 chapters, is the foundational philosophical treatise of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism composed by Nāgārjuna. Through systematic dialectic, Nāgārjuna deconstructs essentialist claims regarding causality, motion, faculties, aggregates, the self, time, karma, and nirvāṇa, establishing that no entity possesses inherent existence (svabhāva). Identifying dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) with emptiness (śūnyatā) and conventional designation (prajñapti), the work articulates the Middle Way free from the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Sanskrit manuscript edited by Giuseppe Tucci. It contains 28 verses plus the closing colophon: an introductory section of 7 verses (with a lacuna in the second half of verse 7), followed by the 20 main kārikās (numbered 1–20 and 8–27), and a concluding stanza (verse 28).

**Also known as:** Mahāyānaviṃśati, Mahāyānaviṃśaka, Theg pa chen po nyi shu pa, Dacheng ershi song lun (大乘二十頌論)

**Attribution:** The colophon attributes the text to Ārya Nāgārjuna ('mahāyānaviṃśikā kṛtirāryanāgārjunapādānāṃ'), as do the Tibetan (D 3833) and Chinese (T 1576, tr. Dānapāla / 施護) canonical records. However, modern scholarship lists Mahāyānaviṃśikā among the works attributed to Nāgārjuna whose authenticity is questioned.

The Mahāyānaviṃśikā ('Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle') is a brief Buddhist treatise traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that synthesizes Madhyamaka and Yogācāra doctrines. It argues that external objects lack independent reality and that the world of saṃsāra is an illusory projection arising from conceptual fabrication (kalpanā) upon mind alone (cittamātra). The text concludes by urging practitioners to rely upon the Mahāyāna vehicle as the only means to cross the ocean of delusion.

**Attribution:** Firmly attributed to Nāgārjuna; traditionally ranked among the works of Nāgārjuna's reasoning corpus (rigs tshogs) in Tibetan doxography.

The Vigrahavyāvartanīkārikā ('Verses on Turning Back Disputes') is a seminal epistemological treatise by Nāgārjuna defending the Madhyamaka doctrine of universal emptiness (sarvadharmaśūnyatā) against realist objections, notably from the Nyāya school. Verses 1–20 set forth the opponent's paradox: if all things lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), Nāgārjuna's own statement lacks reality and cannot negate anything, or else valid means of knowing (pramāṇa) must be conceded. Verses 21–71 provide Nāgārjuna's counter-arguments, showing that negation and conceptual discourse function precisely because of dependently originated emptiness, and that pramāṇa and prameya are mutually established rather than inherently real.

The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Bodhisattva Path') is an 8th-century Sanskrit didactic and philosophical poem by the Madhyamaka master Śāntideva. Arranged in ten chapters, it serves as a practical manual for generating and sustaining the awakening mind (bodhicitta) and cultivating the six bodhisattva perfections (pāramitās). The work is celebrated for its ethical power—notably the exchange of self and other (parātmaparivartana) in chapter 8—and its rigorous philosophical exposition in chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda), which defends Madhyamaka emptiness (śūnyatā) against rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist metaphysical positions.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T06_asmahsbu`

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Sylvain Lévi, ed., Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra: Exposé de la doctrine du Grand Véhicule, vol. I, Paris 1907.

**E-text:** Jens Braarvig, Oslo 2011; Thesaurus Literaturae Buddhicae (TLB) / Bibliotheca Polyglotta; GRETIL.

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL and TEI headers explicitly state: 'Based on the ed. by Sylvain Lévi: Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Exposé de la doctrine du Grand Véhicule, vol. I, Paris 1907. Input by Jens Braarvig, Oslo 2011'.
- Inline pagination markers match Lévi 1907 from '(Msa 1)' at the start through '(Msa 189)' at segment 5831.

**Other editions:**
- Naoya Funahashi, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra (Chapters I, II, III, IX, X), Tokyo: Kokushokankokai, 1985. — Critical revision of selected chapters based on Nepalese manuscripts.

**Translations:**
- Sylvain Lévi, trans., Mahāyānasūtrālamkāra, 2 vols. (Sanskrit text and French translation), Paris, 1907, 1911. (French)
- mdo sde'i rgyan gyi bshad pa (Derge Tengyur D 4026): translated by Śākyasiṃha, ska ba dpal brtsegs (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 21 adhikāras with continuous prose bhāṣya, ending at chapter 21 (Caryāpratiṣṭhādhikāra, segment 5836).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra (Maitreya, root text)
- Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabhāṣya (Vasubandhu, commentary)

**Also known as:** Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārakārikā, Dacheng zhuangyan jing lun, 大乘莊嚴經論

**Attribution:** In the Indo-Tibetan tradition, the root kārikās are attributed to Maitreya revealing the text to Asaṅga, counting as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya' (byams chos sde lnga), with the prose bhāṣya attributed to Vasubandhu. In the East Asian tradition and among some modern scholars, the text is frequently attributed directly to Asaṅga.

The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ('Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras') is a foundational treatise of the Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda tradition, consisting of approximately 800 verse kārikās across 21 chapters accompanied by Vasubandhu's prose commentary (bhāṣya). It establishes the scriptural validity of the Mahāyāna and provides an extensive exposition of the bodhisattva path, synthesizing emptiness with classical Yogācāra tenets including the three natures (trisvabhāva), consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā), and the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparivṛtti). Topics range from lineage (gotra) and the generation of bodhicitta to the perfections (pāramitā), bodhisattva stages (bhūmi), and the resultant bodies of a Buddha (trikāya).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the root verses across all five chapters: 1. Lakṣaṇapariccheda (vv. 1.1–1.23), 2. Āvaraṇapariccheda (vv. 2.1–2.17), 3. Tattvapariccheda (vv. 3.1–3.22), 4. The Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā ('Verses Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Yogācāra school, traditionally counted as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya'. In 111 verses across five chapters—on characteristics (lakṣaṇa), obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), spiritual cultivation and results (pratipakṣabhāvanā-avasthā-phala), and the supreme vehicle (yānānuttarya)—it formulates the middle way (madhyamā pratipad) as avoiding both the extreme of reification and that of nihilistic denial. The treatise provides classical expositions of unreal mental construct (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), and emptiness (śūnyatā) understood as the absence of subject-object duality within that construct.

The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa ('Exposition of the Three Natures') is a concise verse work of 38 kārikās by Vasubandhu presenting the classical Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures: the imagined (kalpita), dependent (paratantra), and consummate (pariniṣpanna). The Yogācārabhūmi is the fundamental encyclopedic compendium of the Yogācāra school of Indian Mahāyāna Buddhism. This digital text comprises the first five bhūmis of the seventeen stages in the basic section (Maulībhūmi): the stage connected with the five sensory consciousnesses (Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā bhūmiḥ), the stage of mental consciousness (Manobhūmiḥ), and the three stages defined by the presence or absence of coarse discursive thinking and subtle investigation (Savitarkā savicārā, Avitarkā vicāramātrā, and Avitarkāvicārā bhūmayaḥ). **Also known as:** Abhidharmadharmaskandhapādaśāstra, Abhidharmadharmaskandha

**Attribution:** Traditional attributions diverge: the Sanskrit/Tibetan tradition attributes it to Śāriputra, whereas the Chinese tradition (T 1537) attributes it to Maudgalyāyana.

The Dharmaskandha ('Aggregation of Dharmas') is one of the seven canonical treatises of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma Piṭaka (specifically counted among the 'six feet' or ṣaṭ-pādāḥ supporting the body of the Jñānaprasthāna) and is regarded alongside the Saṃgītiparyāya as representative of the earliest, sūtra-commentarial stratum of Abhidharma literature (c. 2nd–1st century BCE). The treatise compiles canonical doctrinal categories (mātṛkās)—such as the five precepts, stages of stream-entry, the limbs of awakening, dependent origination, and meditative absorptions—and glosses them with citations from early discourses. While preserved intact in Chinese translation (T 1537), the Indic text survives only in birch-bark manuscript leaves recovered from Gilgit and Central Asia.

The Abhidharmāmṛta (or Abhidharmāmṛtarasaśāstra) is an early, systematic manual of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma attributed to Bhadanta Ghoṣaka, one of the four great venerable masters of the Vaibhāṣika lineage associated with the western/Gandhāran tradition. Organized into sixteen chapters (bindus), it provides a clear exposition of Buddhist scholastic categories, including charity and moral discipline, realms of rebirth, the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas, causal conditions, latent defilements, the path of meditation, and unconditioned dharmas. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the short prose treatise corresponding to Toh 4101 / D 4101 (Derge Tengyur, mngon pa, vol. thu), including opening homage, full exposition of the 'ye dharmā hetuprabhavāḥ' stanza, and the retroverted Tibetan translation colophon.

**Also known as:** Āryadharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa, 'phags pa chos kyi dbyings kyi snying po'i rnam par 'grel pa

**Attribution:** Attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan canonical colophon (Derge Tengyur Toh 4101 / D 4101, translated by Indian Upādhyāya Jñānagarbha and Ska ba Dpal brtsegs).

The Dharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa is a brief prose commentary attributed to Nāgārjuna that analyzes the famous Pratītyasamutpāda stanza ('ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat...'). The text provides an Abhidharmic classification of the twelve links into five causes (hetu: avidyā, saṃskāra, tṛṣṇā, upādāna, bhava) and seven results (phala: vijñāna, nāmarūpa, ṣaḍāyatana, sparśa, vedanā, jāti, jarāmaraṇa), concluding with an etymological gloss on the epithets 'Tathāgata' and 'Mahāśramaṇa' in terms of forward (anuloma) and reverse (pratiloma) dependent origination.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 33 chapters (vargas) containing 1,061 verses, terminating with the final uddāna verses listing all 33 chapters as reconstructed in Bernhard's edition.

**Also known as:** Ched du brjod pa'i tshoms, Fǎjí yàosòng jīng

**Attribution:** Traditionally compiled or redacted by Dharmatrāta. Modern philology regards the work as an evolving canonical verse anthology sharing an archaic common verse corpus with the Pāli Dhammapada, Pāli Udāna, and the Gāndhārī Dharmapada.

The Udānavarga is a canonical northern Buddhist anthology of aphoristic stanzas (udāna) arranged topically across 33 chapters (vargas), primarily preserved in the Sarvāstivāda and Mūlasarvāstivāda traditions. Functioning as the Sanskrit counterpart to the Pāli Dhammapada, the Pāli Udāna, and the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, it shares an ancient core of stanzas while expanding the collection to over a thousand verses. Preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts from Central Asian oasis sites along the Northern and Southern Silk Roads as well as in Tibetan and Chinese translations, it is a crucial witness to early Buddhist verse anthologies and sectarian transmission.

The Abhidharmadīpa along with its prose auto-commentary (Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti) is an important post-Vasubandhu Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika treatise. # Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā (on Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T07_sthtattva4`

**Author:** Sthiramati

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T07 (Abhidharma)

**Source:** Aggregated by Sebastian Nehrdich (Dharmamitra) from the published critical editions of Kazuo Kano and collaborators (2020–2022). Only Sthiramati's constituted Sanskrit is reproduced here.

**Editions used (one per Abhidharmakośa verse):**

- *AK 4.34* — Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, "The Fourth Chapter of the Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā: On Forbidding Intoxicating Liquor," in *Sanskrit Manuscripts from China III* (Proceedings of a panel at the 2016 Beijing International Seminar on Tibetan Studies), Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House, 2020 (critical edition and diplomatic transcription at pp. 122–128).
- *AK 4.35* — Kazuo Kano, Jowita Kramer, Takeshi Yokoyama, Hironori Tanaka, Sebastian Nehrdich, Keiki Nakayama and Kaworu Kominami, "律儀の獲得 ― 倶舎論安慧疏・業品第35偈の梵文和訳 ― [On the Attainment of Restraint: Sthiramati's Tattvārthā on Abhidharmakośa 4.35]," *Taihō zasshi* (対法雑誌 / Journal of Abhidharma Studies) 2 (March 2021): 63–98.
- *AK 4.36ab* — Kazuo Kano, Jowita Kramer, Takeshi Yokoyama, Hironori Tanaka, Sebastian Nehrdich, Keiki Nakayama and Kaworu Kominami, "律儀獲得の範囲と動機 ― 倶舎論安慧疏・業品第36偈ab句の梵文和訳 ― [The Field of Scope and Motivation of the Attainment of Restraint: Sthiramati's Tattvārthā on Abhidharmakośa 4.36ab]," *Taihō zasshi* (対法雑誌 / Journal of Abhidharma Studies) 3 (March 2022): 43–95.
- *AK 4.36cd and 4.37* — Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, "The Fourth Chapter of the Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā: On Attaining Restraint, Non-Restraint and Neither-Restraint-nor-Non-Restraint," *China Tibetology* 36, no. 1 (March 2021): 81–99.

**Textual basis:** Constituted Sanskrit reading text of Sthiramati's Tattvārthā commentary on Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37 (within the fourth chapter, Karmanirdeśa), covering folios 1r1–2r6 of the Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet (Ms. "A," copies of which are kept at the China Tibetology Research Center, Beijing). The text was aggregated across the four editions above and ordered by Abhidharmakośa verse (4.34 → 4.35 → 4.36ab → 4.36cd → 4.37). Where a verse was edited in more than one paper (4.35 and 4.36ab), the later Japanese editions' corrected Sanskrit was preferred. This etext contains only Sthiramati's constituted Sanskrit: the Abhidharmakośa kārikā/bhāṣya, Saṃghabhadra's *Nyāyānusāra* parallels, the Tibetan translation, the critical apparatus (variant readings), and the Japanese/English translations given in the source papers are not included. Bold AKBh lemmata are not separately marked. Segments are split at the daṇḍa; the manuscript folio side (1r/1v/2r) is recorded in the folio field.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Aggregated from four published critical editions by Kazuo Kano and collaborators based on the Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet: (1) AK 4.34 in Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, 'The Fourth Chapter of the Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā: On Forbidding Intoxicating Liquor', in Sanskrit Manuscripts from China III, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House, 2020; (2) AK 4.35 in Kazuo Kano et al., Taihō zasshi 2 (2021): 63–98; (3) AK 4.36ab in Kazuo Kano et al., Taihō zasshi 3 (2022): 43–95; (4) AK 4.36cd and 4.37 in Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, China Tibetology 36, no. 1 (2021): 81–99.

**E-text:** Sebastian Nehrdich (Dharmamitra), aggregating the critical texts edited by Kazuo Kano, Jowita Kramer, et al.

**Evidence:**
- Explicitly stated in the source note of the catalog bundle.
- Exact textual match of constituted Sanskrit readings, verse sequence (4.34 -> 4.35 -> 4.36ab -> 4.36cd -> 4.37), and manuscript folio references (1r1–2r6).

**Other editions:**
- Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō no. 1561 (倶舍論實義疏). — Chinese translation (5 juans).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains Sthiramati's commentary on Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37 only (from chapter 4, Karmanirdeśa), covering folios 1r1–2r6 of the Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet.

**Also known as:** Abhidharmakośabhāṣyaṭīkā Tattvārthā, Tattvārthā, Jushe lun shiyi shu (倶舍論實義疏, T 1561)

**Attribution:** Composed by the Yogācāra master Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE) as an extensive sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

This text preserves the surviving Sanskrit of Sthiramati's commentary (ṭīkā) entitled Tattvārthā on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37, located in the fourth chapter on action (Karmanirdeśa). It treats the debate over whether drinking alcohol constitutes an offense by nature (prakṛtisāvadya) or solely by prohibition (pratikṣepaṇasāvadya), the attainment of the three types of moral discipline (saṃvara: prātimokṣa-, dhyāna-, and anāsrava-saṃvara), their relationship to karmic path stages, and the definition of non-restraint (asaṃvara). The work is historically vital for showing Sthiramati's engagement with the competing views of the Sautrāntika and Sarvāstivāda traditions (especially Saṃghabhadra).

## Overview

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Abhidharma; a commentary on the Abhidharmakośa, by the Yogācāra master Sthiramati)

**Genre:** ṭīkā (sub-commentary)

**Estimated date:** c. 6th c. CE

The portion of Sthiramati's Tattvārthā (Abhidharmakośaṭīkā) commenting on Abhidharmakośa(bhāṣya) 4.34–4.37, within the fourth chapter (Karmanirdeśa, the exposition of action). The passages treat: the status of drinking intoxicating liquor as a transgression "by nature" (prakṛtisāvadya) versus "by prohibition" (pratikṣepaṇasāvadya) (4.34); the attainment of the three restraints — prātimokṣa-, dhyāna- and anāsrava-saṃvara — and the tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi) of their relation to past/present/future and to the preparatory, primary and consecutive parts of an act (4.35); the scope (aṅga), causes (kāraṇa) and objects of restraint, including whether it extends to beings out of reach (4.36ab); and the attainment of non-restraint (asaṃvara) and of neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint (4.36cd–4.37).

**History:** Composed by Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE), among the most prolific commentators of the early Yogācāra tradition. His Tattvārthā commentary on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya was long known only through Tibetan and Chinese witnesses until the recovery of a Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet; these passages were critically edited by Kazuo Kano and collaborators in 2020–2022 and are aggregated here into a single reading text.

**Related works:** Abhidharmakośakārikā and Abhidharmakośabhāṣya (Vasubandhu; cf. `SA_T07_vakobhk`, `SA_T07_vakobhau`), Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā (Yaśomitra; cf. `SA_T07_yabhkvyu`), *Nyāyānusāra* (Saṃghabhadra).

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 492 CE – 587 CE

**Posterior median:** 539 CE

The root verses were preserved embedded in Jayarakṣita's commentary (Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā) and reconstructed by modern editor Sanghasen Singh, whose editorial reconstruction is acknowledged in each chapter colophon ('iti saṃghasenena saṃvihitoddhāre...').

The Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of Conduct according to the Buddha') is a Buddhist Vinaya manual in verse outlining monastic discipline and deportment for novices (śrāmaṇera). Affiliated with the Mahāsāṃghika (or Lokottaravādin) disciplinary lineage, the work is organized into four adhyāyas treating the three refuges, the ten novice precepts (śikṣāpada), and supplementary rules of conduct. **Coverage:** complete — Complete work in 20 Śārdūlavikrīḍita stanzas (Js_1–Js_20) plus closing author colophon line.

**Also known as:** Skyes pa rabs kyi bstod pa

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to Ācārya Jñānayaśas (jātakastava ācāryajñānayaśasaḥ; Tib. Ye shes grags pa).

The Jātakastava ('Praise of the Buddha\'s Former Births') by Jñānayaśas is a 20-stanza Mahāyāna devotional hymn (stotra) composed in the classical Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre. Framed by an opening confession of inadequate poetic capacity (verses 1–3) and a concluding dedication of merit for universal enlightenment (verses 19–20), stanzas 4–18 succinctly celebrate the Bodhisattva's extreme self-sacrificing deeds in previous lives—including feeding the tigress, giving away his wife and children, jumping into fire as the hare, giving up his tusks as Ṣaḍdanta, and slicing off his flesh as King Śibi. ## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Pandit Aiswamy Shastri, Bhavasankrantiparikatha. Madras: Adyar Library, 1938, pp. 1-7.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC) project, University of the West / Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods; later normalized for GRETIL by Reinhold Grünendahl and Maximilian Mehner (bsa067_u.htm).

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL mirror and TEI headers state: 'Based on the edition by Pandit Aiswamy Shastri: Bhavasankrantiparikatha. Madras : Adyar Library, 1938, pp. 1-7.'
- DSBC text no. 67 matches the 16 stanzas of the reconstructed Sanskrit text published in the 1938 Adyar Library edition.

**Translations:**
- srid pa 'pho ba (Derge Tengyur D 3840) (Tibetan)
- srid pa las 'das pa'i gtam (Derge Tengyur D 4162): translated by Śrīratha, Ma nang lo tsA ba dge slong grags 'byor shes rab (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete 16-verse text of Pandit Aiswamy Shastri's reconstructed Sanskrit edition, including opening homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and closing colophon.

**Also known as:** Bhavasaṃkrāntiparikathā, Bhavasaṅkrānti, Bhavasaṃkrānti, Srid pa las 'das pa'i gtam

**Attribution:** Ascribed in the Tibetan tradition (Dergé Tanjur Toh. 4162 and Toh. 3840) to Klu-sgrub (Nāgārjuna) and in the Chinese tradition (Taishō 1574, translated by Shihu) to Nāgārjuna. Furthermore, the original Sanskrit text of this work is reconstructed; the text in this file is a reconstructed Sanskrit edition by Pandit Aiswamy Shastri.

The Bhavasaṅkrāntiparikathā is a short Madhyamaka treatise of 16 stanzas traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna, explaining how transmigration across existences (bhavasaṃkrānti) occurs without an enduring self or transmigrating entity (ātman/pudgala). It reconciles karmic continuity and rebirth with emptiness (śūnyatā) and dependent origination through analogies of dreams, reflections, and city-of-gandharvas illusions. As the original Sanskrit text is lost, this e-text preserves the 1938 modern Sanskrit retroversion prepared by Pandit Aiswamy Shastri from Tibetan and Chinese sources.

The Hetubinduṭīkā is a major 8th-century commentary by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason'), an independent tract dedicated to the logical reason (hetu) and Buddhist inferential theory. The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Percept') is a concise foundational treatise in eight verses by the Buddhist epistemologist Dignāga. **Also known as:** Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhiḥ vyatirekātmikā, Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir vyatirekātmikā, Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi (vyatirekātmikā), Vaidharmyadṛṣṭānte vyatirekarūpavyāptyā kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhiḥ

**Attribution:** Authentic work of the Buddhist logician Ratnakīrti, pupil of Jñānaśrīmitra. The work concludes with the author's colophon ('kṛtiriyaṃ mahāpaṇḍitaratnakīrttipādānām').

The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi vyatirekātmikā is an epistemological treatise by the Buddhist master Ratnakīrti demonstrating the universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) of all existents by way of negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) or contraposition. Developing the earlier insights of his teacher Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti argues that whatever lacks causal efficiency through succession or simultaneity (kramākrama) cannot exist, thereby proving that eternal entities are impossible and that only momentary particulars are real. The treatise is particularly famous for its thorough refutation of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika objection of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) when formulating inferences concerning uninstantiated or fictitious entities.

## Edition and provenance

**Edition used (determined):** Svami Dwarikadas Shastri, Nyayabindu Prakaranam-karika. Bauddha bharati, 1994, pp. 42-50.

- Pages 42–50 of Dwarikadas Shastri's edition contain the standalone continuous root text labeled 'Sūtrapāṭhaḥ', which matches the layout and wording of segments [1]–[314].
- The chapter and sūtra numbering schema (1/1–1/21, 2/1–2/47, 3/1–3/140) and terminal rubric 'nyāyabinduprakaraṇaṃ samāptam' strictly reproduce Shastri's printed text.

**Translations:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete root text comprising all three chapters (paricchedas): 1. Pratyakṣapariccheda (1/1–1/21), 2. Svārthānumānapariccheda (2/1–2/47), and 3. Parārthānumānapariccheda (3/1–3/140), concluding with 'nyāyabinduprakaraṇaṃ samāptam'.

**Attribution:** Authentic work of Dharmakīrti.

The Nyāyabindu is Dharmakīrti's concise primer on Buddhist epistemology and logic. Written in prose aphorisms (sūtras), the work is structured into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines perception as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta), formulates the requirements of logical reasons, and classifies reasons into essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi).

**Also known as:** Santānāntarasiddhiprakaraṇa, Rgyud gzhan grub pa zhes bya ba'i rab tu byed pa

**Attribution:** Attributed to Dharmakīrti. This e-text presents a reconstructed Sanskrit edition based on J. S. Negi from the Tibetan translation (D 4219).

The Santānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mind-Streams') is a treatise by Dharmakīrti. Framed as a dialogue opening with a single verse and proceeding through 93 prose sections, it resolves the philosophical challenge of other minds from within the Vijñānavāda (Cittamātra) idealist system, directly rebutting the objection that idealism logically degenerates into solipsism. Dharmakīrti demonstrates that just as a realist infers intentional consciousness from observing physical movements and speech, an idealist can equally infer distinct intentional mental continua from coordinated sensory appearances without positing mind-independent external matter.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text divided into 93 editorial sections, corresponding to pp. 3–149 of Gokhale's 1993 edition, concluding with the terminal verse (93: 'loke 'vidyātimirapaṭalollekhanas...') and the author colophon.

**Also known as:** Vādanyāyaprakaraṇa, Vādanyāyanāmaprakaraṇa

**Attribution:** Universally accepted across Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophical traditions as the final of Dharmakīrti's seven foundational pramāṇa treatises.

The Vādanyāya ('The Logic of Debate') is the last of Dharmakīrti's seven core treatises on epistemology and logic (pramāṇa), expounding his reform of dialectical and debate theory. Dharmakīrti mounts an extensive critique of the classical Nyāya system of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), arguing that genuine defeat in truthful philosophical inquiry (vāda) occurs under only two fundamental circumstances: the proponent's failure to state an essential component of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the respondent's failure to point out an actual fallacy (adoṣodbhāvana). Preserved in Sanskrit and heavily commented upon by thinkers such as Śāntarakṣita (in the Vipañcitārthā) and Vinītadeva, the text served as a foundational model for Buddhist disputation.

Later traditions and modern scholars (such as Kajiyama) have debated attribution to Nāgārjuna, though it is widely treated as an early debate treatise with uncertain or anonymous authorship (sometimes suggested as Bahuśrutīya).

The Upāyahṛdaya (preserved in the 472 CE Chinese translation Fangbian xin lun 方便心論, T 1632, and represented in Sanskrit by Giuseppe Tucci's retroversion) is an early Buddhist handbook of disputation. In four chapters (prakaraṇa), the text provides a justification of debate (beginning with vādo na kartavyaḥ) to defend the Saddharma, discussing pramāṇas, examples, occasions of defeat (nigrahasthāna), and false rejoinders (jāti). The Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason') is an epistemological and logical treatise by the Buddhist master Dharmakīrti, counted among his seven fundamental pramāṇa works. The text focuses specifically on the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu), elucidating its threefold character (trairūpya) and classifying valid reasons into identity (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi). **Also known as:** Tshad ma rnam par nges pa, PVin

**Attribution:** The Pramāṇaviniścaya is undisputed as one of the seven primary epistemological treatises (tshad ma sde bdun) of Dharmakīrti (fl. c. 6th–7th c. CE), combining verses (kārikā) and prose autocommentary (vṛtti).

The Pramāṇaviniścaya ('Ascertainment of Valid Cognition') is Dharmakīrti's synthetic exposition of epistemology and logic across three chapters: perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). This electronic file preserves only a single palm-leaf folio fragment from chapter 3, identified and published by Kazunobu Matsuda and Ernst Steinkellner in 1991 from the National Archives in Kathmandu before the discovery of complete Sanskrit manuscripts in Tibet. The passage comprises Dharmakīrti's prose autocommentary and a summarizing verse (saṃgrahaśloka v. 84) refuting the non-Buddhist proof of an enduring self (ātman) inferred from bodily activities such as breathing.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of Dharmakīrti's autocommentary on chapter 1 (Svārthānumāna) of the Pramāṇavārttika (340 kārikās embedded in prose vṛtti, preceded by the introductory maṅgala verses), corresponding in full to pages 1–176 of Raniero Gnoli's 1960 edition.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Pramāṇavārttikakārikā (chapter 1: Svārthānumāna) (Dharmakīrti, root work)
- Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛtti (Dharmakīrti, autocommentary)

**Also known as:** Pramāṇavārttikavṛtti, Svavṛtti, Tshad ma rnam 'grel gyi 'grel pa

**Attribution:** Dharmakīrti composed a prose autocommentary (svavṛtti) exclusively on the first chapter (Svārthānumānapariccheda) of his Pramāṇavārttika; the subsequent three chapters were commented upon by his direct pupil Devendrabuddhi and later commentators.

The Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛtti is Dharmakīrti's extensive prose autocommentary on the first chapter (Svārthānumāna, 'inference-for-oneself') of the Pramāṇavārttika. Dharmakīrti composed an autocommentary only for this chapter, establishing core principles of Buddhist logic such as the threefold mark of the reason (trairūpya), the necessary ontological relation (svabhāvapratibandha) underlying vyāpti, and negative reasoning (anupalabdhi). It also contains his seminal exposition of the nominalist apoha ('exclusion') doctrine of semantics and conceptual differentiation, coupled with detailed refutations of rival Brahmanical theories of universals and Vedic scriptural infallibility.

The Vādanyāya ('Logic of Debate') is Dharmakīrti's treatise dedicated to dialectical methodology and the formal rules of philosophical debate. Dharmakīrti mounts a critical examination of the Naiyāyika theory of debate, rejecting the classical Nyāyasūtra taxonomy of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna). He replaces them with two overarching criteria: the proponent's failure to present an essential member of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the opponent's alleging of a defect where none exists (adoṣodbhāvana).

**Other editions:**
