## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete across all three chapters (pratyakṣa, svārthānumāna, parārthānumāna) for Dharmakīrti's Nyāyabindu, Vinītadeva's commentary, and Dharmottara's commentary. The anonymous Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī covers only the first chapter (pratyakṣapariccheda), corresponding to the scope of that text in Shastri's edition.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa (Dharmakīrti, root text)
- Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā (Śiṣyahitā) (Vinītadeva, commentary)
- Nyāyabinduṭīkā (Dharmottara, commentary)
- Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī (anonymous, sub-commentary)

**Also known as:** Nyāyabindu, Nyāyabindunāmaprakaraṇa, Rigs pa'i thigs pa zhes bya ba'i rab tu byed pa

**Attribution:** The root work Nyāyabindu is by Dharmakīrti. The commentary Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā (Śiṣyahitā) is attributed to Vinītadeva. The Nyāyabinduṭīkā is by Dharmottara. The anonymous Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī comments on Dharmottara's text.

The Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa ('A Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's foundational introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic, divided into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines valid cognition (pramāṇa), establishes the threefold mark of a sound logical reason (trairūpya), classifies inferential reasons into essential identity (svabhāva), causality (kārya), and non-perception (anupalabdhi), and details valid arguments and pseudo-reasons. This composite e-text presents Dharmakīrti's complete root treatise interleaved with the commentaries of Vinītadeva (Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā / Śiṣyahitā) and Dharmottara (Nyāyabinduṭīkā), together with an anonymous subcommentary (Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī) for the first chapter.

The Hetutattvopadeśa is an introductory primer on Buddhist logic composed by Jitāri. Closely following the model of the Nyāyapraveśa, the work outlines the three characteristics of a valid logical mark (trairūpya), the varieties of correct inferential reasons, and provides an exhaustive taxonomy of fallacies including defective theses (pakṣābhāsa), fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), and fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of chapter 1 (Svārthānumānapariccheda) as preserved and edited by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana. Dharmakīrti's autocommentary and Karṇakagomin's sub-commentary exist only for this chapter.

Karṇakagomin's Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Dharmakīrti's autocommentary (Svavṛtti) to the first chapter (Svārthānumāna, 'Inference for Oneself') of the Pramāṇavārttika. Composed around the 8th to 9th century CE, it offers thorough expositions of Buddhist epistemology, the exclusion theory of meaning (apoha), the nature of logical grounds (hetu), and extensive polemics against rival traditions. Preserved in a manuscript brought to light by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, the text is a vital witness both for establishing the text of Dharmakīrti's Svavṛtti and for tracing post-Dharmakīrti epistemological debate.

The Vādanyāya ('Logic of Debate') is Dharmakīrti's final treatise on debate theory and the grounds of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Critiquing the classic Naiyāyika scheme of twenty-two defeat situations, Dharmakīrti reduces all points of defeat to two fundamental categories: failure to state an essential component of proof (asādhanāṅgavacana) by the proponent, and falsely alleging a defect where none exists (adoṣodbhāvana) by the opponent. Śāntarakṣita's 8th-century Vipañcitārthā is the sole surviving Sanskrit commentary on the text, providing extensive lexical explanations, contextual arguments, and refutations of rival non-Buddhist schools.

A modern Sanskrit essay on Buddhist epistemology (pramāṇamīmāṃsā). It argues that Buddhist discussion of the means of knowledge cannot be shown to be later than the Nyāyasūtra, as Vidyabhusana and Dasgupta held, pointing to the Buddhist positions criticised in the Nyāyasūtra's pūrvapakṣas and to the canonical emphasis on refuting other doctrines (Udāna). The Anupalabdhirahasya is a treatise on Buddhist epistemology by Jñānaśrīmitra addressing the problem of negative cognition. Building on Dharmakīrti's framework, Jñānaśrīmitra defines non-perception (anupalabdhi) not as a mere absence of awareness (upalabdhivirahamātra), but as an implicative negation (paryudāsa) consisting in the apprehension of something incompatible or distinct. He defends the status of anupalabdhi as a valid inferential sign (liṅga) for proving absence (abhāva) against rival Buddhist formulations and non-Buddhist theories such as the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā doctrine of an independent means of knowledge (abhāvapramāṇa).

**Also known as:** Nyāyapraveśa, Nyāyapraveśaka, Nyāyapraveśasūtra, Nyāyapraveśaśāstra, Nyāyapraveśakaśāstra, Yinming ru zhengli lun, 因明入正理論, Tshad ma rigs pa la 'jug pa'i sgo

**Attribution:** Tibetan tradition (Degé Tengyur D4208) attributes the work to Dignāga (Phyogs-kyi glang-po). However, Chinese tradition (T1630) and modern scholarship attribute the manual to Dignāga's disciple Śaṅkarasvāmin. The Tibetan translation (D 4208) attributes the work to Dignāga (phyogs kyi glang po).

The Nyāyapraveśakasūtra (commonly known as the Nyāyapraveśa), authored by Dignāga's pupil Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE), is an influential introductory manual of Buddhist logic and epistemology (hetuvidyā). It systematically defines the members of formal proof (sādhana) and refutation (dūṣaṇa), the three characteristics of a valid logical reason (trairūpya), the varieties of logical fallacies (pakṣābhāsa, hetvābhāsa, dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), and valid cognition through perception and inference. Translated into Chinese as T1630, it became the standard foundational treatise for East Asian Buddhist logic, and was widely preserved and commented upon in medieval India, notably by Jaina scholars.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā, corresponding to pp. 77–88 of Anantalal Thakur's 1957 edition of the Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī.

**Also known as:** Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir Vyatirekātmikā, Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi (Vyatirekātmikā)

**Attribution:** Authored by the Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti (written about 1000–1050 CE), student of Jñānaśrīmitra. The text closes with the author colophon: iti kṛtir iyaṃ ratnakīrteḥ.

The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā ('Proof of Universal Momentariness by Negative Concomitance') is a philosophical monograph by Ratnakīrti, defending the epistemological arguments of his master Jñānaśrīmitra. Complementing his Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Anvayātmikā, this treatise argues from negative contraposition: non-momentary (enduring) entities cannot exercise causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) either in succession (krama) or simultaneously (akrama), and therefore cannot exist. Ratnakīrti pays particular attention to defusing the Nyāya objection that an inference with a non-existent subject incurs the fallacy of lack of substratum (āśrayāsiddhi).

The Saṃtānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mindstreams') is Dharmakīrti's short philosophical treatise on the problem of other minds and the refutation of solipsism. Beginning with a single introductory verse followed by concise prose dialectic, Dharmakīrti shows that inferring the presence of an external continuum of consciousness by observing bodily and vocal activity operates with equal logical validity in an idealist (cittamātra/vijñaptimātra) ontology as in a realist one. A short modern Sanskrit poem of 15 anuṣṭubh stanzas addressed to Dharmaratna. The poet laments the infirmities of old age: trembling, failing sight that spectacles (upacakṣus) no longer help, loss of memory, and his books lying unread in the library to be gnawed by worms and mice. The Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa is a manual of Buddhist iconometry. Framed as a discourse at Jetavana where the Buddha instructs Śāriputra on how devotees should fashion icons after the Teacher's departure or parinirvāṇa, the text establishes canonical proportions (pramāṇa) for images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Across 54 verses, it details precise measurements in bodily units (aṅgula, mātrā, vyāma) for the uṣṇīṣa, cranial contours, facial features, torso, and limbs, as well as distinct facial types for various classes of divine, human, and semi-divine beings.

**E-text:** Helmut Krasser (data entry); GRETIL / Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages; TEI conversion by Reinhold Grünendahl and Maximilian Mehner.

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL and TEI headers state: 'Based on the ed. by Paramanandan Shastri, Patna 1979 (Tibetan Sanskrit Work Series, 20) Provided by Helmut Krasser'.

Chapter 5 begins 'anumānaṃ dvidhā — svārthaṃ, parārthaṃ ca' (Sh p. 75) and breaks off in the discussion of relation (sambandha, quoting Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā) with the editor's note '[itaḥ praṃ mūlapustakaṃ nopalabhyate /]'. The Tarkarahasya ('Secret of Logic/Reasoning') is an Indian Buddhist philosophical treatise and epistemological manual belonging to the pramāṇa tradition. In five topical chapters, the text presents the definitions and number of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), perception (pratyakṣa) and its subdivisions, epistemic objects, and inference and relations (examining Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā), while refuting rival non-Buddhist views.

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Root text (mūla) consisting of 4 sections (nirdeśas): general orthographic variants, ba/va variants, sibilant variants, and gender variants, followed by closing verses and final colophon.

**Attribution:** By Maheśvara (Maheśvara Kavīndra), author of the Viśvaprakāśa, to which this work is appended, as the colophon shows ('viśvaprakāśe śabdabhedaprakāśaḥ'). The closing verses praise Maheśvara as a physician and poet. Jñānavimalagaṇi composed a commentary on the work.

The Śabdabhedaprakāśa ('Illumination of Distinctions among Words') is a Sanskrit orthographic lexicon composed by Maheśvara as a supplement to his Viśvaprakāśa. In four sections (nirdeśas), it catalogues allowable variations in Sanskrit phonology and spelling: general variants, the interchange of ba and va, alternations among sibilants, and differences of gender. It served as a reference for poets and scholars to verify legitimate variants and support verbal figures of speech like anuprāsa, yamaka, and śleṣa.

The Buddhakapālatantra is a Buddhist Yoginītantra centered on the wrathful deity Buddhakapāla ('Buddha-Skull') and his consort Citrasenā. Originating in the same esoteric milieu as the Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra tantras, it features antinomian yogic discipline, cremation-ground rituals, and a prominent focus on Gāruḍa practices used for curing snakebite and counteracting poison. Chapters 9 through 14 cover post-initiatory caryā conduct, herbal and rasāyana lore, Gāruḍa-vidyādhara rites, sexual yoga, meditation on the subtle channels, and the ritual procedure of initiation (abhiṣeka).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the manual as preserved in Institut Français de Pondichéry transcript T. No. 578 (pp. 40–50), covering the daily ritual procedure (upāsanākrama) for the fifteen Nityās and closing with the colophon.

The Cinmantramālinī (subtitled Nityopāsanākrama) is a brief Śākta liturgical ritual manual (paddhati) expounding the daily worship sequence of the fifteen Nityā devīs of the Śrīvidyā tradition according to the Kādimata. It sets forth initial preparatory acts (snāna, prāṇāyāma, bhūtaśuddhi, guru-dhyāna, mātṛkā-nyāsa, and ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) followed by daily visualizations (dhyāna), bījamantras, mudrās, and recitation rules for each of the fifteen lunar days from Kāmeśvarī to Citrā.

- Muktabodha header states: 'Catalog number : E0005', 'Manuscript : IFP transcript T0088', 'Copied from MS no 68462 belonging to the Adyar Library - Madras'
- Internal transcript pagination markers ('p. 2)', 'p. 3)', through 'p. 12)')
- Scribal postscript by IFP scribe Naṭarāja recording transcription from the manuscript in the Adyar Library

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Short tract (12 transcript pages) with many lacunae marked "* * *"; the final colophon is missing and the copyist Naṭarāja records that the concluding sentence of the work is lost ("samāptibodhakavākyaṃ tu naṣṭam"). **Attribution:** Anonymous Śaivasiddhānta tract. The IFP copyist Naṭarāja remarks that the Adyar palm-leaf manuscript seems to have been written by the copyist Mahāgaṇapati Śivācārya, but the author of the work is unknown.

A brief anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta tract on jñānadīkṣā, initiation through knowledge. It sets out the categories of Pati, Paśu and Pāśa (mala, māyā, karma), citing Siddhāntāgamas such as the Mataṅgapārameśvara and Kiraṇa, and treats the awakening of the soul by Śiva's power, including the role of kuṇḍalinī-śakti (as noted in the Muktabodha description). It is not identical with the jñānadīkṣā chapters of the Acintyaviśvasādākhya or of Vedajñāna's Dīkṣādarśa, which open with a similar verse.

The Āgamaprāmāṇya is a foundational philosophical and polemical treatise by the Śrīvaiṣṇava master Yāmunācārya. The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is an important theological and ritual text of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a revelatory discourse taught by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva) to Nārada. The Akulavīratantra is an early Kaula / Yoginī Kaula scriptural text transmitted within the corpus ascribed to Matsyendranātha. It expounds an uncompromising non-dual realization of ultimate reality designated as the Akulavīra ('Hero of the Transcendent'), identified with innate bliss (sahajānanda) and the all-pervading divine nature within the practitioner's own body. Rejecting the doctrines of scholastic systems (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Bauddha, Jaina, Somasiddhānta, Mīmāṃsā) as well as outward ritual and haṭhayogic technicalities, it teaches immediate liberation through effortless dwelling in the transcendent state.

## Contents

**Works in this e-text:**

- Bhogakārikāvṛtti (Aghoraśiva, commentary)

**Attribution:** The root verses are composed by Sadyojyoti (also known as Kheṭakanandana). The vṛtti is by Aghoraśivācārya.

The Bhogakārikā ('Verses on Worldly Experience') by Sadyojyoti is a foundational philosophical treatise of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta tradition and one of the eight canonical primers known collectively as the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. In 146 verses, Sadyojyoti investigates the nature of bhoga (embodied experience of pleasure and pain), explaining how the bound individual soul (paśu)—whose innate powers of consciousness and action are obscured by beginningless primordial impurity (mala)—is endowed by Śiva with bodies, faculties, and worlds evolved out of māyā to experience karmic fruit and mature its impurity. Aghoraśiva's vṛtti elucidates Sadyojyoti's concise verses line by line, rigorously defending the realist ontology of pati (Lord), paśu (soul), and pāśa (bond) against rival arguments from Sāṅkhya, Nyāya, and Buddhist philosophy.

**Attribution:** The root kārikās are by Sadyojyoti. The commentary (vṛtti) is by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (son of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha), explicitly identified in the final verses and the colophon (itiśrīmadbhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭhātmajaśrībhaṭṭarāmakaṇṭhaviracitā paramokṣanirāsakārikāvṛttiḥ samāptā).

The Paramokṣanirāsakārikā is an early Śaiva Siddhānta polemical and doxographical treatise by Sadyojyoti, accompanied here by the comprehensive commentary (vṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha. Across 59 kārikās expounding a passage of the Rauravasūtra, the work systematically refutes twenty non-Śaiva and heterodox soteriological viewpoints—including Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Vedānta, Pāñcarātra, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, and non-Siddhānta Śaiva models—showing that liberation cannot consist in mere isolation, dissolution, cessation of consciousness, or acquisition of mundane qualities. In their place, Sadyojyoti and Rāmakaṇṭha defend the orthodox Siddhānta doctrine that liberation is the manifestation of the soul's innate, co-equal Śiva-nature (śivatvavyakti), consisting in unobstructed omniscience and omnipotence, actualized through initiation (dīkṣā).

A comprehensive late medieval or early modern tantric ritual handbook (paddhati) setting forth the procedures for initiation (dīkṣā), composed by the Maithila scholar Jīvanātha Śarman following Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa's Tantrasāra. ## Contents

**Also known as:** Īśānaśiva

**Attribution:** Attributed in headers and colophons to Īśānaśivagurudeva (also named Īśānaśiva).

The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati is an encyclopedic manual of ritual, temple consecration, and mantra-śāstra composed by the Kerala Śaiva authority Īśānaśivagurudeva (c. 11th–12th century CE). This opening division, the Sāmānyapāda (paṭalas 1–14), provides the common preliminary framework for ritual activity, including the classifications and recitation of mantras, the nature of letters (mātṛkā), the dimensions and preparation of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and diagrams (maṇḍala), morning ablutions, and the rites of the sacred fire (agnikalpa). Synthesizing Śaivasiddhānta tenets with regional Kerala tantric traditions, it serves as a key witness to medieval South Indian ritual literature.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Volume 1 of the KSTS edition (KSTS 60). Contains Adhikāra 1 (Jñānādhikāra), āhnikas 1–3, concluding on p. 299 of the print edition.

**Also known as:** Bṛhatī Vimarśinī, Īśvarapratyabhijñābṛhatīvimarśinī, ĪPVV

**Attribution:** Authored by Abhinavagupta. The work is a commentary on Utpaladeva's Ṭīkā / Vivṛti.

This text comprises Volume 1 of Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī, his extensive philosophical commentary on Utpaladeva's Vivṛti/Ṭīkā to the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā. Adhikāra 1 (Jñānādhikāra) constitutes Volumes 1 and 2 (KSTS 60 and 62).

The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī (also known as the Bṛhatī Vimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's monumental philosophical commentary on Utpaladeva's auto-commentary (Vivṛti) to the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā. It represents one of the most sophisticated masterworks of classical non-dual Kashmir Śaivism.

- Concluding editorial verse at lines 580–581 names the editor: 'śrīmatkaśmīrabhūbharturājñayā prītaye satām | madhusūdanakaulena saṃpādyeyaṃ prakāśitā ||'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Text of the treatise (56 kārikās interspersed with prose vṛtti).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Īśvarasiddhi (Utpaladeva, root text)
- Īśvarasiddhivṛtti (Utpaladeva, autocommentary)

**Also known as:** Īśvarasiddhi, Siddhitrayī: Īśvarasiddhi

**Attribution:** Both the root kārikās and the autocommentary (vṛtti) are composed by Utpaladeva (son of Udayākara), as confirmed in concluding verse 56 and the final colophon (iti śrīmanmahāmāheśvarācāryotpaladevenodayākarasūnunā viracitā īśvarasiddhiḥ samāptā).

The Īśvarasiddhi ('Establishment of the Lord') is one of the three monographs comprising the Siddhitrayī by Utpaladeva, a master of the Pratyabhijñā school of Kashmir Shaivism. Consisting of 56 kārikās and the author's own prose vṛtti, the work defends the necessity of an intelligent conscious agent (Īśvara) behind the cosmos. It critically examines rival models—particularly the Sāṅkhya theory of insentient material transformation (pariṇāmavāda) and the Nyāya inferential proof—before resolving divine agency into recognition (pratyabhijñā).

**Attribution:** The root text is composed by Puṇyānanda. The commentary Cidvallī is composed by Naṭanānanda.

The Kāmakalāvilāsa is a Śrīvidyā treatise by Puṇyānanda expounding the non-dual cosmogonic and metaphysical doctrine of the Supreme Goddess Tripurasundarī. It details the emanation of the universe from the primordial union of illumination (prakāśa) and reflexive awareness (vimarśa) via the kāmakalā—the creative principle embodied in the three primal bindus. The text articulates the manifestation of sacred speech through the four levels of sound and maps this cosmogony onto the geometry and presiding deities of the Śrīcakra. The accompanying Cidvallī commentary by Naṭanānanda provides essential elucidation of the esoteric terminology and ritual correlations.

**Also known as:** Kaṅkālamālinī, Kaṅkālamālinītantram

**Attribution:** Canonical Śākta tantra cast in the form of a dialogue between Śrībhairavī and Śrībhairava (Śiva).

The Kaṅkālamālinītantra ('Tantra of the Goddess Garlanded with Skeletons') is a five-paṭala Śākta text of the Kālīkula tradition, internally attributed to the Southern transmission (Dakṣiṇāmnāya). Framed as a dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, it expounds the esoteric correspondence between the fifty phonemes of the Sanskrit alphabet (mātṛkā) and Śiva-Śakti, followed by yogic teachings on the six cakras, yonimudrā, and the ascent and descent of Kuṇḍalinī. It further prescribes the worship of the Goddess and her attendant ḍākinīs, along with instructions on puraścaraṇa and devotion to the guru.

The Kulārṇavatantra ('Ocean of the Kula') is one of the foundational scriptural texts of the Kaula tradition within Śākta Tantrism, framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess. Comprising seventeen ullāsas (chapters) and more than two thousand verses, the text presents the doctrine and ritual praxis of the Ūrdhvāmnāya (upper transmission). _LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski; catalog no. M00032).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha catalog header: 'Catalog number : M00032', 'Description: Text is vol. 26 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies', 'Publisher : Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State', 'Publication year : 1918', 'Publication city : Srinigar'.

**Other editions:**

- Parimoo, B. N. The Ascent of Self: A Re-interpretation of the Mystical Poetry of Lalla-Dēd. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1978.

**Translations:**
- Grierson, George A., and Lionel D. Barnett, Lallā-Vākyāni. 1920. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Comprising 60 Kashmiri vākhs, 60 Sanskrit metrical verses, and concluding dedicatory śloka and colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Lalleśvarīvākyāni (Lalleśvarī, root text)
- Arthacchāyāpadya (Bhāskarakaṇṭha, translation)

**Also known as:** Lallāvākyāni, Lallā-Vākyāni, Sayings of Lal Ded

**Attribution:** The root verses are Kashmiri quatrains attributed to the 14th-century female mystic Lallā (Lalleśvarī / Lal Dĕd). Each Kashmiri verse is paired with a metrical Sanskrit verse translation (arthacchāyāpadya) composed by Rājānaka Bhāskara (Bhāskarakaṇṭha, 18th century).

The Lalleśvarīvākyāni ('Sayings of Lalleśvarī') comprises 60 mystical Kashmiri quatrains (vākhs) by the 14th-century poet-saint Lallā (Lal Dĕd), accompanied verse-for-verse by Sanskrit metrical translations (arthacchāyāpadya) composed by the 18th-century Kashmiri Śaiva scholar Rājānaka Bhāskarakaṇṭha. Rooted in nondual Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism, the verses convey internal yogic absorption, prāṇāyāma, mind control, critique of ritualism and external caste distinctions, and the nondual realization of the Self as Śiva. As the earliest attested literary compositions in the Kashmiri language, Lallā's verses hold foundational importance in Kashmiri literary and religious culture, while Bhāskarakaṇṭha's translation represents their earliest formal reception in classical Sanskrit scholarship.

The Mahānayaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Great Way') is an anonymous Sanskrit verse treatise belonging to the esoteric Krama (Mahānaya/Mahārtha) school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Divided into nine ullāsas, it systematically presents the sequential and non-sequential cycles of divine manifestation and reabsorption, focusing on the wheels of deities (cakras), the pīṭhas, and the twelve forms of Kālī. It emphasizes the direct transmission of non-dual realization through the grace and penetrating glance of the guru (gurudṛkpāta) as superior to external ritual practices.

The Mṛgendrāgama (or Mṛgendratantra) is an authoritative scripture of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally regarded as an upāgama of the Kāmikāgama. This e-text contains its philosophical Vidyāpāda and practical Yogapāda, which formulate core Siddhānta ontology across the categories of pati (the Lord), paśu (the bound individual), and pāśa (fetters/bonds), followed by an exposition of tantric yoga. The root text is accompanied by the commentary (Mṛgendravṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and the sub-commentary (Dīpikā) of Aghoraśiva.

The Nareśvaraparīkṣā ('Examination of the Soul and the Lord') by Sadyojyoti is an early systematic treatise of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta. Comprising verses across three kāṇḍas, it establishes the distinct ontologies of the individual soul (nara/paśu) and the supreme Lord (īśvara/pati), countering Buddhist, Sāṅkhya, and Advaitin models. - Textual agreement with KSTS 69, including the opening prose commentary on verse 1, complete 35 kārikās, Lakṣmīrāma's concluding signature stanza ('dṛṣṭvā durghaṭanāṃ śāstre guptapādairvinirmite / rājānalasakenaiṣā trīśikāvivṛtiḥ kṛtā'), and the final colophon ('iti śrīrājānakalakṣmīrāmakṛtā parātrīśikālaghuvivṛtiḥ samāptā').

## Contents

The vivṛti (referred to in the closing verse as Trīśikāvivṛti and in the concluding colophon as Parātrīśikālaghuvivṛti) is authored by Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma (also known as Lasa Kāk).

In 35 verses, Śiva (Bhairava) expounds to the Goddess the mystery of the supreme reality (anuttara), the Goddess Parā as non-dual awareness, and the esoteric phonemic emanations (mātṛkā) through which cosmos and mantra manifest. In this vivṛti, Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma provides an exposition of the text in light of Abhinavagupta's earlier work.

- Muktabodha header names the editor Muralīdhara Jhā, publisher Prabhakari and Co, and publication city Benaras.

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the third and final volume (tṛtīyakhaṇḍa) of the work, comprising taraṅgas 9 to 12 in full. Taraṅgas 1–8 are contained in volumes 1 and 2.

**Also known as:** Puraścaraṇārṇava, Purascharyarnava

**Attribution:** Attributed in all chapter colophons to King Pratāpasiṃha Śāha of Nepal (r. 1775–1777). In keeping with traditional royal digests, the compilation was executed under his patronage by court scholars.

The Puraścaryārṇava ('Ocean of Preliminary Ritual Practice') is an encyclopedic Śākta and Tāntrika ritual digest (nibandha) compiled under the auspices of King Pratāpasiṃha Śāha of Nepal (r. 1775–1777). This third volume contains taraṅgas 9 through 12, completing the twelve-chapter digest. It covers the mantras and puraścaraṇa rituals of the Daśamahāvidyās (taraṅga 9), other deities including Sarasvatī alongside Vaidika mantras like the Gāyatrī (taraṅga 10), the worship of Durgā with an extensive manual for the autumnal Durgotsava / Navarātri (taraṅga 11), and the mantras, yantras, stotras, and kavacas of Brāhmī and various other deities (taraṅga 12). Citing scores of canonical tantras, Purāṇas, and earlier ritual paddhatis, it is an essential reference for northern Indian and Nepalese tantric liturgy.

The Parāprāveśikā ('Initiation into the Supreme') is a concise prose primer (prakaraṇa) of non-dual Kashmirian Śaiva (Trika / Pratyabhijñā) philosophy authored by Kṣemarāja. It serves as an accessible introduction to the school's doctrine, expounding ultimate reality as luminous consciousness (prakāśa) endowed with dynamic self-awareness (vimarśa). The work outlines the manifestation of the thirty-six cosmic principles (tattvas) and explicates the esoteric significance of phonemic emanation centered on the seed syllable of the Supreme Goddess (hṛdayabīja / Parā).

The Mahānirvāṇatantra is an influential Śākta work structured as a discourse between Sadāśiva and the Goddess (Ādyā Śakti) on ritual and moral duty in the degraded Kali Yuga. **Also known as:** Kriyāsāra

**Attribution:** Composed by Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, who characterizes himself in the colophons as an authority on the 101 stages of Vīraśaiva philosophy ('śrīmadviśiṣṭādvaitasiddhāntarahasyaikottaraśatasthalābhijña').

The Kriyāsāra ('Essence of Practice') by Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya (c. 14th–15th century CE) is a major Vīraśaiva metrical treatise harmonizing Śaiva ritual, ethical conduct, and devotional observance with the philosophical framework of the Brahmasūtras. Structured into thirty-one chapters (upadeśas), the text systematically expounds the doctrine of the 101 stages (ekottaraśatasthala) and daily religious duties. This portion comprises Upadeśas 5 through 14, focusing on regular and occasional duties (ācāra), the theological symbolism and rites of holy ash (bhasma) and rudrākṣa, ablutions, sandhyā, and the liturgical manual of Śiva worship (śivapūjā).

**Edition used (determined):** Vāmakeśvaratantrāntargatanityāṣoḍaśikārṇavaḥ śrībhāskararāyonnītasetubandhākhyavyākhyānasahitaḥ, ed. K. V. Abhyaṅkara, Ānandāśramasaṃskṛtagranthāvaliḥ 56, Pune: Ānandāśrama, 1946 (as stated in the Muktabodha header).

**Other editions:**

- Madhusūdan Kaul Śāstrī (ed.), The Vāmakeśvarīmatam with the Commentary of Rājānaka Jayaratha, KSTS 64, Srinagar, 1945. — Kashmirian recension with Jayaratha's Vivaraṇa.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text runs from the edition's title and Bhāskararāya's introductory verses to the final colophon, i.e. all eight viśrāmas: 1–5 on the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava and 6–8 on the Yoginīhṛdaya. Page markers of ASS 56 run from p. 2 to p. 388. Two passages are missing: printed pp. 25–40 and pp. 105–112.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (pūrvacatuḥśatī of the Vāmakeśvaratantra) (root text (viśrāmas 1–5))
- Yoginīhṛdaya (uttaracatuḥśatī) (root text (viśrāmas 6–8))
- Setubandha (Bhāskararāya, commentary on both)

**Also known as:** Vāmakeśvaratantra (with Setubandha), Vāmakeśvarīmata, Catuḥśatī, Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇavatantra, Vāmakeśvaratantrāntargatanityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (title of ASS 56)

**Attribution:** Both root texts are anonymous scriptural tantras of Śrīvidyā. The Setubandha is by Bhāskararāya (dīkṣā name Bhāsurānandanātha), son of Gambhīrarāja Dīkṣita. The final colophon reads 'iti ... gambhīrarājabhāratīdikṣitasūnunā bhāsurānandanāthadīkṣābhidhānena bhāskararāyeṇa praṇīto nityāṣoḍaśikārṇavavyākhyānātmā setubandhaḥ saṃpūrṇaḥ'.

The Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (the pūrvacatuḥśatī of the Vāmakeśvaratantra) and the Yoginīhṛdaya (its uttaracatuḥśatī) are foundational scriptures of Śākta Śrīvidyā. The first sets out the outer worship of Tripurasundarī and the sixteen Nityās: mantras, the Śrīcakra, mudrās and ritual applications. The second treats the inner meaning of cakra, mantra and pūjā. This e-text gives both with the Setubandha, the extensive commentary by the 18th-century scholar Bhāskararāya, which uses Mīmāṃsā methods to treat the two parts as one tantra in eight viśrāmas.

It gathers individual ritual manuals ('tantras') for śākta and related divinities, including the Mahāvidyās, Kumārī, and Pañcāyatana deities, providing meditation verses (dhyāna), mantras, nyāsa rites, worship sequences, kavacas, and sahasranāmas.

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophons to Mahāmahopādhyāya Ṭhakkura Śrī-Narasiṃha (Narasiṃha Ṭhakkura).

The Tārābhaktisudhārṇava ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotion to Tārā') is an extensive Śākta ritual digest (nibandha) dedicated to the worship of the Mahāvidyā Tārā in her various forms (including Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī). Divided into eleven taraṅgas ('waves'), it provides comprehensive ritual guidance on guru-disciple requirements, initiation (dīkṣā), daily worship, mantra recitation (japa), yantra designs, nyāsa, puraścaraṇa, and esoteric rites such as śavasādhana, compiling canonical passages from scriptures such as the Rudrayāmala, Brahmayāmala, and Tārātantra.

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Prāṇatoṣiṇī: tantraśāstrāt saṃkalayya viracitā, compiled by Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya, published by Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācārya. Calcutta: Jivanand Vidyasagar, 1898.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00061; data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski).

**Evidence:**
- Title lines preserve the printed title-page imprint: 'Prāṇatoṣiṇī śrīrāmatoṣaṇa bhaṭṭācaryyeṇa tantraśāstrāt saṃkalayya viracitā | Vi, e upādhidhāriṇā paṇḍitakulapatinā śrījīvānandavidyāsāgarabhaṭṭāacaryyeṇa prakāśitā'.

**Other editions:**
- Prāṇatoṣiṇī, in Tantrasārādivividhatantrasaṃgraha. Calcutta (Bengali script). — Mentioned in Muktabodha description: 'Originally published by kalikātā in Bengali script in the tantrasārādivividhatantrasaṃgraha'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the concluding portion of Kāṇḍa 5 (Bhaktikāṇḍa, pariccheda 4, pp. 691–782, covering Dvārakāśilā, Viṣṇu, Devī/Mahāvidyā rituals, and Kumārīpūjā), the full Kāṇḍa 6 (Jñānakāṇḍa, lines 2816–7038, covering yogic anatomy, nāḍīs, cakras, and svarodaya), and the full Kāṇḍa 7 (Nirguṇakāṇḍa, lines 7038–11609, treating paśu, vīra, and divya bhāvas, Kaula worship, and closing recipes), ending at line 11609 with 'iti śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī samāptā'.

**Also known as:** Prāṇatoṣiṇī Tantra, Prāṇatoṣaṇī, Prāṇatoṣiṇī part 6, Prāṇatoṣiṇī Jñānakāṇḍa

**Attribution:** Compiled in 1820 CE by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṃkāra.

The Prāṇatoṣiṇī is an extensive Śākta tantric digest (nibandha) compiled in 1820 CE by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra. Bringing together citations from scores of Tantras, Purāṇas, and ritual compendia, it forms an encyclopedic reference work of the late traditional Bengali Śākta school. This segment contains the latter part of the Bhaktikāṇḍa (worship of sacred stones and Kumārīpūjā), the entire Jñānakāṇḍa (yogic subtle physiology, cakras, and breath divination in Svarodaya), and the entire Nirguṇakāṇḍa (the three spiritual temperaments or bhāvas, Kaula worship, and culminating verses of the entire text).

The Kulapradīpa ('Lamp of the Kula') is a Sanskrit Śākta-Kaula compendium (nibandha) in seven chapters (prakāśa) composed in verse by Śivānandācārya. Drawing heavily upon authoritative Āgamic sources such as the Kulārṇavatantra, it provides an exposition of the doctrines and ritual practices of the Kaula path, including the distinction between dakṣiṇa and vāma conduct, the purification and use of the five substances (pañcamakāra), dūtīyāga, and cakra worship.

The Jñānārṇavatantra ('Ocean of Knowledge') is an authoritative scripture of the Śākta Tantric tradition and one of the principal scriptural sources for the Kādi division of Śrīvidyā. Cast in 26 paṭalas as a revelation by Īśvara to Devī, the work begins with esoteric expositions of the sacred alphabet (akṣamālā / mātṛkā), the phonematic matrix, and the threefold bindu. The remaining chapters detail the internal and ritual pūjā of Mahātripurasundarī and her attendants, yantra meditations, mantra recitation, and seasonal observances, culminating in the damanāropaṇa rite.

It functions as an indispensable textual compendium preserving liturgical quotations from numerous otherwise obscure Tantras and Purāṇas.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Text of the 90-paṭala recension of the Uttaratantra (paṭalas 1–90, ending at verse 90.51).

**Also known as:** Rudrayāmala, Rudrayāmalatantra, Rudrayāmala (Uttaratantra), Rudrayāmala (Uttarakhaṇḍa), Rudrayāmalatantra (Uttarakāṇḍa), Rudrayāmalottaratantra

**Attribution:** Revealed Tantric scripture cast as a dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.

The Rudrayāmala is traditionally celebrated as one of the major early Śaiva-Śākta Yāmala tantras, although the ancient scripture cited by non-dual Kashmirian Śaiva authors survives only in fragmentary quotations. The extant Uttaratantra (presented here in its extensive 90-paṭala recension) is a later Kaula-Śākta compilation devoted to esoteric yoga, ritual, and mantra practice. It provides detailed expositions of Kuṇḍalinī yoga, subtle bodily physiology, the cakras along with their presiding Śaktis (Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī), guru-sevā, and the worship of goddesses such as Kumārī, Tripurasundarī, and Mahākālī.

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophons to Śrīmad-Ativarṇāśramācāryavarya-Śaivaparipālaka-Śivāgrayogīndra-Jñānaśivācārya (Śivāgrayogin).

The Śaivaparibhāṣā is a Sanskrit manual of Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy composed by Śivāgrayogin, patterned after dialectical manuals such as the Vedāntaparibhāṣā. In five chapters, the work methodically details the epistemology (pramāṇa) and the three central ontological categories—the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu), and the fetters of bondage (pāśa)—before concluding with the path of initiation and liberation (mukti). Drawing heavily on the Saiddhāntika Āgamas (particularly the Pauṣkarāgama), it represents a major milestone in the late Sanskrit scholasticism of the school.

**Evidence:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Sambandhasiddhi and its autocommentary, comprising 20 numbered verses, one unnumbered concluding stanza, and the interspersed prose vṛtti, corresponding precisely to pp. 1–15 of KSTS 34.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Sambandhasiddhi (Utpaladeva, root text)
- Sambandhasiddhivṛtti (Utpaladeva, autocommentary)

**Also known as:** Saṃbandhasiddhi, Siddhitrayī: Sambandhasiddhi

**Attribution:** Utpaladeva explicitly identifies himself as the author in the final colophon as the son of Udayākara (śrīmadudayākaraputrotpaladevācāryaviracitā saṃbandhasiddhiḥ samāptā). He composed both the kārikā stanzas and the prose vṛtti.

The Sambandhasiddhi ('Establishment of Relation') is one of the three foundational polemical monographs constituting Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī. Composed in verse with an integral prose autocommentary (vṛtti), the text defends the ontological and linguistic reality of relations (sambandha) against Buddhist nominalist critiques, particularly Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā. Integrating Bhartṛhari's grammatical philosophy with non-dual Pratyabhijñā metaphysics, Utpaladeva argues that relation as identity-in-difference cannot subsist purely among insentient entities, but necessarily depends on the synthesizing, reflective awareness (vimarśa, anusaṃdhāna) of universal consciousness (Śiva).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Spandasaṃdoha, which constitutes an exhaustive commentary on the first verse of the Spandakārikā.

**Attribution:** The Spandasandoha is a work of Kṣemarāja.

The Spandasaṃdoha ('Essence/Collection of Vibration') is an early exegetical work by Rājānaka Kṣemarāja dedicated exclusively to commenting on the opening verse of the Spandakārikā ('yasyonmeṣanimeṣābhyāṃ...'). In this text, Kṣemarāja demonstrates how this single benedictory stanza encapsulates the full metaphysical doctrine of Spanda—the dynamic pulsation and self-awareness of Śiva—along with the divine fivefold cosmic act (pañcakṛtya). Integrating Spanda doctrine with Pratyabhijñā and Krama concepts, it serves as an introduction to his later, comprehensive commentary on the entire kārikā corpus, the Spandanirṇaya.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains all four pādas—Kriyāpāda, Caryāpāda, Yogapāda, and Jñānapāda—but terminates abruptly at verse 3.230 of the Jñānapāda without an explicit or final colophon.

**Also known as:** Suprabheda

**Attribution:** Canonical Śaiva Siddhānta scripture; anonymous revealed text.

The Suprabhedāgama is one of the twenty-eight canonical Mūlāgamas of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally categorized among the five Śivabhedas emanating from the Vāmadeva face of Śiva. It is one of the relatively few Āgamas preserved across all four classical divisions (pādas): Kriyāpāda (temple layout, iconography, installation of liṅgas, and daily/occasional worship rituals), Caryāpāda (initiation, duties of devotees, royal rites, and expiation), Yogapāda (subtle anatomy, prāṇāyāma, and meditation), and Jñānapāda (cosmogony, thirty-six tattvas, and the adhvans). It has long served as a prominent ritual authority for South Indian temple architecture and liturgical performance.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Tārātantra in 6 paṭalas (concluding at segment 328 with '[ samāpto'yaṃ granthaḥ ]'), followed by the editor's three appendices of related extracts on Mahācīnācāra from the Brahmayāmala, Rudrayāmala, and Mīnanātha's Smaradīpikā (segments 329–575).

- Rudrayāmala (extract) (appendix)
- Smaradīpikā (extract) (Mīnanātha, appendix)

**Also known as:** Tārātantram, Taratantra

**Attribution:** Revealed Śākta scripture framed as a dialogue between Śiva (Bhairava) and the Devī (Bhairavī). No human author is attributed.

The Tārātantra is a short Śākta scripture in six paṭalas formatted as a dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, devoted to the worship of the Mahāvidyā goddess Tārā (in forms such as Ugratārā and Ekajaṭā). It details her five-syllable root mantra, visualizations (dhyāna), daily liturgy (prātaḥkṛtya, guru-pūjā), and magical rites (ṣaṭkarman). The text is especially renowned for its integration of the Mahācīnakrama ('Chinese/Tibetan rite'), recounting how both the sage Vasiṣṭha and the Buddha attained spiritual perfection (siddhi) through this esoteric discipline.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 4 paṭalas, matching the 82 pages of the Calcutta print edition.

**Also known as:** Tārārahasyatantra

**Attribution:** Authored by Brahmānandagiri (also referred to as Śrī Brahmānanda Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka).

The Tārārahasya ('Secret of Tārā') by Brahmānandagiri is a fundamental ritual manual (nibandha) dedicated to the worship, mantras, and meditative forms (dhyāna) of the Mahāvidyā Tārā and her manifestations (such as Ugratārā, Nīlasarasvatī, and Ekajaṭā). Divided into four chapters (paṭalas), it incorporates both normative tantric ritual procedures and the esoteric Mahācīnakrama. Synthesizing citations from older authorities such as the Nīlatantra, Mahācīnatantra, and Rudrayāmala, it served as one of the primary handbooks of the Tārā cult across Bengal and Assam.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 36 paṭalas, containing both the root kārikā verses and the running Manoramā commentary up to the closing praśasti and final colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Tantrarājatantra (root text)
- Manoramā (paṭalas 1–22) (Subhagānandanātha, commentary)
- Manoramā (paṭalas 23–36) (Prakāśānandanātha, commentary)

**Also known as:** Tantrarāja, Kādimatatantrarāja

**Attribution:** The root Tantrarājatantra is an anonymous scriptural revelation of the Kādimata division of Śrīvidyā Śāktism, framed as a dialogue between Śiva and Devī. The running commentary Manoramā was composed through paṭala 22 by Subhagānandanātha and completed for the remaining fourteen chapters (paṭalas 23–36) by his disciple Prakāśānandanātha (Prakāśānandadeśika), as explicitly recorded in the closing verses of paṭala 36.

The Tantrarājatantra is one of the primary canonical scriptures of the Kādimata lineage within the Śākta Śrīvidyā tradition, structured in 36 chapters as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and the Devī. It presents comprehensive instruction on the worship of Lalitā Mahā-Tripurasundarī and the fifteen Nityā goddesses, detailing mantra formulas, yantra geometry, the nyāsa rites of the Śrīcakra, and non-dual Śākta metaphysics. In this edition, the scripture is accompanied by the running Manoramā commentary, written up through chapter 22 by Subhagānandanātha and finished for chapters 23–36 by his disciple Prakāśānandanātha.

**Edition used (determined):** Kriyākramadyotikā of Aghoraśiva with the Commentary of Nirmalamaṇi. Cidambaram: Jñānasambandham Press, 1927 (Grantha script, 523 pp.).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00126), data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski from a printed Grantha edition supplied by Richard Davis.

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha catalog header: 'Description: Transcribed from a 1927 cidambaram edition in Grantha script supplied by Richard Davis. Publisher : cidambaram, Publication year : 1927'.
- Printed page markers matching the 523-page 1927 Chidambaram publication appear throughout the text ('p. 2)', 'p. 3)', through 'p. 523)').
- Concluding colophon at p. 523: 'iti śrīmatkamalālayanivāsi bhaktādhyakṣasantānaprabhavatyāgarājācāryātmajanirmalamaṇiguru viracitāyāmasphuṭārtha prakāśikāyāṃ prabhāsamākhyāyāṃ kriyākramadyotikā vyākhyāyāṃ damanavidhissamāptaḥ ||'.

**Other editions:**
- Mahotsavavidhi. Reprinted after resetting by the South India Arcaka Association, 1974. — Standalone printed edition of the festival manual portion.

- Davis, Richard H. Ritual in an Oscillating Universe: Worshipping Śiva in Medieval India. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991. (English)
- Davis, Richard H. A translation and study of the Mahotsavavidhi attributed to Aghoraśiva (2010). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Corresponds to pages 1–523 of the 1927 Chidambaram edition, breaking off at the end of the Damanavidhi. It contains daily worship (nityakarma/śivapūjā), initiations (dīkṣā), and seasonal renewal rites (pavitrāropaṇa, damanāropaṇa), but lacks later sections such as funerary and post-mortuary rites (antyeṣṭi, śrāddha), temple installation (pratiṣṭhā), the festival manual (mahotsava), and expiations (prāyaścitta).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kriyākramadyotikā (Aghoraśiva, root text)
- Prabhā (Nirmalamaṇi, commentary)

**Also known as:** Aghoraśivapaddhati, Kriyākramadyotikāpaddhati, Asphuṭārthaprakāśikā

**Attribution:** The root paddhati was composed by Aghoraśiva. The commentary Prabhā (formally titled Asphuṭārthaprakāśikā) was composed by Nirmalamaṇi, son of Tyāgarājācārya, resident in Kamalālaya.

The Kriyākramadyotikā is a ritual handbook of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition by Aghoraśiva. This e-text transmits the paddhati alongside Nirmalamaṇi's commentary Prabhā (Asphuṭārthaprakāśikā) up through the Damanavidhi section.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete Sundarīkhaṇḍa (the third of four khaṇḍas comprising the Śaktisaṅgamatantra), consisting of 21 paṭalas.

**Also known as:** Śaktisaṅgama Mahātantrarāja, Śaktisaṃgamatantra, Sundarīkhaṇḍa

**Attribution:** A Śākta tantric scripture framed as a dialogue between Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā.

The Sundarīkhaṇḍa is the third section of the extensive Śākta compendium Śaktisaṅgamatantra, framed as a dialogue between Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. In 21 chapters (paṭalas), it expounds rituals, mantras, and esoteric doctrines centering on the goddess Tripurasundarī (Lalitā) and the Śrīvidyā tradition, detailing initiation (dīkṣā), nyāsas, Śrīcakra worship, and related Mahāvidyās such as Dhūmāvatī. The section is also well known in South Asian historiography for its seventh paṭala (the Deśavyavasthāniyama / Ṣaṭpañcāśaddeśavibhāga), which provides a valuable late-medieval geographical gazetteer dividing the subcontinent into fifty-six regions.

The Tantrasāra ('Essence of Tantra') is an influential prose compendium composed by the Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta as an accessible digest of his monumental encyclopedic treatise, the Tantrāloka. Arranged into 22 āhnikas ('daily lessons'), the work systematically expounds the metaphysics, ritual, yoga, and soteriology of the non-dual Trika and Pratyabhijñā traditions. It is centrally structured around the hierarchy of means to spiritual liberation—anupāya, śāmbhavopāya, śāktopāya, and āṇavopāya—alongside an extensive treatment of the descent of divine grace (śaktipāta) and initiation rituals (dīkṣā).

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha catalog header explicitly identifies KSTS vol. 32 (misnumbered 31) published by the Research Department Jammu and Kashmir State in Srinagar, 1921.
- The e-text title page text (lines 11–24) faithfully reproduces the printed KSTS front matter: 'kāśmīrasaṃskṛtagranthāvaliḥ | granthāṅkaḥ 31 | śrīmālinīvijayavārtikam... madhusūdanakaula śāstriṇā... 1921'.
- Concluding editorial verses at lines 3285–3286 explicitly state: 'śrīmatpratāpabhūbharturājñayā prītaye satām | madhusūdanakaulena saṃpādyedaṃ prakāśitam ||'.

**Other editions:**
- Jürgen Hanneder, Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998. — Critical edition and annotated translation of Kāṇḍa 1, vv. 1–399.

**Translations:**
- Jürgen Hanneder, Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in two books (kāṇḍas): Kāṇḍa 1 contains 1,079 verses and Kāṇḍa 2 contains 335 verses. Although the treatise itself expounds only the opening verse/portion (ādimavākya) of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, both surviving kāṇḍas that comprise the full work are present.

**Also known as:** Mālinīślokavārttika, Mālinīvijayottaraślokavārttika, Mālinīvijayavārtika

**Attribution:** Firmly attributed to Abhinavagupta in the opening verses and the colophons of both kāṇḍas.

The Mālinīvijayavārttika (also known as the Mālinīślokavārttika) is a major verse commentary composed by Abhinavagupta interpreting the opening sentence of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the foundational scriptural authority of the Trika Śaiva lineage. Arranged in two books (kāṇḍas), the text formulates a comprehensive theology of revelation (āgama), hermeneutics, and nondual metaphysics while mounting extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā.

**Edition used (determined):** Jagaddhar Zadoo (ed.), The Uddamareshvara Tantram, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS), Srinagar: Research Department of Jammu and Kashmir State, 1947.

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha catalog metadata explicitly specifies: 'Uniform title: uḍḍāmeśvaratantra', 'Editor : Zadoo J. D.', 'Description: Photographic facsimiles from vol 70 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies', 'Publisher : Research Department Jammu and Kashmir State', 'Publication year : 1947', 'Publication city : Srinigar'.
- E-text preamble and footer confirm: 'Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Catalog number : M00169'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text comprising all 15 paṭalas (chapters), preceded by the introductory table of contents (viṣayānukramaṇī) and followed by the editor's comparative index/glossary of 140 botanical and mineral preparations with Hindi names and Latin binomial identifications.

**Also known as:** Uḍḍāmareśvaramahātantra, The Uddamareshvara Tantram

**Attribution:** Anonymous Śaiva-Śākta tantra cast as a dialogue between Gaurī and Śiva. The colophons at the conclusion of each chapter describe the work as an extraction from the Vīrabhadreśvaratantra (iti śrīśivaprokte vīrabhadreśvaratantroddhṛte uḍḍāmareśvaramahātantre).

The Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra (also styled Uḍḍāmareśvaramahātantra) is a 15-chapter applied Tantric manual dedicated primarily to pragmatic magic and ritual pharmacology (ṣaṭkarman rites such as vaśīkaraṇa, uccāṭana, stambhana, and māraṇa). It details incantations, herbal and mineral recipes (auṣadhi), and counter-sorcery remedies for curing fevers, expelling demonic and planetary possession (bhūtas, grahas, brahmarākṣasas), counteracting poisons, and evoking yakṣiṇīs and related semi-divine entities for material acquisition. The work is structured as an instruction delivered by Śiva to Gaurī and belongs to the wider milieu of practical medieval grimoire literature closely allied with the Uḍḍīśa/Uḍḍāmara traditions.

The Jñānasaṅkalinītantra ('Tantra of the Collection of Gnosis') is a concise Śākta-Śaiva tantric treatise framed as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Śiva and the Devī. It subordinates external ritualism, caste prescriptions, and scholastic learning to internal non-dual knowledge (brahmajñāna) and subtle yogic contemplation. The text expounds the esoteric anatomy of the body (piṇḍa) as identical to the cosmos (brahmāṇḍa), identifying the internal channels iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā with sacred rivers (Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī), and explains the symbolic significance of the Praṇava (Oṃ) alongside inner mudrās such as khecarī and śāmbhavī.

- Literature citation (Bühnemann 2000): 'MT Merutantra Merutantram. Edited by R. Ojha. Bombay: Śrīveṅkaṭeśvar Steam Press 1908'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 35 prakāśas (chapters), concluding with the final colophon of prakāśa 35 ('iti śrīmahāmāyāmahākālānumate merutantre śivapraṇīte kārttavīryyārjunamantrakathanaṃ nāma pañcatriṃśattamaḥ prakāśaḥ || 35 || samāptaścāyaṃ granthaḥ ||').

- Merutantra (root text)
- Ṭippanī (Raghunātha Śāstrī Ojha, commentary)

**Also known as:** Merutantra, Merutantram

**Attribution:** Revealed scriptural tantra presented as a dialogue between Śiva and Śivā (śrīśivaśivāsaṃvādopanibaddha, śrīmahāmāyāmahākālānumate merutantre śivapraṇīte). The bracketed glosses, liturgical clarifications, and variant readings (ṭippanī) embedded in the text are by Paṇḍita Raghunātha Śāstrī Ojha.

The Merutantra is an encyclopedic Śaiva-Śākta tantric manual comprising 35 chapters (prakāśas), framed as a revelation given by Sadāśiva on Mount Meru to the gods after their distress under the demon Jalandhara. Functioning much like a nibandha (digest) of mantra-śāstra and ritual practice, it details initiation (dīkṣā), preliminary discipline (puraścaraṇa), nyāsa, and rituals for numerous deities, including Mahākāla, Devī, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, and Kārtavīryārjuna. Containing notable historical anachronisms, such as predictions naming London, Christianity, and the British (chapter 35), the text in its present form dates to the early modern period (ca. 16th–18th century CE).

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Acephalous and truncated transcription of a single manuscript witness; the text opens abruptly in the midst of ritual/mantra instructions on folio 18b/19a and breaks off mid-word at line 712 ('paraśi----------------') without a concluding colophon or formal chapter division.

**Also known as:** Kiñcittantra, Kiñcit tantra, NGMPP MS 4-1867

**Attribution:** Anonymous Kaula Śākta-Śaiva tantric text. The title 'Kiñcitatantra' appears to stem from a descriptive cataloguer's label in Nepal (kiñcit tantram, i.e., 'a certain [unidentified] tantra') rather than an intrinsic textual title.

An acephalous and truncated Kaula Śākta-Śaiva ritual fragment preserved in an unedited Nepalese manuscript, focusing on Guhyakālikā and associated fierce deities such as Cāmuṇḍā, Siddhilakṣmī, and the Aṣṭamātṛkās. The text details esoteric mantra vidyās, nyāsa prescriptions, samayavidyā recitation, and fierce Kaula rites (including māraṇa and samādhividhi). The Sanskrit exhibits extensive non-standard orthography and vernacular corruption characteristic of medieval Nepalese tantric transmission.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_TridasadaamaratantresiddhikaaliistotramHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition; unpublished transcription of the Nepalese manuscript microfilmed by the NGMCP as reel H 334/6 (Muktabodha catalog no. M00203).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (data-entered by Muktabodha staff under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, Release 0: February 12, 2010; catalog number M00203).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha file header: 'Uniform title: tridaśaḍāmaratantre siddhikaalīstotra', 'Manuscript : NGMCP reel no. H 334/6', 'Catalog number : M00203'
- Muktabodha header: 'Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Release 0: February 12, 2010'
- Manuscript folio markers embedded in text ('p. 1b', 'p. 2', 'p. 3a', 'p. 3b', 'p. 4a')
- Colophons of the individual pieces (segs 124, 750, 834, 1003, 1040, 1077) and Newari ritual rubrics show this is a single ritual manuscript, not a printed edition.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete transcription of the manuscript on NGMCP reel H 334/6 as filmed (ms pp. 1b–71b), ending 'śubhaṃ || pūrṇam'. The first lines (segs 7–10) duplicate the closing cakrapūjā rubrics (a misplaced final leaf). The Siddhikālīstotra itself is complete but forms only a small part of the e-text.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Rāhugrahapūjā and Navagrahapūjā (ritual instructions (segs 11–26))
- Mahāmāryāṣṭakastotra (ascribed to the Rudrayāmala, Kālīkhaṇḍa; ṛṣi Vararuci) (stotra with nyāsa (segs 27–125))
- Koṭhalāccha kṣetrapāla- and cakrapūjā (ritual instructions (segs 126–248))
- Parānityārcanavidhi (ritual (segs 249–329))
- Trailokyavijaya mantragarbha Śyāmāsahasranāmastotra (ascribed to the Rudrayāmala) (stotra (segs 373–751))
- Pratyaṅgirāpūjā (ritual (segs 525–586))
- Pañcamukhīhanumatkavaca (ascribed to the Sudarśanasaṃhitā) (kavaca (segs 754–834))
- Pratyaṅgirāstotra (ascribed to the Kubjikāmata) (stotra/mālāmantra (segs 837–1004))
- Siddhikālīstotra (ascribed to the Tridaśaḍāmara) (stotra (segs 1018–1040))
- Siddhikālīmantroddhāra (ascribed to the Tridaśaḍāmara) (mantra section (segs 1043–1077))
- Tritattvaśodhanapūjāvidhi and concluding cakrapūjā (ritual (segs 1099–1200))

**Also known as:** Tridaśaḍāmaratantre Siddhikālīstotra, Siddhikālīstotra (Tridaśaḍāmara)

**Attribution:** Anonymous Nepalese (Newar) ritual compilation; individual pieces are ascribed in their colophons to the Rudrayāmala, Sudarśanasaṃhitā, Kubjikāmata and Tridaśaḍāmara(tantra). The Mahāmāryāṣṭaka names Vararuci as its ṛṣi (traditional viniyoga), not as an author.

A Nepalese Śākta ritual manuscript with Newari rubrics, combining navagraha worship, the Mahāmāryāṣṭaka (a protective hymn to Mahāmārī/Kālī ascribed to the Rudrayāmala), a mantra-laden Śyāmā-sahasranāma, a Pañcamukhī-Hanumat-kavaca, a Pratyaṅgirā hymn ascribed to the Kubjikāmata, and the brief Siddhikālīstotra and Siddhikālī mantroddhāra ascribed to the Tridaśaḍāmara, framed by pūjā, bali and cakrapūjā procedures. It documents the Newar practice of assembling stotras and kavacas from different tantric sources into a single liturgical handbook.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the 10 paṭalas comprising the Kriyāpāda in this recension, closing with the tenth paṭala colophon: iti śrīkāraṇāgame uttarabhāge pārvatīparameśvarasaṃvāde kriyāpāde prāyaścittavidhikathanaṃ nāma daśamaḥ paṭalaḥ.

**Also known as:** Karaṇāgama, Kāraṇāgama (Uttarabhāga, Kriyāpāda), Kāraṇāgamottarabhāga: Kriyāpāda

**Attribution:** Revealed Śaiva scripture presented as a dialogue between Pārvatī and Parameśvara (Śiva). In the Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyata) tradition, the Uttarabhāgas of the Siddhāntāgamas are regarded as foundational revelations establishing Vīraśaiva ritual and theological doctrines.

The Kāraṇāgama is traditionally ranked fourth among the twenty-eight canonical Siddhāntāgamas; this e-text contains the ten-chapter Kriyāpāda section of its Uttarabhāga preserved in the Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyata) tradition. Structured as a divine discourse between Pārvatī and Śiva, the text establishes the supremacy of Vīraśaiva dharma, the observance of the śāmbhavavrata, and the transmission of the threefold initiation (vedhā-, mantra-, and kriyādīkṣā). It provides extensive ritual prescriptions for the worship, wearing, and maintenance of the personal liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga), culminating in expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) to be performed in the event of ritual errors or the loss of the liṅga (naṣṭaliṅga).

The Śrīvidyārṇavatantra is an encyclopedic Śākta and Śrīvidyā compendium attributed to Vidyāraṇyayati. It synthesizes various lineages and ritual streams (including Kādimata and Kālikāmata), detailing yantras, nyāsas, mantraśāstra, initiation rituals, and deity worship. This file contains the complete Pūrvārdha (śvāsas 1–18).

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished manuscript transcription: NGMPP reel no: B 133/3 manuscript no. 5-5148, transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (Muktabodha Catalog No. M00218, 2010–2011).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha file header: 'Catalog number : M00218', 'Manuscript : NGMPP manuscript 5-5148 Reel no: B 133/3', 'Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.'
- Muktabodha file header note: 'Revision 0: Sept. 18, 2010 chapter 15 to end added'

## Contents

**Coverage:** unclear — Transcribes 56 chapters (paṭalas) preserved in National Archives Kathmandu MS 5-5148 (NGMPP reel B 133/3). Internal colophons indicate a composite manuscript or sections from two closely related texts: paṭala 24 concludes the Meruddhāra section of the Pārameśvarīmata ('iti pārameśvarīmate navakoṭisaṃhitāyāṃ caturāśītisahasrameruddhāraḥ caturviṃśatimaḥ paṭalaḥ'), while the final colophon at paṭala 56 reads 'iti śrīkubjikāmate ṣaṭpañcāśatitamaḥ paṭalaḥ samāptaḥ'.

**Also known as:** Parameśvarīmata, Pārameśvarīmata, Meruddhāra, Kubjikāmata

**Attribution:** Anonymous canonical Śākta/Śaiva scripture revealed by Śrī Mahābhairava to the Devī.

The Parameśvarīmatatantra is a scripture of the Western Transmission (Paścimāmnāya) of Kaula Śaivism, intimately connected with the Kubjikā cycle. Set as a dialogue between Mahābhairava and the Devī, the text treats the esoteric symbolism of Mount Meru (Meruddhāra), the sixfold lineage (ṣaḍvidha kulāmnāya), mantras, mudrās, and yantras. In this manuscript transcription, paṭala 24 marks the conclusion of the 24-chapter Meruddhāra of the Pārameśvarīmata, while the remainder continues through to chapter 56, ending with a colophon to the Kubjikāmata.

# Kriyāsāratattvaprakāśinīvyākhyā (paṭalas 3–15) with an anonymous commentary on Sureśvara's Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika (fragment)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished manuscript transcript: IFP/EFEO transcript T00934 (Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient, Pondicherry), transcribed from a palm-leaf manuscript belonging to Nārāyaṇankuññu Nambūdiripad, Ernakulam.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00232), under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revised Sept. 18, 2011.

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header lines 1-4: 'Catalog number : M00232 ... Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T00934'
- Transcript title lines 8-11: 'ṭ.ṇo. 934 ... copied from a manuscript belonging to ṇārāyaṇankunju ṇambūdiripad Ernakulam'

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Part 1: the Tattvaprakāśinī starts at paṭala 3 ('tṛtīyapaṭalādārabhyate'), with colophons for paṭalas 3-14, and breaks off within paṭala 15. Part 2: a Vedāntic commentary on Sureśvara's Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika, starting around BĀU 2.1 and breaking off in the Gārgī section (BĀU 3.8, 'kasmin na khalv ākāśa ...'), marked 'īncomplete'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kriyāsāratattvaprakāśinīvyākhyā (Tattvaprakāśinī on the Kriyāsāra) (Nārāyaṇa, commentary (root text cited by pratīkas only), paṭalas 3-15)
- commentary on Sureśvara's Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika (unidentified) (separate work in the same transcript (fragment))

**Also known as:** Kriyāsāratattvaprakāśinī, Tattvaprakāśinī

**Attribution:** The opening rubric of the transcript ('śrīḥ nārāyaṇaviracitā') and the Muktabodha header name Nārāyaṇa as author of the Kriyāsāra commentary. The author of the Vārttika commentary is not named in the fragment.

Nārāyaṇa's Tattvaprakāśinī is a commentary on the Kriyāsāra, an āgamic/tantric ritual manual; the preserved paṭalas 3-15 explain site purification, the maṇḍapa and Kumbheśa worship, adhivāsana, fire ritual, expiations, and installation preparations. The same IFP transcript (T00934) continues with an unrelated fragment of a commentary on Sureśvara's Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika covering roughly BĀU 2.1-3.8.

The Gītārthasaṃgraha is Abhinavagupta's philosophical commentary on the Bhagavadgītā written from the perspective of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism (Pratyabhijñā). It interprets Kṛṣṇa's instruction to Arjuna as a revelation of supreme non-dual consciousness (anuttara-saṃvid), synthesizing action (karma), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhakti) as integrated expressions of divine sovereignty and self-awareness (svātantrya). _LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition; transcription of manuscript no. 2379, Research Library, Jammu & Kashmir Government, Srinagar (Muktabodha catalog no. M00245, revision 0, 5 Feb. 2012). Marginal additions are given in round brackets.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (data entry by staff under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski)

- Header note: 'This manuscript contains copious additions written in smaller characters on the margin … These noted in round brackets.'

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Day 1 (preliminary rites, kalaśa, fire), day 2 (adhivāsa, caru, the disciple's preparation, mapping of kalās and bhuvanas, the disciple's bed and dream rite; ends 'ity adhivāsaḥ') and the start of day 3 ('atha tṛtīya dine…': interpretation of dreams, then construction of the maṇḍala). It breaks off mid-word ('pūrvapatraṃ prasādyaivami') without a colophon.

**Attribution:** Anonymous Kashmiri compiler.

An anonymous Kashmiri manual for Śaiva (Bhairava-oriented) initiation, which Muktabodha describes as showing an intensely tantric local pantheon like Nepal's. The surviving part covers the preparatory days in detail: purification of the officiant, kalaśa installation, fire consecration, caru, and preparation of the disciple. It also maps the six paths (kalās, tattvas, bhuvanas) onto the disciple's body and gives the dream rite of the adhivāsa night. It then begins the third day (interpretation of dreams, drawing of the maṇḍala) before breaking off. Extensive marginal glosses in the manuscript are transcribed in round brackets.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Starts at the beginning (maṅgala to Bhairavāgama, then 'atha vistare satyagnikāryapaddhatirlikhyate'). It breaks off mid-verse in the rules for the sacrificial animal (paśu), where it distributes the victim's parts to the deities. Muktabodha marks the end 'uncomplete', and there is no final colophon.

**Attribution:** Anonymous manual of the Kashmiri Tantric Śaiva/Śākta ritual tradition.

An anonymous Kashmiri ritual manual (paddhati) for the fire ritual (agnikārya/homa) in a Bhairava/Kaula-oriented Śaiva setting. It begins with worship of Pustakavāgīśvarī (Sarasvatī) and Gaṇapati, kalaśa worship, purification of the subtle body, and preparation and consecration of the kuṇḍa and fire. It then gives oblation and tarpaṇa sequences for many deities, including Durgā, the Lokeśas and the planets, and ends with an incomplete section on animal sacrifice. The Muktabodha description stresses its incidental information on Kashmiri cults, e.g. the goddess Siddhalakṣmī.

# Ṣaṭsahasrakālottarāgama (selected chapters) with an anthology of extracts from other Āgamas

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_satsahasrakalottaragamaHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished transcript: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient Transcript No. T0767 (transcribed from IFP MS RE 20294).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00249), data-entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (Revision 0: 5 Feb. 2012).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Catalog number : M00249', 'Uniform title: ṣatṣahasrakālottarāgama', 'Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T0767', 'Description: Copied from a MS belonging to the French Institute of Pondicherry, No. RE 20294'.
- Transcript page markers 'p. 2)' to 'p. 158)' and continuous verse numbering 1–2343 in the e-text.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcript T0767 pp. 2–158, verses numbered continuously 1–2343. Kālottara section (pp. 2–36, vv. 1–495): opens without title in a passage on maṇḍala and exegesis (vv. 1–2 repeated as 20–21), then chapters with Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara colophons: gaṇapatipūjā, aghorakalpa, rudraśānti, āśrama, gocara (paṭala 14), samayācāra, guruvicāra (16) and aṃśakatālakṣaṇa (17); paṭala numbering is irregular and many chapters of a 6,000-verse work are absent. From v. 496 (p. 36) the text is a compilation on worship, homa, kuṇḍas, iconography, pratiṣṭhā, festivals and Śivarātri, with source rubrics such as 'iti kāraṇe', 'iti bhīmakāraṇe pratiṣṭhātantre vināyakavratavidhipaṭalaḥ', 'sūkṣmatantre', 'dīptatantre', 'iti vijayākhya mahātantre śivarātrividhiḥ'; it ends abruptly at v. 2343 (flower/leaf substitutes in worship) with no colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Ṣaṭsahasrakālottarāgama (selected paṭalas) (root text (verses 1–495))
- Anthology of ritual extracts from Kāraṇa, Bhīmakāraṇa, Sūkṣma, Dīpta, Vijaya and other Āgamas (appended compilation (verses 496–2343, incomplete))

**Also known as:** Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara, Ṣaṭsahasrakālottara

**Attribution:** Revealed scriptural work belonging to the Siddhāntatantra / Kālottara corpus of the Śaiva tradition.

The e-text begins with selected chapters of the Ṣaṭsahasra ('6,000-verse') recension of the Kālottara, a Śaiva Siddhānta scripture known in recensions of very different length; they deal with Gaṇapati worship, an Aghora ritual (aghorakalpa), the rite of pacification (rudraśānti), the āśramas, astrological suitability (gocara), the conduct of ācāryas and initiates, the examination of the guru and the aṃśaka division. Most of the transcript, however, is a South Indian temple-ritual compilation quoting the Kāraṇa, Sūkṣma, Dīpta, Vijaya and other Āgamas on homa and kuṇḍas, images, liṅgas, installation, festivals and Śivarātri.

An anonymous Kaula/Tantric yoga treatise on subtle-body physiology centered on the standard schema of the six cakras (ṣaṭcakra), sixteen bodily supports (ṣoḍaśādhāra), three gazing targets (trilakṣya), and five internal spaces (vyomapañcaka). **Attribution:** Anonymous; a dialogue in which Śiva (Īśvara) teaches Skanda (addressed as Guha, Śikhidhvaja, Śikhivāhana).

An anonymous Śaiva yoga text in which Śiva instructs Skanda. It covers the subtle body (the nine doors, nāḍīs such as piṅgalā and suṣumṇā, the vital winds), the 'joining to brahman' (brahmasandhāna) through the brahmadvāra, and yogic exit at death (utkrānti). It closes with an internal fire worship (agnipūjā), in which the five breaths are offered into the fire in the heart.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_nirvanayogottaraHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Diplomatic transcription of Banaras Hindu University manuscript BHU C4246 (fols. 86a–93a), transcribed by Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00267).

**E-text:** Staff of Muktabodha Indological Research Institute under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Uniform title: nirvāṇayogottara; Manuscript : BHU C4246; Catalog number : M00267; Revision 0: April 7, 2012'
- Folio markers in the e-text: 'p. 86a)', 'p. 86b)', 'p. 87a)' through 'p. 93a)'

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete short tract of 90 verses as preserved in MS BHU C4246 (fols. 86a–93a), ending with the final concluding statement, a damaged colophon string (transcribing [iti] śrī-nirvāṇayogottaraṃ samāptam), and the closing benediction 'śivaṃ bhavatu'.

**Attribution:** Cast as a divine dialogue between the Bhagavān (Śiva) and his son Guha; no human author is named.

A short Śaiva yoga text of 90 anuṣṭubh verses structured as an instruction delivered by Bhagavān to Guha. It details internal breath retention (pūraka and kumbhaka), cessation of mental fluctuation (niścala citta), the contemplation of voidness (triśūnya, sāmarasya), five symbolic mudrās, and the synthesis of ascetic vows (vrata) with yoga practice leading to liberation (mokṣa).

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_pranagnihotraHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unedited manuscript: Banaras Hindu University Library MS BHU C4257. Transcription of the manuscript.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00268, data-entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 0 of 7 Apr. 2012.

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Uniform title: prāṇāgnihotra / Manuscript : BHU C4257 / Revision 0: April 7, 2012'.
- ilx_skt metadata (M00268): 'incomplete', colophon 'no'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcription of a short text within a manuscript, BHU C4257 (beginning at leaf marker 'p. 251a)'). The e-text ends mid-word with 'sa', with no closing colophon. ilx_skt metadata: 'incomplete', colophon 'no'.

**Attribution:** An anonymous Śaiva dialogue. Ṣaṇmukha (Skanda) asks Śiva (addressed as Śūlabhṛt) for the prāṇāgnihotra on behalf of 'alpavittā narāḥ' who cannot keep the Vedic agnihotra, and Śiva answers. Its question list ('śarīre'smin katy agnayaḥ, ko yajamānaḥ, kā patnī ...') belongs to the tradition of the inner, bodily fire sacrifice. No source for the text was identified.

A short anonymous Śaiva text in verse and prose on the 'agnihotra in the breath' (prāṇāgnihotra), taught by Śiva to Ṣaṇmukha for people who cannot afford the Vedic fire ritual. It maps the elements of the sacrifice onto the body, its faculties and the cosmos. It then describes the vital breaths and their deities, and the eating of food as an inner fire offering. The surviving text breaks off in this section.

**Also known as:** Svabodhodayamañjarī

The Subodhamañjarī (also referred to in verse 44 as Svabodhodayamañjarī) is a short Sanskrit treatise in 44 verses by Vāmanadatta, son of the Mīmāṃsaka Harṣadatta. It outlines an effortless method of mental absorption (samāveśa / nirodha) by dissolving sensory perceptions into the nature of the self (ātman), leading to jīvanmukti.

**Attribution:** A traditional didactic dialogue framed between King Janamejaya and an interlocutor, recounting an exchange between Vyāsa and his son Śuka.

The Śukavākya is a didactic dialogue in Purāṇic verse recounting an exchange between the sage Vyāsa and his son Śuka. Narrated within a traditional frame addressed to King Janamejaya, Śuka describes the suffering and transience of saṃsāra, detailing his past incarnations across various animal and plant forms, before reflecting on dispassion (vairāgya), devotion, and release from rebirth.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcribed from folios 73a–85b of BHU manuscript C4245; the text preserves the verse sequence up to the traditional concluding verse (ityuktvā nanditā devī kaṇṭhe lagnā śivasya tu), but lacks a closing scribal colophon or explicit.

The Vijñānabhairava is a celebrated nondual Śaiva tantric scripture of the Trika tradition, cast as a dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess (Bhairavī). In response to questions on the ultimate nature of reality beyond ritual forms and dualistic concepts, Bhairava presents 112 dhāraṇās (meditative centering practices) utilizing the breath, void, sound, sensory perception, and direct nondual awareness to realize spontaneous identity with divine consciousness.

**Also known as:** Acintyaviśvasādākhyatantra, Cintyopabheda Acintyaviśvasādākhya

The Acintyaviśvasādākhya is an Upāgama belonging to the Cintyāgama cycle within the Śaiva Siddhānta canon. It deals with āgamic ritual (kriyā), ascetic and daily observances (caryā, dāsamārga, putramārga, sahamārga), temple worship, nyāsa, and prāsādamantra theology. # Unmattabhairavahṛdaya

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_unmattabhairavaHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Diplomatic transcript of Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient transcript T1020 (IFP/EFEO transcript T1020).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00275), entered by Muktabodha staff under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (2011–2012).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Catalog number : M00275', 'Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T1020'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete ritual text as preserved in IFP/EFEO transcript T1020, comprising the yantroddhāra, kīlaka, nyāsa, dhyāna, gāyatrī, and the hṛdaya hymn ending with verse 54 and colophon.

**Also known as:** Unmattabhairava, Pārameśvaratantrāntargata-unmattabhairavahṛdaya

**Attribution:** Ascribed in the colophon to the Vārāṇasīpaṭala (Unmattabhairavopākhyāna) of the Pārameśvaratantra.

The Unmattabhairavahṛdaya is a Śaiva tantric ritual manual focused on Unmatta Bhairava, one of the classical eight Bhairavas (Aṣṭabhairava). Claimed in its colophon to belong to the Pārameśvaratantra (Vārāṇasīpaṭala), the text presents instructions for drawing the yantra (yantroddhāra), the kīlaka, nyāsa, dhyāna, and the protective 'heart' recitation (hṛdaya), along with standard tantric applications (ṣaṭkarman) such as māraṇa, vaśīkaraṇa, and uccāṭana.

The Kāmakalāvilāsa is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Śrīvidyā tradition of Śākta Tantra, attributed to Puṇyānandanātha. In 55 verses, it sets forth the non-dual metaphysics of Kāmakalā—the creative pulsation and self-manifestation of pure consciousness (Prakāśa-Vimarśa / Śiva-Śakti)—and elaborates the esoteric emergence and symbolic structure of the Śrīcakra and the fifteen-syllabled mantra (Kādimata / Hādimata). The text is accompanied by the Cidvallī, the classic Sanskrit commentary by Naṭanānanda, which elucidates its dense philosophical vocabulary and meditative correspondences.

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished manuscript transcription of Nepalese manuscript catalogued as NGMCP 5-4798 (reel no. A 204/6), data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, e-text M00283, 2003/2011).
