**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha e-text header lines [1]–[3]: 'Catalog number : M00283', 'Uniform title: hāhārāvatantra', 'Manuscript : NGMCP 5-4798 reel number A 204/6'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete transcription of the manuscript up to the concluding colophon (catalog records note 18 chapters; description notes chapters up to chapter 15).

**Also known as:** Hāhārāva Tantra, Atharvaṇasaṃhitā (Hāhārāvatantra)

**Attribution:** Canonical Śākta-Kaula tantric scripture presenting itself as an Atharvaṇasaṃhitā (associated with the Atharvaveda tradition).

The Hāhārāvatantra is a Nepalese Śākta-Kaula tantra affiliated with the Atharvaveda tradition (Atharvaṇasaṃhitā), centering on the worship of Kaula goddesses with an emphasis on Guhyakālī and Pratyaṅgirā. The text details dhyānas, yantras, a thousand names (sahasranāma) of Guhyakālī, protective hymns (kavaca), indrajāla and other magical rites, and Kaula ritual worship using sacrificial vessels (pātras). It survives primarily in Kathmandu Valley manuscript collections.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** hāhārāvatantra

**Description:** The Hāhārāvatantra (the Tantra of the Roaring Haa, Haa) teaches the worship of Kaula goddesses, especially forms of Kālī, with a very clear preference for Guhyakālī. Guhyakaalii is one of the most popular form of Kaalii in the Kathmandu Valley, although hardly known outside it. The main Tantra of Guhyakālī is the massive Mahākālasaṃhitā which may well have been redacted in Kathmandu Valley probably after the 14th century. It is likely that the Hāhārāvatantra is also of Nepalese as its preference for Guhyakālī suggests and absence of manuscripts or references to it outside the Valley. Another indication that this so is the presence in the text of the typical Nepalese corruption mahākarmārcana for mahaakramārcana denoting the Kaula liturgy for the worship of Kaula goddesses. This Tantra calls itself an atharvanasaṃhitā and so affiliates itself to the tradition of the Atharva Veda. This is probably because of its extensive treatment of magical rites, incantations and magical potions.

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, Catalog number M00284, data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, Revision 0 of December 17, 2003.

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Uniform title: kulānandādi / Manuscript : NGMCP 1-1376/ v reel number A40/6 / Catalog number : M00284 / Revision 0: December 17, 2003'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — A collection of fragments marked 'īncomplete' at the end. Contains the Kulānanda (first 7 folios), a 4-folio passage on kapāla from the Picumata, and ritual texts ending after 'bhairava vali'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kulānanda (Matsyendranātha, first work (folios 1–7))
- Kapālalakṣaṇa (Picumata / Brahmayāmala) (scriptural fragment)
- Kaula ritual prescriptions (ritual fragments)

**Also known as:** kulānandādi

**Attribution:** The Kulānanda colophon reads 'iti matsyendrapādāvatārikaṃ kulānandasamāptam'. The skull-bowl passage has the colophon 'iti kapālakṣaṇaṃ picumate', referring to the Picumata / Brahmayāmala. The ritual sections are anonymous.

A transcription of a Kaula manuscript (NGMCP 1-1376/ v). It opens with the Kulānanda, a dialogue attributed to Matsyendranātha dealing with Kaula Yoga, subtle body piercing (vedha), and the rising of Kuṇḍalinī. This is followed by a section on the characteristics of skull-bowls (kapāla) drawn from the Picumata (Brahmayāmala), and prescriptions for Kaula rituals addressing goddesses including Kubjikā, Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Bhagamālinī, and Kāmeśvarī.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulānandādi

**Description:** The manuscript called Kulānandādi contains short tracts and fragments of early Kaula works. The first is called Kulānanda covers the first seven folios. As it attributed to Matsyendranātha, it is important although short. It deals with aspects of Kaula Yoga, focused around the -piercing - (vedha) of spiritual energy through centres of the subtle body following from above and the piercing of Kuṇḍalinī upwards. The character and form of the exposition, which is in line with other Kaula tracts attributed to Matsyendranātha, supports the view that this is indeed an early Kaula work. The next 4 folios deal with the charateristics of a skull bowl (kapāla) which is said to be drawn from the Picumata (i.e. the Brahmayāmala) which is quite possible as this text does indeed deal with this topic. The rest of the manuscript contains prescriptions for Kaula ritual. The goddesses belong to the early period, including Kubjikā, Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Bhagamālinī and others. Notably Tripurā is absent, although Kāmeśvarī, one of her precursors is not.

**Notes:** In the manuscript anusvāra and visarga occur together.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Manuscript NGMCP 3-251 reel number A 150/16 contains fragments of three Kaula works: Kaulsārasaṃgraha (begins with chapter 24 and extends up to chapter 26), Kulācāranirṇaya (chapters 1 to 5), and an 18th ullāsa dealing with funerary rites of a Kaula ('iti tatvāmarśāṃtyaṣṭikramaḥ aṣṭādaśollāsaḥ saṃpūrṇaṃ'), ending with 'samvat 1929 śubham'.

- Kulācāranirṇaya, paṭalas 1–5 (root text, excerpt)

**Attribution:** According to Muktabodha, the manuscript is a collection of fragments of three Kaula tracts in the format of Tantras outlining Kaula ritual and practice, belonging to the period after the 13th century. After the final chapter, a note reports that in the view of Subhagānandanātha (subhagānandanāthamate tu) it cannot be said whether this 18th ullāsa was spoken by Īśvara or composed by ācāryas. A manuscript labelled Kulasāra containing fragments of three Kaula works in Tantra format: chapters 24–26 of Kaulsārasaṃgraha (part of Somabhujavalī), chapters 1–5 of Kulācāranirṇaya, and chapter 18 of a work belonging to the Śrīvidyā lineage of Subhagānandanātha dealing with the funerary rites (antyeṣṭi) of a Kaula. Muktabodha dates such Kaula works to after the 13th century.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulasāra

**Description:** This manuscript is called Kulasāra, but is in fact a collection of fragment of three Kaula tracts. The first is Kaulsārasaṃgraha which, according to the colophons is a part of the Somabhujavalī. It begins with chapter 24 and extends up to to chapter 26. It is followed by the Kulaacāranirṇaya which extends from chapter 1 to 5. The third fragment is chapter eighteen of a work belonging to the śrīvidyā lineage of Subhagānandanātha. It deals with the funerary rites of a Kaula. The texts of which these are fragments in the format of a Tantra, outlining the principles of Kaula ritual and practice. They are typical Kaula work belonging to the latter period, that is, after the 13th century. Indeed such texts can be treated as an independent class of Kaula works of which the Kulārṇavatantra is one of the earliest.

The Āścaryayogamālā ('Rosary of Wondrous Recipes/Applications'), also known as Yogaratnamālā or Yogaratnāvalī, is a medieval manual of magic and occult recipes (ṣaṭkarman) attributed to Nāgārjuna. It details preparations and spells for subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), immobilization (stambhana), and other powers. It is accompanied by the concise commentary (Laghuvṛtti) of the Śvetāmbara Jaina scholar Guṇākara.

This Nāgārjuna is famous as the author (or the namesake of various authors) of works on magic (ṣaṭkarma). A manuscript in the Asiatic Society in Bombay dates the composition of the work as 1240 CE. It was written, the text tells us, to serve people needs and delight them. It deals with standard matters of magic beginning with control of others (vaśīkaraṇa), then the checking of an enemies army (stambhana), killing of enemies (śatrumāraṇa), attraction of women (akarṣaṇa) and ways of attaining various magical powers (siddhi) through the preparation of potions, which the text describes in detail, and mantras.

**Attribution:** Revealed tantric and rasaśāstra treatise framed as a dialogue between Bhairava and the goddess Kākacaṇḍeśvarī (Kākacāmuṇḍā).

The Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata is an early Śākta-Śaiva alchemical (rasaśāstra) and iatrochemical tantra presented as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Bhairava and the goddess Kākacaṇḍeśvarī (a form of Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā). The text details mercurial processing, calcination, mineral operations, and herbal recipes (kalpas) for rejuvenation (rasāyana) and therapeutic medicine. Preserved in Nepalese manuscripts, it represents an important early stratum in medieval Indian tantric alchemy.

**Description:** Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata (the Teaching for the Fierce Crow Goddess). The text is framed as a dialogue between Kākacaṇḍeśvarī (also called Kākacāmuṇḍā) who is equated with Kaṃkālī (the Skeleton) and Kālarātrī (Dark Night), both forms of Kālī. She is the consort (Umādevī) of the five headed Bhairava, who is probably with Svacchandabhairava, who is in some of his aspects a medicine god. They are seated on mount Kailāsa. After imploring him for the knowledge that leads to liberation, the god promising to do so, teaches the preparation of herbs for healing and magic most especially he focuses on the magical preparation of alchemical mercury making this an important unpublished work on Indian alchemy.

It describes the subtle body as an internal microcosm containing the sacred Kaula sites, sacred rivers, sun, moon, and cakras, and teaches prāṇāyāma, bandhas, and the unification of prāṇa and apāna for physical and spiritual liberation.

**Also known as:** Kalpadrumavivekinī

**Attribution:** Traditionally catalogued by Muktabodha under Gorakṣanātha, but the internal text is cast as a Tantric dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī (Haragaurīsaṃvāda) from the Kalpadrumavivekinī praising Gorakṣanātha.

The Gorakṣaguṭikā ('Pill/Amulet of Gorakṣa') is a late Nātha liturgical and mythological text framed as a Tantric Haragaurīsaṃvāda (dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī), claiming affiliation to the Kalpadrumavivekinī. Unlike standard Haṭha Yoga treatises, it centers on devotional ritual and Guru worship, recounting the miraculous birth and deeds of Gorakṣanātha in its opening chapter, followed by protective kavacas, mantras, and stotras (including his dvādaśanāma, aṣṭottaraśatanāma, and sahasranāma) across nine chapters (taraṅgas).

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** gorakṣaguṭikā

**Author:** gorakṣanātha

**Description:** The Goraksaguṭikā (the Magic Pill of Gorakṣa) is attributed to Gorakṣa (alias Gorakhnātha) the famous founder of Haṭha Yoga. The colophons state that it is part of the Kalpadrumavivekinii and that it is a commentary (bhyāsa) on Yoga. It is framed in the format of a Tantra as a dialogue between śiva and Gaurī. Although Gorakṣanātha was a yogi, as are his followers the Naatha Yogis today, and so should not be concerned with ritual practice, in actual fact the Nātha tradition has developed an extensive liturgy centered on the worship of its Gurus. This short tract contains a series of hymns (stotra) praising Gorakṣanātha and myths that narrate their origins.

# Kulasāra (fragment)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_kulasaraHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished manuscript transcription of Nepalese-German Manuscript Cataloguing Project (NGMCP) MS 4-137/vi (microfilm reel A 40/11), transcribed by Muktabodha Indological Research Institute under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, 2011.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (dir. Mark S. G. Dyczkowski)

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Catalog number : M00294', 'Uniform title: kulasāra', 'Manuscript : NGMCP 4-137/vi reel number: A 40/11', 'Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.'

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Preserved fragment of an incomplete Nepalese manuscript; opens abruptly in chapter (paṭala) 4, followed by chapters 8 to 17, where it ends abruptly.

**Attribution:** Scriptural Kaula tantra presented as divine revelation in dialogue form.

The Kulasāra is an early Kaula Śaiva scripture surviving in archaic Nepalese manuscripts and cited by non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva authors prior to the eleventh century. It expounds Kaula metaphysics—including the categories of piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, and rūpātīta, as well as Akula and Kula—combined with yogic practices for bodily internalization, mantra protection, visualization of Bhairava and yoginīs, non-dual ritual purity, and internal pilgrimage (caryā). This e-text preserves an unedited diplomatic transcript of chapters 4 (fragment) and 8–17 (incomplete).

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulasāra

**Description:** The manuscript is incomplete. It begins abruptly in the middle of chapter (paṭala) four and then continues from chapter eight to seventeen where it ends abruptly. The Kulasāra is quoted by non-dualist Kashmiri Shaiva authors and so preceeds the 11th century. It belongs to a genre of Kaula Tantras that are focused on the attainment of the direct experience of essential metaphysical principles and yogic powers through the practice of Yoga and insight. Through knowledge of these principles the Kaula Yogi attains liberation in this life (jñānāvabhāsena jīvanmuktye vyavasthitaḥ fl. 33b) and numerous yogic powers. The text focuses also on the worship of Bhairava and Devī and the host of Yoginīs. The first chapters are concerned with the four principles commonly mentioned in Kaula works, namely, Piṇḍa, Pada, ṛūpa and Rūpātīta. Unfortunately, here the manuscript is incomplete. Chapter nine deals with the attainment of the pervasion of transcendental śiva by the abandonment of śakti (9). The following chapter teaches the attainment of the supreme reality which is the Inexplicable free of phenomenal qualities, immobile and pervasive like the sky by merger with the space contained in the jar of the psycho-physical body (10). The next chapter deals with transcendent Akula and immanent Kula along with Kaula which is the union of the two (11). Chapter twelve describes the ascent through the centres of the body from the feet to the head. Corresponding to the spheres of the gross elements, they are the abodes of numerous types of Yoginīs the text describes and the damage they can do. The Yogi should know them and by his devotion to the deity, fire and the guru and practice of Yoga be protected from them. Those who are immoral are consummed by them. The chapter ends with a series of visualizations designed to protect the body of the Yogi (12). The next chapter continues with similar concerns for protection and the overcoming of disease and death by the use of Bhairava Mantra and visualization of his form which appears to be that of Svacchandabhairava and accompanying forms and their consorts (13). The next chapter discusses non-duality in the sense of the absence of pure and impure with regards to food and drink and the defects of those who do not follow this path. It goes on to talk about freedom from dualistic thought constructs and the purification of the mind and purification of the sacrificial substances that takes place in this way. It is applied to the sacrificial meat and then wine (14). Chapter fifteen deals with the observance (caryā) of the Kaula adept (vīra). He should travel to the inner Kaula sacred sites (pīṭha, kṣetra) in the body following the vital breath rather than the outer ones. There he plays with the Yoginīs and worships them and does so externally also with a pure mind. The manner the pilgrimage is to be performed externally is described next.The last chapter deals with the Three Jewels of Shiva, Shakti and the Self, their attainment and experience.

**Attribution:** Attributed in the text and colophon tradition to Vimalaśiva, a 13th-century Śaiva Siddhānta master who resided in Benares.

The Vimalāvatītantra (also termed Vimalāvatī) is an extensive Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual composed by Vimalaśiva, who lived in the thirteenth century and took a vow of residing in Benares (kāśīvāsa). The work details worship procedures (pūjāsiddhi), fire sacrifices (vahnikārya, homa), festive ritual observances such as pavitra and dāmana, subtle breath yoga with Kuṇḍalinī, and various degrees of initiation (dīkṣā) alongside conduct codes for initiates.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** vimalāvatītantra

**Author:** vimalaśiva

**Description:** This is a work on Siddhānta ritual written by Vimalaśiva who lived in the thirteenth century. He declares with pride that he had taken the vow of residing all his life in Benares (kāśīvāsa). The first chapter deals with the accomplishment and fruits of worship (pūjāsiddhi). Chapter two deals with the procedure for making the sacrificial; fire (vahnikārya) and three the offerings to it (homa). Four deals with the seasonal offering to the deity of a sacred thread (pavitra) and the next with the offering of garlands (dāmana). The fifth deals with the rites of initiation. The text continues to elaborate on the details concerning initiation. It includes several interesting inner purificatory practices linked with the movement of the vital breath and the movement of Kuṇḍalinī. The rules of right conduct for initiate of various kinds are ennumerated and other matters taught concerning his duties and those of Shaivites in general both as householders and renouncers. Various initiatory rites are described for different types and levels of initiands.

The Mohacūḍottara is an early Śaiva scriptural manual on installation (pratiṣṭhā-tantra) framed as a dialogue between Skanda and Śakra (Indra). A comprehensive compendium of Śākta liturgical, hymnological, and mantric literature centered on the Mahāvidyā goddess Bhuvaneśvarī. It opens with the Bhuvaneśvarīmahāstotra attributed to Pṛthvīdharācārya alongside the commentary by Kavi Padmanābha, and collects various ancillary texts including a pañcāṅga, pūjāpaddhati, kavaca, sahasranāma, aṣṭottaraśatanāma, and hṛdaya attributed largely to the Rudrayāmala, Anantadeva's ritual manual Bhuvaneśvarīkramacandrikā, and Pṛthvīdharācārya's Laghusaptaśatīstotra.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete e-text of the printed edition, covering the Devīrahasya (Pūrvārdha in 25 paṭalas and Uttarārdha in 35 paṭalas), the Kashmiri goddess Pariśiṣṭas, and the Uddhārakośa in 7 kalpas.

**Also known as:** Devīrahasyatantra, Rudrayāmalāntargata Devīrahasya

**Attribution:** The Devīrahasya is presented as belonging to the Rudrayāmala. Its regional focus on Kashmiri shrines (Śārikā, Jvālāmukhī, Mahārājñī, Śāradā) and late vocabulary indicate medieval Kashmiri compilation. The appended Uddhārakośa is attributed in its colophons to Dakṣiṇāmūrtimuni.

The Devīrahasya is a Śākta tantric digest and ritual compilation framed as part of the Rudrayāmala, composed in Kashmir. It is structured into a Pūrvārdha of 25 paṭalas dealing with initiation, mantra vitalization and unlocking, puraścaraṇa, yantras, and ritual ingredients, followed by an Uttarārdha of 35 paṭalas providing pañcāṅgas (paṭala, kavaca, paddhati, sahasranāma, and stotra) for various deities. The appended text is the Uddhārakośa of Dakṣiṇāmūrtimuni, a 7-kalpa lexicon defining and deciphering tantric mantras.

The Troṭalātantra (or Troṭalamahātantra) is an early medieval Śaiva/Śākta tantric scripture framed as an exposition delivered by Śiva to Garuḍa (Tārkṣya). The work covers her visual iconography, mantra formulas, internal yogic ascent through the centers to union with Bhairava, and rites for protection against poison and the subjugation of spirits.

The Tantracintāmaṇi is an extensive Śākta Tantric digest (nibandha) composed in the late seventeenth century by Navamīsiṃha (Ādyānanda), a minister in the Newar Malla kingdom of Kathmandu. Organized in forty prakāśas, it compiles citations from numerous Āgamic and Tantric authorities to delineate cosmology, mantra lore, the worship of the Daśamahāvidyās (focusing particularly on Dakṣiṇakālikā/Śyāmā), Kulācāra rites, and dīkṣā ceremonies. This digital transcription covers chapters 1 through 30 with its autocommentary (Pañjikā).

An anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta doctrinal compendium in mixed prose and verse that synthesizes tenets of the Śaivāgama tradition. It quotes foundational scriptures and commentaries including the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha, Kiraṇatantra, Mālinīvijayottara, Rauravatantra, and Mataṅgapārameśvara, as well as Rāmakaṇṭha. The treatise addresses the divine origin and transmission lineages of scriptural revelation (mahaughakrama and pratisaṃhitākrama), the ontological categories of pati, paśu, and pāśa, and initiatory praxis (dīkṣā).

The Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā is a Vīraśaiva apologetic and theological treatise composed by Nandikeśvara. Applying Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to Vedic, Upaniṣadic, Āgamic, and Smṛti citations, the work establishes the scriptural validity, necessity, and orthodoxy of constantly bearing the personal liṅga on the body (iṣṭaliṅgadhāraṇa) and examines associated funerary practices. The first book (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa, 33 sargas) of the Yogavāsiṣṭha describes the profound disillusionment and existential grief of the young prince Rāma after his pilgrimage across the country. Confronting the transience of life, wealth, youth, and the physical body, Rāma articulates his despair before king Daśaratha and the royal assembly, creating the need for sage Vasiṣṭha's extensive exposition of non-dual liberation. Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī's accompanying commentary Tātparyaprakāśa provides word-by-word glosses and an orthodox Advaita Vedānta framing.

The Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa is the second book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (or Mokṣopāya), consisting of twenty chapters. Addressing Rāma's spiritual disaffection introduced in the opening book (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa), this section analyzes the nature of human striving (pauruṣa) versus fate (daiva), details the narrative of Śuka's attainment of peace through King Janaka, and introduces the four 'gatekeepers of liberation' (dvārapālas: śama, vicāra, santoṣa, and sādhasaṅgama). **Attribution:** The Yogavāsiṣṭha is traditionally attributed to Vālmīki. The commentary Tātparyaprakāśa is by Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī, pupil of Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī.

The Sthitiprakaraṇa constitutes the fourth book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (consisting of 62 sargas), elucidating the apparent preservation and sustenance (sthiti) of the manifest phenomenal cosmos from the perspective of radical non-dualism. Sage Vasiṣṭha instructs Prince Rāma through philosophical discourse and pedagogical narratives—such as the allegorical tales of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the story of the ascetic Dāśūra—demonstrating that the universe possesses no independent reality and is merely an ungrounded vibration of consciousness (cittaspanda) sustained by delusion. The accompanying commentary, the Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī, elucidates the text in terms of classical Advaita Vedānta epistemology and metaphysics.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary on all four adhyāyas of the Brahmasūtra, concluding at Brahmasūtra 4.4.22 (anāvṛttiḥ śabdād anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt).

The Śrīkarabhāṣya is the primary Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) bhāṣya on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtras, expounding the doctrine designated as Viśeṣādvaita or Bhedābhedātmaka-Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita. Śrīpati establishes Paraśiva as the supreme non-dual Brahman, arguing for a relation of natural difference during bondage and non-difference upon liberation (bhedābheda) between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. The text also integrates and validates distinctive Vīraśaiva socio-religious practices such as liṅgadhāraṇa, bhasma, and rudrākṣa on Vedic and Upaniṣadic authorities.

**Edition used (determined):** Pārānanda Sūtra, critically edited by Swami Trivikrama Tīrtha, Gaekwad's Oriental Series, Baroda: Baroda Oriental Institute, 1931.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The whole work is present: the pūrvādhyāya with 7 āhnikas and the uttarādhyāya with 7 āhnikas, ending with the final colophons 'iti pārānandasūtre uttarādhyāye saptamamāhnikam || samāptaṃ cedaṃ pārānandasūtram | samāptā ceyaṃ pārānandamīmāṃsā'. The Pārānandasūtra (also called Pārānandamīmāṃsā) is an anonymous Śākta-Kaula ritual code written in sūtras, in two adhyāyas of seven āhnikas each, modelled on the Vedic and Mīmāṃsā sūtra style. It teaches one supreme Self, the Īśvaras and the countless souls. It describes the three paths of practice (dakṣiṇa, vāma and uttara), the qualifications of guru and disciple, initiation and order of precedence, daily and special worship, sacrificial sessions (satra) with offerings of wine and animals, expiations, and rules of conduct, and it often cites the differing opinions of named authorities.

The Guhyasamājatantra is the foundational scripture of the Buddhist Mahāyoga / Anuttarayoga tantric class, centered on Akṣobhya and the fivefold Buddha family maṇḍala. Structured in eighteen chapters, it details deity visualization, mantras, ritual enactments, and subtle-body meditation forming the basis of generation (utpattikrama) and completion (niṣpannakrama) stage yogas. Celebrated for its paradoxical, antinomian imagery representing non-dual gnosis, it gave rise to two prominent Indian exegetical schools: the Jñānapāda school and the Ārya school.

The Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa is an encyclopedic Buddhist ritual work belonging to the early Mantrayāna (traditionally classified in Tibetan canonical taxonomies as a Kriyātantra), framed as a Mahāyāna vaipulyasūtra delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha. It represents one of the earliest preserved Indian Buddhist tantric sourcebooks, integrating esoteric ritual technology with classic Mahāyāna doctrine.

A 3,000-verse 'Sārasaṅgraha' recension of the Makuṭāgama (Makuṭatantra), one of the 28 Siddhāntāgamas of Śaiva Siddhānta, transmitted in an IFP transcript. It begins with the descent of the scripture (tantrāvatāra) and treats bathing and ācamana, daily worship, initiation, the festival, expiation, kṛttikādīpa, snapana, iconography and installation, pavitrārohaṇa, prāṇāyāma, the qualities of the ācārya, Kālī and Bhairava worship, funerary rites, and the ūrdhva- and ambā-cakras, ending with a meditation on Śiva as dancer and Dakṣiṇāmūrti in Cidambaram.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** Manuscript transcript: IFP/EFEO transcript T01046.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00230 / M0230, data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 0 of Sept. 18, 2011.

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Uniform title: kuladīpikā / Main title: Kuladīpikā uttaraṣaṭkam ṣaḍvidyāprakāśikā / Author : tryambakabhaṭṭaraka / Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T01046 / Revision 0: Sept. 18, 2011'.
- ilx_skt metadata (M00230) classifies the file as '4 excerpts' and lists the colophons.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Composite transcript. The Uttaraṣaṭka begins abruptly mid-verse ('koṭisamaprabham |'). It runs to the colophon 'iti śrīrudrayāmale ... uttarabhāge nityaklinnāprakaraṇe ṣaḍvidyāprakāśāyāmuttaraṣaṭkaṃ saṃpūrṇam'. The Kuladīpikā has the colophons 'ityuttaraṣaṭkavivaraṇe kuladīpikāyāṃ prathamaḥ paṭaḥ' to '... pañcamaḥ paṭalaḥ'. The Tripurāsārasamuccaya has paṭalas 1–10, ending 'iti śrī bhaṭṭanāgaviracite tripurāsārasamuccaye daśamaḥ paṭalaḥ'. The Saṃpradāyadīpikā has paṭalas 1–10, followed by the scribal verse. After that, a short unidentified passage of Tripurā pūjā prose breaks off mid-sentence.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Uttaraṣaṭka (Ṣaḍvidyāprakāśa, ascribed to the Rudrayāmala, Nityaklinnāprakaraṇa) (root text (6 paṭalas; segs. 9–332; beginning missing))
- Kuladīpikā (Uttaraṣaṭkavivaraṇa) (commentary on the Uttaraṣaṭka (5 paṭas/paṭalas + conclusion; segs. 333–904))
- Tripurāsārasamuccaya (Bhaṭṭanāga, independent Śrīvidyā manual (10 paṭalas; segs. 905–1613))
- Saṃpradāyadīpikā (commentary on the Tripurāsārasamuccaya (10 paṭalas; segs. 1614–1793))

**Also known as:** Kuladīpikā (uttaraṣaṭkam) ṣaḍvidyāprakāśikā (Muktabodha main title), Ṣaḍvidyāprakāśa, Uttaraṣaṭkavivaraṇa

**Attribution:** The text itself nowhere names Tryambakabhaṭṭāraka; the attribution in the Muktabodha catalogue header is unverified and rejected as author in ilx_skt. The Tripurāsārasamuccaya colophons read 'iti śrī bhaṭṭanāgaviracite tripurāsārasamuccaye ... paṭalaḥ'. The verse following the Saṃpradāyadīpikā, 'tejānandasya śiṣyena kṛṣṇānandasya sūriṇā | likhitaṃ saṃpradāyasya dīpikā cāmbikājñayā', likely identifies Kṛṣṇānanda merely as copyist ('likhitam').

The e-text transcribes a South Indian composite manuscript of Kaula and Śrīvidyā works. It contains (1) the Uttaraṣaṭka or Ṣaḍvidyāprakāśa, ascribed to the Rudrayāmala (Nityaklinnā section), on yonimudrā, the revival of defective mantras, kuṇḍalinī yoga and the six vidyās; (2) the Kuladīpikā, an anonymous commentary on it in five chapters; (3) Bhaṭṭanāga's Tripurāsārasamuccaya, a ten-chapter Śrīvidyā manual on Tripurasundarī worship, nyāsa, the cakras, yantras and homa; and (4) the Saṃpradāyadīpikā, a commentary on the Tripurāsārasamuccaya.

Spoken by Śāriputra, it organizes fundamental doctrinal categories (dharmas) into ten numerical sections (1 to 10), each classified under ten functional sets (dharmas to be developed, abandoned, cultivated, realized, etc.). ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 18 lambakas comprising 124 taraṅgas and over 21,000 verses, ending with Somadeva's epilogue verses praising Queen Sūryavatī and King Kalaśa.

**Attribution:** Somadeva, son of the Brahmin Rāma, composed the work at the court of King Kalaśa of Kashmir for Queen Sūryavatī (c. 1063–1081 CE), adapting Guṇāḍhya's Bṛhatkathā into Sanskrit verse.

The Kathāsaritsāgara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story') is an encyclopedic 11th-century Sanskrit narrative poem composed in Kashmir by Somadeva for Queen Sūryavatī. Arranged into 18 lambakas and 124 taraṅgas, it preserves a major Kashmiri verse recension of Guṇāḍhya's lost Paiśācī epic, the Bṛhatkathā. The central frame tale follows Prince Naravāhanadatta's romantic adventures and quest to attain sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, embedding numerous cycles of folk tales, fables, and romances, including the Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā.

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete across all 8 adhyāyas (chapters) and their respective khaṇḍas, covering both the mūla text and Śaṅkara's bhāṣya up to the final colophon at 8.15.

**Works in this e-text:**

- Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya (Śaṅkara, commentary)

The Chāndogyopaniṣad is one of the earliest and most important mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads, belonging to the Kauthuma/Rāṇāyanīya recension of the Sāmaveda. In eight adhyāyas, it progresses from esoteric meditations on the chanting of the Sāman and the sacred syllable Om (udgītha) to quintessential metaphysical doctrines of early Vedānta, including the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the dialogue of Satyakāma Jābāla, Uddālaka Āruṇi's instruction to Śvetaketu culminating in the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' (6.8.7), and Prajāpati's teachings on the four states of the self. The accompanying commentary by Śaṅkarācārya interprets the text as an exposition of non-dual reality (advaita), demonstrating that ritual action produces transient heavenly realms, whereas direct knowledge of the non-dual Brahman-Ātman leads to absolute liberation (mokṣa).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of Chapter 9 (prose treatise without root kārikās), from the opening inquiry ('kiṃ khalvato 'nyatra mokṣo nāsti') to the final verse, concluding colophon, and scribal dedication ('uttarāpathikapaṇḍitasthaviraśrīlāmāvākasya').

**Attribution:** Vasubandhu's authorship of this prose treatise, appended as the ninth chapter to his Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, is unanimously accepted in Indian, Tibetan, Chinese, and modern scholarship.

Chapter 9 of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, commonly titled Pudgalaviniścaya ('Examination of the Person') or Ātmavādapratiṣedha ('Refutation of the Self Theory'), is an independent prose treatise appended to the main eight-chapter auto-commentary. Vasubandhu demonstrates that liberation is impossible without relinquishing belief in an enduring self, establishing that 'person' (pudgala) or 'self' (ātman) is merely a conventional designation (prajñapti) applied to the causal continuum of the psycho-physical aggregates (skandha). The work contains an extensive critique of both the Buddhist Personalist (Vātsīputrīya/Pudgalavādin) concept of an ineffable pudgala and the Brahmanical (Vaiśeṣika and Nyāya) ontologies of a substantial ātman.

**Also known as:** Īśvarapratyabhijñā, Pratyabhijñākārikā, Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikāvṛtti

**Attribution:** Both the root kārikās and the vṛtti are the work of Utpaladeva.

The Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā along with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Utpaladeva constitutes the foundational philosophical treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') system of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Structured into four sections (adhikāras on knowledge, action, scriptural authority, and a summary of tattvas), the work argues dialectically against Buddhist epistemologists and other rivals to establish that all reality and individual consciousness are identical with the autonomous, self-luminous Lord (Maheśvara / Śiva), and that liberation consists in the explicit recognition of this identity.

**Attribution:** Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa is the author of the Stavacintāmaṇi. Kṣemarāja is the author of the Vivṛti commentary.

The Stavacintāmaṇi ('Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Hymns') is a 120-verse devotional hymn to Lord Śiva by Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa, synthesizing non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva metaphysics (Pratyabhijñā and Spanda) with ecstatic devotional surrender (bhakti). The Viṃśatikākārikā ('Twenty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda polemical treatise composed by Vasubandhu. The text refutes the reality of mind-independent external physical objects (bāhyārtha) through a rigorous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), demonstrating that atomic partlessness and spatial extension are mutually incompatible. Vasubandhu defends the thesis that all experiential phenomena are appearances only (vijñaptimātra), answering realist objections by showing that spatial-temporal determination, intersubjective consistency, and practical efficacy can function without external objects, as seen in dreams, collective karmic hallucinations, and demonic mental projections.

The first adhyāya of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Kāṇva recension of the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa, Śukla Yajurveda) along with the Advaita Vedānta commentary (bhāṣya) attributed to Śaṅkara. - Bouy, Christian. Gauḍapāda: L'Āgamaśāstra. Un traité védāntique en quatre chapitres. Paris: Collège de France / De Boccard, 2000. (French)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all four prakaraṇas: 1. Āgamaprakaraṇa (29 kārikās), 2. Vaitathyaprakaraṇa (38 kārikās), 3. Advaitaprakaraṇa (48 kārikās), and 4. Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa (100 kārikās), totaling 215 verses.

**Also known as:** Gauḍapādakārikā, Gauḍapādīyakārikā, Māṇḍūkyakārikā, Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Gauḍapāda. Modern scholarship (notably Vidhushekhara Bhattacharya, Tilmann Vetter) has debated whether the four prakaraṇas were composed by a single author or represent distinct treatises assembled together, with the fourth prakaraṇa (Alātaśānti) displaying especially strong ties to Buddhist terminology and dialectic.

The Āgamaśāstra (frequently called the Gauḍapādakārikā or Māṇḍūkyakārikā) is the earliest extant systematic verse treatise of Advaita Vedānta, traditionally attributed to Gauḍapāda (c. 6th century CE). Consisting of four prakaraṇas—Āgama, Vaitathya, Advaita, and Alātaśānti—the work expounds the doctrine of radical non-duality and absolute non-origination (ajātivāda). The first chapter interprets the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's four states of consciousness culminating in turīya, while the subsequent chapters systematically deconstruct the ontological reality of external objects, change, and plurality, drawing extensively on the dialectic and terminology of contemporary Buddhist philosophy.

The Vajrabhairavatantra (also known as Vajramahābhairavatantra) is a central Anuttarayogatantra text centered on the wrathful deity Yamāntaka/Vajrabhairava, closely affiliated with the Mañjuśrī cycle. In seven kalpas, it details the construction of the wrathful maṇḍala in cremation grounds, ferocious magical and protective rites (ṣaṭkarmāṇi), visualisations of the buffalo-headed deity, and initiation protocols. First critically edited in Sanskrit by Aleksandra Wenta in 2020, it holds major historical significance for Tibetan Buddhist esoteric ritualism, particularly within the Sakya and Gelug traditions.

The text survives in manuscript Add. 1699 copied in Eastern India during the reign of Govindapāla.

The Caryāgītikoṣa is an anthology of 50 esoteric Buddhist Tantric songs (caryāgīti) composed in an early New Indo-Aryan vernacular (Old Bengali / Apabhraṃśa) by various Mahāsiddhas of the Sahajayāna tradition, accompanied by the Sanskrit commentary of Munidatta. The Nairātmyasiddhi is an extremely succinct Buddhist epistemological treatise by Jitāri refuting the existence of an enduring self (sthirātman). **Attribution:** Attributed to Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīla, as confirmed by the opening and concluding colophons of both authors in the e-text.

The Tattvasaṅgraha ('Compendium of True Realities') is an encyclopedic philosophical and epistemological treatise by the Buddhist master Śāntarakṣita, consisting of 3,646 metrical verses divided into topical investigations (parīkṣā). From a late Madhyamaka-Yogācāra perspective informed by Dharmakīrtian pramāṇa methodology, it systematically examines and refutes rival non-Buddhist ontologies and epistemologies (including Sāṅkhya, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Jaina, and Cārvāka) as well as internal Buddhist positions on topics such as the soul (ātman), God (īśvara), substance, universals, causality, external reality, testimony, and omniscience. Kamalaśīla's companion commentary, the Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, meticulously elucidates Śāntarakṣita's terse verses and preserves crucial quotations and arguments from otherwise lost classical Indian philosophical works.

Blending kārikā verses with extensive prose, the text established the influential 'Alaṅkāra' sub-school of Buddhist epistemology. Prajñākaragupta interprets Dharmakīrtian logic from a sākāravāda and ultimate non-dual (advaita) standpoint, addressing foundational epistemological topics including the nature of valid cognition, perception, reflexivity (svasaṃvedana), and omniscience.

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to Śāntarakṣita (written in the manuscript as 'sāntarikṣapādānām').

The Vādanyāyaṭīkā Vipañcitārthā is an extensive 8th-century commentary by the Buddhist philosopher Śāntarakṣita on Dharmakīrti's debate treatise, the Vādanyāya. In the work, Dharmakīrti simplified the classical Indian debate theory by reducing the traditional twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) to two fundamental categories: failure to state an essential part of the proof (asādhanāṅgavacana) and stating a non-existent defect in the opponent's argument (adoṣodbhāvana). Śāntarakṣita's commentary clarifies Dharmakīrti's dialectical definitions and engages extensively with opponent objections from Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Sāṅkhya traditions.

The Avayavinirākaraṇa is a short philosophical treatise by the late Buddhist logician Paṇḍita Aśoka (c. 10th–11th century CE) dedicated to refuting the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika doctrine of the 'whole' (avayavin) as an ontological real distinct from its parts (avayava). Operating in the tradition of Dharmakīrti, Aśoka utilizes the epistemological reason of vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi (perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader) to demonstrate that positing a single entity that simultaneously admits contradictory properties (such as moving and unmoving, covered and uncovered, or coloured and uncoloured) violates basic principles of non-contradiction.

The Sāmānyadūṣaṇa is a Buddhist epistemological tract by Paṇḍita Aśoka refuting the realist doctrine of universals (sāmānya / jāti) maintained by Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā thinkers. - Ṭippaṇa (Jambūvijaya, sub-commentary)

**Also known as:** Dvādaśāranayacakra, Nayacakra, Nayacakravālavṛtti

**Attribution:** The original root work by Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa does not survive in independent manuscripts; its text is reconstructed through pratīkas preserved in Siṃhasūri Gaṇin's commentary Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī (Nayacakravālavṛtti). The e-text also incorporates the editorial Sanskrit Ṭippaṇa by Muni Jambūvijaya.

The Dvādaśāranayacakra ('Twelve-Spoked Wheel of Standpoints') by the Śvetāmbara Jaina dialectician Mallavādin is an influential masterwork of classical Indian doxography and Jaina philosophical pluralism (anekāntavāda). Mallavādin arranges twelve non-Jaina philosophical standpoints into a self-contained dialectical wheel where each school systematically refutes the preceding one and is in turn overthrown by the next, demonstrating how partial viewpoints fall into internal contradiction unless synthesized within Jaina anekāntavāda. Because Mallavādin's original text survives only embedded as pratīkas within Siṃhasūri Gaṇin's commentary Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī, the commentary forms an integral part of the surviving tradition.

The Padārthadharmasaṅgraha (also known as the Praśastapādabhāṣya), composed by Praśastapāda around the 6th century CE, is the defining classical exposition of the Vaiśeṣika philosophical school. Rather than commenting sequentially on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, it presents an independent systematic categorization of reality into six fundamental ontological categories (padārthas: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya), establishing the conceptual foundation for all subsequent classical Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophy.

**Evidence:**
- SARIT TEI metadata directly records Kāśinātha Śāstrī Āgāśe's 1904 Ānandāśrama edition (ASS 47) as the printed source.

**Other editions:**

- Pātañjalayogasūtrabhāṣyavivaraṇam, ed. Polakam Sri Rama Sastri and S. R. Krishnamurthi Sastri, Madras Government Oriental Manuscripts Series 94, Madras: Government Oriental Manuscripts Library, 1952. — Editio princeps of the Vivaraṇa sub-commentary attributed to Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda.

**Translations:**
- Woods, James Haughton, The Yoga-System of Patañjali; or, The Hindu Doctrine of Concentration of Mind, Harvard Oriental Series 17, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1914. (English)
- Hariharānanda Āraṇya, Swāmi, Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali: Containing His Yoga Aphorisms with the Commentary of Vyāsa, Calcutta: University of Calcutta, 1963 (rev. ed.. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all four pādas of the sūtras along with the bhāṣya: Samādhipāda (YS 1.1–1.51), Sādhanapāda (YS 2.1–2.55), Vibhūtipāda (YS 3.1–3.55), and Kaivalyapāda (YS 4.1–4.34), ending at segment 1795 with the final colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Yogasūtra (Patañjali, root text)
- Vyāsabhāṣya (Vyāsa, commentary)

**Also known as:** Yogasūtra with Vyāsabhāṣya, Yogabhāṣya, Sāṅkhyapravacana Yogaśāstra

**Attribution:** While later Indian tradition distinguishes the sūtras composed by Patañjali from an independent commentary (bhāṣya) composed by Vyāsa (hence 'Vyāsabhāṣya'), philological research demonstrates that the sūtras and bhāṣya form an integral textual whole (the Pātañjalayogaśāstra), composed or compiled by a single author named Patañjali.

The Pātañjalayogaśāstra is the foundational philosophical text of classical Yoga (Pātañjala Yoga). Organized into four chapters (Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda), it presents an eightfold discipline of practice (aṣṭāṅgayoga) and meditative absorption within a dualist Sāṅkhya metaphysical framework. The system directs the practitioner toward the cessation of mental operations (cittavṛttinirodha) and ultimate spiritual liberation (kaivalya), defined as the isolation of pure consciousness (puruṣa) from material nature (prakṛti).

The Cakradatta (or Cikitsāsaṃgraha) is an 11th-century Sanskrit compendium of Ayurvedic therapeutics and clinical medicine composed by Cakrapāṇidatta, the celebrated commentator on the Carakasaṃhitā. Structured largely along the nosological classification established by Mādhava's Rugviniścaya (Mādhavanidāna), the treatise systematically details medicinal recipes, dietetics, and panchakarma treatment regimens. It is a landmark text in the history of Indian medicine for its early, widespread integration of metallic and mercurial preparations (rasaśāstra) into standard medical practice.

- SARIT metadata header directly states the source: 'पण्डितकेदारनाथशर्मणा, सरस्वतीकण्ठाभरणम्, मुम्बय्याम्, पाण्डुरङ्ग जावजी, ख्रिस्ताब्दाः १९३४ (काव्यमाला ९४)'.
- The opening title line ([0]: 'sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇam | śrīratneśvaraviracitayā ratnadarpaṇākhyayā vyākhyayā sametam') and introductory dedication stanzas naming Rāmasiṃhadeva match the text.

**Other editions:**

- Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa of Bhojadeva, ed. T.R. Chintamani, Madras: University of Madras, 1937 (Madras University Sanskrit Series, No. 11). — Critical edition in the Madras University Sanskrit Series.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in five paricchedas (chapters 1–5), containing Bhoja's kārikās with prose exposition and illustrative stanzas, accompanied throughout chapters 1–3 by Ratneśvara's Ratnadarpaṇa and chapters 4–5 by Jagaddhara's commentary.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa (Bhoja, root text)
- Ratnadarpaṇa (Ratneśvara, commentary)
- Vivaraṇa (Jagaddhara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇālaṃkāra, Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa

**Attribution:** The root work is attributed to King Bhoja. Ratneśvara composed the Ratnadarpaṇa on paricchedas 1–3 naming Rāmasiṃhadeva. The commentary on paricchedas 4–5 was supplied by Jagaddhara.

The Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa is an encyclopedic treatise on Sanskrit poetics and dramaturgy (Alaṃkāraśāstra) attributed to King Bhoja (11th century). In five exhaustive paricchedas, it systematically classifies poetic flaws (doṣa), excellences (guṇa), verbal figures (śabdālaṃkāra), semantic figures (arthālaṃkāra), and aesthetic experience (rasa), highlighting Bhoja's synthesis of poetic ornament with rasa theory. This digital text transmits the complete work alongside its primary classical commentaries: Ratneśvara's Ratnadarpaṇa on chapters 1–3 and Jagaddhara's gloss on chapters 4–5.

**Other editions:**

Part II: Commentarial Works, Hamburg: Department of Indian and Tibetan Studies, Universität Hamburg, 2020. — Edition of the Sanskrit text with Tibetan translation and annotated translation.

**Translations:**
- kye rdo rje'i sgrub thabs kyi mdor bshad pa dag pa rdo rje sgron ma zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1237): translated by Mañjuśrī, thar pa lo tsA ba nyi ma rgyal mtshan (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary explaining thirty-two sadhana limbs (dvātriṁśatsādhanasūtra), from the opening udghātaḥ to the concluding verses and colophon at segments 361–365.

**Also known as:** Vajrapradīpā nāma ṭippaṇī, Vajrapradīpā nāma ṭippaṇiviśuddhiḥ, Hevajrasādhana-vajrapradīpa-nāma-śuddha-ṭippanī, Viśuddhikramaṭippaṇī

**Attribution:** The author calls himself Suratavajra ('kṛtvā suratavajreṇa viśuddhikramaṭippaṇīm') and says he is known as Jālandharī ('mayā jālandharīti khyātena'); the colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṁ paṇḍitācāryaśrīmatsuratapādānām'. Gerloff calls him Jālandharipāda. DSBC lists Saroruha as author, which is wrong: Saroruha wrote the root sādhana. The Tibetan translation is in the Tengyur (D 1237).

The Vajrapradīpā (also known as Vajrapradīpā nāma ṭippaṇī or Viśuddhikramaṭippaṇī) is a Vajrayāna commentary composed by Suratavajra (also known by his mahāsiddha epithet Jālandhari/Jālandharipāda) on Saroruhapāda's (Saroruhavajra's) Hevajrasādhana. Adhering to the utpattikrama (generation stage) of the Hevajra cycle, the work systematically explains thirty-two sadhana topics (dvātriṁśatsādhanasūtra), analyzing the purificatory symbolism (viśuddhi) of the mandala deities, the eight cremation grounds (śmaśāna), ritual implements, and seed syllables.

The Śrīhevajrabhaṭṭārakasya Cakraviṃśatikāstotra is a 20-verse tantric hymn of praise (stotra) composed by the siddha Saroruhavajra honoring the Anuttarayogatantra deity Hevajra and his retinue. The verses systematically praise the eight-faced, sixteen-armed form of Hevajra embracing Nairātmyā (vv. 1–8), followed by individual invocations of the eight yoginīs of his maṇḍala (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī; vv. 9–16), their collective qualities (vv. 17–19), and a concluding philosophical praise of the nondual deity (v. 20).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete sādhana from the opening homage (upodghāta) to the final colophon.

**Attribution:** The author calls himself Bhadra, a descendant in the lineage of Saroruhapāda ('saroruhapādanaptṛsutaputreṇa bhadranāmnā'), writing at the request of Kodāli, and names Rāhulapāda among his gurus. The colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṁ siddhācāryaśrīmadbhadrapādānām'.

A Hevajra sādhana by Bhadrapāda, a later member of the lineage of Saroruhavajra. Following the Hevajratantra and Saroruha's instructions, it teaches the meditation on Hevajra/Heruka with Nairātmyā as 'Dveṣavajra' (the hatred-vajra form). It covers the preliminaries, worship by the eight goddesses (Gaurī, Caurī, etc.), the sevenfold worship and the brahmavihāras, the generation of the maṇḍala, consecration, mantra recitation, bali and subtle yoga, and closes with the assignment of the vajrīs to the senses. The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way') is the foundational treatise composed by Nāgārjuna. Across 27 chapters, it examines and deconstructs core metaphysical categories and conceptual frameworks—including causation, motion, sense faculties, the skandhas, the self, time, suffering, defilements, the four noble truths, and nirvāṇa. ## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Opening verse 1: 'buddhaṃ praṇamya lokeśaṃ vāgīśaṃ tāriṇīm api / teṣāṃ pūjākramaṃ brūmo yathāmnāyaṃ samāsataḥ'. The e-text gives the daily preliminaries, the maṇḍalaka of the Pañcatathāgatas and their consorts, the pūjā and mantras (verses 1–35), 'buddhamaṇḍalaṃ samāptam', and the arghya/pādya offerings with the iconography of the eight Bodhisattvas. It then begins 'atha śrīmatkhasarpaṇabhaṭṭārakapūjā…' and breaks off mid-sentence ('pūrve pūrvavidehe vairocanam | dakṣiṇe'). The sections on Lokeśa/Khasarpaṇa (most of it), Vāgīśa (Mañjuśrī) and Tārā are missing.

An anonymous Sanskrit manual (pūjākrama) for the daily worship of the Buddha and of the deities named in the opening verse: Lokeśa, Vāgīśa (Mañjuśrī) and Tāriṇī. The surviving part covers the morning observances and bath mantras, the preparation and consecration of the maṇḍalaka, and the visualisation of the Pañcatathāgatas with their consorts on Sumeru and the four continents, with mantras, offerings and praise. It then gives the arghya and pādya offerings with the iconography of the eight great Bodhisattvas, and breaks off at the beginning of the worship of Khasarpaṇa Avalokiteśvara.

The Mahāvastu (or Mahāvastvavadāna) is an extensive canonical biography of the Buddha preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit, representing the Vinayapiṭaka tradition of the Lokottaravāda branch of the Mahāsāṅghika school. It frames the life of Śākyamuni Buddha within a cosmic perspective of past buddhas and numerous rebirth stories (jātakas and avadānas), reflecting early Lokottaravāda docetism. Volume 2 details the Bodhisattva's final rebirth from his descent from the Tuṣita heaven, conception, birth, princely life, and great renunciation through the attainment of awakening, interspersed with major narratives including the Śyāmajātaka and Kuśajātaka.

The Pāiyalacchīnāmamālā ('Garland of Names of the Prakrit Fortune') is a Prakrit synonym lexicon (koṣa) composed in 279 Āryā/Gāhā stanzas by the Jain poet Dhanapāla. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the 1,000 verses (numbered GāSa.1 to GāSa.1000) collected in Albrecht Weber's 1881 critical edition.

**Also known as:** Gāhāsattasaī, Gāthāsaptaśatī, Gāthākośa

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla (ca. 1st–2nd century CE) as collector/author. Modern scholarship treats the collection as an evolving anthology of Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit muktaka stanzas compiled and augmented over several centuries (roughly 3rd to 8th centuries CE).

The Sattasaī (Gāhāsattasaī, Sanskrit: Gāthāsaptaśatī) is an anthology of lyric stanzas (muktaka) in the āryā (gāhā) metre in Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit, traditionally attributed to the Sātavāhana ruler Hāla. The poems evoke vignettes of pastoral and domestic life in the Deccan, focusing primarily on the nuances of erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), courtship, jealousy, and the distress of separation. It holds a pivotal place in Indian poetic tradition and was frequently cited by classical Sanskrit rhetoricians as the exemplar of dhvani (poetic suggestion).

The Gāhārayaṇakosa (Sanskrit: Gāthāratnakośa) is a Prakrit poetic anthology compiled by the Śvetāmbara Jain monk Jineśvarasūri in VS 1251 (1194 CE). The Paümacariya (Padmacarita) of Vimalasūri is the earliest surviving Jaina retelling of the Rāma story (Rāmāyaṇa), composed in Jaina Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit verse across 118 uddesas. The work explicitly rationalizes and corrects Vālmīki's epic in light of Jaina doctrine, presenting Rāvaṇa and the Rākṣasas as civilized Vidyādhara aerial beings rather than blood-drinking demons, and Sugrīva and the Vānaras as a dynasty bearing the monkey emblem rather than beasts. Emphasizing karma, ahiṃsā, and monastic renunciation, it culminates in Rāma's attainment of omniscience (kevalajñāna) and ultimate liberation (nirvāṇa), serving as the foundational prototype for subsequent Jaina Rāmakathā literature in Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Apabhraṃśa.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete as extant; contains all 1209 verses (gāthās) of the introductory section (gāthāpīṭha), which is all that survives of the poem in the manuscript tradition.

**Also known as:** Gauḍavaha, Gauḍavadha, Gaüḍavaho, Gaüḍavahaṁ

**Attribution:** Vākpatirāja explicitly names himself in the text and colophon (kaïrāa-lañchaṇassa vappaïrāassa gauḍavahē gāhāvīḍhaṁ samattaṁ).

The Gaüḍavaha ('The Slaying of the Gauda [King]') is an 8th-century Maharashtri Prakrit mahākāvya composed in āryā meter by Vākpatirāja, court poet of King Yaśovarman of Kanauj (c. 725–753 CE). Although planned to celebrate Yaśovarman's digvijaya and victory over the Gauda monarch, the extant text preserves only the introductory portion (gāthāpīṭha, 1209 verses), concluding before the actual battle. The text contains elaborate invocations of Viṣṇu and Vindhyavāsinī (Durgā), reflections on the nature and sweetness of Prakrit poetry, descriptions of seasons and village life, and eulogies of King Yaśovarman.

The Āyāraṅgasutta (Sanskrit: Ācārāṅgasūtra) is the first of the eleven surviving Aṅgas of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. The Daśavaikālikasūtra (Prakrit: Dasaveyāliyasutta) is one of the four Mūlasūtras of the Śvetāmbara Jain canonical tradition (Siddhānta). Composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit in ten adhyayanas and two supplementary cūlikās, it is one of the foundational texts studied by newly ordained ascetics. It systematically sets forth the core vows, monastic rules of conduct (ācāra), the strict requirements for begging alms (piṇḍaiṣaṇā), and the cultivation of non-violence (ahiṃsā) and self-restraint.

The Uttarajjhayaṇasutta (Sanskrit: Uttarādhyayanasūtra) is one of the four Mūlasūtras of the Śvetāmbara Jain canonical corpus, traditionally held to record the final discourses delivered by Vardhamāna Mahāvīra before his parinirvāṇa. The Nirvikalpastuti (commonly known as the Prajñāpāramitāstotra) is a 21-verse devotional and philosophical hymn praising the perfection of wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) in classical Madhyamaka terminology. Depicted as non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), beyond conceptual elaboration (niṣprapañca), and indistinguishable from the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā is revered as the mother and grandmother of all Buddhas.

The Smṛticandrikā is an influential South Indian Dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) compiled by Devaṇabhaṭṭa. Its Vyavahārakāṇḍa treats civil and criminal jurisprudence in two parts: judicial court organization, plaint, reply, and proof (vyavahāramātṛkā, including documents, witnesses, and divine ordeals); and substantive adjudication over the eighteen classical titles of dispute (vyavahārapada, such as non-payment of debt, partition/inheritance, boundary disputes, and assault). It remains one of the foundational legal authorities of the Southern school of Hindu law.

Chapter 3 of the Manusmṛti and Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya addresses the rules governing the householder (gṛhastha). It begins with the student's return ceremony (samāvartana), qualifications for marriage, and a detailed discussion of the eight forms of marriage (brāhma, daiva, ārṣa, prājāpatya, āsura, gāndharva, rākṣasa, paiśāca). Medhātithi utilizes classical Mīmāṃsā principles to interpret injunctions (vidhi) and eulogistic explanations (arthavāda).

Medhātithi applies Mīmāṃsā principles and legal reasoning to interpret these rules and reconcile conflicting smṛti traditions.

The Dakṣasmṛti (or Dakṣasaṃhitā) is a metrical Dharmaśāstra text in seven chapters traditionally attributed to the sage Dakṣa Prajāpati. The Praśna Upaniṣad is a classical Vedic text associated with the Pippalāda recension of the Atharvaveda, numbered among the principal (mukhya) Upaniṣads. Structured as an inquiry by six seekers of Brahman addressing the sage Pippalāda, the work unfolds in six sections (praśnas) addressing cosmogony through the polarity of rayi (matter) and prāṇa (breath/energy), the supremacy and functions of vital breath, physiological and psychic functions, the dream and deep sleep states, meditation on the syllable Om, and the nature of the sixteen-part Puruṣa.

The 'Buddhamuni' section summarises the Buddha's life from his birth at Kapilavastu to his nirvāṇa, dating events in the Kali era and ending with the Purāṇic view of the Buddha as an avatāra of Viṣṇu.

Nālandādahana ('The Burning of Nālandā') is a Sanskrit dance-drama of the ḍima type. Composed with songs (pallavi, anupallavi, caraṇam) in various classical rāgas (such as Durgā, Pūrvakalyāṇī, Ābhogi, Siṃhendramadhyamam, Vihag) and ādi tāla. Students sing praise of Nālandā, the abbot and senior monks discuss the approaching Turkish army attack, followed by the assault and destruction. It concludes with the head librarian nun dancing and proclaiming the enduring fame of mother Nālandā.

The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Truth'), traditionally attributed to Ādiśeṣa, is a concise philosophical poem of 85 āryā stanzas setting forth an early form of non-dualist Vedānta with strong Vaiṣṇava and Sāṅkhya-Yoga affinities. Identifying the ultimate reality (Brahman) with Viṣṇu, it elucidates the relationship between prakṛti and puruṣa, the nature of cosmic illusion (māyā/avidyā), and final release through knowledge. It is historically notable as the source text reworked by Abhinavagupta into his prominent treatise of the same title.

The Narmamālā ('Garland of Mirth' or 'Garland of Satires') is a satirical poem in three chapters (parihāsas) composed in 11th-century Kashmir during the reign of King Ananta. The Vaidyajīvana ('Physician's Life') is an Āyurvedic treatise composed in ornate poetic verse (kāvya) by the poet-physician Lolimbarāja (17th cent.). In five vilāsas, it treats fevers, bowel and digestive disorders, women's diseases and aphrodisiacs, pulmonary consumption, and general ailments. Uniquely within Indian medical literature, the medical prescriptions and dietary rules are formulated as playful, erotic addresses to the author's beloved.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Karl Gustav Hoefer (ed.), Kāvyarākṣasaṃ saṭīkam, in Sanskrit Lesebuch mit Benutzung handschriftlicher Quellen, Berlin: Besser, 1849, pp. 86–93; collated and critically constituted for the poem by Christophe Vielle against 19th-century editions (Häberlin 1861, Haridas Hirachand 1864, Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara 1872, K. P. Parab).

**E-text:** Christophe Vielle for GRETIL (converted to TEI by Maximilian Mehner)

**Evidence:**
- TEI header: 'The text of the poem (‘RaKa’) has been established on the basis of Hoefer’s text compared with the text of several other available editions or manuscripts... The text of the ṭīkā relies on Hoefer’s edition only, slightly corrected when needed, and with a few additions in brackets.'
- The apparatus explicitly cites Hoefer ('H') along with Häberlin ('C'), Jīvānanda ('J'), Parab ('P'), etc.

**Other editions:**
- Johannes Häberlin (ed.), Kāvyasaṃgrahaḥ, Calcutta, 1847 (2nd ed. 1861), pp. 586–589. — Early printed edition of the root verses.
- Haridas Hirachand (ed.), Kavya Kalapa, Number First, Bombay: Ganpat Krishnaji’s Press, 1864, pp. 137–139. — Under title Vidvadvinodakāvyam.
- Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara (ed.), Kāvyasaṃgrahaḥ, vol. 3, Calcutta: Sarasvati Press, 1888, pp. 343–353. — Includes editor's own vyākhyā.
- Kāśīnāth Pāṇḍuraṅg Parab (ed.), Rākṣasakāvyam, saṭīkam, Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgara Press. — Standard NSP edition with Sanskrit commentary.
- Śrīnavakiśorakara Śāstrī (ed.), Rākṣasakāvyam with commentary, Haridas Sanskrit Series 73, Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1938. — Haridas Sanskrit Series edition.

**Translations:**
- Raja Pṛthvīpāla Siṃha (transl.), Allahabad: Indian Press, 1909. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete work of 20 verses (viṃśatihṛdyapadyasameta) with corresponding commentary, word-division, and textual apparatus.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Rākṣasakāvya (Ravideva, root text)
- Sajjanānandadāyinī (Ravideva, commentary)

**Also known as:** Kāvyarākṣasa, Vidvadvinodakāvya, Rākṣasakāvyaṭīkā

**Attribution:** Colophons of the root text and commentary name Ravideva of the Malaya region as the author. The commentary colophon notes expansion/gloss by Kṛṣṇadhara Vyāḍi (kṛṣṇadhareṇa vyāḷinā prapañcitā).

The Rākṣasakāvya is a brief 20-verse poem in the vasantatilakā meter describing the arrival of the monsoon season. Notable for its dense wordplay, alliteration (yamaka), and obscure periphrastic expressions, the poem depicts a youthful traveler admiring rain clouds, peacocks, and flowering trees before returning home in a bullock cart with his wife. It is accompanied by the Sajjanānandadāyinī commentary, traditionally attributed to Ravideva and expanded by Kṛṣṇadhara Vyāḍi.

**Works in this e-text:**

- Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣya (Śaṅkara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Taittirīyopaniṣad-Śāṅkarabhāṣya, Taittirīyabhāṣya

**Attribution:** The root text is a canonical Vedic Upaniṣad belonging to the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. The commentary is universally accepted in both tradition and modern scholarship as an authentic work of Śaṅkarācārya.

The Taittirīyopaniṣad is a principal Upaniṣad of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, comprising three chapters: Śikṣāvallī, Brahmavallī (or Brahmānandavallī), and Bhṛguvallī. It covers traditional phonetic instruction, meditative upāsanās, the fivefold sheath analysis (pañcakośa), and the quintessential definition of absolute reality as satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma. Śaṅkara's commentary provides an authoritative Advaita Vedānta exposition, establishing that liberation is achieved not through ritual action (karman) but solely through direct knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self.

The Dvayasaṃpattivārttika is a short Kashmirian Śaiva work in 23 verses by Vāmanadatta (ca. 10th century CE). It comments on two scriptural verses outlining 'dvayasampatti' (the simultaneous realization/perfection of Śiva and Śakti), analyzing phonemic mysticism centering on 'a' (Śiva) and 'ha' / nādabindu (Śakti), and incorporates yogic techniques referenced from the Vijñānabhairava.

## Contents

While mundane branches of learning emerge during the evolution of the world, they cannot eliminate suffering; only the Buddhas disclose the supreme science—the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to nirvāṇa.

The Nirukta of Yāska is the foundational treatise of the Nirukta (Vedic etymology and semantic interpretation) Vedāṅga, composed c. 5th century BCE. Serving as an exegesis of the Vedic lexical list (Nighaṇṭu), it elaborates early linguistic theory regarding word classes (nāma, ākhyāta, upasarga, nipāta), root derivation, and Vedic theological-mythological hermeneutics across the Naighaṇṭuka, Naigama, and Daivata sections.

The Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred Thousand Lines') is the longest canonical recension of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras. It expounds universal emptiness (śūnyatā), the non-arising and non-apprehendability (anupalambha) of all dharmas, and the comprehensive path of the bodhisattva through dialogues between the Buddha, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and other disciples. This volume covers chapters 1 through 12 (the first khanda), beginning with the opening assembly on Gṛdhrakūṭa and systematically examining the emptiness and ungraspability of the skandhas, dhātus, āyatanas, and pāramitās.

Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai's 13th-century Maṇipravāḷam commentary provides a line-by-line grammatical, theological, and devotional exposition reflecting classical Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.

**Coverage:** complete — Text of ritual procedures (vidhis), beginning with opening verses at p. 47 and concluding with the final verses and colophon at p. 516.

**Also known as:** Vajrāvalīnāmamaṇḍalopāyikā, Vajrāvalīnāmamaṇḍalasādhana, dKyil 'khor gyi cho ga rdo rje phreng ba

**Attribution:** Work of Abhayākaragupta; explicitly named in the opening verse (0.1: '... abhayasya mahasā vajrāvalī mīlatu') and closing colophon (p. 516: 'mahāpaṇḍita-abhayākaragupta-racitā vajrāvalī nāma maṇḍalopāyikā samāptā').

The Vajrāvalī (or Vajrāvalīnāmamaṇḍalopāyikā) by Abhayākaragupta is a comprehensive ritual compendium of late Indian tantric Buddhism. Structured around sequential rites (vidhi), it details the selection and purification of the ritual ground, maṇḍala construction and coloration, installation and consecration of images and monastic dwellings (pratiṣṭhā), the progression of tantric initiations (abhiṣeka), post-initiatory observances (vrata), fire rituals (homa), and maṇḍala dissolution. Providing the liturgical framework for maṇḍalas also described in Abhayākaragupta's Niṣpannayogāvalī, the work became a foundational ritual authority in Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (also known as the Ekallavīratantra) is an Anuttarayoga tantra centered on the wrathful deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (Acala) and his consort Dveṣavajrī. Across 25 chapters, it covers maṇḍala construction, initiation rituals (abhiṣeka), the subtleties of the energetic channels and drops (nāḍī and bindu), the generation of the four joys (caturānanda) through yogic and erotic union, fierce magical and subjugation rites, and meditation upon non-duality.

The Krīḍākhaṇḍa ('Book of Divine Play') is the second and concluding part of the Gaṇeśapurāṇa, an Upapurāṇa central to the Gāṇapatya tradition. ## Contents

**Also known as:** Śrījvālāmālinīkalpa, Jvālinīkalpa

**Attribution:** According to the introductory narrative (vv. 5–25), the vidyā was originally revealed by the goddess Jvālāmālinī (Vahnidevī) to Helācārya of the Draviḍa Saṅgha on the Nīlagiri hill to exorcise a demon possessing his disciple Kamalaśrī. It was subsequently passed down through a lineage of disciples to Guṇanandin, from whom Indranandin received it and composed this manual.

The Jvālāmālinīkalpa is a Digambara Jaina tantric manual in ten paricchedas attributed to Indranandin (ca. 10th century CE), dedicated to the propitiation of Jvālāmālinī (Vahnidevī), the yakṣī of the eighth Tīrthaṅkara, Candraprabha. According to the opening narrative, the rites trace back to Helācārya of the Draviḍa Saṅgha, who obtained them on the Nīlagiri hill to exorcise a brahmarākṣasa from his disciple Kamalaśrī. The text details mantra recitation, yantra diagram construction, homa rituals, mudrās, and various protective and pacifying rites.

**Translations:**
- Sabine Gudrun Klein-Schwind, annotated English translation in her dissertation (Universität Hamburg, 2012). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Covers all ten tattvas announced in v. 2 (rakṣācakra, cakra, jāpa, two sekas, haṭha, bali, two pratyaṅgirās, puṭodghāta) up to the concluding verse and colophon, but with lacunae from the incomplete manuscript: a folio is missing at the beginning of the rakṣācakra section (segment 'FOLIO MISSING') and another near the end of the puṭodghāta section (segment '[folio missing]'). The ilx/Hamburg header marks the file as '(not final)'.

**Also known as:** The Compendium of the Ten Fundamentals

**Attribution:** Colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ daśatattvasaṃgrahaḥ paṇḍitakṣitiga⟨rbha⟩syeti' (supplement by the editor). Kṣitigarbha (paṇḍita) of the Jñānapāda school of Guhyasamāja exegesis.

The Daśatattvasaṃgraha is a manual of the Jñānapāda school of Guhyasamāja exegesis setting out ten ritual 'fundamentals' (tattva) of the tantric master: the protective circle, the maṇḍala visualisation centred on Vajrasattva/Samantabhadra, mantra recitation, the secret and wisdom-knowledge consecrations, forceful practice (haṭha), bali offerings, two kinds of counter-magic (pratyaṅgirā) and the 'opening of the casket' (puṭodghāta). It combines verse with prose explanation and quotes tantras.

Tribe, 'The Names of Wisdom: A Critical Edition and Annotated Translation of Chapters 1–5 of Vilāsavajra's Commentary on the Nāmasamgīti, with Introduction and Textual Notes', D.Phil. thesis, University of Oxford, 1994. — Doctoral dissertation containing a critical edition and annotated translation of chapters 1–5.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains chapters (adhikāras) 1 to 5 only, ending with the colophon of chapter 5: āryanāmasaṃgītiṭīkāyāṃ nāmamantrārthāvalokinyāṃ bodhicittavajrasya vajradhātumahāmaṇḍalādhikāraḥ pañcamaḥ. The complete work comprises 14 chapters.

**Also known as:** Nāmasamgītiṭīkā Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī, Āryanāmasaṃgītiṭīkā Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī

**Attribution:** Traditional attribution to Vilāsavajra (Tibetan: sGeg pa'i rdo rje).

The Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī is an influential late 8th-century Sanskrit commentary by Vilāsavajra on the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, interpreting the root text through the esoteric framework of the Māyājālatantra and the Vajradhātumaṇḍala of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha. This critical edition covers chapters 1 through 5 (adhikāras 1–5), which detail the preliminary overview (śarīravyavasthāpana), the setting, the request of Vajrapāṇi, the response of Śākyamuni, and the exposition of the 86 name-mantras mapped onto the Vajradhātu mandala deities. It is the earliest surviving dated Sanskrit commentary on the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti.

**Attribution:** The root grammatical sūtras of the Kātantra (or Kalāpa) are traditionally attributed to Śarvavarman (revealed by Kumāra/Kārtikeya). The primary vṛtti is composed by Durgasiṃha.

The Kātantra (also known as Kalāpa or Kaumāra), attributed to Śarvavarman, is the foundational work of the earliest post-Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammatical school. Designed as an accessible alternative to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī without employing the complex Śivasūtra pratyāhāra apparatus, it systematically treats phonology and sandhi, nominal morphology and compounds, verbal conjugation, and primary derivatives across four books. The Amṛteśatantra (commonly known as the Netratantra) is an influential Śaiva tantra dedicated to the worship of Amṛteśa / Mṛtyuñjaya and Amṛtalakṣmī. Across 24 chapters, it presents mantric procedures, yogic visualizations, initiation (dīkṣā), and extensive rites for pacification, healing, royal protection, and liberation. This e-text is a diplomatic transcription of an early dated palm-leaf manuscript from Nepal copied in Nepāla Saṃvat 320 (c. 1101 CE).

**Coverage:** partial — IFP palm-leaf manuscript 30687 (160 fols.; incomplete, some folios out of order). Present: the Jñānapāda (colophon '[jñānapādaṃ samāptam]'); the Kriyāpāda, of which according to the IFP description only 90 of 118 verses survive (colophon); and the Yogapāda (8 verses, colophon). The Siddhāntasārāvalī of Trilocanaśivācārya (12th c.) is a verse compendium of Śaiva Siddhānta doctrine and ritual, arranged in the four pādas: jñāna, kriyā, yoga and caryā. Anantaśambhu's commentary explains it with extensive quotations from the Siddhāntāgamas and ritual manuals. Its topics include the categories pati, paśu and pāśa, the tattvas, daily and occasional worship, initiation (dīkṣā), yoga, and festivals and pratiṣṭhā (installation). This e-text transcribes a single incomplete and partly disordered IFP palm-leaf manuscript.

**Attribution:** Scriptural (āgamic) text. The colophon 'iti candratajñāne' ascribes the material to the Candrajñāna, associated with the Siddhāntāgama tradition.

Verse sections of the Śaiva Siddhānta scripture Candrajñāna(āgama) on the 'dwelling of mantras' (mantravāsa) and on the daily worship of Śiva (nityārcana), transcribed from a badly damaged South Indian palm-leaf manuscript. The surviving text covers the times of worship, images of wood, pedestals, the worship of Sūrya and Indra, the fruits of worship, the seats and the five purifications (bhūta-, mantra-śuddhi etc.), the lion-throne, the Sadāśiva form, invocation, food offering and bathing, and the bathing of the liṅga with various substances.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete transcription of manuscript 4919, preserving the introductory pīṭhikā and the eight thematic sections (adhikāras) treating the ṣaṭkarmas, śānti, rakṣā, and bandhamokṣa, ending with the concluding colophon: iti śrīdāmodareṇa śivājñākareṇa paṇḍitarājena viracito yantracintāmaṇiḥ samāptaḥ.

**Also known as:** Kalpacintāmaṇi

**Attribution:** Dāmodara introduces his lineage in the opening stanzas (vv. 1–6: Mahādeva -> Devadatta -> Gaṅgādhara -> Dāmodara) and states that Śiva inspired him in a dream to compile this yantra treatise based on various Śaiva, Saura, and Śākta texts.

The Yantracintāmaṇi is a widely cited medieval Sanskrit tantric treatise on yantras composed by Dāmodara, son of Gaṅgādhara. Structured as a dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara upon Mount Kailāsa, the work provides detailed instructions for constructing, inscribing, and ritually activating yantras across eight principal sections corresponding to the ṣaṭkarman (vaśya, ākarṣaṇa, stambhana, vidveṣaṇa, māraṇa, uccāṭana) as well as rites for pacification (śānti), protection (rakṣā), and liberation from physical confinement (bandhamokṣa).

An anonymous South Indian ritual handbook made up mainly of dhyāna verses, which describe the forms, attributes and mounts of deities for visualization in worship. It includes Śaiva forms (Sadāśiva, Dakṣiṇāmūrti), forms of the Goddess (Durgā, the Lakṣmīs), Vaiṣṇava deities and the nine planets with their gotras and directions. It also contains ritual notes such as the examination of coconuts (nālikeralakṣaṇa), the visualization of the yāgaśālā as a divine body, and, towards the end, verses on ancestral offerings (śrāddha, pitṛtarpaṇa).

This chapter establishes the authoritative 700-mantra breakdown (saptaśatīmantrasaṅkhyāvibhāga) of the Devīmāhātmya / Durgāsaptaśatī necessary for ritual applications such as homa, japa, and saṃpuṭīkaraṇa. The Nityādisaṅgraha is an extensive Kashmiri Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati) composed by Rājānaka Takṣakavarta. After this come further rites: trikhaṇḍāpūjana, mūlasthāna devārcana, the catuḥṣaṣṭiyoginī-, mahā-, samaya- and śānti-bali, and gift/dakṣiṇā formulas with Newari rubrics ending '... upadohanārthaṃ || śubha ||'. The ilx_skt Muktabodha metadata marks the transcription as 'incomplete, lacking final colophon', with the colophon located 'in middle'. It could not be checked whether folios are missing, because the NGMCP description of the manuscript was not accessible.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Paścimāmnāyāṣṭāviṃśatikramārcana (worship of the 28 kramas of Kubjikā) (root text (paddhati))
- Supplementary rites: Trikhaṇḍāpūjana, Mūlasthāna-devārcana, Catuḥṣaṣṭiyoginībali, Mahābali, Samayabali, Śāntibali, dakṣiṇā and gift formulas (appendix (further ritual sections copied after the colophon of the main krama-worship, in the same manuscript))

**Also known as:** Paścimajyeṣṭhāmnāyāṣṭāviṃśatikramārcana (manuscript colophon: 'śrīpaścimajeṣṭhānjeṣṭhe āmnāya aṣṭāviṃśati krammārccaṇaṃ')

This is a Newar ritual manual (paddhati) of the Kubjikā cult (Paścimāmnāya, the 'Western Transmission'), mixing Sanskrit mantras with Newari ritual instructions. It sets out the worship of the goddess Kubjikā and her retinue in 28 sequences (aṣṭāviṃśatikrama): guru veneration, purification of the hands and of the vessels for water and arghya, bhūtaśuddhi, extensive nyāsas, meditation on the kramas, and worship of the lineages of Siddhas/Nāthas (navanātha, the 'ānanda' teachers). The manuscript then gives supplementary rites, chiefly bali offerings to Vaṭuka, the 64 yoginīs and other deities, and closing formulas for dakṣiṇā and gifts.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Manuscript transcription of Uttar Pradesh Sanskrit Sansthan (UPSS), Lucknow, MS 5144 (diplomatic transcription).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00643; transcribed under the supervision of Anirban Dash, April 4, 2024)

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha TEI header: 'Manuscript : Uttar Pradesh Sanskrit Sansthan (UPSS) 5144. Notes: Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Anirban Dash. Revision 0: Apr. 4, 2024 Diplomatic transcription'

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Six prakāśas, each closed by a colophon: (1) pretādi-agni-upaśamana; (2) śarīraja-ādi-upaśamana; (3) bandhamokṣa, uccāṭana, garbharakṣā, bālarakṣā; (4) sthāvara-jaṅgama viṣa; (5) māraṇa, mohana, vidveṣaṇa; (6) dvārācakra etc., ending with jvara mantras. A scribal colophon follows ("yādṛśaṃ pustakaṃ ... saṃvat phālguṇa saptamī ..."), so the copy in UPSS MS 5144 is complete as transmitted. The work's extent outside this manuscript is unknown. The language is mostly early modern Hindi with Sanskrit mantra and colophon material.

**Also known as:** Śābaratantramantrasaṃgraha, Sāvaratantra

**Attribution:** Only the final colophon (6th prakāśa) names the compiler: "iti śrīsāvaratantre mantrasaṃgrahe durge rāmasiṃhakṛte ...". The colophons of prakāśas 1–5 name sections or sub-collections (Bhānumatī-carita, Sonā ciraiyā, Kavūtarakalā, Durgomadanā-vicitrakalā) but no author.

A compendium of Śābara (vernacular folk-tantric) incantations, protective mantras, and healing rituals attributed to Rāmasiṃha. The text interweaves early modern vernacular North Indian formulas invoking deities (Śiva, Pārvatī, Hanumān), Nātha siddhas (Gorakhnāth), and Muslim pīrs (Sulaimān) to treat physical ailments, fevers, and encounters with wild animals.
