## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text begins with the maṅgala and frame verses and the thesis on the supremacy of the Vīraśaiva, supported by quotations from Śāṅkarasaṃhitā, Pārameśvara, Kūrma and Sūtasaṃhitā. It continues through arguments on aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra and ṣaṭsthala, and on iṣṭaliṅga versus sthiraliṅga worship. It breaks off mid-sentence ("tathā ca jaṅgamatattvasya sarvābhya..."). ilx_skt: "Completeness: incomplete".

**Attribution:** The frame verses (vv. 3–7) praise Toṭada Siddheśvara and Murigā Śāntavīra Yati, and present the guru Vīracannabasava(ārya) ("vīracaṃna basavāya edhate", v. 5) answering the paṇḍita Muragaya. The author is therefore Vīracannabasava or a pupil recording his teaching. The attribution rests only on these verses.

A late Vīraśaiva theological and polemical treatise composed in mixed verse and prose by Vīracannabasava of Sudhāpurī, writing within the lineage of the 15th–16th century saint Tōṭada Siddhēśvara and Murigā Śāntavīra. The work expounds classical Vīraśaiva doctrine, focusing on the eight protective shields (aṣṭāvaraṇa), five conducts (pañcācāra), six stages (ṣaṭsthala), and the superiority of personal liṅga worship (iṣṭaliṅga) over temple idols (sthiraliṅga). It supports its positions by citing extensive passages from Purāṇic and Tantric/Āgamic texts such as the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā, Pārameśvara, Kūrmapurāṇa, and Sūtasaṃhitā.

**Attribution:** Canonical Śaivasiddhānta scripture traditionally classified as the second of the 28 Mūlāgamas (specifically one of the ten Śivabhedas), revealed by Śiva (Paraśiva) to Sudhākhya, Vibhu, and Bhasma.

The Yogajāgama is traditionally enumerated as the second of the twenty-eight Mūlāgamas of the Śaivasiddhānta canon, categorized as one of the ten Śivabhedas. The text deals primarily with kriyā and caryā aspects of Śaiva temple ritual and architecture, including temple planning (prāsādalakṣaṇa), iconometry (pratimālakṣaṇa), the installation of attendant deities (parivārasthāpana), liṅga installation (liṅgasthāpana), fire rituals (agnikārya), and initiation rites (dīkṣā). This e-text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of an incomplete palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the French Institute of Pondicherry (IFP MS 39691).

**E-text:** Institut Français de Pondichéry Indology team under the supervision of Deviprasad Mishra, for the IFP–Muktabodha project; Muktabodha catalogue no. I00037 (rev. 0: 30 Jan 2025; rev. 2: 11 Jun 2025); TEI conversion by Intellexus (ilx_skt).

The appended Dūtikānyāsa, Devīśrīkaṇṭhanyāsa and Devīṣaḍadhvanyāsa also end with closing formulas; the last ends at seg. 810 with 'ṣaḍoddhvā [= ṣaḍadhvā] samāptaḥ'. The manuscript then gives the vaktra- and kalānyāsas and a Śrīkaṇṭhamātṛkānyāsa (seg. 843ff.), which breaks off mid-formula on p. 59b / f. 55a (seg. 879). The rest of the bundle (pp. 59b–62b) is blank. The IFP description calls the Devīṣaḍadhvanyāsa the incomplete section. The e-text shows that it is the following mātṛkānyāsa that is cut off.

**Attribution:** An anonymous South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta ritual compilation preserved in manuscript form.

An anonymous South Indian ritual manual of the late Śaiva Siddhānta for worship of the Goddess in the sacrificial pavilion (śaktimaṇṭapa / śaktiyāga). It prescribes the preparation of the pavilion and vessels (vardhanī), the worship of the four doorways and their toraṇas (caturdvārapūjā), the altar (vedikārcana) and the āvaraṇa deities, and the invocation of Gaurī. Appended are several nyāsa procedures: Dūtikānyāsa, Devīśrīkaṇṭhanyāsa, Devīṣaḍadhvanyāsa, kalānyāsa and Śrīkaṇṭhamātṛkānyāsa.

The Śambhunirṇaya (also known as the Śambhunirṇayatantra) is an influential Śāmbhava Kaula tantric ritual work divided into 26 avacchedas. This first volume, the Māheśvarāṃśa, details the transmission of secret Śaiva doctrine to the sage Jaigīṣavya, praises of Śiva and Devī by Skanda and other divinities, the religious merit of liṅga worship and temple building, and theological arguments asserting Śiva's transcendence over all other deities.

**E-text:** Institut Français de Pondichéry: Sambandhan Anandavardhana and Arul Nandi, under the supervision of Deviprasad Mishra, for the IFP–Muktabodha project; Muktabodha catalogue no. I00021 (© 2023); TEI conversion by Intellexus (ilx_skt).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The transcription runs from picture P5b to P200a of the 200-picture bundle; 'P' numbers are photograph numbers, and the folio numbering restarts within sections. It starts with a section heading on P5b, so the first pictures probably contain only covers or blank leaves; this was not verified. It ends mid-sentence on P200a (seg. 5838) in the rites after the utsavavidhi that ends at seg. 5733, without a colophon. The material on the following leaves is therefore lost or not photographed. Individual Āgama chapters are mostly complete with paṭala colophons. Muktabodha marks completeness as 'uncertain'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Dhanurmāsapūjāvidhi, Kṛttikādīpanirṇayavidhi, Dīpāvalisnāna, Navarātryutsavavidhi (short ritual tracts with Āgama quotations (seg. 1–253))
- Skandaṣaṣṭhīvratotsava from the Kāmika utsavapaddhati (extract (colophon seg. 254))
- Ekākṣaranighaṇṭu (lexical tract (from seg. 257))
- Rakṣoghnahomavidhi (ritual tract (seg. 425–468))
- Mudrālakṣaṇa, Ṣoḍaśopacāra (ritual tracts (seg. 546ff., 860ff.))
- Dravyāhutihomavidhipaṭala from the Sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha (extract (seg. 984–1083))
- Navarātrividhi; Cintya (Pratiṣṭhātantra): mahānavamī/śamīpūjā and the śivotsava chapters (utsavaprakaraṇa, aṅkurārpaṇa, dhvajārohaṇa ... maunabali) (Āgama extracts (seg. 1085–2327; colophon 'kālīśvaraguruṇā likhite cintye śivotsavavidhi samāptaḥ'))
- Cintya: utsava-prāyaścitta chapters (Āgama extracts (seg. 2328–2883))
- Sūkṣmāgama utsavavidhipaṭala (Āgama extract (to seg. 4108))
- Makuṭāgama utsavavidhipaṭala (Āgama extract (to seg. 4629))
- Kāraṇa (Pratiṣṭhātantra): āḍipūra utsavavidhi (Āgama extract (to seg. 5156))
- Navarātrividhi from the Sakalāgamasaṅgraha (Aghoraśiva (as attributed in the colophon), extract (colophon seg. 5313: 'iti sakalāgamasaṅgrahe aghoraśivācāryaviracitāyāṃ navarātrividhiḥ samāptaḥ'))
- Utsavavidhi (ends seg. 5733) and the kṛṣṇagandhalepana/Naṭeśa rites (ritual prose, incomplete (seg. 5314–5838))

**Also known as:** Cintye śivotsavavidhi (seg. 2327)

**Attribution:** Anonymous compilation. The colophon at seg. 2327 names one Kālīśvaraguru as the writer or copyist of the Cintya śivotsava section ('kālīśvaraguruṇā likhite'). A note at seg. 1083 records the dravyāhuti section as written in the owner's own hand ('(அப்பா/அய்யா) svahastalikhitam'). One colophon attributes a Sakalāgamasaṅgraha to Aghoraśivācārya; that attribution is reported, not verified.

A composite South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta manuscript on temple festivals (utsava) and seasonal observances. It contains short tracts on the Dhanurmāsa worship, the Kṛttikā lamp festival, Dīpāvali and Navarātri, as well as rakṣoghnahoma, mudrās, the sixteen upacāras and dravyāhuti homa. Its core is a series of festival chapters from the Cintya (Pratiṣṭhātantra), covering sprouting, flag-hoisting, drum-beating, bali processions, vehicle and chariot processions, tīrtha and cūrṇotsava, with the corresponding expiations (prāyaścitta). It also has utsava chapters of the Sūkṣma, Makuṭa and Kāraṇa Āgamas.

An anonymous Śrīvaiṣṇava manual of domestic (gṛhya) rites in Sanskrit with Tamil rubrics, preserved in IFP manuscript 31231. Its main subject is the annual śrāddha for the father (pratyābdikaśrāddha), performed both by the pārvaṇa procedure with homa and in the shortened saṅkalpa form, with Mahāviṣṇu as protector of the rite. It also gives procedures for rekindling the domestic fire (agnisandhāna), aupāsana, the student's aupāsana and pañcagavya. It ends with a cosmographic saṅkalpa formula and fragmentary Tamil–Maṇipravāḷa notes.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — The text begins '[śrīvyāsoktabasavapurāṇaṃ prārabhyate] [prathamo'dhyāyaḥ] agastyapraśnaḥ' and ends with the colophon of the 43rd adhyāya: 'iti śrībādarāyaṇamaharṣipraṇīte śrībasaveśvarapurāṇe svarūpagraṃthe paramarahasye skaṃdāgastyasaṃvāde tricatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ śrībasaveśvarapurāṇaṃ saṃpūrṇaṃ'.

Colophons present the work as a 'svarūpagrantha' and 'paramarahasya' in the form of a dialogue between Skanda (Kumāra) and Agastya. It is a Sanskrit Vīraśaiva work and should not be confused with the Telugu Basavapurāṇamu of Pālkuriki Somanātha.

The Sanskrit Basavapurāṇa (Basaveśvarapurāṇa) is a Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) purāṇa in 43 adhyāyas, framed as a dialogue in which Skanda answers Agastya's questions. It narrates the birth of Basava (Basaveśvara) as a partial incarnation of Nandin, his marriage, his service at the court of Bijjala and his miracles. It also tells the legends of many Śaiva and Vīraśaiva devotees (e.g. Kannappa, Dīpada Kaliya, Moligemāra, Śivanāgadeva) and argues for Vīraśaiva doctrine and practice against Vedic ritualism and rival sects. It closes with a scene in which Viśvakarman weighs the work against Vyāsa's other compositions and finds it the best of all purāṇas.

The Advaitapañcaratna (also known as Ātmapañcaka) is a concise philosophical stotra of five verses attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Employing standard Advaita analogies such as the rope and the snake, the dream state, and reflections in a mirror, each verse refutes identity with the body, senses, intellect, or external possessions and concludes with the refrain 'śivo'ham' ('I am Śiva/pure consciousness').

**Also known as:** Bhedojjīvanam, Bhedojjīvanabhāvapradīpa (Bhagavantarāya's commentary, also called Bhedojjīvanapañcikā), Bhedacintāratna (Ānandatīrtha), Bhedacandrikā (Vāsudevācārya), Bhedasañjīvanī / Bhedasañjīvinī (Śrīnātha), Kāśikā (Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya's commentary, as it is commonly called)

**Attribution:** The root text is by Vyāsatīrtha (Vyāsarāja, 1478–1539; also given as c. 1460–1539); the root colophon reads 'brahmaṇyatīrthapūjyapādaśiṣyeṇa vyāsayatinā kṛtaṃ bhedojjīvanaṃ samāptam'. The commentators as identified in the e-text: (1) Bhagavantarāya, 'bhagavannāmnā', a pupil of Bhāskarī Veṅkaṭavarāhācārya (seg. 4 and 8661). (2) Ānandatīrtha, son of Mudgalārya, of Janārdanapura (seg. 66 and 8706–8710); he is not Madhva. (3) Vāsudevācārya, son of Kumbhārī Nārāyaṇācārya (seg. 91 and 8725). (4) Śrīnātha, called Hulagī Śrīnāthācārya in the heading, of Vyāghrapurī and son of Vāsudevārya (seg. 156 and 8740–8744). (5) Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya, called Kāśī Tirumalācārya in the colophon (seg. 173 and 8748). (6) Śarkarā Śrīnivāsācārya (seg. 192 and 8788–8792). None of the commentators is dated here.

The Bhedojjīvana ('Reviving Difference') is a short polemical treatise by the Dvaita scholar Vyāsatīrtha. It defends the reality of difference (bheda) against Advaita. In this e-text each passage of the root text is followed by six later Mādhva commentaries and glosses, by Bhagavantarāya, Ānandatīrtha (son of Mudgalārya), Kumbhārī Vāsudevācārya, Hulagī Śrīnātha, Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya and Śarkarā Śrīnivāsa.

**Attribution:** Śaṅkara is traditionally credited with two separate commentaries on the Kenopaniṣad: the Padabhāṣya (a literal, word-for-word commentary) and the Vākyabhāṣya (a sentence-by-sentence exposition). The text here is the widely accepted Padabhāṣya.

The Kārikāvalī (also known as Bhāṣāpariccheda) together with its auto-commentary, the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī, is a standard 17th-century manual of the syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system composed by Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. The Pañcadaśī ('Fifteen Chapters') is an influential 14th-century manual of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Vidyāraṇya (and in part to Bhāratītīrtha). It is divided into three pentads corresponding to the tripartite nature of Brahman: Viveka-pañcaka (discrimination of existence, sat), Dīpa-pañcaka (illumination of consciousness, cit), and Ānanda-pañcaka (nature of bliss, ānanda). The Smṛtimuktāvalī of Kṛṣṇācārya, a pupil of Rāghavendra Tīrtha, is a dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) written for the Mādhva (Dvaita) community. It argues that Mādhva practice rests on smṛti, that ritual duties are to be done without desire for results as worship of Hari, and that smṛti and purāṇa are authoritative. It then sets out calendrical rules (seasons, months, intercalary and 'empty' months, Cāturmāsya, fortnights). The e-text breaks off in the section on the time for the single daily meal (ekabhukta).

The Tithinirṇaya is a short astronomical and calendrical treatise of 29 verses composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha) as part of his Sarvamūlagrantha corpus. It sets forth mathematical procedures, sine tables (jyāvākya), and correctional calculations (saṃskāra) for establishing the exact duration of lunar days (tithi). The text is intended to settle the proper timing for ritual fasts (upoṣaṇa), particularly Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī, in accordance with Dvaita tradition.

It also discusses related questions such as the inner self's entering (anupraveśa) and the soul's departure and movement.

The Saṅgītaratnākara is a foundational medieval treatise on Indian music and performing arts. Arranged into seven chapters (saptādhyāyī), it provides an exhaustive analysis of notes and intervals (svara), melodic modes (rāga), miscellaneous musicological concepts (prakīrṇa), song and meter forms (prabandha), rhythm and metrics (tāla), musical instruments (vādya), and dance (nartana). The treatise forms an essential transition between ancient dramatic musical theory (gāndharva/mārga) and regional performance traditions (deśī).

The Caṇḍikāṣṭaka is a 20th-century Śākta devotional stotra addressed to the goddess Caṇḍikā (Durgā/Umā), written in ornate, highly alliterative Sanskrit verse (including yamaka and anuprāsa). It was composed by Umāpatidvivedin ('Kavipati') and presented to the Śākta scholar Jagadānandaśarman on Mahāṣṭamī in VS 1983 (1926 CE).

Cārudatta (also known as Daridracārudatta) is a classical Sanskrit-Prakrit play in four acts attributed to Bhāsa. It relates the romance between Cārudatta, an impoverished and noble merchant of Ujjayinī, and the wealthy courtesan Vasantasenā, intertwined with scenes involving the thief Sajjalaka (Śarvilaka) and the thief's burglary of Cārudatta's house. The surviving text breaks off at the end of the fourth act without a formal conclusion or bharatavākya, paralleling the first four acts of Śūdraka's ten-act Mṛcchakaṭikā.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Kuvalayānanda in 172 verses with prose commentary (vṛtti), running from the maṅgala verses to the concluding verse 172 and colophon.

**Attribution:** Composed by Appayadīkṣita (c. 16th century) under King Veṅkaṭapati. The work adopts and supplements the alaṅkāra stanzas from Jayadeva's Candrāloka along with Appayadīkṣita's own prose commentary (vṛtti).

The Kuvalayānanda is an influential manual of Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) composed by the 16th-century polymath Appayadīkṣita under the patronage of King Veṅkaṭapati. Taking the fifth chapter of Jayadeva's Candrāloka as its structural baseline, it organizes and elaborates upon over one hundred figures of sense (arthālaṅkāra), providing definition verses (lakṣaṇa), illustrative examples (lakṣya), and explanatory prose comments.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Eight stanzas with refrain plus phalaśruti (refrain repeated after it); no verse numbers and no colophon.

The Kālabhairavāṣṭaka is an eight-stanza devotional hymn (with an appended phalaśruti verse) eulogizing Kālabhairava, the fierce manifestation of Śiva acting as the guardian protector of the sacred city of Vārāṇasī (Kāśī). Each stanza ends with the refrain 'kāśikāpurādhinātha-kālabhairavaṃ bhaje', celebrating the deity's awe-inspiring iconography, dread cosmic sovereignty, and mercy in purging sins and bestowing liberation.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete Sanskrit translation corresponding to the Marathi text, followed by concluding stanzas and the closing prayer 'āpadāmapahartāraṃ...'.

**Also known as:** Śrīmanobodha, Manāce Śloka (Sanskrit translation)

**Attribution:** Original Marathi composition by Samartha Rāmadāsa. This Sanskrit verse translation was composed by an unnamed devotee ('śrīrāmadāsānudāsaḥ') residing on the banks of the Tapatī (Tapti) river.

The Manobodha (widely known in Marathi as Manāce Śloka) is a devotional and philosophical poem by Samartha Rāmadāsa. Addressed to the human mind (manas), the work instructs it to renounce worldly infatuations, transcend bodily identification, and cultivate ethical righteousness and surrender to Rāma. This e-text preserves an anonymous metrical Sanskrit translation composed on the banks of the Tapti river.

- E. E. Veṅkaṭanāthācārya (ed.), Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotram with Mānasollāsa, Tattvasudhā, and Mānasollāsavṛttāntavilāsa, 2 vols., Mysore, 1972. — Edition with sub-commentaries.

- Harshananda, Dakshinamurti Stotra with Manasollasa of Suresvaracharya, Bangalore, 1992. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of both works: the 10 stanzas of the Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra followed by all 10 ullāsas (chapters) of the Mānasollāsa (ending with daśamollāsasaṅgrahaḥ and final colophon).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra (Śaṅkara, root text)
- Mānasollāsa (Sureśvara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotrabhāvārthavārtika

**Attribution:** The root hymn Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra is traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya, and the metrical commentary Mānasollāsa is traditionally ascribed to Sureśvarācārya. Scholars note doctrinal differences between the Mānasollāsa and Sureśvara's undisputed vārttikas.

The Mānasollāsa is an influential metrical exposition (vārttika) in ten chapters (ullāsas) expounding Śaṅkara's celebrated ten-verse hymn, the Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra. Traditionally ascribed to Sureśvara, the text systematically develops the hymn's pithy Advaita Vedānta doctrines, treating themes such as the illusory nature of phenomenal diversity (māyā/vivarta), the mirror-like reflection of the world in pure consciousness, the critiques of rival philosophical views (including Buddhist Śūnyavāda and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika), and the ultimate identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Parameśvara (Śiva-Dakṣiṇāmūrti).

The Naiṣadhīyacarita (or Naiṣadha) by the philosopher-poet Śrīharṣa (12th century CE) is one of the five celebrated mahākāvyas ('great court epics') of classical Sanskrit literature. Across 22 cantos, it narrates the story of King Nala and Princess Damayantī up to their wedding and honeymoon, elaborating on the Nalopākhyāna from the Mahābhārata. Famed for its intricate linguistic craftsmanship, double entendres (śleṣa), and profound philosophical references, the work is traditionally regarded as the ultimate test of scholarship ('naiṣadhaṃ vidvad-auṣadham').

The Śivasahasranāmastotra ('Hymn of the Thousand Names of Śiva') is a major Śaiva devotional hymn extracted from the Anuśāsanaparvan of the Mahābhārata (adhyāya 17). It synthesizes Vedic, cosmogonic, and philosophical aspects of Śiva and forms one of the standard liturgical sahasranāmas of the Hindu tradition.

The Śivānandalaharī ('Wave of the bliss of Śiva') is a hymn of 100 verses to Śiva in various metres, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. It joins Advaita themes to fervent bhakti, using extended images for the devotee's mind: an elephant to be bound with the chain of devotion, a monkey, a bride. The concluding verse ('karacaraṇakṛtaṃ vākkāyajaṃ...') is widely recited across Hindu tradition as a general prayer of absolution.

The whole is framed by invocations of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi Pīṭha.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete short devotional stotra in 27 segments, consisting of introductory dhyāna verses, a core stotra praising Dattātreya with the refrain 'dattātreyaṃ namāmy aham', and a phalaśruti.

**Also known as:** Śrīdattātreyastotra, Bhṛguviracita Dattātreyastotra

**Attribution:** Ascribed to the mythical ṛṣi Bhṛgu in the concluding stanzas.

A Sanskrit devotional hymn (stotra) dedicated to Dattātreya, venerated as the unified manifestation of the Trimūrti and supreme yogic guru. It describes his visual iconography as an ascetic with matted hair, ash-besmeared limbs, and attributes of Śiva and Viṣṇu, closing with verses describing the spiritual and material benefits (phalaśruti) of regular recitation.

The Ūrubhaṅga ('The Shattering of the Thighs') is a one-act Sanskrit drama (often classified as an utsṛṣṭikāṅka) attributed to Bhāsa, based on the final mace duel between Duryodhana and Bhīma in the Mahābhārata. The Skandopaniṣad is an Upanishad associated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Opening with a speaker's declaration to Mahādeva of his identity with Acyuta and Śiva, the text teaches radical non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva, as well as the ultimate identity of Śiva and Viṣṇu ('śivāya viṣṇurūpāya śivarūpāya viṣṇave'). It synthesizes Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional motifs into Advaita Vedānta, concluding with the Vedic refrain 'tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam'.

The text correlates the component morphemes and phonemes of the mantra with deities and figures of the Rāmāyaṇa—equating them with Jāmbavān, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, and Rāma as the supreme Puruṣottama.

The Chāndogyabrāhmaṇa (widely known as the Mantrabrāhmaṇa) is a Vedic ritual text of the Kauthuma śākhā of the Sāmaveda comprising two prapāṭhakas of eight khaṇḍas each. The Mādhavanidāna (originally titled Rogaviniścaya) is a foundational 7th–8th-century Ayurvedic treatise devoted to pathology and clinical diagnosis (nidāna). Composed by Mādhavakara, the text systematizes the five diagnostic factors (pañcanidāna: nidāna, pūrvarūpa, rūpa, upaśaya, and saṃprāpti) across sixty-nine disease classifications, forming part of Ayurveda's 'shorter triad' (laghutrayī).

## Contents

**Coverage:** excerpt — Anthology of excerpts treating the tantrayuktis across different Āyurvedic treatises, including Suśrutasaṃhitā Uttaratantra 65 with commentary.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Exposition of tantraguṇas: 36 tantrayuktis, 7 kalpanās, arthāśrayas, 17 tācchīlyas, 15 tantradoṣas (lines 1–140), with examples from the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and a citation of the Saṅgraha (Uttara 50) (commentary passage)
- Śaśilekhā on Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha, Uttarasthāna 50 (tantrayukti section), headed 'indu tantrayuktiḥ' (Indu, commentary (with root verses))
- Carakasaṃhitā, Siddhisthāna 12.41–48 (tantrayukti verses) with commentary (Āyurvedadīpikā) (Caraka, Cakrapāṇidatta, root text with commentary)
- Suśrutasaṃhitā, Uttaratantra 65 (Tantrayuktyadhyāya) with Nibandhasaṅgraha (Suśruta, Ḍalhaṇa, root text with commentary)
- Indu's tantrayukti section again (duplicate) and a further exposition of the tantrayuktis (duplicate / unidentified commentary passages)

**Also known as:** Tantrayuktayaḥ, Tantrayuktyadhyāya

**Attribution:** Composite Wikisource compilation including passages from the tantrayukti sections of the Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha (with Indu), Carakasaṃhitā (with Cakrapāṇidatta), and Suśrutasaṃhitā Uttaratantra 65 with Ḍalhaṇa's commentary.

An anthology of Sanskrit passages on tantrayukti, the devices used to compose and interpret technical treatises, as discussed in Āyurvedic classics including the Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha, Carakasaṃhitā, and Suśrutasaṃhitā Uttaratantra 65.

## Contents

The Āyurvedaprakāśa of Upādhyāya Mādhava is a rasaśāstra treatise on preparing and using mercury, minerals, metals, gems and poisons in medicine. The first chapter covers the processing (saṃskāra) of mercury and related alchemical procedures, and the later chapters cover the uparasas, metals, gems and poisons. It quotes many earlier rasa authorities (Rasārṇava, Rasendracintāmaṇi, Rasaratnasamuccaya and others).

The Baudhāyanaśrautasūtra, of the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, is generally regarded as the oldest extant Śrautasūtra. It prescribes, largely from the Adhvaryu's standpoint, the solemn rites from the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnyādheya, Agnihotra, Paśubandha and Cāturmāsya through the Agniṣṭoma, Agnicayana, Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Aśvamedha and sattras. The Dhātukārikā (subtitled Bālarañjanī) by Śrīkaṇṭha is a versified grammatical mnemonic handbook on Sanskrit verbal roots according to the Pāṇinian system. Composed as a pedagogical aid complementary to Dharmādhikāri Cakravarti Ayyaṅgār's Śabdakārikā, it systematically covers the verbal roots across all ten classes (bhvādi to curādi), classifying their meanings, voice (parasmaipada, ātmanepada, ubhayapada), augment iṭ behaviors (seṭ, aniṭ, veṭ), and marker letters (anubandhas).

The second part opens with a homage to Nārāyaṇa and an anonymous author's statement ('nirūpya coccasvaranirṇayo mayā'). It lists Taittirīya words alphabetically by accent type (antodātta first, then ādyudātta).

The Lakṣmīkāntaśikṣā (Varṇakramacatuḥślokī) is a very short Taittirīya śikṣā. In four verses it states the rules of varṇakrama (gemination of consonants, abhinidhāna, insertion of yamas and other transition sounds, nasal treatment), drawing on the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya. On Wikisource, and so in this e-text, it is followed by a second, anonymous text under the same heading: a verse list of Taittirīya words sorted alphabetically by accent type (antodātta and ādyudātta).

A short Vedic lakṣaṇa (śikṣā) tract from the Taittirīya tradition. It explains the Nāradabaiṭ, a mnemonic syllable code ascribed to Nārada that encodes the counts of anuvākas and vākyas in the Taittirīyasaṃhitā. Seven paribhāṣā verses set out the rules (which vowels count, how conjunct consonants count in kaṭapayādi fashion, and the bindu-marked syllables ma, da, ga, ta, sa standing for tens). The author's prose commentary, Bhāvaprakāśikā, follows, and then the code strings for all seven kāṇḍas.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — 37 short numbered sections. The source itself notes 'mātṛkāyāmapyasaṃpūrṇam' ('also incomplete in the exemplar'). The original extent is unknown.

**Attribution:** Anonymous. The examples ('brahmavādinaḥ', 'caturhotṛṇām', 'prajananaṃ jyotiḥ') and the reference to Gautama's rule ('gautamokteḥ') point to the Taittirīya (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda) lakṣaṇa tradition. The numbered segments mix rule statements with explanatory prose ('ityarthaḥ', 'atra … viśeṣaḥ'), so the text may be a short lakṣaṇa with an embedded explanation.

The Piṇḍalakṣaṇa is a short Vedic phonetic treatise (Lakṣaṇa/Śikṣā) examining the pronunciation and tightness of cohesion in consonant clusters (varṇapiṇḍa). It classifies clusters into analogical categories such as ayaḥpiṇḍa (compact like an iron ball), dārupiṇḍa (moderately bound like wood), and tūlapiṇḍa (loosely bound like cotton), depending on whether stops, semivowels, sibilants, or nasals are conjoined. It also details the articulation of clusters containing hakāra, citing traditional Śikṣā rules on chest (urasya) versus guttural (kaṇṭhya) voicing.

The Prathamatṛtīyavarṇavibhāgalakṣaṇa is a concise five-verse Vedic phonetic tract (lakṣaṇagrantha) designed for oral recitation. It sets out mnemonic rules to distinguish whether a first (voiceless unaspirated, prathama) or third (voiced unaspirated, tṛtīya) consonant within a varga is articulated when conjoined with nasals (vargottama) in specific Vedic mantra occurrences.

The Pāṇinīyaśikṣā is the principal Vedāṅga treatise on phonetics and pronunciation associated with the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition. It systematically describes the inventory of 63 or 64 speech sounds (varṇa), the physiology of speech production, places of articulation (sthāna), internal and external effort (prayatna), pitch accents (udātta, anudātta, svarita) and their correlation with musical notes, as well as rules and faults in Vedic recitation. This e-text contains the widely cited vulgate metrical recension in 61 verses.

The Taittirīyaprātiśākhya is the phonological and phonetic treatise belonging to the Taittirīya recension. In 24 adhyāyas, it provides detailed rules on phonetic inventory, euphonic combination (sandhi), accentuation (svara), moric quantity, and pronunciation necessary to transition between the continuous saṃhitāpāṭha and the uncombined padapāṭha. It cites numerous early phoneticians, including Pauṣkarasādi, Plākṣi, and Vālmīki.

The Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā (commonly referred to as Bṛhanmañjūṣā to distinguish it from the Laghu- and Paramalaghu-mañjūṣā) is Nāgeśabhaṭṭa's masterwork on the philosophy of language and semantic theory in the Pāṇinian tradition. The Vyāsaśikṣā is a prominent phonetic manual (śikṣā) belonging to the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Arranged in 28 sections (prakaraṇas) comprising 525 verses, it details rules of accentuation (svara), sandhi, consonant gemination (dvitva), and recitation modes (pada, krama, and jaṭā) characteristic of the Taittirīya textual tradition. It shares a deep structural relationship with the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya.

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete across all three kāṇḍas: Kāṇḍa 1 (Brahmakāṇḍa / Āgamasamuccaya), Kāṇḍa 2 (Vākyakāṇḍa), and Kāṇḍa 3 (Padakāṇḍa / Prakīrṇaka, 14 samuddeśas, ending at the colophon of the Vṛttisamuddeśa).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vākyapadīya (Bhartṛhari, root text)
- Vākyapadīyavṛtti (Bhartṛhari, commentary (on Kāṇḍa 1))

**Also known as:** Trikāṇḍī, Vākyapadīyam

**Attribution:** The root kārikās are by Bhartṛhari. The ancient Vṛtti is traditionally ascribed either to Bhartṛhari himself (svopajñā vṛtti) or to Harivṛṣabha. The commentary on Kāṇḍa 3 is by Helarāja (son of Bhūtirāja).

The Vākyapadīya by Bhartṛhari is the foundational treatise of the philosophy of grammar (Vyākaraṇadarśana) and classical Indian semantic theory. Comprising three books—Brahmakāṇḍa (on Śabdabrahman and the metaphysics of language), Vākyakāṇḍa (on sentence-meaning wholism and the sphoṭa doctrine), and Padakāṇḍa or Prakīrṇaka (fourteen specialized treatises exploring universals, particulars, relations, time, action, and case-roles)—it articulates a non-dualist linguistic philosophy that shaped subsequent debates across Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya traditions. This e-text contains the complete kārikās across all three books together with their principal classical Sanskrit commentaries.

It deals with the accent of finite verbs (kriyāpada) in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā: it lists the contexts in which a verb that is normally unaccented in a main clause takes the udātta, for example after particular preceding words or in clauses with yad and hi. Each rule is illustrated with Taittirīya passages and counter-examples ('... iti kim').

A short anonymous Sanskrit hagiographical narrative recounting the legendary life of the celebrated 8th-century Madhyamaka master Śāntideva. It relates his birth as prince to King Mañjuvarman, his renunciation following his mother's warning, spiritual attainment under the siddha Mañjuvajra, service as a royal bodyguard (under the name Acalasena) armed with a wooden sword, and admission to the Nālandā monastery under the name Śāntideva (nicknamed Bhusuku). The account culminates in his recitation of the Bodhicaryāvatāra, his levitation into the sky upon reciting 9.34 (9.35), and the subsequent discovery of his written works (including the Bodhicaryāvatāra and Śikṣāsamuccaya) in his monastic cell.

The first section (vv. 1–34) details a method of post-mortem revival and transference (mṛtasaṃjīvanī) based on Guhyasamājatantra chapter 14, in which the officiant reinstalls the deceased's consciousness into the body to bestow initiation and direct it through the cranial aperture toward liberation or a pure land. The Ātmasādhanāvatāra is a major doctrinal treatise by Buddhajñānapāda (c. late 8th–early 9th century CE), founder of the Jñānapāda school of the Guhyasamājatantra. Integrating Madhyamaka epistemological analysis and Yogācāra philosophy with Anuttarayogatantra ritual principles, the text argues that saṃsāra is merely conceptual fabrication (vikalpa), refutes external reality, and defends the soteriological validity of self-worship (ātmasādhana/ātmapūjā) through identity with the maṇḍala deities.

A small manuscript (CUL Or. 155) of Cakrasaṃvara texts by the lay devotee (paramopāsaka) Chātrakumāradatta, in the tradition of Luyīpāda's sādhana. It contains a list of the names of the heroes and heroines (vīra/vīreśvarī) of the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala; a pūjā manual; and an annotated outline of the stages of the sādhana, from the preliminary pūjā and brahmavihāras through the purification of skandhas, protective circle, emptiness, generation of the maṇḍala, consecration, nectar, nyāsa, mantra recitation and bali. The author names his guru 'residing in Kanyārāma' (Rāḍhā, Bengal) and the mahāmaṇḍalācārya Sauṣṭhavapāda; Szántó dates the toponym's attestation to c. 1100–1150 CE.

**Evidence:**

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to Paṇḍita Kumudākaramati (Tibetan: ku mu da 'byung gnas blo gros).

The Trisamayarājasādhana is a detailed ritual manual (sādhana) composed by Kumudākaramati dedicated to the practice of Trisamayarāja. It lays out the requirements of initiation, samaya vows, maṇḍala construction, mantra recitation, and visualization techniques associated with Kriyā/Caryā tantric traditions. It is famously preserved as the opening text of the Sādhanamālā collection.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 32 dohā verses of Kāṇhapāda with the full Sanskrit commentary Mekhalāṭīkā, ending with the colophon 'ity ācāryapādīyadohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā samāptā'.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Also known as:** Kāṇhapādadohākoṣa, Kāṇhasya Dohākoṣaḥ, Dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā

The Dohākoṣa of Kāṇhapāda is a cycle of 32 rhymed Apabhraṃśa verses (dohā) teaching non-dual realization and sahaja. It criticizes external scholastic and Vedic rituals while elucidating esoteric internal yogic physiology (including the channels lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī). The accompanying Sanskrit commentary, the Mekhalāṭīkā (attributed to Amṛtavajra), provides word-for-word grammatical and doctrinal interpretations supported by citations from Buddhist tantric texts such as the Caturdevīparipṛcchā.

**Also known as:** Viṃśatividhi, Śrīguhyasamājamaṇḍalopāyikāviṃśatividhi, Guhyasamājamaṇḍalaviṃśatividhi, Samājamaṇḍalavidhiviṃśati

**Attribution:** Attributed to the Guhyasamāja Ārya-lineage master Nāgabuddhi (Nāgabodhi), traditionally considered a close disciple of the tantric Nāgārjuna.

The Samājamaṇḍalopāyikā (commonly known as Viṃśatividhi) is a fundamental ritual manual (maṇḍalopāyikā) of the Guhyasamāja Ārya tradition (Āryasaṃgha/Āryapakṣa), attributed to Nāgabuddhi (Nāgabodhi). The text systematically expounds the twenty ritual stages (viṃśatividhi) required to prepare, consecrate, and construct the thirty-two deity Guhyasamāja sand maṇḍala (rajomaṇḍala), followed by the procedure for admitting and conferring tantric initiations (abhiṣeka) upon disciples.

The Abhisamayamañjarī is an extensive Anuttarayogatantra ritual manual (sādhana) dedicated to the visualization and realization of Vajrayoginī / Vajravārāhī within the Cakrasaṃvara cycle. It outlines purification procedures, mantra recitations, bali offerings, the generation of the maṇḍala with accompanying retinue deities, and internal yogic meditations. Produced in late North Indian Buddhist circles (ca. 11th–12th century), it represents an important source for the development of late medieval Vajrayoginī practice.

The Pañcasthānasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse prescribing five facts that householders and monastics alike should frequently contemplate (abhīkṣṇaṃ pratyavekṣitavyam): vulnerability to disease (vyādhidharmatā), aging (jarādharmatā), death (maraṇadharmatā), separation from loved ones (viprayoga), and ownership of one's own actions (karmasvakatā). Contemplation of these realities dismantles pride in health, youth, and life, and motivates cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path to eliminate the fetters (saṃyojana).

**Attribution:** Composed by Sarvarakṣita, a Buddhist poet associated with Saṃmatīya cosmological traditions.

Chapters 3 and 4 treat the re-evolution of the world (vivṛttāvasthā), the physical and moral devolution of sentient beings as material foods are consumed, the appearance of sex differentiation and private dwelling, and the descent into the degenerate age (kali).

The Amanasikārādhāra ('Justification of Non-Mental Engagement') is a short doctrinal treatise by Advayavajra (Maitrīpa) vindicating the term and practice of amanasikāra ('absence of conceptual mental engagement') against critics. Drawing citations from canonical Mahāyāna scriptures (Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra) and tantras (Hevajra), he establishes that amanasikāra culminates in the realization of inseparable emptiness and compassion (śūnyatākaruṇābhinnayuganaddhādvayavāhisaṃvedanam).

- Explicit header lines 2–5: 'edited by MM Hara Prasad Shastri in Advayavajrasaṃgraha GOS 1927 Baroda' and 'edited by Mikkyou-seiten-kenkyūkai 3. in Taisho Daigaku Sougou Bukkyou Kenkyūjo Nenpou'
- In-text edition milestones: '^S p.49.' (Shastri) and '^M (56/309)', '^M (58/307)' (Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 10 verses, concluding with '|| yuganaddhaprakāśaḥ samāptaḥ ||'.

**Also known as:** Zuṅ-du ḥjug-pa rab-tu-gsal-ba bstan-pa shes-bya-ba

**Attribution:** Advayavajra is also known as Maitrīpa. The work is no. 15 in the collected corpus conventionally known as the Advayavajrasaṃgraha.

The Yuganaddhaprakāśa is a 10-verse philosophical text by Advayavajra (Maitrīpa) on the principle of indivisible union (yuganaddha). Synthesizing Madhyamaka reasoning with Tantric Mahāmudrā view, it explains that appearances and emptiness, as well as compassion and voidness, are intrinsically non-dual rather than artificially combined. Because all entities arise dependently and lack intrinsic existence, the yogin transcends the extremes of existence and non-existence.

# Daśatattvasaṃgraha (excerpts: rakṣācakra, cakra and seka sections)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T02_Kṣitigarbha_Daśatattvasaṃgraha`

**Author:** Kṣitigarbha

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T02

**Source:** OCR / Dharmamitra

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished partial transcription from the manuscript IASWR MBB-II-208 (missing fol. 2).

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- E-text header [0]–[2]: 'Kṣitigarbha's Daśatattvasaṃgraha apud Jnānapāda / [in the retinue of Vanaratna, died at mChims phu] / IASWR MBB-II-208 (missing folia: 2 )'.
- Folio markers [1r], [1v], [3r], '[on 22r]', '[on 28r]', '[ends on 41r]' show a selective transcription of the manuscript.
- Editorial brackets and conjectures ('[rbha]', '<dma>') indicate a working transcription, not a printed edition.

**Other editions:**
- Klein-Schwind, S.G., 'The Compendium of the Ten Fundamentals, Dasatattvasamgraha of Pandita Ksitigarbha: Critical Edition of the Sanskrit Text with Introduction and Annotated English Translation', diss., Hamburg University, 2012.

**Translations:**
- Klein-Schwind, S.G., diss., Hamburg University, 2012. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** excerpt — The manuscript runs to fol. 41r, and folio 2 is missing in the manuscript itself (header [2]; lacuna at [13]). The transcription covers fols. 1v–ca. 9 (introductory verses, rakṣācakra, maṇḍala/cakra visualisation up to [177]). It then jumps ('[on 22r]', [178]) to the seka section (guhyābhiṣeka, prajñājñānābhiṣeka, vidyāvrata, [179]–[255]) and stops at '[on 28r]' ([256]). Only the final colophon of fol. 41r follows ([257]–[260]). Of the ten tattvas listed in v. 2, the rest of the cakra section, japa, haṭha, bali, the two pratyaṅgirās and the saṃpuṭodghāṭa are not transcribed, except for the closing line 'iti saṃpuṭodghāṭavidhiḥ'.

**Attribution:** The colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṃ daśatattvasaṃgrahaḥ paṇḍitakṣitiga[rbha]sya' ([260]). The Dharmamitra header ([1]) adds that Kṣitigarbha was in the retinue of Vanaratna and died at mChims phu. The work follows the Jñānapāda tradition of the Guhyasamāja ('jñānapādakrameṇa', [5]).

The Daśatattvasaṃgraha of the paṇḍita Kṣitigarbha (in the retinue of Vanaratna) is a manual in the Jñānapāda tradition of the Guhyasamāja. It sets out ten ritual 'principles' (tattva): protective circle, maṇḍala (cakra), recitation, the two higher consecrations, haṭha, bali, the two pratyaṅgirā rites and the opening of the box (puṭodghāṭa). The e-text gives the opening verses, the rakṣācakra and much of the maṇḍala visualisation, and the guhya and prajñājñāna consecrations with the vidyāvrata. The remainder is untranscribed apart from the final colophon.

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 584 CE – 1472 CE

**Posterior median:** 1019 CE

**Author:** Samantabhadra

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T02

**Source:** OCR / Dharmamitra

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished working edition / diplomatic transcript of the 'Pāla recension' from a 45-folio manuscript.

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- Header explicitly reads: 'Sāramañjarī Pāla recension / cleaned-up e-text'.
- Embedded manuscript folio markers from [ 1a5--2a2] to [ 45b3].

**Translations:**
- yan lag bzhi pa'i sgrub thabs kyi rgya cher bshad pa snying po snye ma zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1869): translated by Nyāyaśrī, rngog blo ldan shes rab; at bal yul mthil (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary on the 164 verses of Buddhajñānapāda's Caturaṅgasādhana (fol. 1a to fol. 45b3), concluding with the author's closing verse, colophon, and scribal Pratītyasamutpāda verse.

**Also known as:** Caturaṅgasādhanaṭīkā Sāramañjarī, Caturaṅgasādhanavyākhyā Sāramañjarī

**Attribution:** Samantabhadra was a master in the Jñānapāda lineage of the Guhyasamāja tantra.

The Sāramañjarī is an extensive Sanskrit commentary by the master Samantabhadra on Buddhajñānapāda's Caturaṅgasādhana (also known as the Samantabhadrasādhana), a fundamental manual of the Guhyasamāja creation stage (utpattikrama). It provides detailed exegesis of the four limbs of yoga (caturaṅga) according to the Jñānapādamata tradition, elucidating visualization, deity generation, mantra recitation, and the philosophical defense of tantric deity yoga.

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 488 CE – 1064 CE

**Posterior median:** 885 CE

**Author:** Virūpa

**Tibetan:** D 1555

## Edition and provenance

**Translations:**
- dbu bcad ma'i sgrub thabs zhes bya ba (Derge Tengyur D 1555): translated by Varendraruci, rma lo tsA ba rma ban chos 'bar (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — The Sanskrit original survives only as a two-folio fragment in Kathmandu, Kaiser Library MS 139 (beginning at folio 10r); missing portions at the beginning and end are supplied in Tibetan transcription from D 1555.

**Also known as:** dBu bcad ma'i sgrub thabs

**Attribution:** Attributed in the Tibetan colophon to the master Bar bi pa (Virūpa). The Tibetan translation was produced by the Nepalese paṇḍita Bharendraruci and the Tibetan translator rMa Chos 'bar (Rma-ban chos-'bar).

The Chinnamuṇḍāsādhana ('Sādhana of the Severed-Headed Goddess') is an esoteric Buddhist tantric visualization manual dedicated to the severed-headed form of Vajrayoginī / Vajravārāhī. It details the self-generation of the goddess holding a cleaver (kartrikā) and severed head / skullcup. Previously considered lost in Sanskrit and known through its Tengyur translation (D 1555), a two-folio Sanskrit fragment was identified in Kaiser Library MS 139.

Kolff, M. S. Oort (eds.), Ritual, State and History in South Asia – Essays in Honour of J. C. Heesterman. Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1992, pp. 222–243 (text on pp. 226–229).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete ritual text including sections on bhāvanā, pūjā, japa, and bali, concluding with the final dedication and author colophon.

**Also known as:** Āryabhagavatītrikāyavajrayoginīsādhana, Guhyasamayasādhana no. 25

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Mahāsiddha Virūpa (Virūpapāda). The sādhana presents the severed-headed form of Vajrayoginī (Chinnamuṇḍā / Trikāyavajrayoginī) flanked by Vajravarṇanī and Vajravairocanī, closely related to Sādhanamālā nos. 232, 234, and 238, as well as Guhyasamayasādhana no. 25.

A short Vajrayāna sādhana dedicated to Trikāyavajrayoginī (the decapitated Vajrayoginī flanked by Vajravarṇanī and Vajravairocanī), attributed to the Mahāsiddha Virūpa. The text details the visualization (bhāvanā) of the self-decapitated deity drinking her own blood alongside her two attendants, worship (pūjā) with offerings directed to the sacred sites (pīṭhas) and four Buddha bodies (kāyas), japa recitation, and bali offering. It represents one of the earliest Buddhist witnesses to the severed-headed goddess motif shared with the Hindu Chinnamastā tradition.

The liturgy prescribes visualisations, protective mantras, flower offerings, the eight-line praise, the mālāmantra, and concludes with a samayagīti ('kollaïre ṭṭhia bola...') and dismission rites.

- Moriguchi, Mitsutoshi. 'Vajradhātu-mukh'ākhyāna-deguri-vidhiḥ III'. Mikkyō Bunka (Quarterly Reports on Esoteric Buddhism) 161 (1988). — Continuation of Moriguchi's edition.

**Attribution:** An anonymous Newar Buddhist ritual and iconographical manual associated with Vajradhātumaṇḍala practice.

The Vajradhātumukhākhyāna is an illustrated ritual handbook (vidhi) preserved in the Newar Buddhist tradition of Nepal. It details the liturgy, mantras, protective circles (rakṣācakra), nyāsa rituals, and hand gestures (mudrā) associated with the Vajradhātumaṇḍala. In Nepalese manuscript culture, copies of this handbook typically accompany iconographical drawings illustrating the mudrās and deities of the Vajradhātu system.

The Yogāmbarīsādhanaratnamālā ('Ratnamālā') is an anonymous Catuṣpīṭha-cycle text, written by a disciple of Kalyāṇavarman. The sole source for this text is an incomplete Sanskrit manuscript in a composite codex.

# Unidentified work in the Pañcakrama tradition (fragment)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T02_Āryadeva-tāntrika_Pañcakrama-unidentified`

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Preserves verses 1–18 and the beginning of verse 19 (fol. 29r–30v of NAK 1-1697), breaking off abruptly at 'iti kurva[]'.

**Attribution:** Unidentified and anonymous in the manuscript. The tentative attribution to Āryadeva-tāntrika in earlier metadata has no manuscript basis.

A brief metrical Buddhist tantric fragment (18 complete verses and one incomplete line) expounding internal yogic practices associated with the Guhyasamāja completion stage (Pañcakrama). It discusses the control of vital winds (prāṇavāyu), vajrajāpa, the experience of clear light (prabhāsvara), the realization of all phenomena as devoid of inherent existence (sarvaśūnya) and like an illusion (māyā/svapna), and the attainment of the unified state (yuganaddha).

## Edition and provenance

**Translations:**
- bdag med ma'i dkyil 'khor gyi 'khor lo'i sgrub thabs (Derge Tengyur D 1313) (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Text of the sādhanopāyikā concluding with the colophon '|| amṛtaprabhā nāma sādhanopāyikā samāptā ||'.

**Also known as:** Amṛtaprabhā nāma sādhanopāyikā, Amṛtaprabhā, Sādhanamālā 228

**Attribution:** Explicitly attributed in verse 1 (ḍombīherukapādair devīcakrasya bhāvanā kathitā) and in the final verses mentioning the author riding a tiger and ornamented with serpents.

The Amṛtaprabhāsādhanopāyikā is a Vajrayāna ritual text detailing the visualization and realization of the fifteen-deity maṇḍala of Nairātmyā, based on the Hevajratantra. Attributed to the mahāsiddha Ḍombīheruka, it guides the practitioner through the protective circle, bījamantras of the yoginīs, generation stage (utpattikrama), and completion stage (utpannakrama).
